thales-of-miletus.context_blurb:
Thales lived around 600 BC in Miletus, a Greek port on the shore of modern Turkey. Later Greeks called him the first philosopher and counted him among their Seven Sages. He left almost no writing, so he lives on in a handful of vivid stories that show how differently his mind worked from the minds of the people around him.

The most famous story mocks his absent-mindedness. One night, walking with his eyes fixed on the stars, he stepped straight off the edge of a well and tumbled in. A quick-witted servant girl laughed that he was so eager to know the heavens that he could not see what lay at his feet.

In his day most Greeks explained thunder or a raging sea by naming a god. Thales looked for causes in nature itself, and that turn is why Aristotle, two centuries later, called him the first philosopher. He asked what everything is made of, deep down, and answered: water. Every living thing needs it, seeds and food are moist, and even warmth seemed to feed on wetness. People teased him that philosophy kept him poor. So one winter, reading the skies, he judged that the olive harvest would be huge, and he quietly put cheap deposits on every olive press around while no one bid against him. At harvest everyone needed a press at once, and he rented them out at whatever price he pleased. In Egypt he was challenged to measure the Great Pyramid's height. He waited until his own shadow was exactly as long as he was tall; at that moment the pyramid's shadow had to equal its height. Herodotus credits him with foretelling the day the sky went dark during a battle between the Medes and the Lydians. Terrified, the two armies stopped fighting and made peace on the spot.

Thales threw out the gods for earthquakes too. Most Greeks blamed Poseidon, but Thales pictured the flat Earth floating on water like a piece of wood, so that when the water grew rough the land rocked like a boat on the waves. That darkness was a solar eclipse, dated to 28 May 585 BC. Later scholars doubt he could really have predicted it, but if he did, it would be the earliest eclipse in recorded history known to have been forecast. He saw a lodestone drag iron to itself, and saw amber, once rubbed on wool, pull bits of straw. Anything that causes motion seemed to him alive, so he concluded that even a magnet and a piece of amber must have souls, and he said that all things are full of gods. He also reasoned that the Moon makes no light of its own and shines with the Sun's light bouncing off it. His student Anaximander kept his method but not his answer: the source of all things, Anaximander said, is not water but the apeiron, a boundless something without any limits.

anaximander-and-anaximenes.context_blurb:
In the 500s BC the coastal Greek town of Miletus produced the first philosophers. After Thales came Anaximander, probably his pupil, and then Anaximenes, who learned from Anaximander. Each asked what the world is really made of, and each argued against his teacher with better reasons instead of simply repeating him, a habit Greek philosophy never lost.

Thales had said everything comes from water. Anaximander objected that water is just one common substance among many, and any limited supply would one day be used up. Since things are born and pass away forever, the source must be boundless, an endless store that can never run dry. Anaximenes kept the question but chose air, for a shrewd reason. Air is everywhere, unseen and always moving, and above all it is what every living creature has to breathe: the breath of life itself.

Anaximander also wondered where people came from. Human infants need years of care before they can fend for themselves, so humanity's first members must have started life some other way. He guessed that they grew inside fish-like creatures, sheltered and fed like embryos, until the creatures burst open and grown men and women stepped out. Anaximenes, meanwhile, had to explain how one stuff becomes flame, fog, river and rock. His answer was squeezing. Thinned out, air becomes fire; packed tighter, it becomes wind, then cloud, water, earth and finally stone, so a rock is simply air pressed far more tightly than a flame. Differences of kind became differences of amount, the first real mechanism of change in Western thought. He even tested the idea on his own breath. Blow on your hand through pursed lips, a tight narrow gap, and the squeezed breath feels cold; open your mouth wide and the loose breath feels warm.

Anaximander's most daring answer was about the Earth itself. Earlier thinkers took it for granted that the Earth needed a support beneath it. He said nothing at all holds it up. The Earth hangs free at the exact center of everything, the same distance from every edge, so it has no more reason to fall down than up or sideways, and it stays where it is.

heraclitus-and-the-doctrine-of-flux.context_blurb:
Heraclitus lived in Ephesus, a Greek city on the coast of Asia Minor, around 500 BC. His book survives only in scattered quotations, riddling lines that readers already found obscure in his own day. His great subject is change: what it is, where it comes from, and what holds steady beneath it. With Parmenides, who took the opposite side, he framed the oldest fight in Greek metaphysics.

Ancient writers paired him with Democritus. As the writer Sotion told it in the first century AD, Democritus laughed at human folly, while Heraclitus answered the same sight with tears, earning the name of the weeping philosopher. Born heir to the royal house of Ephesus, he gave up his claim to the kingship in favor of his brother. By one story, astonished citizens later found him in the temple of Artemis, throwing knucklebones with a group of children, and he asked whether that was not better than governing alongside them. His sayings pack huge claims into a few words, such as his warning that nature loves to hide. In one he denies that a single sun rises and comes back each morning: each day's sun is a new one, a fresh fire, not yesterday's returning. His end, by legend, was grim. Ill with dropsy, a swelling of the body with water, he packed himself in warm cow dung, hoping its heat would draw the water out. It did not, and he died at about sixty.

His most famous image is the river. The real fragment does not say you cannot step in twice; it says that fresh waters keep flowing over anyone who wades into the same river. The river stays one river because its water keeps changing, since the constant replacing of its water is exactly what makes it the same river. Opposites, for him, are partners. The way uphill and the way downhill are a single road, because the climb and the descent are one track, named by your direction of travel. A bow and a lyre work only because the string pulls against the frame; take away the strain and neither can shoot an arrow or sound a note. Through everything runs one hidden order, the logos, which most people miss. Listen not to me but to the logos, he urged, and you will agree that all things are one. Yet people live as though each owned a private wisdom, sleepwalking through the common world.

Parmenides went the other way. Taking as his starting point only that whatever exists, exists, he argued by logic alone that reality must be a single, changeless whole, and all the motion our senses report is illusion; the quarrel between the two is still unsettled. Earlier thinkers had named water or air as the world's basic stuff. Heraclitus chose a fire that lives forever, flaring up by measure and dying down by measure, and he insisted that neither god nor man created this world-order; it has always existed and always will. All things are traded for fire and fire for all things, he said, as goods are bought with gold and gold with goods, so fire is the currency the world keeps trading itself into and back out of. War, he wrote, is the father and king of all, and strife is justice. He was not cheering bloodshed: the tug of opposites against one another is what keeps the cosmos in order.

parmenides-and-the-one.context_blurb:
Parmenides lived in Elea, a Greek colony on the coast of southern Italy, in the early 400s BC. He wrote his philosophy not as a treatise but as a poem in the style of Homer, and only fragments survive, quoted by later writers. Its teaching tries to overrule common sense by pure reasoning, and the puzzle it set haunted Plato, Aristotle and nearly every Western thinker after them.

The poem opens with a wild ride. Immortal mares pull Parmenides' chariot along a blazing road, its axle shrilling like a pipe. The guides who lead him out from the House of Night are the Daughters of the Sun, maidens who push the veils back from their heads as they go. At the end of the ride a goddess greets him, and every surviving line of his teaching comes from her mouth, so a goddess's revealed speech is literally all we have of Parmenides. She warns him that the eye wanders and the ear rings with noise, and tells him to trust argument alone. So when the eye shows a world full of motion and change, that sight is only a trick of the senses, an error that reason must overrule.

The goddess divides her teaching into two roads, the Way of Truth and the Way of Opinion, the beliefs of mortals, which deserve no real trust. Everything turns on her claim that only the Way of Truth can be thought or put into words at all, which dooms the other road. On that road reality is one unbroken whole, since nothing but non-being could split it, and non-being does not exist. To picture that seamless whole, Parmenides compares reality to a perfectly rounded ball, equal in every direction from its center and complete out to its edge. His pupil Zeno of Elea defended him with famous brain-twisters, such as swift Achilles, who can never catch the tortoise, and the flying arrow that never really moves. They were no party tricks: Zeno meant to show that the everyday world of many moving things leads to contradictions, so that the believer in motion, not Parmenides, ends up holding the absurd view. His rule that nothing comes from nothing pressed hard on the next generation. Empedocles, Leucippus and Democritus answered by making change nothing but the rearranging of permanent stuffs: Empedocles' four roots, shuffled by Love and Strife, and the atoms of the atomists. Parmenides may have had a second calling, too. A stone head dug up at Velia in 1962 names him beside the cult titles Ouliades and Iatromantis, physician-seer, and from that thin clue some scholars guess, without proof, that he was remembered as a healer-seer in a cult of Apollo the Healer.

At the deepest level the goddess allows just two ways of thinking: either it is, or it is not. She rules the second out completely, because no mind can point itself at nothing: what is not cannot be thought or spoken of at all. The lever behind that move is a famous identity, "it is the same thing that can be thought and that can be," which welds thinking and being into one. From there Parmenides passes a startling verdict on time. A past would mean that reality once was not yet, and a future would mean that it will someday cease to be, and both need the banned non-being. So there is no past and no future, only one undivided, continuous now, all at once. Plato honored Parmenides like a father, but the ban trapped him: if nobody can speak of what is not, every false statement becomes impossible, though liars plainly exist. In the Sophist, a character begs not to be called a parricide before he defies his master and insists that what is not, in a certain sense, somehow is. Refuting Parmenides felt to Plato like killing a forefather.

zenos-paradoxes-of-motion.context_blurb:
Zeno of Elea, in southern Italy, was a devoted pupil of Parmenides in the 5th century BC. Parmenides taught that reality is one unmoving whole and that change is illusion, and crowds laughed. Zeno defended him indirectly. He granted the common belief in a world of many moving things, then showed that it collapses into knots worse than his teacher's. His short puzzles about a race, a walk and an arrow have challenged philosophers and mathematicians ever since.

The Achilles. Swift Achilles gives a tortoise a head start. Before he can pass it, he has to get to where the tortoise is now; yet when he arrives, it has crept forward a little, and by the time he gets to that point, it has moved on again. Every time he arrives, the tortoise has already opened a fresh small gap, so the list of stops never ends. The argument concludes that the swiftest runner never catches even the slowest.

The Dichotomy. To cross your bedroom you must first reach the halfway point, but before that the quarter point, and before that the eighth. Crossing one ordinary room seems to demand endlessly many separate distances. A nastier twin attacks even starting a step: no stretch can be the first, because a still smaller one always lies before it.

The Arrow. At any single instant, an arrow in flight occupies a space just its own length and covers no ground. If time is nothing but a string of instants, Zeno concluded, the flying arrow is in fact motionless throughout.

A story told about seven hundred years later, and probably invented, says Zeno was caught plotting against a tyrant. Offering to whisper his fellow plotters' names, he leaned to the tyrant's ear, sank his teeth into it and hung on until they stabbed him to death.

The answers took a long time. Aristotle distinguished divisions you could always go on making from divisions actually completed, and held that a body can pass through endlessly many possible pieces in a finite time. The philosopher Marc Cohen notes that the Arrow misuses rest: being at rest is a matter of staying put across a span of time, and a single instant has no span, so a frozen snapshot shows neither rest nor motion. The decisive tool came in the nineteenth century, when Cauchy, in 1821, and then Weierstrass made precise the idea of a limit, the value an endless sum can be proven to settle on. Give the tortoise a ten-pace lead and make Achilles ten times quicker. The gaps run ten paces, one, a tenth, a hundredth and so on forever, yet their total is a finite distance, just over eleven paces, and there Achilles passes the tortoise.

pythagoras-and-the-pythagoreans.context_blurb:
Pythagoras lived in the 500s BC and settled in Croton, a Greek colony in southern Italy, where he founded something between a philosophical school and a religious order. His followers, the Pythagoreans, lived together under strict secret rules and cared as much about the fate of the soul as about numbers and ratios. Many of the stories about him are legends, and that is part of their fame.

Pythagoras forbade his followers to eat beans, believing they held the souls of the dead, and legend says that when a mob chased him in old age, he halted at the edge of a bean field and let his pursuers kill him rather than trample the plants. The brotherhood also lived by odd secret sayings, the acusmata, passed on by word of mouth and never written down, and one of them was simply this: don't stir a fire with a knife.

A newcomer had to hold a vow of complete silence for five years before he could so much as listen to the master lecture. Disciples claimed their master was no mere man and pointed to a golden thigh, which he is said to have shown off at the Olympic Games as proof that he was divine.

Behind the odd rules lay a bold claim about reality. The Pythagoreans found that a string halved in length sounds an octave above the whole string, and that the sweetest musical intervals all come from simple whole-number ratios. So they decided that a hidden mathematical order runs beneath the whole world and that everything is built from number: whole numbers and their ratios. Legend says Pythagoras made the discovery while walking past a blacksmith's forge, where hammers of different weights rang out the octave, the fifth and the fourth. The hammer story is physically false, but the string version truly works. Pythagoras also believed that souls pass after death into new bodies, animal as well as human. Xenophanes mocked him with a story: seeing a man beat a puppy, Pythagoras cried out for him to stop, because he had recognized the soul of a dead friend in the puppy's yelp.

The Pythagoreans carried their music into the heavens. Each planet, they held, sounds its own note, and together the spheres ring one endless harmony. No one hears it, they explained, because it has been sounding since the day we were born, and nobody can notice a sound he has never once heard stop. Pythagoras claimed to remember his past lives, including one as Euphorbus, a warrior killed at Troy, and as proof he entered a temple and picked out the battered shield of Euphorbus, hanging among the old war relics, as his own. The brotherhood guarded its secrets fiercely. Hippasus, one of its members, revealed that certain lengths, the diagonal of a square among them, fit no ratio of whole numbers at all, a crack in the claim that everything is number. The brotherhood, legend says, answered his betrayal by drowning him in the sea.

democritus-leucippus-and-the-atom.context_blurb:
In fifth-century BC Greece, Leucippus and his far more famous student Democritus reasoned their way to one of the boldest guesses in history: that everything is built from pieces too small to see. They had no microscope, only argument, and the word they chose still names those pieces today. Most of Democritus's many books are lost, so we meet him mainly through later writers who quoted him.

Democritus chose the name for what could never be done to such a piece. Atom comes from the Greek atomos, meaning not-cut: uncuttable, a piece that can never be split. Old writers called him the laughing philosopher and set him beside Heraclitus, who wept at the same human folly. Democritus was not sneering, though. The aim of life, he taught, was euthymia, cheerfulness: a calm, contented mind, and fretting over the wrong things was the very folly that made him laugh. He prized knowledge far above riches, saying he would rather find the true cause of one single fact than win the kingdom of the Persians, the richest empire on earth.

Why must the cutting stop somewhere? Picture slicing gold in half, then in half again, forever. If the dividing never ended, you would arrive at nothing at all, and nothing cannot build a real thing, so there must be a smallest piece that no blade can divide. His picture of infinite atoms tumbling through an infinite void led him to a second startling thought: there is more than one world. According to the later writer Hippolytus, he taught that there are countless worlds, large and small, thriving and decaying, some with suns and moons bigger than ours, and some with no sun or moon at all.

His boldest claim still unsettles people. Tastes such as sweet and bitter, feelings of hot and cold, and every color, he said, exist only by convention, as effects of the way atoms strike our senses, while in reality there are only atoms and the empty void. The sweetness is not out there in the honey. Then how can identical bits make things as different as iron and a dog? Atoms differ, he said, in just three ways: shape, order and position. Aristotle explained it with the alphabet. The letters A and N have different shapes, AN and NA hold the same letters in a different order, and a letter lying on its side has a new position. In just that way the same few letters can spell out both a tragedy and a comedy.

empedocles-and-the-four-roots.context_blurb:
Empedocles lived in the fifth century BC in Acragas, a wealthy Greek city on the south coast of Sicily. He was as much a performer as a philosopher: he wore purple robes, hinted that he was more than mortal, and set out his ideas in two long poems that people memorized. He tackled the old question of what everything is made of and why it changes.

Legend gave him a showman's death. Wanting people to believe he had become a god and vanished without a trace, he jumped into the fiery mouth of Etna, Sicily's great volcano, so that no body would ever turn up. The volcano betrayed him by tossing up a single bronze sandal, for he liked to wear slippers of bronze, proof that a mortal man had died there. Another ancient writer, Timaeus, said Empedocles simply moved away. His answer to the great question was that everything is built from four roots, earth, water, air, fire, mixed in different amounts the way paints blend into new colors. Aristotle credited him as the first to single out those four, and the scheme ruled Western thought for two thousand years.

Two cosmic forces work on the roots: Love, which unites unlike things, and Strife, which tears them asunder. So when a baby is born or a fire burns out, nothing truly new appears and nothing vanishes. The same basic ingredients remain, and only their arrangement changes, an early glimpse of the idea that matter is conserved. His account of how animals first arose is stranger still. Lone body parts sprang up from the earth, heads without necks and arms without shoulders, and Love joined them at random into ox-faced men and man-faced oxen. Only the combinations that worked could stay alive and last, while the unworkable ones perished, which is why Aristotle and later scholars saw in him a distant forerunner of natural selection. He also held that a single soul passes through life after life, as boy and girl, bush, bird and fish. Since any animal might house a soul, he kept to a diet of plants and grain, refusing all meat.

He offered one of the first physical theories of sight as well. Every object, he said, gives off fine streams of matter, which he called effluences, and these fit into matching openings, or pores, in the eye. Those lines of his poem had been lost to readers for more than two thousand years, until in April 2026 the papyrologist Nathan Carlig identified thirty of them on an ancient scroll held in Cairo.

anaxagoras-and-mind-nous.context_blurb:
Anaxagoras came from Clazomenae in Ionia and moved to Athens in the mid-400s BC, the first major philosopher to live and teach in the city. He was the friend and teacher of Pericles, the great Athenian statesman. Like the thinkers of Miletus before him, he asked what the world is made of and what puts it in order, and his answers scandalized Athens.

Asked why it is better to be born than never to exist, Anaxagoras gave a single reason: to look up and understand the sky, the sun and moon and all the heavens. He looked hard. To most Athenians the sun was Helios, a god with a fiery chariot, but Anaxagoras declared it a mass of red-hot metal, larger even than the Peloponnese, the whole southern landmass of Greece. The city's most worshipped light, in his telling, was a burning rock.

The moon, he said, has no light of its own and shines by catching the sun's. Up close it would show plains and mountains like the earth's ground, because it is made of earth, and with that picture he correctly explained eclipses as one body blocking the sun's light from another. His boldest idea concerned how the world began. In the beginning all things lay mixed together in one mass. Then Mind, which he called Nous, pure and all-knowing, set the mass spinning, and the spin sifted it into the stars, the land and the sea, and every living creature; Mind governs everything.

In his view nothing ordinary is pure: a bone or a tree holds a little of every other kind of stuff. Mind alone had to be the exception, pure and mixed with nothing. His reason was about control: anything blended into Mind would hold it back and stop it from ruling, so the one unmixed thing is the one thing able to steer all that is mixed.

Such talk made enemies. Cleon, a politician who wanted to wound Pericles, took the old philosopher to court instead, accusing him of impiety against the city's gods for calling the sun a lump of hot metal. Pericles defended him, but Anaxagoras was fined five talents and driven from Athens. He died in exile in Lampsacus, a Greek town on the Turkish coast, where the people held him in honor. Asked how the town should remember him, he made one request: give the schoolchildren a holiday every year in the month he died, a custom still kept in the days of the biographer Diogenes Laertius.

socrates-the-gadfly-of-athens.context_blurb:
Socrates lived in Athens in the 400s BC. He was the son of a stonemason and served bravely as a foot soldier in the Peloponnesian War. Afterward he spent his days in the streets and the marketplace, stopping people to ask them hard questions. Athens finally put him on trial for it, and he has shaped how Western philosophy sees itself ever since.

Athens prized fine looks and fine clothes, and Socrates ignored both. Winter or summer he walked barefoot and unwashed, in a single plain cloak, with a rough stick in his hand; he owned almost nothing and never wanted more. Other teachers, the Sophists, charged rich families large fees, but Socrates would talk with anyone and never took a single coin for it.

Strangely for a man who shaped all of Western thought, Socrates never wrote down a single line. Everything we know of him comes secondhand, chiefly from his students Plato and Xenophon. At his trial he refused to apologize for pestering the city. Athens, he said, was like a great, noble horse made sluggish by its own size, and he was the gadfly that clung to it all day, stinging it awake. Offered his life if he would stop questioning and live quietly, he refused, declaring that a life never examined is not worth living, and he was executed by drinking hemlock. His home was stormy too. His wife Xanthippe was famous for her temper; once, the story goes, she scolded him until she was hoarse and then emptied a pitcher of water over his head. Socrates only remarked that he had always said her thunder would end in rain.

His mission began with a riddle. The oracle at Delphi announced that no man was wiser than Socrates. Baffled, he spent years questioning the city's famous wise men, and he concluded that the god meant this: he alone knew how little he really knew, while they thought they knew what they did not. His mother Phaenarete was a midwife, and Socrates said his own work was the same. He taught nothing, he claimed; his questions only helped a person bring to birth the truths he already carried within. His concentration amazed the army. On campaign at Potidaea he stopped to think through a problem and stood rooted to one spot from one dawn right through to the next, while soldiers carried their bedding outside to watch.

At a drinking party in Plato's Symposium, a tipsy Alcibiades compared Socrates to the small carved statues of Silenus that shopkeepers sold, ugly on the outside but splitting open to reveal tiny golden gods within. Popular memory has polished his humility into a neat slogan about knowing only his own ignorance, but that line appears nowhere in Plato. At his trial Socrates claimed something subtler: unlike the experts, he neither knew nor fancied that he knew. Long before, the comic playwright Aristophanes had mocked him in The Clouds as the head of a school of clever nonsense. Socrates' first entrance got a roar of laughter: he dangled overhead in a hanging basket, treading the air, a joke that Plato later blamed for turning Athens against him.

the-socratic-method-elenchus.context_blurb:
In the dialogues of Plato, Socrates of Athens has a signature way of talking, called the elenchus, Greek for cross-examination. He meets someone famous for knowing about justice, courage or piety, and instead of lecturing, he asks questions. The real work happens inside the other person as he tries to answer. The method still shapes teachers, lawyers and debate coaches, and Athens eventually put it on trial.

The method itself is simple. If a cousin is certain he knows what fairness means and challenges everyone to prove otherwise, you do not declare the opposite. You go on questioning him until his own replies collide, so that he refutes himself. Socrates usually opened with one demand: what is it? A student asked about courage might point to a firefighter running into a burning building. Socrates would say that is one example, not an account of what makes every brave act brave.

Pressed this way, people end in aporia, a stuck, honest puzzlement. A young man named Meno complained that his mind and tongue had gone numb. For Socrates that was the goal, not a failure, because you cannot search for an answer while you still believe you have it. Meno compared him to the torpedo fish, a sea creature whose touch stuns. Socrates accepted the picture with one correction: this torpedo fish is numb itself before it numbs anyone else, since he spreads a puzzlement he truly feels.

He also called himself a midwife, like his mother, Phaenarete. He helped minds give birth instead of bodies, drawing out ideas already inside the other person and adding nothing of his own.

The method has a story behind it. His friend Chaerephon once put a question to the oracle at Delphi, and the priestess replied that no man was wiser than Socrates. Sure he knew nothing, Socrates went hunting for a wiser man to show that the oracle had erred. He questioned a politician famous for wisdom and found that neither of them knew anything fine and good. His one edge: he was aware of his own ignorance, while the politician fancied himself wise.

Watch the method work. The general Laches defined courage as holding your place in the ranks and never fleeing. Socrates only mentioned the mounted Scythians, who fight while riding away, and the Spartans, who won battles by pretending to retreat. So standing firm cannot be the whole of courage, since brave fighters sometimes flee. Euthyphro defined piety as what the gods love, yet he also believed the old stories of gods at war with one another. Then one act could be loved by some gods and hated by others, pious and impious at once.

At his trial in 399 BC, Socrates told the jury he was a gadfly sent to sting a big, lazy horse. That was why powerful Athenians hated him: he went about all day stinging the city's leading men with questions they had no answers for. He would not promise to stop, because a life that is never examined is not worth living, and he applied that to his own life as much as to anyone's.

The method has a limit. When a person's beliefs collide, at least one of them must be false, but the contradiction alone cannot tell you which one. That is why so many of the dialogues end in puzzlement rather than answers.

the-oracle-at-delphi.context_blurb:
High on the slopes of Mount Parnassus stood Delphi, the temple of Apollo and the most respected oracle in the Greek world. Kings and cities sent envoys to put questions to its priestess, the Pythia. One of her answers changed the life of Socrates, the barefoot philosopher of Athens, and Plato tells the story in the Apology, his account of Socrates' trial.

Socrates never asked the question himself; he would have found it absurd. His close friend Chaerephon, an impulsive man whom the comic poet Aristophanes nicknamed the bat, climbed to Delphi and asked whether anyone was wiser than Socrates. The priestess said no one was. Carved at the temple's entrance was a two-word command, Know thyself, and Socrates' whole life reads like obedience to it.

The verdict baffled him, since he was sure he had no wisdom at all. Rather than preen, he went looking for a wiser man, meaning to bring him back as proof that the god was mistaken. He tried a politician famous for wisdom. Neither of them knew anything worth much about the great questions, but the politician believed he knew things he did not, while Socrates claimed nothing. That honest admission was his one advantage. Then he tried the craftsmen. They truly knew their trades, the shoemaker his shoes and the smith his iron, but because each was good at one craft, each assumed he understood every great matter too, and that conceit hid the wisdom he had.

At his trial, insisting he was telling hard truths about the city's famous men, Socrates swore his odd private oath. Where other Athenians swore by Zeus or Apollo, he swore by the dog.

Two of his students wrote the story down, and their reports differ. In Plato's version the priestess names no one wiser than Socrates. Xenophon remembers a different verdict that praised his character rather than his wisdom: no man was more free, more just or more self-controlled.

the-trial-of-socrates.context_blurb:
In 399 BC, when Socrates was about seventy, three Athenian citizens took him to court. Athens had just lost a disastrous war and lived through a bloody tyranny, and many blamed the cheerful questioner whose old companions included some of the guilty men. A huge jury of ordinary citizens heard the case. Our main account is Plato's Apology, Socrates' defence in his own voice; his student Xenophon left a shorter and tougher one.

The indictment had two charges: corrupting the young men of Athens, and refusing to honour the city's gods while bringing in new divine beings. Behind them lay an older grudge. Critias, once his student, had headed the bloodthirsty Thirty Tyrants, and another, Alcibiades, had betrayed Athens in wartime. But an amnesty passed in 403 BC, after the Thirty fell, made it illegal to prosecute anyone over those old political ties, so the case was built on religion instead.

Socrates explained how his strange life began. His friend Chaerephon asked the oracle at Delphi about him, and the priestess answered that no man alive was wiser than Socrates. Puzzled, Socrates questioned the city's proudest experts and found his one advantage: they thought they knew things they did not, while he alone admitted he did not know.

He turned his accuser Meletus's own words against him. Meletus swore that Socrates believed in no gods at all, yet the indictment charged him with introducing new divinities. Teaching about new divine beings means believing in divine things, Socrates pointed out, so the charge of atheism collapses.

He refused to beg, telling the jury he would obey God rather than them. If the court spared him on condition that he give up philosophy, he said, he would go on teaching and questioning for as long as there was breath in him, because an unexamined life is no life worth living for a human being. He called himself a gadfly stinging a great, lazy horse awake; swat the fly, and the city would simply doze off again. Nor did he fear death. To dread it, he argued, is to claim to know that death is bad, and no living person knows that.

The jury convicted him by a fairly close vote; thirty votes the other way would have acquitted him. Under Athenian law he then had to propose his own penalty, and he proposed that the city feed him at public expense for the rest of his life, an honour Athens kept for its heroes and Olympic champions. The jury voted again, on death, and about eighty more jurors voted for his death than had found him guilty. Socrates took his leave calmly: he was going to die and they to live, and which of them was better off, he said, only God knows.

the-death-of-socrates.context_blurb:
Socrates, the great questioner of Athens, was condemned to death by an Athenian court on charges of impiety and of corrupting the young. He spent his last weeks in prison, where his friends could visit him, and Plato retold those days in two famous dialogues, the Crito and the Phaedo. Painted most famously by Jacques-Louis David in 1787, the scene is often called the founding martyrdom of Western philosophy.

One morning before sunrise Crito, a wealthy friend, crept into the prison with an escape plan: the guards were bribed and a safe house waited in Thessaly. Socrates refused to run, and when the day came he drank the hemlock. On that last morning his wife Xanthippe sat by him in tears, their infant son in her arms, and Socrates quietly asked that someone take her and the child home before the long final talk with his friends began. When the jailer brought the cup, Socrates drank the poison readily and cheerfully, without a tremor. His friends broke down, with Apollodorus, always excitable, wailing loudest, and Socrates rebuked them: he had sent the women away precisely so that he might die in peace, and their outcry was spoiling it.

The sentence had waited about a month. Athens allowed no executions while its sacred ship was away on the yearly voyage to the island of Delos in honour of Apollo, and contrary winds kept the ship out for thirty days. When the end came, even the jailer who brought the poison wept as he said goodbye, calling Socrates the noblest, gentlest and best man who had ever come to that place. Before drinking, Socrates bathed, so that the women would not have to wash his body after death. Afterward he was told to pace the cell until his legs grew heavy, then to lie down. An attendant pressed his foot hard, and Socrates felt nothing. The cold was climbing upward, and when it reached his heart, the man said, that would be the end. Then Socrates uncovered his face and spoke his last words to Crito: they owed a rooster to Asclepius, and Crito must not forget to pay the debt.

Those last words haunt readers. Sick Greeks who got well offered Asclepius, the healing god, a rooster as thanks for the cure. Read that way, Socrates was quietly calling death itself the cure that freed his soul from the body. In the Crito he explains why he would not flee by imagining the Laws of Athens speaking to him like stern parents. Without us, they say, you would not exist, since your father married your mother under our authority, and we saw to your raising and schooling.

The Crito's deepest arguments still divide thinkers. Socrates granted that the verdict against him was unjust, and Crito said the injustice freed him to escape. Socrates stood on a principle: one must never repay a wrong with another wrong, whatever has been done to you. The Laws added a second argument. For seventy years Socrates had been free to leave Athens if he disliked its rule, yet he stayed all his life. That lifelong staying, they argued, amounted to an unspoken promise to obey the city's laws, one that still held. Thinkers who believe an unjust state forfeits a citizen's obedience take the other side of a real dispute.

the-examined-life.context_blurb:
"The examined life" comes from one of the most quoted lines in ancient philosophy, spoken by Socrates in Plato's Apology, the speech he gave at his trial in Athens. Already convicted, he was expected to propose a lighter penalty and promise to go quiet. Instead he explained why he could not, and the speech became the clearest statement of what Socrates thought philosophy is for: not a job or a system, but a way of spending a human life.

Athens, he told the jurors, was a fine, noble horse grown lazy with its own bulk, and the god had set him on it as a gadfly, stinging it awake all day; kill him, and the city would doze again. It all began when the oracle at Delphi declared no man wiser than Socrates. Sure that he had no special wisdom, he tested the city's experts and concluded that the god meant something odd: unlike them, he never fancied that he knew things he did not know.

He named the best thing a person can do: to talk every day about virtue and what makes a person good, examining himself and others. Exactly that habit was what his accusers wanted ended. Asked to propose his own punishment, he proposed a reward instead: free meals for life in the Prytaneum, the city's public dining hall, an honour kept for Olympic champions and war heroes.

Why not simply ask for exile or prison and live? Socrates reasoned that he did not know whether death is good or bad, while he did know that exile and prison are evils, so he would not take on a sure evil to dodge one no one can prove is an evil. He called the common fear of death a false show of wisdom. To feel sure that death is a harm we must flee is to claim knowledge no living person has, the same pretended knowledge he had exposed in expert after expert.

socratic-irony.context_blurb:
Socratic irony is the name later readers gave to a favourite trick of Socrates in Plato's dialogues. The word comes from the Greek eironeia, a show of ignorance, a kind of shamming. Writers from Cicero to Kierkegaard have argued over how sincere Socrates really was when he played his part.

The trick runs like this. A man boasts that he is an expert. Socrates replies that he himself knows nothing and humbly asks to learn. Then come a few gentle questions, each one simple, until the expert has talked himself into a corner and it is plain that he never grasped what he was claiming. The confusion Socrates puts on is a tactic, not real bewilderment.

The classic case is Euthyphro, who is on his way to court to charge his own father with a killing, confident that he knows exactly what holiness demands. Socrates asks to become his pupil. The meek request is a trap: it pushes Euthyphro to say plainly what holiness is, and he fails five times over. At last he announces that he is late and hurries off.

the-sophists.context_blurb:
The Sophists were travelling teachers who flourished in Greek cities in the 400s BC, above all in democratic Athens, where a young man who could speak well in the assembly and the law courts could rise fast. Protagoras, Gorgias, Prodicus and others sold that skill for a living. Plato, who disliked them, is a main source for them, and in his dialogues they stand as the great rivals of Socrates.

The movement's famous boast, credited to Protagoras, was that a Sophist could teach you to make the weaker argument look like the stronger. That is persuasion cut loose from truth, a real skill every lawyer and campaigner uses, which is why it pays to recognise it. Protagoras held that every question has two opposing arguments and drilled his pupils in both: argue the case one way, then turn round and argue it the other. The drill trained a young man to defend whichever side of a case he was handed.

Socrates questioned generals, poets and workmen all over Athens, but he refused the one thing every Sophist did: he never took a fee for teaching. In Plato's Apology he flatly denies charging money.

Not every Sophist lesson was cynical. Prodicus told a story children still hear. At a crossroads young Heracles meets two women. One, Vice, offers an easy, downhill life of pleasure; the other, Virtue, offers a hard climb that ends in honour.

Gorgias showed off in the opposite direction. He chose the most blamed woman in Greek legend, Helen, whose elopement with Paris supposedly set off the Trojan War, and argued that she was entirely innocent, to prove he could win any case.

In the Republic, Plato has the Sophist Thrasymachus claim that justice is nothing but the advantage of the stronger: rulers make laws to serve themselves. Socrates meets him on his own ground. Rulers can blunder and pass a law that harms their own side, and then obeying it would hurt the stronger, so the definition breaks.

A story told by Aulus Gellius has Protagoras teaching a penniless pupil, Euathlus, who would pay only after winning his first lawsuit. When the pupil never argued a single case, Protagoras took him to court, claiming that he would be paid whichever way the verdict went. Euathlus turned the trick around: if I win, the court frees me from paying; if I lose, I still have not won a case, so under our deal I owe nothing. The two arguments cancelled out, and the puzzled judges reportedly put off the case indefinitely.

protagoras-man-the-measure.context_blurb:
Protagoras of Abdera, who lived roughly from 490 to 420 BCE, was the first to take the title sophist for himself: a paid teacher of argument who grew rich on famously high fees. He is remembered for one short saying that opened a debate philosophers have pursued ever since. Plato devoted a long dialogue, the Theaetetus, to working out what the saying commits its author to, and whether it can survive its own logic.

Protagoras moved in the highest circles. Pericles, the leading man of Athens, chose him in 444 BCE to draft the entire law code for Thurii, a new colony, an irony given what Protagoras taught about justice. His relativism shows in a simple case. Two travelers stand in the same gust, and one finds it cold while the other does not. Protagoras would not call the wind simply cold or not cold: for the shivering traveler it is cold, for his companion it is not, and each report is true. He was just as cautious about the gods. His book On the Gods opened by admitting he could not know if they existed, because the subject is obscure and human life is short. It was agnosticism, not a denial, but it earned him a name for impiety.

His book Truth opened with the most famous line of ancient relativism: of all things the measure is man. By man he meant each individual, so whatever seems true to a person is true for that person, with no higher standard set by the wise, the city or the gods. In the Theaetetus, Socrates traces this to one premise: perceiving is always perceiving something that exists, so a perception can never be false, and every appearance is true for the one who has it. Protagoras carried the idea from hot and cold into right and wrong. Whatever seems just to a city is just for that city, so long as it keeps thinking so, because on his view justice has no fixed source above human communities. Behind it all lay his classroom method, built on the claim that any question can be argued from two opposite sides, and critics charged that he trained students to turn the weaker argument into the winning one.

The doctrine faces a famous trap, known in Greek as peritrope, the table turned. If every belief is true for the one who holds it, then the common belief that Protagoras's doctrine is false must be true as well. His own principle makes that judgment true, so the doctrine refutes itself. A defender may reply that the doctrine is false only for its critics while staying true for Protagoras, but critics answer that a truth held only for one man asks nothing of anyone else, and the objection has dogged relativism ever since.

gorgias-the-rhetorician.context_blurb:
Gorgias came from Leontini in Sicily in the fifth century BC. He first reached Athens as an ambassador seeking military help, and his speeches so stunned the assembly that his fame as a master of eloquence spread across Greece. With him, Western thinking about the sheer power of words begins.

One surviving showpiece defends Helen of Troy, whom Greeks blamed for the war because she ran off with Paris. In ornate, rhyming prose Gorgias lists the forces that might have moved her: fate, violence, words or love. His sly payoff concerns words. Speech, he argues, is a mighty lord that grips a listener as forcibly as an abductor's hands, so anyone swept away by words was taken, not freely choosing. A defense of Helen becomes a hymn to rhetoric.

Stranger still was On Non-Being, aimed at Parmenides, who had called Being one, eternal and knowable. Gorgias argued three escalating claims: nothing exists; if anything did exist, no one could know it; and if anyone knew it, he could never pass that knowledge on. Whether he meant parody or real skepticism is still debated.

the-euthyphro-dilemma.context_blurb:
The Euthyphro is a short early dialogue by Plato, named after a self-assured young Athenian whom Socrates meets on the steps of a court. Out of their talk comes one of the most important questions ever asked about religion and morality: is something right because the gods command it, or do they command it because it is right? Neither answer escapes cleanly, and believers and skeptics still argue over it.

Socrates has come to court as the accused, charged with impiety. Euthyphro claims to be an authority on holiness, so Socrates, the man accused of impiety, asks him to say what holiness is. Euthyphro is there to prosecute his own father for murder. Back on Naxos, a labourer working for the family had killed a servant while drunk. Euthyphro's father tied the killer up, left him lying in a ditch and sent word to Athens seeking a priest's ruling; before an answer came, the man died of hunger, cold and his bonds. Euthyphro is certain that prosecuting is holy, yet he cannot define holiness. Every definition he offers, Socrates picks apart, and at the end, pressed once more, Euthyphro says he is in a hurry and walks off, leaving the question unanswered.

Along the way Euthyphro defends himself with a myth. Zeus, best of the gods, bound his own father Cronos, who had swallowed his children as soon as they were born, so surely a mortal son may punish his father as well. His last definition is that holiness is the skill of pleasing the gods with prayer and sacrifice. Socrates recasts that as a kind of trade with the gods, offerings handed over in hope of something back. The famous question comes when Euthyphro says holiness is what the gods love. Socrates asks: is the holy loved by the gods because it is holy, or does their love make it holy?

Each answer has a price. If holiness is nothing but the gods' liking, with no reason behind it, then had they loved cruelty, cruelty would have been holy, and goodness becomes divine whim. If instead the gods love things for a goodness they already have, their love merely registers a goodness that is there anyway, adding nothing to its being good. Socrates argued for the second order. Something counts as carried only because a person carries it; so too the gods love what is holy because it is holy, and their love comes after the holiness, not before it. Divine-command thinkers dispute that direction. The friar William of Ockham bit the first horn hard: if God commanded theft, adultery or even hatred of God, he held, those acts could be done meritoriously. Gottfried Leibniz answered that if goodness is simply whatever the strongest being wills, then justice comes down to a tyrant's whim, whatever the ruler pleases to call just, and praising God's goodness becomes empty.

plato-and-the-academy.context_blurb:
Plato was born in Athens around 428 BCE into a powerful aristocratic family. In his twenties he watched Athens put his teacher Socrates to death, and the killing turned him from politics to philosophy. He went on to found the first enduring school of advanced study in the Western world, and he did his thinking in staged conversations, called dialogues, that rank among the finest prose in Greek.

Even his name was a nickname. Born Aristocles, he wrestled in competition and had a powerful build, and his wrestling coach, the story goes, called him Plato, from the Greek platos, meaning broad. Ancient writers argued over why: his broad frame, his broad eloquence, or a wide forehead. Around 387 BCE, a short walk beyond the city walls, he began gathering students, not in a built hall but in a sacred olive grove named for the hero Academus, which gave us the word academic.

A legend tells that on the eve of Plato's arrival as a student, Socrates dreamed that a young swan settled on his knees, grew its feathers all at once and flew off singing. The next morning, meeting the young man, Socrates declared that this was the swan. Socrates was executed by hemlock in 399 BCE, when Plato was in his late twenties. Plato could not save him, but he gave Socrates the leading role in almost every dialogue he wrote, so his teacher's questioning voice carried on for centuries. The Academy long outlived its founder. Teachers in Plato's tradition kept meeting on the same ground for about nine hundred years, until the Christian emperor Justinian closed the pagan schools in 529 CE.

Life at the Academy had its comic moments. Plato once defined a human being as a featherless biped, a two-legged creature without feathers. The Cynic Diogenes plucked a chicken, carried it into the Academy and announced, "Here is Plato's man!" The definition was patched to add broad, flat nails, and one counterexample had beaten a tidy definition. Another legend says a carved warning over the door turned away anyone ignorant of geometry. Scholars doubt it, because Aristotle studied there for twenty years without mentioning it, and the first reports come about a thousand years after Plato.

the-allegory-of-the-cave.context_blurb:
The allegory of the cave opens Book VII of Plato's Republic and is perhaps the most famous image in Western philosophy. In it Socrates asks his friends to picture people held underground, then walks them through what those people believe, what happens when one escapes, and what happens when he returns. It is Plato's picture of what education is and of how discovering the truth feels from the inside.

Picture people who have lived in an underground den from early childhood, bound so tightly at the legs and neck that they can look only straight ahead at a bare wall. Behind them, things pass before a fire and throw moving shadows on that wall. Since shadows are all they have ever seen, the prisoners take the shadows to be the only real things there are. They are not stupid; they simply have no way to know of anything more.

Plato fills in the machinery. Between the fire and the prisoners runs a raised walkway with a low wall along it, like the screen puppeteers hide behind at a puppet show. Unseen people walk behind it holding up carved figures of men and beasts in wood and stone, so the prisoners are watching shadows of copies, two steps away from anything real. When one prisoner is freed and dragged up the steep path into daylight, the light hurts his eyes, and his first wish is to turn back to the shadows he can bear to look at. Glaucon, listening, calls them strange prisoners in a strange picture. Socrates answers in two words: like ourselves.

Down in the cave, the prisoners even hand out honours and prizes. The glory goes to whoever is quickest to name each passing shadow and best at predicting which one will come next, which is mastery of an illusion. The freed man, meanwhile, comes to see real trees, animals and at last the sun itself, and he reasons that the sun governs the seasons and the years and rules over everything visible. Out of duty he goes back down to tell the others. But his eyes, used to sunlight, are useless in the dark, and he fumbles the shadow game. The prisoners laugh at him and decide the climb has ruined his eyes, so the journey up is not worth making.

Plato then explains the symbols. The climb out is the soul rising from appearances to truth, and the sun stands for the Good, from which all truth and all knowing flow; it makes things knowable and gives the knower the power to know. Education, then, is not stuffing knowledge into empty heads, as if putting sight into blind eyes. The power to understand is already in everyone, and the teacher's work is to turn the student's whole soul around, away from the shadows and toward the light. Plato ends with a chilling line: anyone who tried to release the prisoners and lead them upward would be killed by them. Many readers hear in it a memory of his own teacher, Socrates, whom Athens executed.

the-theory-of-forms.context_blurb:
Plato's theory of Forms is the centre of his philosophy. It begins with a simple-sounding question: how can many different wooden chairs all count as chairs, and how can the mind know what perfect equality is without ever having seen two perfectly equal things? Plato's answer, the Forms, carried his ethics, his politics and his theory of knowledge. His own student Aristotle rejected it, and philosophers still argue over it.

Picture a carpenter's chair. It wobbles, one leg is uneven, and someday it will rot, yet you know at a glance that it is a chair, because you hold it up to a flawless chair that exists only in thought. Plato's startling claim is that the flawless chair no eye has seen is more real than the wooden one under you. The same goes for every shared feature. A basketball, a bowling ball and a circle drawn in chalk differ in every way except roundness, so Plato posited a single Roundness, the perfect original that each round object imitates and shares in. The clearest Forms are things like Justice and Beauty. Asked whether he has ever seen justice itself with his eyes, a young friend of Socrates admits he never has; such things are real, Socrates says, but grasped by the mind alone.

Plato ranked three beds. God makes the one true Bed. A carpenter looks to it and builds a wooden bed, which stands one step below the true Bed. A painter then paints the carpenter's bed, a copy of a copy, standing further off still.

The arguments go deeper. Two sticks can look equal from one angle and unequal from another, but Equality itself can never look unequal. Whatever can fall short of equality cannot be identical with the Equal that never falls short. And because no flawed stick could ever have given you the idea of perfect equality, Plato concluded that your soul met Equality before you were born, so that all learning is a kind of recollection of what it knew then. He added that a face beautiful from one side and plain from another, or an act just in one city and unjust in the next, is no fit object for knowledge. Such things slide into their own opposites, so they offer the mind nothing stable to grasp; they can be matters of opinion only, and real knowledge needs the Forms.

In the Republic Plato imagines people held in chains inside a cave from birth, facing a wall where shadows flicker. They take the shadows for the whole of reality, though the shadows are only copies of real things. One prisoner is freed and climbs past the fire into blinding daylight. Over all the Forms Plato set one supreme Form, the Good, which he compared to the sun: as the sun lets the eye see and makes living things grow, the Good lets the mind know the Forms and gives them their being. Yet the Good is not one more being among them. It stands beyond being, the source that lets everything else exist.

Plato also wrote the strongest attacks on his own theory. In his dialogue the Parmenides, the aged Parmenides corners young Socrates. If large things are large by sharing in Largeness, and that Form is large as well, the large things and Largeness together call for yet another Largeness over them, and that group for another. The Form meant to stop the chain has started an endless tower of higher Forms. Worse, if the Forms are perfectly separate from our world, our minds, which reach only things here, could never know them at all. Yet Parmenides warns Socrates not to give the Forms up. Deny that anything stays always the same, and you destroy the very power of careful reasoning, since thought would have nothing stable to hold onto.

the-ring-of-gyges.context_blurb:
In Book II of Plato's Republic, Socrates' young friend Glaucon tells a story he does not believe, to force Socrates to defend justice against the strongest case he can build. The story is about a shepherd and a magic ring, and the question behind it is simple and hard: if you could never be caught, would you still be good? The rest of the Republic is Socrates' answer.

Before the story, Glaucon ranks good things by the reason we want them. Some we enjoy for themselves; some we put up with only for what they bring. He files justice among the unpleasant ones, like a dose of bitter medicine or a punishing workout, and dares Socrates to prove it belongs with the highest goods.

Then comes the tale. Gyges, a shepherd of Lydia, climbs into a chasm and pulls a gold ring from a dead man's finger. He learns by accident that turning the ring makes him invisible, and turning it back makes him reappear. Sure he can never be caught, he gets himself sent to the royal court, seduces the queen, murders the king and takes the throne. Glaucon's lesson is blunt. Hand such a ring to a decent man and a matching one to a crook, and both would end up behaving exactly alike. Ordinary people stay honest, he claims, only because they fear being caught. Socrates must answer this challenge, and thinkers who believe people are good from love of the good hold a real rival view.

Readers have long seen the same ring in Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings. The One Ring also makes its wearer vanish, but over time it corrupts and poisons his soul. Tolkien never named Plato as a source, so the likeness is one scholars draw.

The historian Herodotus told an older story of a real Gyges, a bodyguard of King Candaules of Lydia. Candaules, proud beyond sense of his wife's beauty, hid Gyges in the royal bedroom so he could see her undressed. The queen caught him and gave him a choice: kill Candaules and take both her and the throne, or die himself. Gyges killed the king.

Glaucon then sharpens the contest. Take the perfectly just man and rob him of his reputation until everyone thinks him a villain, and let him be whipped, racked, chained and finally impaled, while a perfectly unjust man is honoured by all. Which life is better? If justice is worth having for its own sake, Socrates must answer that the just man on the rack still lives the happier life.

His reply runs through the rest of the Republic. Reason, spirit and appetite make up the soul, and justice means each of the three doing its proper job in harmony. Injustice is a disease of the soul, just as illness is disorder in the body, so the unseen wrongdoer ruins himself from within even if no one ever finds out. As for the tyrant who grabs total power to help himself to anything he likes, he is no winner. Socrates finds him the wretchedest man alive, enslaved to his own lusts.

justice-in-the-republic.context_blurb:
In Plato's Republic, Socrates and a circle of friends ask what justice really is and why a sensible person should care about being just. Early challenges set the agenda: a blunt teacher insists justice is a cover for power, and Glaucon tells the tale of a magic ring. Plato's surprising method is to study justice in a whole city first, then carry the result back to the single soul.

Justice in one person, Socrates says, is like small print read from a distance, but the same letters appear writ large elsewhere: in an entire city, a community of people living and working side by side. So he reads the big copy first. To show that the soul has parts, Plato tells of Leontius, who passed the corpses of executed men, craved to stare and was disgusted with himself for craving it. At last he ran over, cursing his own eyes as he gave in. The soul cannot be a single thing, Plato reasoned: one part of him craved while another fought the craving at the same moment. Glaucon's challenge is the ring of Gyges, a legend about a shepherd who finds a ring of invisibility and uses it to win the queen, kill the king and take the crown, all without paying any price. The ring forces the hardest question: whether a person sure he could never be caught would have any reason to remain just.

Late in building his city, Plato gives his own answer. Justice is every person sticking to the one task his nature suits him for and not interfering in the work of others. It is his position to weigh, set against rivals in the dialogue such as the view that justice means paying your debts. It is also his reply to the blunt teacher Thrasymachus, who had declared that justice is simply the advantage of the stronger, since rulers make the laws to suit themselves.

Inside one person, Plato says, injustice is a kind of civil strife inside the soul, one part rising up against the whole. The just person, by contrast, binds reason, spirit and appetite together until the many pulls inside him become a single self. Plato pictures this as tuning the high, middle and low notes of a musical scale into one harmony. For him justice is this inner order, not merely a list of correct outward deeds.

the-philosopher-king.context_blurb:
Around 375 BC, in the Republic, Plato has Socrates make a proposal he admits will sound outrageous to democratic Athens: the best city would be ruled by philosophers. The idea rests on the Republic's whole theory of knowledge and the Good. It has been attacked and defended for twenty-five centuries, and the argument is still alive.

Deep in an all-night conversation about the just city, Socrates says cities will never be free of their troubles until philosophers become kings, or kings become true philosophers. What qualifies the philosopher is not wit or eloquence. He has turned away from shadows and climbed until he sees the Good itself, which lights up truth for the mind the way the sun lights up the world for the eye. Everyone else can only steer by opinion, which keeps shifting and never reaches the real thing.

Plato knew how the crowd would react. Imagine a vessel owned by a big, dim-sighted, hard-of-hearing man who knows nothing of the sea. His sailors fight over the helm, though not one has learned navigation. Aboard sits one man who has studied the stars, winds and seasons and could truly pilot her, yet the sailors dismiss him as a useless star-gazer, a dreamer lost in the clouds. That, Plato says, is how a mob treats the one person fit to govern.

Plato's rulers, the Guardians, live under harsh rules. They own no gold, no house and no land, and they are not even told which children are their own. Without wealth to grow or an heir to favour, nothing remains that a bribe or a family faction could use to bend a Guardian's judgment. They do not even want power, since they would rather keep studying, and the city must compel them. A good person rules anyway, Socrates says, chiefly to escape the penalty of being governed by someone worse.

Plato's own character Glaucon sees the weak spot: who keeps watch over the watchmen? Surely, he jokes, a guardian needing a guard of his own would be ridiculous. Plato's answer is education. Raised and trained rightly, the Guardians become their own guardians. The famous Latin line about guarding the guards is not Plato's at all. The Roman satirist Juvenal wrote it about a jealous husband who sets guards on his unfaithful wife; the joke is that she will simply seduce the guards themselves.

In 1945 Karl Popper read the Republic as a warning. Plato's rulers value the unity of the city over any individual's interest and are allowed to tell the people convenient myths. Popper argued that handing such power to the supposedly wise ends in a power no one can remove once it turns bad. Against those who say a true philosopher could never rule well, Plato's defenders point to Marcus Aurelius, the second-century Roman emperor who filled a private notebook with Stoic thoughts while governing Rome. The fork remains: trust the one who knows, or never hand anyone that much unchecked power.

the-tripartite-soul-and-the-chariot.context_blurb:
In the Republic and the Phaedrus, Plato gives his picture of what a person is like inside. His ethics rests on it: justice, self-control and the trouble with a bad character all depend on this one model. Centuries later Freud admitted it came close to his own.

Start with an everyday fight. You promised yourself not to check your phone while studying, but your fingers keep sliding toward it, so part of you reaches for it while part of you holds to your promise. Plato argued that this could not happen if the mind were one simple thing. It must be made of several drives that can pull against each other at the same moment. His own example was a thirsty man who refuses to drink.

In the Republic the soul has three parts. Reason loves truth and wisdom. Appetite hungers for food, drink, sex and money. The third, the spirited part, loves honour and winning, and flares with anger at any insult. Justice in the soul means every part minding its own job: reason rules, appetite obeys, and spirit fights on reason's side, carrying out what reason decides when appetite pulls the other way.

In the Phaedrus, Socrates paints the same soul as a charioteer driving two winged horses. The driver is reason, and the two horses are the soul's other drives, which he must steer: one calm and obedient, the other wild and stubborn. The noble horse answers the reins; the dark, crooked one fights them. When the dark horse bolts toward what it lusts after, the driver hauls back so hard that he bloodies its mouth and forces it to the ground. After this has happened many times, the beast is finally tamed, so that merely seeing beauty makes it shake with fear and submit.

These chariots are not in a race. They follow the gods up to the edge of the sky, hoping to glimpse what lies beyond: a realm without colour or shape, where true being lives and justice and wisdom themselves dwell. A soul that misses the sight sheds its wings and drops to earth, into a mortal body.

the-ladder-of-love-symposium.context_blurb:
Plato's Symposium is set at a drinking party in the house of the Athenian playwright Agathon, where the guests take turns giving speeches in praise of love. The speeches are brilliant and often funny; one is interrupted by hiccups. When Socrates' turn comes, he reports a step-by-step teaching about love, the source of the dialogue's famous nickname. Christian mystics, Renaissance humanists and modern philosophers have all started from this scene.

Socrates does not speak as the expert. He presents his speech as a lesson he was once taught by a wise woman, Diotima of Mantinea, which he merely repeats, so the most celebrated philosopher in Athens casts himself as the pupil. For Diotima, love is an ascent. It starts when a young person is drawn to one beautiful body, an attraction that is real and strong but meant to be a rung the lover leaves behind, not a home, and not something to be ashamed of.

What is love for? Not the beautiful thing itself, Diotima says, but giving birth in beauty, to children or to great ideas and noble deeds, so as to leave something of ourselves behind. At bottom, love is how a being that must die reaches for what never dies. The climb goes on in order. From one beautiful body the lover learns to love all beautiful bodies, and next the beauty of souls, of fine minds and characters, then laws and customs, then knowledge.

At the top the lover glimpses Beauty itself, unlike anything below it. A face fades and a custom admired in one city is scorned in another, but Beauty itself is everlasting and always the same, never lovely in one way and ugly in another. Readers have long called the passage the ladder of love, in Latin the scala amoris, yet scholars point out that Plato's Greek never once uses the word ladder; his image is of climbing as if on steps.

recollection-and-the-slave-boy-meno.context_blurb:
Plato's dialogue Meno opens with a young nobleman, Meno, asking Socrates whether virtue can be taught. The talk soon jams on an older puzzle: how can you search for something you do not already know? Socrates answers with one of philosophy's most famous classroom scenes, a geometry lesson for an untaught slave boy, and Plato draws from it a startling claim about where knowledge comes from. The scene is still argued over.

First Meno lost patience. Each confident definition of virtue he offered fell apart under Socrates' questions, until he complained that talking with Socrates was like touching the torpedo fish, the rounded electric ray of the seabed whose shock leaves its prey numb; his mind and his tongue both went numb. Then came the lesson. Socrates drew a square 2 feet on a side, 4 square feet in area, and challenged the boy to find the side of a square with twice that area, 8 square feet. The boy confidently proposed doubling the side to 4 feet. Socrates simply had him count: a square 4 feet on every side holds 16 square feet, four times the original rather than twice.

Socrates kept asking questions and never gave answers. After a second wrong guess of 3 feet, the boy saw that the side he wanted had been hiding inside the first square all along: the diagonal, running corner to opposite corner. Four of the triangles it cuts off fit together into a square of exactly double the area. Though Socrates supplied no answers, the boy, who had never studied geometry, arrived at a genuine geometrical truth. Where did it come from? Socrates' explanation was recollection: his soul had already seen it before birth, so all learning is really remembering.

The demonstration answers a trap Meno had set, now called Meno's paradox. If you already know a thing, you need not search for it; if you do not know it, you will not recognize it when you find it, so inquiry seems hopeless. Recollection offers an escape, since a soul that half-knows has somewhere to begin. Critics point to Socrates' own admission that the boy holds only true opinions, roused as if in a dream, which would need many more rounds of questioning to become knowledge. A skeptic concludes that skilled questioning alone drew out the answer, and no memory from before birth is required. Plato leaves the dispute open.

platos-banishment-of-the-poets.context_blurb:
In the Republic, Plato has Socrates argue that a well-ordered city would refuse citizenship to most of Greece's honored poets, with Homer and the great tragedians first in line. The case is striking because Plato was himself a brilliant writer, steeped in Homer. It is one of the earliest critiques of popular art ever written, and defenders of poetry from Sir Philip Sidney to Shelley have felt bound to answer it.

The truest bed, for Plato, is its Form, the single perfect bed that is completely real. A carpenter builds a wooden bed by looking toward that Form. A painter then paints the carpenter's bed, copying only how it looks and not what it is, so his picture sits at the bottom, a copy of a copy, third in line from the truth. Plato admits the exile costs him. He confesses a lifelong reverence and love for Homer, so strong that he can hardly bring himself to pronounce the sentence. He banishes the poet anyway, because a man must not be honored above the truth. His deepest charge concerns what happens inside the audience. As a tragic hero weeps over his losses, the viewer grieves with him, and the play feeds and waters those passions instead of letting them dry up, strengthening the very feelings reason ought to govern. Other thinkers have judged tragedy very differently, and the quarrel is still alive.

the-myth-of-er.context_blurb:
Plato's Republic, his long dialogue on justice in the city and in the soul, ends not with an argument but with a story. Socrates tells of Er, a soldier who saw the land of the dead and came back to describe it. Plato offers it as a teaching tale, not a doctrine, yet it gathers up everything the Republic has argued about how a person should live.

Er fell in battle, and his body lay with the other dead for ten days without decaying. Two days later, stretched on his own funeral pyre, he revived and began to tell what he had seen.

The dead, he said, choose their next lives from sample lives spread out on the ground. A prophet scatters lots among them and proclaims the tale's one lesson: each soul picks its own life, so the blame for a wretched life falls on the soul that chose it, and God is cleared. Odysseus came up last of all, holding the final lot. Cured of ambition by the memory of his old hardships, he hunted for ages and gladly took the quiet life of a private man free of cares, which everyone else had passed over. He said he would have picked it even if his lot had come first.

atlantis-as-platos-invention.context_blurb:
Atlantis, the drowned island empire of novels and documentaries, has one ancient source: the Greek philosopher Plato. He tells the story in two late dialogues, the Timaeus and the unfinished Critias, and almost every modern version of Atlantis traces back to those two short texts. What Plato was doing with the tale is the real puzzle.

In Plato's telling, Atlantis was a mighty empire beyond the Pillars of Hercules that grew proud and violent and attacked Athens. After its defeat, earthquakes and floods struck, and in a single day and night the whole island sank beneath the sea. An empire that took ages to build vanished almost at once, which is the sting of the cautionary tale.

Was it real? Aristotle, who studied under Plato, judged bluntly that his teacher had invented the island whole to teach a lesson. Atlantis appears in no text older than Plato, and the classicist A.E. Taylor agreed that the narrative is plainly Plato's own invention. Plato's insistence that the story was true and very old is a storyteller's old trick of dressing fiction up as history.

The opening of the Timaeus shows the lesson. It is set the morning after the long talk of the Republic, in which Socrates built an ideal city in words. Words alone no longer satisfy him, he confesses; he longs to see it in motion, tested against a worthy rival in a real war. That wish is what prompts Critias to tell the Atlantis story. Atlantis is a deliberate foil, a swollen, arrogant empire built so that Plato's smaller, virtuous Athens could defeat it.

aristotle-and-the-lyceum.context_blurb:
Aristotle was born in 384 BC in Stagira, in northern Greece, the son of a court doctor to the kings of Macedon. At seventeen he joined Plato's Academy in Athens and stayed twenty years. He later tutored the young Alexander the Great, then returned to Athens to found his own school, the Lyceum. For nearly two thousand years, scholars writing in Latin and Arabic called him simply the Philosopher.

Alexander, legend says, loved the copy of Homer's Iliad that Aristotle had marked up for him so much that he slept with it under his pillow, beside his dagger, throughout his campaigns in Asia. Back in Athens, Aristotle's school picked up a nickname, the Peripatetic school, meaning given to walking about. Its classes met along the Lyceum's covered colonnades, and teacher and students strolled the walkways as they argued, instead of sitting still.

The two schools disagreed about where truth lives. For Plato, what is most real is a world of perfect, unchanging Forms that only reason can reach. Aristotle turned to the world you can touch, cutting open animals and collecting observations. Even his school's site reflected his status. As a foreigner from Stagira, he could not legally own land in Athens, and he had no property to teach on the way Plato did. In 335 BC he taught instead in a precinct belonging to the god Apollo Lykeios, land open to the public, which gave the Lyceum its name.

His habit of looking for himself paid off in surprising ways. Wading off the island of Lesbos, he heard from fishermen that the male octopus has a special arm for mating that can even snap off. Scholars mocked the report as a fisherman's tale for some two thousand years, until the French naturalist Georges Cuvier dissected octopuses in the early 1800s and found the arm exactly as described. He cracked open hen's eggs at daily intervals to follow the growing chick. The first organ to come alive, he saw, was the heart, beating before the rest of the body had taken shape. His school also gathered the written constitutions of 158 different Greek cities, but only the one for Athens survived, and even it was lost for over a thousand years. Then copies on papyrus turned up, preserved in the dry sands of Egypt. Two leaves arrived in Berlin in 1879, and whole rolls came to the British Museum in 1890.
