the-golden-mean.context_blurb:
The golden mean is the traditional name for the central idea of Aristotle's ethics, set out in his Nicomachean Ethics. Each virtue of character, he held, sits between two failures, one of too much and one of too little. The mean is not a bland halfway compromise; it is a target sharper than either extreme, and finding it takes real self-knowledge. The idea remains the backbone of modern virtue ethics.

Picture a village terrorized by a dragon. One knight, sick with fear, gallops away; another, reckless with pride, rushes the beast single-handed and is burned to cinders. Aristotle would praise neither. The truly brave knight stands his ground and fights when he has a real chance of winning, feeling the right amount of fear and acting well despite it. Money works the same way. Between the miser who hoards every coin and the spendthrift who throws money at strangers, the generous person gives a sensible amount to those who truly need it.

Anyone can get angry, Aristotle said; that is easy. The hard part is to be angry with the right person, to the right degree, at the right time, for the right purpose and in the right way. Too little anger misses the mark as well. A boy who watches a bully rob a smaller child and feels nothing is not admirably calm; his failure to feel anger at a real wrong is itself a flaw. Aristotle compared virtue to archery. There are countless ways to overshoot or fall short, but only one way to hit the centre, which is why being bad is easy and being good is hard.

Some extremes are rare. Many people chase pleasure too hard, but a person who finds no pleasure in anything is so unusual that the failing barely has a name. Honesty about yourself has two failures as well: the braggart who claims too much, and the falsely modest man, like Socrates pretending to know nothing, because playing yourself down departs from the truth as surely as puffing yourself up. Since the exact middle is hard to find, Aristotle advised noticing which fault you lean toward and pulling hard the other way, the way men straighten a bent stick by bending it back, so that over-correcting lands you nearer the middle. False courage gives itself away: the rash man boasts about danger in advance and then draws back when the real terror comes, while the brave man is quiet beforehand and keen when it counts. Pleasure, Aristotle warned, is hard to judge fairly. Treat it the way Troy's elders treated Helen, the beauty who had caused the war: grant frankly that she is lovely, and send her off.

The mean is relative to the person. If ten pounds of food is too much for a wrestler and two too little, a trainer will not simply order six, which might starve the champion Milo and overstuff a beginner; the right amount depends on who is eating. Nor does the mean mean everything in moderation. Theft, adultery and murder have no right amount or right occasion, because some acts are wrong in the very doing.

virtue-ethics-and-eudaimonia.context_blurb:
Alongside rule-based ethics descended from Kant and results-based ethics descended from the utilitarians, virtue ethics is the third great family of moral theory, and Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics is its founding book. Aristotle starts with neither rules nor results. He asks what final goal a human life is really aiming at. His word for it, eudaimonia, is usually translated happiness, but he means flourishing, a whole life lived well, not a passing mood.

Most people, Aristotle noticed, think the good life means piling up pleasure. He took them seriously enough to argue with them, but judged that life a life fit for grazing cattle, the kind beasts would choose. He also rejected a life aimed at honour, because honour depends on the people who give it rather than on the one who receives it, and the highest good cannot be so easily taken away. To find what is truly good for a human being, he reasoned from crafts. A flute-player has his own work, and so do the eye and the hand. Plants merely grow and animals merely sense; the work peculiar to a human being is reasoning, done well over a lifetime.

Flourishing takes a whole life. A girl who has one perfect afternoon has not yet made her life a happy one: a single swallow is no proof that summer has come, and a single good day does not make a happy life. The ending matters too. King Priam of Troy prospered for decades, then in old age watched Troy burn and his sons die before he too perished miserably. So a catastrophe at the close can undo a life's happiness, and flourishing must be measured across the entire span.

Virtues are built, not born. A boy who plans to be brave once he understands courage has the order wrong: the only road to bravery is acting bravely, again and again, until courage hardens into his character. Each virtue sits at a middle point between two vices. Courage lies between cowardice, which fears too much, and rashness, which fears too little, so fearlessness is not courage perfected but one of courage's two failures, overshooting the target just as cowardice falls short. Knowing the good is not enough either. A person who knows an act is wrong and does it anyway because desire drags him is like a city that passes all the right decrees and then makes no use of them. And two equally brave, equally trained officers may still part ways at a crisis: what separates them is practical wisdom, the judgment to deliberate well about this very case.

Aristotle could be playful. His great-souled man, who rightly judges himself fit for great things, walks slowly, speaks in a deep voice and never hurries his words. Nor did he sneer at pleasure. It is not the goal, but it rides along with an activity done well and completes it, the way the bloom of youth sits on young people in their prime. Highest of all is contemplation, the godlike activity of reason. Rather than keep our thoughts on mortal things, Aristotle urged, we should reach as far as we can toward the immortal, putting every effort into living by the highest part of ourselves.

virtue-as-habit.context_blurb:
In the Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle makes a claim about character that is simple to state and hard to live by: virtues such as courage, honesty and fairness are not gifts handed out at birth but skills built by practice, like a craft. The idea shaped medieval ethics, faded after the Reformation, and has come roaring back in modern philosophy and in character education.

Aristotle took his model from the workshops of his day. Nobody turns into a builder except by building, or into a musician except by making music. In the same way, a boy hoping to become courageous and just gets there only by doing courageous and just deeds, again and again. Justice in particular is trained in our dealings with others: it is by acting fairly or unfairly toward the people around us that we become just or unjust.

To show that character is not fixed by nature, Aristotle pointed to a stone. Toss a stone into the air ten thousand times and it will still never learn to fly upward by itself, because falling is its nature. Virtue, by contrast, can be trained into us by habit, so it cannot be a fixed part of our nature. Even the name tells the story. Ethike, the Greek term for moral character, is a small variation on ethos, the ordinary word for habit or custom, and it gave us our word ethics. So the habits a child forms from youth are no small matter; they make all the difference.

How can you tell when a virtue has really taken root? Aristotle's sign is pleasure. Once acting rightly has become a pleasure instead of a struggle, so that the brave man no longer dreads standing firm and the temperate man no longer pines for the feast he gave up, the virtue is built into him rather than forced on him from outside.

That is why Aristotle studied ethics at all. The aim, he said, is not merely to know what virtue is, which alone would be useless, but to make us good people, which only practice in good deeds can do, just as no one becomes a harpist by understanding music.

the-four-causes.context_blurb:
The four causes are Aristotle's tool for explaining anything, set out in his Physics and Metaphysics. The English word cause misleads a little: Aristotle offers four different kinds of answer to the question of why a thing exists or is the way it is. A full explanation, he held, touches all four, and he thought earlier Greek thinkers had each grabbed one or two and mistaken them for the whole.

Take a wooden table. One answer names whatever started the change, the one who did the making: the carpenter, who did the building. This is what we usually mean today by cause. A second names the stuff it is made of. Aristotle's examples were the bronze of a statue and the silver of a bowl; for a marble statue honouring a hero, it is the marble the sculptor carved. A third, the slippery one, is the form, the arrangement that turns loose timber into a table instead of a woodpile. For a table that pattern is simply four legs and a flat top. The fourth is what a thing is for. Ask why anyone builds a house, and a child's answer is the right one: for the shelter it gives.

Form can be surprising. Cut a vibrating string to half its length and its note climbs exactly one octave, on any string. So the octave's nature lives not in gut or bronze but in a proportion between the two notes, the ratio of 2 to 1. Purpose can seem backward. Aristotle said health is the cause of a man's walk after dinner, even though the health arrives later than the stroll. He meant that the man strolls in order to be healthy, so the end he is aiming at explains the stroll. Since nature does nothing in vain, natural things have purposes too: an acorn is for the mature oak it grows into.

The Greek word behind cause is aition, and it began in the lawcourt, where it named the person to blame. So Aristotle's real question is what is answerable for a thing, and scholars say explanation fits better than cause. That is why even an absence can be a cause. A ship's pilot at the helm causes its safety; when he leaves and the ship strikes the rocks, his very absence is the cause of the wreck. Aristotle crowned the final cause the queen of causes, for one reason: the goal ranks first because every other part of the work is done for its sake. The builder gathers bricks and follows a plan in order to make a shelter.

telos-and-the-final-cause.context_blurb:
Telos is Greek for end, goal or completion. For Aristotle, the great Greek philosopher and a serious working biologist, the telos or final cause answers the question of what something is for, and he held that natural things, above all living ones, have real answers to it. His purpose-filled picture of nature ruled European thought for about two thousand years, until the scientific revolution challenged it. Whether science can truly do without it is still argued.

Aristotle's classic image is an acorn. Nothing pushes it from outside, yet it is already heading somewhere: its end is the mature oak it will slowly become, a goal hidden in the seed itself. He leaned again and again on one slogan, in Greek he phusis ouden poiei maten: nature never does anything in vain, so every part of a creature exists for some job. His favourite proof was teeth. In every animal the front teeth are sharp, made for tearing, while the broad back teeth are flat, made for grinding. A pattern that reliably serves the animal's good, he argued, points to a purpose, not to luck.

To explain a bronze statue fully, Aristotle named four causes: the bronze it is made of, the shape it takes, the sculptor who makes it, and the end it aims at. Its final cause, which answers "for the sake of which?", is the finished statue itself, standing complete as its own goal. A thing's purpose is what makes it the thing it is. A painted eye on a statue, or the dead eye of a corpse, is an eye in name only, because a true eye must be able to do the work of seeing.

His hardest case was rain on a field of grain. An opponent said rain is pure mechanism, warm air rising, cooling and dropping its water, and that the grain growing is mere coincidence. Aristotle answered that nature has ends built into things themselves. His purposes are not planted from outside by a designing mind or a meddling god; they live inside the things. Modern science took the opponent's road. In 1605 Francis Bacon, helping to launch the new science, called the hunt for final causes barren, like a virgin vowed to God who bears no children, and urged that nature be explained by matter and force instead.

the-syllogism-and-valid-form.context_blurb:
Aristotle was the first person we know of to study good reasoning as a subject of its own, the way geometry studies shapes. His logic books, later gathered as the Organon, or instrument, focus on a short pattern in which two statements lead to a third: the syllogism. His catalogue of which patterns are reliable shaped Western thought for two thousand years.

The classic example: every human is mortal, and Socrates is a human. Grant both and you are trapped. You cannot accept the two and still deny that Socrates is mortal; the conclusion is forced. Not every forced conclusion uses Aristotle's all and some. If Elizabeth owns just one car, either a Honda or else a Saturn, and she truly has no Honda, then her car is a Saturn, since ruling out one option leaves only the other.

Look closely at this one: Greeks are all men, men are all mortal, so Greeks are all mortal. One word sits in both premises, joins the two ends and then vanishes from the conclusion. That hinge is men, the middle term, and without a shared middle term there is no syllogism. True starting sentences alone do not make a good argument. Every basketball is round and the planet is round, but that does not make the planet a basketball. A shape like that forces nothing, so whenever it happens to land on a true conclusion, the truth is a lucky coincidence.

Aristotle's great stroke was to swap names like Socrates for bare letters, A, B and C, so that a shape of argument could be studied alone. Historians call this the birth of the variable, a placeholder letter that can stand for any term, still used in algebra and computer code. Write a form using only letters, with no subject named at all, and what you judge is the arrangement of its terms, without knowing whether any sentence is true.

That is what valid means. A valid form rules out one situation: all the premises true and the conclusion false at the same time. It does not promise the premises are true. Suppose every toaster were solid gold and anything golden could travel through time; then every toaster could travel through time. Every line is false, yet the argument is valid, because validity protects the step from premises to conclusion and says nothing about whether the facts are right. The stronger word is sound. A sound argument is valid and its premises are actually true, and only a sound argument truly proves its conclusion.

Medieval teachers turned the catalogue into memory games. The four kinds of statement (every, none, some, and some-not) were tagged A, E, I and O, letters taken from two Latin words: affirmo, I affirm, which gave A and I, and nego, I deny, which gave E and O to the denials. Students sang nonsense words such as Barbara and Celarent, recorded in William of Sherwood's thirteenth-century logic book. The vowels of each name, read in order, spelled out the three statement types of that form.

Some shapes only look valid. Cats are mammals and dogs are mammals, so cats are dogs? Mammals appears in both premises, but it sits above cats and dogs separately and never links them to each other. For some two thousand years Aristotle's account simply was logic, hardly altered; Kant even called the subject finished. Then in 1879 Gottlob Frege's short book, the Begriffsschrift, broke past it and began modern logic.

the-function-argument.context_blurb:
In the first book of his Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle tries to learn what a good human life is by first asking a simpler question, the kind you would ask about a good knife or a good flute-player. The move, now called the function argument, is the hinge of his whole ethics. Biologists have attacked it and modern defenders of virtue ethics have rebuilt it, and the fight is still open.

The opening rule is plain. A knife's job is to cut and a flute-player's job is to play, and a good one of either kind is simply one that does its own job well. Aristotle piles up example after example, the musician, the sculptor, the painter, so that the pattern feels obvious for anything with a job before he turns it on human beings. Then he looks at the body. The eye has a job, seeing; the hand, gripping; the foot, walking. If every part has a job, he asks, must not the whole human being have a job too, beyond all its separate parts?

To find it, Aristotle hunts for the work that belongs to humans alone. Merely being alive, taking in food and growing, fails at once, since plants do that too. A life of perceiving, seeing colours and hearing sounds, fails as well, because the horse, the ox and every other beast perceive. Only one kind of life is left, an active life guided by reason. So the good human life, for Aristotle, is reasoning well, the activity of the soul in keeping with virtue.

Critics have pressed hard. A knife's purpose was given to it by the smith who forged it. But no one built a whole human being for a task, so perhaps a human has no built-in function at all. Aristotelians reply that natures can carry ends without a designer. A second critic turns Aristotle's own words against him. He wrote that only humans laugh, but he never named laughter as our purpose. Being the only creature to do something, the critic concludes, does not prove that thing is your true job, so the argument needs one more step from "only we do it" to "this is what we are for."

practical-wisdom-phronesis.context_blurb:
Phronesis is Aristotle's Greek word for practical wisdom, a kind of knowing distinct both from the general truths of geometry and from the hand-skill of a carpenter. Its home is the particular case. Moral life, Aristotle held, does not run like a flowchart, and no rulebook can cover every situation an adult must handle. Medical, military and legal ethics have all returned to his account in recent decades.

Aristotle compared it to navigation. A captain heading into a sudden gale carries a good chart, but the chart was made long ago and knows nothing about tonight's wind and waves. To get the ship home safely, he has to see the storm as it actually is and decide what tonight's sea demands. A real case shows the cost of lacking that skill. At a baseball game in Detroit, the archaeologist Chris Ratte bought his young son a lemonade, not realizing it was the alcoholic kind. Everyone involved, from the police to the judge, saw a loving father's innocent mistake, yet the boy was taken into foster care for three days. What the case lacked was someone in charge with the experienced judgment to act on the plainly right outcome in this one case.

Aristotle noticed that a bright youngster can become a fine mathematician, but a practically wise youth is nowhere to be found. Practical wisdom is built from experience, and only the passing of years supplies that. It also needs two things joined: the general rules, and the reading of the case at hand. An officer who knows the field manual by heart but keeps blundering in battle has the rules and lacks the second part, the ability to see this battle, here and now, for what it is.

Good character and practical wisdom divide the labor. A warm-hearted woman eager to aid a neighbor in trouble, whose clumsy efforts only make things worse, has the right aim but not the means. Virtue, Aristotle wrote, makes the goal right; practical wisdom adds the know-how to find the means that will truly succeed here. Nor is practical wisdom mere cleverness. A swindler who sizes up his marks perfectly and always finds a way to fleece them is clever, because cleverness will work for any goal, a villain's included, whereas practical wisdom works only toward what is good. Fittingly, the Greek word for clever, deinos, also means terrible. Finally, Aristotle separated knowledge of eternal, unchanging things, such as the heavens and pure mathematics, from the knack of acting well in shifting human affairs. They are different virtues, so a genius about the eternal order may still blunder foolishly through ordinary life.

the-three-kinds-of-friendship.context_blurb:
In Books VIII and IX of his Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle spends two whole books on friendship, which he counts among the central goods of a human life. His key move is to notice that one word, friend, covers bonds that run on very different motives, and to ask which bonds survive when circumstances change.

People find three things lovable, Aristotle says: what is useful, what is pleasant, and the good man himself. So there are three kinds of friendship. The first is a friendship of use. Tomas sits beside his classmate Dmitri only on the days when homework is hard and never looks for him after the final exam; the bond rests on nothing but the use Dmitri is to him. The second is a friendship of pleasure. Priya drops in on her neighbour Kofi on dull afternoons because he makes her laugh, and admits she would stop coming if he lost his spark. She is drawn by how much fun he is, not by the man himself.

Aristotle does not sneer at these bonds; most ordinary friendships are made of them. But they rest on things that change, and he gives an easy test for them. Cease to be useful or amusing, and anyone who stayed only for the benefits drops away, since the bond was never really about you.

The third kind lasts a lifetime. A friendship of virtue rests on the goodness of each friend's character, each wishing the other well for the other's own sake, and it endures as long as they stay good. Aristotle called such a friend a second self, someone you care for as you care for yourself.

He also separated friendship from goodwill. A man may admire a famous stranger and truly wish him well, though the stranger has never heard of him. That goodwill is only the seed of friendship. The grown friendship needs time together and a bond that is returned.

man-the-political-animal.context_blurb:
In the opening pages of his Politics, written around 335 BCE, Aristotle set down a famous claim about what kind of creature a human being is. Some Sophists before him had called the city, the polis, an artificial bargain struck to protect individuals from one another. Aristotle took the opposite line, and the quarrel over whether political life is natural or invented, later revived by Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau, is still open.

Why do people build towns instead of scattering across the countryside? Aristotle's answer was that a human being is by nature a political animal. We are made for shared life, the urge toward community is planted in us, and only in community does a human life become complete. Hence his striking line about a being who needed no community at all: so self-sufficient a creature would fall outside humanity, below it as a beast or above it as a god. People first band together simply to stay alive, he granted, but survival is not what a city is for. A city comes into being for the sake of life and goes on existing for the sake of the good life, to help its members live well and flourish.

What sets us apart? Many animals have voice, a dog's yelp or a bird's cry, which signals pain or pleasure. Humans alone have speech, and speech exists so that we can reason together about what helps and what harms, and so about right and wrong, rather than merely announce how we feel. That is also why Aristotle called humans more political than bees. A hive may be perfectly orderly, but bees cooperate by instinct. The gap is not that humans choose freely while bees obey a queen; it is that humans alone deliberate together about what is good and just for the community.

Aristotle's case for the purpose of speech leans on one hidden premise. Of all the animals, only humans were given speech; nature, he liked to say, makes nothing in vain; therefore speech must serve a purpose, and that purpose is shared deliberation about justice. Without the middle step, the "therefore" collapses. He also claimed that the city is prior to the individual, as a whole comes before its parts. A hand cut off from the body is a hand in name only. In the same way, a person cut off from all community is not self-sufficient, and so is no longer fully what a person should be.

the-unmoved-mover.context_blurb:
Near the end of the twelfth book of his Metaphysics, Aristotle argued that all motion in the cosmos depends on a first mover that is itself never moved. Centuries later Thomas Aquinas built the first of his Five Ways on the same reasoning. Aristotle offered it as a first principle of motion, not as a verdict on the God of any religion.

Trace any motion back. The cart is pulled by the horse, the horse is driven by its rider, and the rider is driven by his desires. Each link in between only passes along motion it was given, so a chain made entirely of such relays never explains where the motion began. There must be something that moves others without being moved.

But how can something perfectly still move anything? A pusher must move in order to push. Aristotle's answer is that the first mover moves things by being desired and loved, as a beloved draws a lover toward her without stirring.

What does such a being do? It is a perfect mind that never stops thinking, and whatever it thinks about must be the best thing there is, or the mind itself would be lessened. The best thing is that mind, so it eternally thinks about itself, in one unbroken act of thought thinking about thinking.

catharsis-and-the-poetics.context_blurb:
Aristotle's Poetics is a short, unfinished study of Greek tragedy, written when the great playwrights of the century before, Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, were already classics. Taking stage practice as his evidence, Aristotle asked what makes some tragedies hit an audience hard. Underneath lies a strange puzzle: why do we enjoy watching a good person suffer?

Audiences pay to see a hero ruined, leave oddly satisfied, and come back for more. Aristotle's answer is catharsis, a Greek word for cleansing borrowed from medicine and ritual. A tragedy stirs up the audience's pity and fear and then safely washes those feelings out, so the spectators go home lighter. He uses the word only once and never explains it, and scholars have argued over it for two thousand years.

His model of a great reversal, which he called peripeteia, comes from Sophocles' Oedipus the King. A messenger comes hoping to set Oedipus's mind at rest about his parents. Instead, the cheering message, simply by being delivered, exposes who Oedipus really is and ruins him. The good news is itself the catastrophe, and the turn springs from the story's own events rather than from chance.

Aristotle said the tragic hero falls through hamartia, an archery word for an arrow missing its mark. He misjudges honestly, missing the mark the way an arrow does, and his fall does not punish a wicked heart. That is why we feel he did not deserve it, and why we pity him and fear for him. The popular phrase "tragic flaw" is itself disputed; some scholars argue that tragedy is never about flaws at all.

zeno-of-citium-and-the-founding-of-stoic.context_blurb:
Zeno of Citium, not to be confused with Zeno of Elea and his paradoxes, was a merchant from Cyprus who reached Athens around 312 BC. There he founded Stoicism, one of the most influential schools of the ancient world, later embraced by Roman senators, emperors and former slaves alike.

His road to philosophy began with disaster. His ship sank near Athens, taking his whole cargo, and left him stranded and penniless. Wandering into a bookshop, he read about Socrates, the barefoot Athenian who had questioned everyone about how to live while claiming to know nothing. Thrilled, Zeno asked where such men could be found. The bookseller pointed at a figure passing in the street, the ragged Cynic Crates of Thebes, who begged for his living, and told Zeno to follow him. Years later Zeno called the day of his shipwreck the most prosperous voyage he ever made.

An oracle told Zeno to take on the colour of the dead. Rather than despair, he decided it meant he should steep himself in the books of authors long dead.

Crates set out to cure his painful shyness. He handed Zeno a full pot of lentil soup to carry through the busy market, and when Zeno tried to hide it, Crates smashed the pot with his staff so the soup ran down his legs. As Zeno fled, Crates called after him that nothing terrible had happened.

Zeno taught in the Stoa Poikile, the Painted Porch, a roofed public colonnade beside the marketplace, and that porch gave the school its name: stoa became Stoic. Unlike the walled schools of Plato and Aristotle, the porch was open to anyone, and his listeners were remembered as merchants, slaves and day labourers. Athens came to trust this foreigner so much that it reportedly entrusted him with the keys to its walls, and after his death it honoured him with a golden crown.

Legend says that as a very old man he tripped leaving his school and wrenched his toe. Taking it as a summons, he struck the ground, quoted a line from a tragedy, and stopped breathing by his own will until death came.

the-dichotomy-of-control.context_blurb:
The dichotomy of control is the keystone practice of Stoicism, a school of philosophy founded in Athens around 300 BCE that became the working philosophy of educated Romans. The practice is to sort everything in your life into two piles: what is truly in your power and what is not. The Stoics held that peace of mind lies on that line, and the idea echoes today in modern therapy and the Serenity Prayer.

Picture two farmers whose wheat is flattened by the same storm the night before harvest. One is wretched all day; the other shrugs and gets to work. The Stoic teacher Epictetus taught that people are upset not by things but by their judgments about them, so what made the first farmer miserable was his own judgment that the loss was a disaster. The path to a steady life, he said, is not to demand that events go your way but to want events to turn out exactly as they do turn out. Epictetus knew both piles from the inside. As a young man he was a slave in the household of Epaphroditus, a rich official serving the emperor Nero. When something is taken from you, even someone you love, never say you have lost it, he taught; say instead that you have given it back, since it was only ever on loan.

One famous story says his master once twisted his leg for sport. Epictetus calmly warned that it would break, and when the bone snapped he only remarked that he had told him so. He limped for life, but his composure was never the master's to break. Epictetus opened his teaching by sorting life into two bins, what is up to us and what is not. On the second side he put the body, property and, most surprisingly, reputation, which most people would defend before almost anything. He never wrote a word himself. Arrian, the same man who wrote the history of Alexander the Great's campaigns, took down his lectures and boiled them into a pocket handbook, the Enchiridion. Even love falls under the rule. When you kiss your child or your spouse goodnight, Epictetus said, remind yourself that the one you kiss is a mortal human being, so that your love can stay steady and unafraid.

Epictetus pointed to ball players chasing a ball that is nothing but a cheap scrap of leather. The lesson is to throw yourself into playing well, which is up to you, while holding the outcome loosely, since it is not. Some events cannot be escaped at all: I must die, I must go into exile. Yet even then one thing stays yours, the manner in which you meet it, whether groaning or serene.

The harder cases test the line. A young athlete who longs for the crowd's love has staked his peace on something he can never control. He can master his training and his conduct, but the opinions of the crowd are formed in the spectators' heads, not in his. Even the body is not fully ours. Epictetus called it borrowed clay, a little donkey on loan, because chains, illness or injury, all forces beyond your will, can seize it. Picture a tyrant gloating over a man in chains. He can seize the man's goods, ruin his name and even take his life, but he cannot make him a worse man. Your calm, Epictetus thought, can be shaken; your moral character, whether you become vicious, is yours alone to keep or to corrupt, since only your own assent can make you bad.

epictetus-from-slave-to-sage.context_blurb:
Epictetus was a Greek-speaking philosopher of the first century and one of the three great teachers of Roman Stoicism. Born a slave and lame for life, he ended up schooling senators, and his words later shaped an emperor. His central puzzle is an everyday one: why does the same loss crush one person and barely ruffle another? His answer reads like the ancestor of modern cognitive therapy.

He was born around 55 CE at Hierapolis in Phrygia, in what is now Turkey, and his birth name is lost. The household that owned him called him Epictetus, from the Greek epiktetos, meaning acquired: not a name so much as a note that the boy had been bought. His philosophy began from a gap he saw between people. Two traders see the same storm sink their whole fortune; one is shattered, the other shrugs and walks off calm. Since the event was identical, the difference must lie elsewhere. People are upset not by things, Epictetus taught, but by the judgments they form about things. So he split life into two groups. Your opinions, desires and choices of what to pursue or avoid are truly yours to command, while your body, reputation and property are not.

Legend says his lameness came from cruelty. The writer Celsus told how a master once twisted the young slave's leg; Epictetus neither begged nor raged, only warning that it would break, and when the bone snapped he remarked coolly that he had told his master it would break. Another ancient source blames rheumatism instead, but either way he limped for the rest of his life. Life, he said, is like a drama on a stage. You are an actor, and whether your part is a king's or a beggar's, brief or lengthy, the author chose it, not you. Your one real task is to perform the part you were given as well as it can be performed.

His boyhood was spent inside Nero's imperial court, owned by a powerful official named Epaphroditus, and the bitter irony is that Epaphroditus had himself been a slave before winning his freedom. Epictetus wrote nothing at all. A devoted student, Arrian of Nicomedia, took down his spoken lectures as the Discourses and boiled them into a small handbook, the Enchiridion. Those notes reached the emperor Marcus Aurelius through his teacher Junius Rusticus, and the former slave became the writer Marcus quoted most in his private Meditations, including his picture of each of us as a little soul hauling a corpse about.

marcus-aurelius-and-the-meditations.context_blurb:
From 161 to 180 CE Marcus Aurelius governed the empire of Rome through plague, long wars on the northern border and plots at home. Trained in Stoic philosophy, he spent his reign trying to live by it while holding absolute power, the kind of power that had ruined many emperors before him. The short book he left behind, the Meditations, has become one of the most-read works of philosophy ever written.

The Meditations was never meant for any reader but its author. It was a private notebook that Marcus kept for his own eyes alone, and its Greek title means "to himself." He wrote much of it not in a palace in Rome but in his army camp on the Danube frontier, during the long wars against Germanic tribes, jotting reminders between campaigns. One entry catches him on a chilly morning, snug under the blankets and unwilling to rise. Was he made only to lie there keeping warm? No, he told himself: he was getting up to do a human being's work.

Marcus feared what the throne could do to him. He cautioned himself against becoming "Caesarified," dipped in the purple dye of the emperors, because, he wrote, it does happen: absolute power could corrupt his character. His defense was the core Stoic idea he learned from the former slave Epictetus, that events do not disturb us, but our judgments about them do. That explains why two people struck by the same illness can come out so differently, one broken and one almost untouched: the difference lies in how each one judges what has happened. He opened the whole notebook not with conquests but with gratitude. Book One names about sixteen people, among them his grandfather, his mother and his teachers, and thanks each for one thing that person taught him.

History added bitter ironies. Marcus's son and heir, Commodus, became everything his father warned against, a vain megalomaniac who fancied himself Hercules reborn and fought as a gladiator in the arena. And the great plague of his reign, probably smallpox, which killed millions while Marcus wrote calmly about accepting death, is called the Antonine Plague after Marcus's own family name, Antoninus.

seneca-the-tutor-and-his-calm-death.context_blurb:
Lucius Annaeus Seneca was a Roman statesman, playwright and Stoic philosopher of the first century AD, famous for letters on how to live well, from wasted time to the fear of death. He was also fabulously rich, and he spent years as tutor and adviser to the boy who became the emperor Nero. His death became the test of everything he had written.

In AD 65 a conspiracy against Nero failed, and the emperor turned on his old teacher. Soldiers came to Seneca's villa, and when word came back that the old man showed no fear, Nero sent a centurion with the sentence. The order was that Seneca must die by his own hand, the forced suicide Rome granted its nobles instead of the executioner, which meant opening his own veins. He cut the veins of his arms, but his aged body bled slowly and death took hours to come. So Seneca summoned his secretaries and spoke a long essay aloud for them to take down, words that Tacitus says were later published just as he spoke them.

His blood crept out so slowly for a grimly ironic reason: the wealthy Seneca had eaten so sparingly for years that his aged body was wasted thin, and he had to open the arteries of his legs and behind his knees as well. Poison did no better. At last his friends placed him in a warm bath, and Seneca sprinkled water on the slaves standing nearest him as a drink-offering to Jove the Liberator, a last Stoic salute to freedom. The steam of a vapor bath finally ended his life. It was the death his letters had rehearsed. Philosophy, he taught, is practice for hardship, and the dreaded last day is the birthday of eternity. Whoever has learned to die, Seneca wrote, has unlearned slavery, because no threat can own a man who does not fear death.

Yet his life sat uneasily beside his teaching. His accuser Publius Suillius Rufus charged in Rome that this preacher against greed had piled up three hundred million sesterces in only four years at Nero's side, when a Roman legionary earned under a thousand sesterces a year. Seneca's reply came in On the Happy Life. Wealth, he argued, is indifferent, not good or bad in itself, so a wise man may keep a fortune provided he came by it honestly and puts it to right use, owning his riches without being owned by them. Whether his life matched the argument, each reader may judge for himself.

apatheia-not-emotionless-but-unenslaved.context_blurb:
Apatheia is the Greek word behind one of philosophy's worst translations. Today "stoic" means cold and unmoved, but the ancient Stoics, from Zeno's school in Athens to Seneca and Epictetus, aimed at something else: holding steady under rage, grief or craving without turning into a block of wood. Modern cognitive therapy owes their idea a large and rarely admitted debt.

Being stoic in the old sense does not mean feeling nothing when the family dog dies. The Stoic feels the grief but refuses to let it rule him or drag him around; he still loves and still acts, he simply is not the slave of his impulses. Even bodily shocks do not count against him. Seneca wrote that the bravest soldier goes pale as he straps on his armor and the general's heart leaps before battle, yet this is not fear. Those are the body's involuntary jolts, first movements that arrive before the mind has agreed to anything, and they become fear only if the mind says yes.

Epictetus located where suffering really lives. The same blow, exile for instance, can crush one man and leave another calm. Were the harm inside the event, both would suffer equally, so the real hurt lies in the opinion each man forms about his exile, and that opinion is his to choose.

Critics called the Stoic sage cold and dead-hearted. The Stoics answered that he feels three good feelings, finely and well: joy grounded in reason, caution that keeps him wary, and goodwill that wishes others well. What he lacks is a healthy form of grief, since, judging rightly, he has nothing truly bad to mourn. Seneca's book On Anger shows how the Stoics saw the passions. The angry man pleads that rage swept over him like a wave, but for a Stoic a passion is a judgment the mind has just assented to, not an ambush from some animal part of the soul. Because he gave that assent, he can take it back this instant.

amor-fati-loving-your-fate.context_blurb:
Amor fati is Latin for "love of fate." The idea grew out of Stoic philosophy in Greece and Rome, and it asks for more than patience. Accepting what you cannot change is only the start; the Stoic goal was to welcome it, as if the universe had handed you exactly what you needed. Friedrich Nietzsche gave the attitude its two-word Latin name in the 1880s and praised it as the formula for human greatness.

Zeno and Chrysippus, early Stoics, used the image of a dog tied to a moving cart. The cart rolls on whatever the dog does, so the dog controls only one thing: whether the journey is miserable or pleasant. The wise dog trots along willingly and enjoys the ride, while the foolish one is dragged. Epictetus, a teacher born a slave, used the stage instead. The playwright hands you your role, rich man or beggar, ruler or nobody, and choosing it is someone else's business. Only one thing is truly yours: how well you act the role you are given.

Epictetus summed up his cure for misery in one rule about wanting. People make themselves wretched by insisting that events bend to their wishes. Instead, he said, wish for things to happen exactly as they do happen, and your life will go smoothly; fit your wishes to events, not events to your wishes. The emperor Marcus Aurelius went a step further in his private notebooks. He pictured fate as a loom weaving everything that befalls you into the thread of your life, and he told himself not merely to put up with what it wove but to love it, welcoming each experience with his whole heart.

The difference between love and mere surrender is the core of the idea. Picture two pupils, each ruined by the loss of a fortune. The first shrugs that nothing can be done and bears it; he has simply given up. The second has done something harder: he wills the loss as if he had chosen it himself, turning his desire toward what is. Seneca packed the whole teaching into a line he translated from the Stoic Cleanthes at the end of one of his letters, which says that fate leads those who are willing and drags those who refuse. It is the dog and the cart again, set down as a maxim.

memento-mori-and-premeditatio-malorum.context_blurb:
Two Latin phrases name a pair of linked Stoic exercises: memento mori, "remember that you will die," and premeditatio malorum, "rehearsing misfortunes in advance." Both ask you to call dark pictures into your mind before you need them. Their defenders insisted this was preparation, not gloom, like the drill a soldier runs before battle, and later monks and painters filled whole genres with skulls and hourglasses to keep the habit alive.

Rome's victorious generals rode through the city in a golden chariot while the crowds roared. The Christian writer Tertullian reports that a slave stood behind the general and kept murmuring that he too would die, so that the cheering could not blind him to the plain fact of his own mortality. The former slave Epictetus gave fathers similar advice: when bending to kiss a sleeping son or daughter, tell yourself quietly that tomorrow the child may die. He meant no curse, and the aim was not to numb the father against future grief. The point was to turn careless love into grateful love, since the father holds a treasure he can never truly keep. Hence Epictetus's rule for speech: never say you have lost something you love, but that you have given it back, because it was only ever on loan.

Marcus Aurelius turned the same tool on himself. Most people picture their own death as something far off; Marcus reminded himself that he could leave life right now, and that the closeness of death should steer every word, deed and thought of the present day, with no waiting on a future that may never arrive. Zeno of Citium, who founded Stoicism, had been a rich merchant shipping purple dye until a wreck near Athens swallowed his whole fortune. Stranded in Athens, he drifted into a bookshop, fell for philosophy and never went back to trade, and he later called the shipwreck the most prosperous voyage he ever made. Seneca made the rehearsal physical. He told his young friend Lucilius to live a few days on coarse bread, a straw pallet and rough clothing, then ask himself whether this was really the condition he had dreaded, so that real poverty could never ambush him with terror.

Marcus also punctured pride by setting Alexander the Great, conqueror of the known world, beside the servant who drove his pack-mule. The king and the muleteer both died and came to the same end, which levels every boast of rank. When the Roman colony of Lugdunum, today's Lyons, burned down in a single night, Seneca wrote that the thing which makes a disaster hit hardest is surprise. Strangeness makes any blow heavier, so the wise send their minds forward to meet troubles before they arrive.

Seneca could be severe. When his friend Marullus lost a small child, Seneca sent not soft comfort but a scolding. Loving a child, he argued, gives a father reason for joy that he had the boy at all, and not only for sorrow at his loss. The same rehearsal that braces you for loss can turn grief toward gratitude. It is a demanding view, offered as Seneca's counsel, not as a rule for how anyone must grieve.

the-view-from-above.context_blurb:
Marcus Aurelius was a Stoic philosopher and a Roman emperor who governed through wars, rebellion and plague, often from army camps on the frontier. His private notebook, the Meditations, holds one of the Stoics' sharpest tools for a worry that feels too large to bear: the view from above, an exercise of the imagination that later astronauts would recognize.

Borrowing the idea from Plato, Marcus would picture himself lifted high above the earth, gazing down on the swarming crowds until his own city shrank to a dot and his grievance shrank along with it. He aimed the same zoom at his own pride: gazing at the endless multitudes below, he reminded himself that most of humanity has never heard of him and that today's admirers will soon turn critics, so fame is worth nothing.

Then he pushed the move to its limit, shrinking even the grandest things in the world: Asia and Europe are corners of the universe, Mount Athos is a little clod of earth, and all the sea is a single drop. If the sea is a drop, a human problem is smaller still. The passage ends with the reminder that all things are little, changeable and perishable.

the-obstacle-is-the-way.context_blurb:
Marcus Aurelius ruled the Roman Empire in the second century and kept a private notebook we now call the Meditations. In it he observed that whatever blocks our action ends up advancing it, because the thing standing in our path turns into the path. The modern writer Ryan Holiday made the idea a bestseller, and sports teams took it up as a slogan.

Marcus did not mean that a barrier is secretly a blessing. His move is that the obstacle itself becomes the material you work on. Blocked from one task, you turn to the hard case in front of you and exercise patience on the rude person, ingenuity on the dead end and courage on the danger.

Epictetus, a former slave who became a famous teacher, compared us to a dog tied behind a cart. The dog may strain against the rope and get hauled along, bruised and angry, or it may walk with the cart and look about. Either way it ends up wherever the cart is going. So the obstacle lies in the dog's own resistance: the rope and the cart are beyond its control, but how it meets them is its own choice.

That keeps the idea from becoming mere denial. People are troubled not by events, Epictetus taught, but by their judgments about events. An injured athlete need not pretend the injury is good news. He can meet it as the very workout he has been training for, using patience and nerve on the one hard thing now before him.

cato-the-younger-dying-free.context_blurb:
Cato the Younger was a Roman senator and Stoic of the first century BC, one of the last defenders of the Roman Republic against one-man rule. Even his enemies could not accuse him of taking a bribe. He led the Senate's resistance to Julius Caesar in the civil war, and when Caesar won and offered him a pardon, Cato's response became one of history's most debated acts.

Defeated, and staying at Utica, Cato resolved to die rather than live under Caesar. His family hid his sword; when it was at last returned, he checked that it was sharp and remarked that now he was master of himself, then went back calmly to his book, Plato's dialogue on the soul.

Caesar had hoped to show mercy to Cato, and to be known for it. When he heard of the death, he cried out bitterly that he grudged Cato his death, because Cato had grudged him the sparing of his life. Cato had died precisely so that Caesar could never claim the glory, or the right, of saving him.

Cato's reason, as Plutarch reports it, went deeper than pride or misery. To accept a pardon is to admit that the pardoner had the standing to grant it. Taking the pardon would be admitting Caesar was entitled to decide whether he lived, as though Cato's life belonged to Caesar to return, and Cato would not grant a tyrant that ownership. Later Stoics made him their model: virtue alone is the true good, and integrity could outweigh survival itself.

living-according-to-nature-and-the-cosmo.context_blurb:
"Live according to nature" was the great motto of the Stoics of Athens and later of Rome. The motto is easy to mangle; it never meant "go wild." With it came a bolder claim: understand human nature properly and you discover you belong to something far larger than your own city, the whole human race.

Many people hear the motto as "follow your gut." The Stoics meant nearly the opposite. Each living thing has a nature of its own: a plant's is to grow, and an animal's is impulse and sensation. What sets a human apart from plants and beasts is reason, so living by your nature means living by reason rather than chasing every urge. The second idea began with Diogenes the Cynic, who made his home in a large clay jar. A Greek asked where he came from was expected to name his city, because his city was his whole identity. Diogenes refused to name Sinope and called himself a kosmopolites, a world citizen, the root of our word cosmopolitan.

The Stoic Hierocles pictured your loyalties as rings, with you at the center, your family next, then relatives, neighbors and fellow citizens, and on the outermost ring all of humankind. The work of a good life, he taught, is to draw the outer rings inward until distant people feel more like your own kin. He even offered a trick: call your cousins "brother" and your aunts "mother," because the warmer name trains warmer care. The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius reached the same place in his private notebook. If reason is shared by everyone, he argued, then law is shared too, and if law is shared, every person, peasant or emperor, is a fellow citizen of one world-wide community, the cosmopolis.

Inside the school, Cleanthes taught that following nature meant following the nature of the whole universe. His student Chrysippus, the school's great systematizer, answered that a person must live in agreement with both the universe's nature and his own human nature, because each individual nature is a part of the nature of the whole. That two-part answer became standard Stoic teaching for centuries.

virtue-is-the-only-good.context_blurb:
Virtue is the only good: that is the hard core of Stoic ethics. Much Stoic advice is easy to like, such as separating what you control from what you don't and preparing for setbacks. Beneath it lies a far more demanding claim, that nothing but good character makes a human life good. It deserves to be met at full strength.

Seneca, the Roman Stoic who advised the emperor Nero, said a wise man would rather be honest in chains than wicked in a palace. Fortune can take away health, freedom, wealth and even life, but the only thing truly yours, which no blow of fortune can seize, is your own good character; everything else is only on loan.

The Stoics had a favourite real-life proof. Around 255 BC, in the First Punic War, Carthage captured the Roman general Marcus Regulus and sent him home on his word of honour to plead for an exchange of prisoners. Before the Senate he urged the opposite: refuse the swap, since it would hurt Rome. Then he kept his oath, went back to Carthage and was put to death. Later writers added gruesome details that historians treat as legend, but his choice is the point.

The doctrine does not mean caring about nothing. Health, wealth and good reputation are what the Stoics called preferred indifferents: worth pursuing, but never what makes a life good or bad. Antipater, another Stoic, compared the good life to archery. A gust of wind may blow even a flawless shot aside, so what counts as the archer's success is the skill of his aim and release, not where the arrow ends up.

Why can't wealth or health be the real good? Cicero gave a blunt reason: a completely wicked man can enjoy every one of them in abundance, so owning them cannot be the thing that makes anyone good. The Stoics then pushed the doctrine to its limit. Aristotle's followers held that virtue needs some outward good fortune to make a life happy. The Stoics answered that a good man being tortured on the rack is still fully happy, because his good character alone is enough.

diogenes-of-sinope.context_blurb:
Diogenes of Sinope was a Greek philosopher of the fourth century BC, a contemporary of Plato and Aristotle, and the founder of the Cynic school. He lived rough on the streets of Athens and later Corinth, by choice, and taught through public stunts and acid wisecracks. Most of his stories were collected centuries after his death, so his life and his legend are tangled, but the point beneath the showmanship is clear.

He slept in a pithos, a huge clay wine jar, out in the marketplace of Athens; the famous barrel is a later mistranslation, since barrels did not yet exist. He owned almost nothing on purpose, to prove by living it that a good life needs very little and that chasing more only wastes your effort. When Alexander the Great, the young conqueror of half the known world, found him lying in the sun and offered him anything he wished, Diogenes asked only that the king move aside, because he was standing in his light.

A free man wants nothing a king can give. Walking away, Alexander told his startled followers that if he were not Alexander, he would wish to be Diogenes. Other stunts drove the same point home. Diogenes carried a lit lamp through the crowded market in broad daylight, peering into face after face, and said he was looking for a man, meaning that among all those people he could not find one living as a true human being should; the honest-man version is a later embellishment. Once he saw a boy drink from a stream out of his hands and threw away his wooden cup, his last possession, because the child had shown that even a cup was one thing more than he needed. When a vain rich man showing off his gilded house warned him not to spit on the floor, Diogenes spat in the man's face, explaining that nothing else in the house was filthy enough.

His targets included philosophers. Plato had defined a human as a featherless two-legged animal, so Diogenes plucked a chicken and presented it as Plato's man. The definition fit the bird perfectly yet captured nothing real about people, and Plato had to tack on broad, flat nails. Seized by pirates and put up for sale as a slave, Diogenes told the auctioneer that his trade was governing men and pointed to a rich buyer, Xeniades, who he said needed a master. Even in chains, he claimed, no owner could touch the freedom inside his mind. He ate and slept in the open marketplace, reasoning that an act which is not shameful in private cannot become shameful because the public watches. Plato summed him up as a Socrates gone mad: he chased the same examined, virtuous life as Socrates, but by outrageous, shameless public stunts instead of polite questions.

People threw the word dog at him as an insult, and from kynikos, dog-like, comes the word Cynic. He wore it proudly, because a dog follows nature openly and feels no false shame before anyone; he said a dog fawns on those who feed it, barks at those who refuse, and bites scoundrels. Legend adds that an oracle once told him to deface the currency. He had in fact been exiled from Sinope for spoiling its coins, and he made the command his life's program: strike down a society's counterfeit values the way a mint cancels a bad coin.

diogenes-defacing-of-convention.context_blurb:
Diogenes of Sinope, a Greek of the fourth century BC, founded the Cynic school and ranks among the great disruptors of Western thought. Instead of writing treatises, he staged public stunts aimed at what ordinary Athenians and Corinthians assumed a decent life must look like. The stunts seem crude at first glance, but each one carries a precise argument.

Athenians called him the Dog, and the word Cynic comes from kynikos, dog-like. Asked about the name, he embraced it with a three-part boast: like a good dog, he fawned on people who gave him something, yapped at people who refused, and sank his teeth into scoundrels. He also did in the crowded marketplace what everyone agreed was perfectly fine indoors and out of sight. His argument was that if an act is not shameful in private, doing it in public cannot make it shameful, so the shame comes from custom and not from nature. The claim was his own, and it was meant to scandalize.

He went after philosophers too. Plato had won applause for defining a human being as a two-legged animal without feathers. Diogenes plucked a chicken bald, dropped the bird in front of Plato's students and announced that here was Plato's man. The joke was an argument: a neat list of outward features fit a plucked fowl perfectly, so it had never grasped what a person actually is. His whole life ran on a pun about money. He had been exiled from Sinope for tampering with the city's coinage, and he turned the crime into his motto, defacing the currency. In Greek the word for coin shares its root with the word for custom, so restamping bad coin became restamping bad convention, striking out the counterfeit values a society circulates as if they were the real thing.

Crowds cheered these shows, and Diogenes saw the catch. He called himself a hound of the kind all men praise, yet not one of his admirers dared go out hunting beside him: they applauded the man who exposed false convention, but none would share that bare, exposed life with him. Plato, meanwhile, repaired his definition by adding broad, flat nails. Diogenes pounced on the patch itself. If a definition can be mended by bolting on one more trait, there is no point at which such a list is ever finished, so it is an open-ended tally of outer features rather than a grasp of what a human being is.

antisthenes-and-the-birth-of-cynicism.context_blurb:
Antisthenes was an Athenian philosopher of the late 400s and early 300s BC and one of Socrates' most devoted students, a classmate of Plato. He decided that the hard parts of Socrates' life, the toughness, the rough living and the owning of almost nothing, were not side details but the whole point. The Cynic school traces itself to him.

Antisthenes once shocked Athens by declaring he would rather go mad than feel pleasure. He did not deny that pleasant things feel good. His worry was that chasing pleasure makes it your master: it enslaves you and wears away the self-sufficiency that real freedom depends on. So he lived needing almost nothing. He was the first to fold his cloak double, wear it as his only garment and sleep in it, and to carry a staff and a beggar's wallet, a kit that became the uniform of every Cynic for centuries.

Even poverty can be worn for show. Antisthenes once turned his torn cloak so that everyone could see the holes, and Socrates was not impressed: through those holes, he said, he could see Antisthenes' love of fame peeping out. Rags displayed to win admiration are just vanity in another costume.

Antisthenes also mocked Plato, who held that beyond our world stands a perfect Form of horseness, of which every real horse is a copy. Antisthenes answered that he could see a horse well enough, but never horseness. His point was that only particular, concrete things are real: this horse in front of you exists, while horseness is a mere word, not a thing in some other world. Aristotle recorded the view, and philosophers still argue about it.

His deepest legacy was ethical. He held that virtue alone is enough for a happy life, needing nothing but the strength of a Socrates, while wealth, fame and comfort can all be done without. That idea passed from him to Diogenes of Sinope, from Diogenes to Crates, and from Crates to Zeno, who founded the Stoics around 300 BC and made it the heart of Stoic ethics. That is why Antisthenes is sometimes called the grandfather of Stoicism.

crates-and-hipparchia.context_blurb:
Crates of Thebes was a Greek philosopher of the fourth century BC and the best-known pupil of Diogenes, the Cynic who taught that a good life needs almost nothing. Where Diogenes was harsh and provoking, Crates was gentle, witty and widely loved. His story is bound up with Hipparchia of Maroneia, a well-born young woman whose choice made her one of the earliest named women philosophers of the West.

Crates was born to great wealth in Thebes, and he opened his life as a philosopher with a grand gesture. He turned his inheritance into money and shared the whole sum out among the people of Thebes, by one account about 200 talents, then lived as a beggar who owned only a cloak and a knapsack. Hipparchia, courted by rich and handsome men, fell instead for this older, famously ugly, penniless thinker and his teaching. When her parents refused the match, she swore she would take her own life if they kept her from him, and they gave way.

In Athens Crates earned the nickname Door-opener, because he walked uninvited into any house he liked, and families were glad to see him. Once inside, he settled their quarrels and gave counsel, patching up relatives who had fallen out.

Hipparchia's parents had even begged Crates to talk her out of the marriage. When he failed, he stood up, threw off every stitch before her and pointed to his naked body and his shabby cloak: here was the bridegroom, and here was everything he owned. He was making her choose the hard Cynic life itself, with nothing softened or hidden, since she could be no partner of his unless she shared his way of living. She chose him. Crates showed the same indifference to comfort before a conqueror. Alexander the Great had razed Thebes in 335 BC, and he later offered to rebuild it for its most famous son. Crates refused, reasoning that whatever Alexander put back up, some later conqueror would simply knock down once more. Poverty and obscurity, he wrote in a verse, were a wise man's true country.

Hipparchia argued as an equal. At the banquet of Lysimachus, Theodorus, a fellow thinker, scoffed that a woman had no business matching wits with men, and she replied with a chain of logic. Anything Theodorus may do without blame, she may do without blame; Theodorus may hit himself without blame; therefore she may hit Theodorus without blame. Because the argument was valid, the only way to escape its conclusion was to throw out a premise he had already granted. Theodorus found no answer and instead tugged at her cloak to shame her.

the-cynic-idea-live-according-to-nature.context_blurb:
The Cynics followed a few famous Greek teachers, above all Diogenes, who made his home in a big clay jar in Athens and spent his days deflating everyone's pretensions. Their stunts and one-liners all argue one thing: most of what people chase is fake, and the free life lies in giving nearly all of it up.

Diogenes owned almost nothing but a wooden cup, and when he saw a boy drink from a stream with his cupped hands, he threw the cup away, because each desire he shed was one less handle fortune had on him. When Alexander the Great came and offered him any gift he liked, Diogenes asked only that the king step aside, because he was blocking the sun. Walking off, Alexander told his laughing courtiers that if he were not Alexander, he would wish to be Diogenes. Another bright morning Diogenes carried a lit lamp through the marketplace, peering into faces, and said he was searching for a real, honest human being, because among people chasing money and status he could hardly find one living a rational, natural life.

When Plato's students boasted that man is a two-legged animal without feathers, Diogenes answered with a prop instead of an argument: he plucked a chicken and let it loose in the school, announcing, "Behold, Plato's human being!" The scholars had to add "with broad flat nails" to their definition. Asked which city he came from, he refused the local loyalty every Greek was expected to have and called himself a kosmopolites, a citizen of the world, the birth of the word cosmopolitan. He trained himself on purpose, hugging snow-covered bronze in winter and rolling in scorching sand in summer. He also begged coins from a stone statue again and again, because he was rehearsing refusal, so that when a real person turned him down it would no longer sting.

The name Cynic means dog-like and began as an insult, but Diogenes embraced it, holding that a stray dog lives more honestly than most civilized people: it eats whatever it finds, sleeps wherever it lies down, and never blushes over its own body. To a Cynic, a thing that is not wrong at home does not become wrong in the public square; the blush is custom, not nature.

Diogenes had been banished from his birthplace after a coin-tampering scandal, and he turned that very crime into his motto: deface the currency. The Greek word nomisma meant both coin and custom, so the slogan became his whole program: unmask society's most trusted customs as counterfeits, the way a forger's coin is exposed as fake. His creed in one line was "to fortune oppose courage, to convention nature, to passion reason." His pupil Crates taught Zeno, who carried the call to live according to nature into Stoicism.

epicurus-and-the-garden.context_blurb:
Epicurus was a Greek philosopher of the late fourth and early third centuries BC who taught in a walled garden outside Athens. He is a victim of word drift: today epicurean means a lover of rich food, yet the man had famously plain tastes and firm views about which pleasures are worth chasing. His school, called the Garden, was known for whom it let in and for the quiet happiness it taught.

The proud schools of Athens kept their doors narrow. Plato's Academy trained mostly the sons of the Athenian elite, and Aristotle tutored young nobles. The Garden admitted women and slaves as equals, so noblewomen, courtesans and slaves argued philosophy side by side; two women remembered by name are Leontion and Themista. A slave named Mys, whose name meant Mouse, studied beside the free students, and in his will Epicurus set him free, along with several other slaves of the household. The founder himself lived simply. He said he was content with bread and water, and when he wanted a feast he asked a friend to send him a pot of cheese.

So what did he mean by pleasure, which he called the highest good? Not banquets and parties, as his rivals claimed. The steadiest pleasure, he taught, is freedom from every pain and every fear: aponia, no pain in the body, and ataraxia, no turmoil in the mind. Among the greatest goods he ranked close friends, and he said that what matters most is less the help friends give than the sure trust that they would help if trouble came. Friendship, he wrote, dances around the world, calling every one of us to wake up to happiness. The motto of his school, lathe biosas, told students to live unnoticed, staying out of politics and the scramble for fame. He even reasoned away the fear of dying. As long as you exist, death is absent, and when death comes, you are no longer there to feel it, so death can never hurt you.

He met his own death that way. On his final day, in agony from a blocked kidney, he wrote to Idomeneus that this was a blissful day, because the glad memory of conversations he had shared with his friends outweighed all the torment in his body. In the same letter he asked his friend to look after the children of the late Metrodorus. Later followers boiled his teaching into a four-part cure, the tetrapharmakos, that students memorized like a doctor's remedy: no fear of the gods, no worry about death, the good is easy to obtain, and the terrible is easy to endure. One copy survived on a charred scroll by Philodemus at Herculaneum, the Roman town that the volcano Vesuvius buried in ash in AD 79.

ataraxia-and-the-limits-of-desire.context_blurb:
Ataraxia is the Greek word for a settled calm, a mind free of worry, and the Athenian philosopher Epicurus made it the real goal of life. His school put pleasure first, which earned him a reputation for feasting. In fact his idea of pleasure was strikingly plain: a body without pain and a mind without fear, reached by sorting your wants and dropping the ones that can never be filled.

Epicurus watched men with full tables and sound roofs still feel poor. His diagnosis fit in one line: nothing is enough for the man who has decided that enough is too little. Once a person judges a fair supply to be too small, no fortune can satisfy him, because the trouble lives in the wanting, not the having. Of everything wisdom can win for a happy life, he ranked one far above the rest: a true friend. And he praised simple food for what it does to the rest of your life. A man content with bread and water cannot be ruined by losing a fortune, so his simple habits make him free and fearless whatever happens, while the man who needs luxury is a hostage to luck.

His master tool was a pair of questions asked of every want: does it come from nature, and do you truly need it? Hunger for food passes both tests. The dangerous kind, the empty wants such as fame, statues and endless money, is neither natural nor necessary, born of groundless opinion. Such cravings can never be filled, because they have no natural stopping point. Hunger ends when you have eaten, but the wealth of vain fancies, he wrote, recedes to an infinite distance, so there is always more to want. That is why the sign over his garden gate, promising that pleasure was the highest good, came with a joke, as the Roman writer Seneca told it. The guest who walked in expecting a feast was served barley porridge and water.

Epicurus also explained why a king's feast gives no more pleasure than a poor friend's bread once both men have eaten their fill. When the pain of hunger is gone, bodily pleasure cannot grow any larger; the king's dozen courses only vary it, changing its flavor but not its amount. He did not condemn the hunt for riches as wicked, but he named its hidden price. Great wealth can scarcely be won without becoming a servant of crowds or politicians, so the man who piles it up pays with his freedom, the very thing a calm life most needs.

His own death tested the teaching. When it came for him around 270 BC, a bladder stone and dysentery brought pain he said could not have been worse, yet he named it a happy day. In a last letter to his friend Idomeneus he explained why: remembering, with joy, the philosophical talks he had shared with friends balanced every agony of the body. The calm mind he had taught held to the end.

death-is-nothing-to-us.context_blurb:
"Death is nothing to us" is one of the most quoted lines of Epicurus, the Greek philosopher of the fourth and third centuries BC. With it he tried to cure the fear of death by reasoning alone, with no promise of an afterlife and no heroic distraction. The argument is cleaner than most people expect, and for more than two thousand years philosophers have argued over whether it actually works.

Epicurus reached calm by an unusual route. You and your death never meet, he argued: while you are alive, death has not yet arrived, and once it arrives, you are no longer there, so it never touches anyone at all. The Roman poet Lucretius gave the idea its most vivid picture. An eternity passed before you were born, and you never lost a moment of sleep over it. That stretch, he said, is a mirror held up to the matching eternity after you die, which is the very nonexistence you now dread.

Two premises sit beneath the slogan. First, everything good or bad is something felt, and death puts an end to every sensation, so a thing you can never feel can be neither good nor bad for you. Second, Epicurus held that the soul is itself a cluster of atoms, as physical as a stone. At death those soul-atoms fly apart and can no longer feel anything, so no self survives to be rewarded or punished, and the calm rests on physics, not on hope. Lucretius dramatized the lesson. In his poem, Nature herself scolds a man who weeps that he must die: he has enjoyed a full life, so why hang on at the table pleading for second helpings of the same dishes? He should leave like a dinner guest who has eaten his fill and go to his rest content.

The sharpest reply came in 1970, in Thomas Nagel's essay Death. Nagel attacked the premise that what you never feel cannot harm you. A friend who betrays you in secret wrongs you even if you never find out, so a harm need not be a sensation. Death is bad, he argued, because it robs you of all the good things your future would otherwise have held. He also argued that Lucretius's mirror is cracked. It makes sense to picture you yourself living on for extra years, but a baby born decades earlier would not have been you at all, only a different person, so a late birth costs you nothing while an early death does. In his 1984 book Reasons and Persons, Derek Parfit probed why the mirror feels wrong. A patient wakes with amnesia and learns that either he already went through ten hours of agony in surgery yesterday, or he faces one hour of it today. Nearly everyone would choose to be the patient whose ten hours are behind him. We care far more about suffering ahead than about identical suffering behind, which is why the eternity ahead frightens us and the one behind does not. Parfit judged that bias irrational but almost universal, and whether Epicurus or his critics have the better case remains open.

the-tetrapharmakos-the-four-part-cure.context_blurb:
The tetrapharmakos, Greek for four-part cure, is a four-line summary of the teaching of the Greek philosopher Epicurus, memorised by his followers to calm an anxious mind. Its lines say that the gods are not to be feared, death is nothing to fear, the good is easy to get, and what is terrible can be borne.

The name was borrowed from the pharmacy. Long before the philosophers took it up, a tetrapharmakos was a real wound salve made of beeswax, pine resin, pitch and animal fat, smeared on open cuts. The Epicureans offered four sentences as an ointment for the soul.

Epicurus was no atheist; he held that the gods truly exist. But a god perfectly happy and indestructible is troubled by nothing, so it feels no anger and punishes no one, and there is nothing to dread.

Death is no threat either. While you live, death is absent, and once death arrives, you are gone and feel nothing. Epicurus packed this into one line: while I am here, death is not, and when death has come, I am no more.

Pain, he claimed, has a built-in limit. Intense pain burns out quickly, and pain that lasts a long time stays mild, so no suffering is both unbearable and endless.
