lucretius-and-the-swerve.context_blurb:
Titus Lucretius Carus was a Roman poet of the first century BCE who poured the philosophy of Epicurus, already centuries old and fading, into one long Latin poem, On the Nature of Things. It argues that everything, the soul included, is tiny particles in empty space, and that grasping this frees a person from two ancient fears: of meddling gods and of punishment after death.

Lucretius explained his verse with a doctor's trick. A doctor who wants a feverish child to take bitter wormwood first coats the edge of the cup with honey. The hard Epicurean teaching is the medicine, and his beautiful poetry is the honey, the lure that gets the lesson swallowed. He also retold the death of Iphigenia, whom her father King Agamemnon let the priests kill at the altar so the Greek fleet could sail for Troy. Lucretius capped the scene with a famous line laying the whole horror on religious fear, which can persuade people into monstrous deeds; in his view superstition, not true piety, did the killing.

Lucretius reasoned his way to atoms nearly two thousand years before the microscope. He began from one rule: nothing is ever created out of nothing, and nothing ever vanishes into nothing. It follows that the world's smallest building blocks can never be destroyed and must always have existed.

The soul, he argued, is made of atoms too, fine particles woven all through the living body. So when the body dissolves at death the soul's atoms scatter with it, and no one is left to suffer anything at all; death, he wrote, is nothing to us. In his universe atoms rain straight down through the void, all at the same speed. Into that steady fall he added the swerve: at random moments and random spots, an atom veers a hair's breadth aside. Without that veer, atoms falling side by side would never meet or collide, so they could never clump together into any world.

The swerve had a second job. Suppose every atom moved only when the atom behind it pushed, in one unbroken chain; then every act you will ever perform was fixed at the start of time, which is fate with no room for free will. The swerve breaks the chain with a touch of real chance, so the future is not wholly settled in advance and a living creature can begin a motion of its own. In Lucretius's phrase, it snaps the bonds of fate. Critics have objected ever since that a random veer might make actions accidental rather than chosen, and the free-will dispute remains open.

confucius-kongzi-and-the-analects.context_blurb:
Confucius, called Kongzi or Master Kong in his own language, taught in the small Chinese state of Lu around 500 BC. In his lifetime the old Zhou order was cracking into rival states, and he spent years trying to persuade their rulers to govern well. He died believing he had failed, yet his remembered sayings shaped China for more than two thousand years.

His advice to learners was a matter of balance. Learning that is never thought through is labour lost, he warned, while thinking with no learning beneath it is perilous. Facts memorized without reflection lie dead, and reasoning with nothing solid underneath drifts into nonsense. He also said that walking with any two companions, he could find a teacher. He would copy what was good in them and steer away from what was bad, so even a poor example taught him something.

His disciple Zigong once asked for a single word to live by. Confucius offered shu, reciprocity, and unfolded it as a plain rule: never do to others what you would hate to have done to you. It is the Golden Rule in a careful negative form, given centuries before the Christian version. Confucius never wrote a book. He taught by talking, and after his death his pupils gathered the sayings and short conversations they remembered into the Analects. That is why nearly every passage opens with the same three words, "The Master said," one remembered voice repeated line after line. His beginnings were humble. He lost his father at about age three, his mother raised him poor, and his first jobs were lowly clerk's posts, keeping the accounts of grain stores and the records of farm animals; the later philosopher Mencius calls him a Foodstuffs Scribe.

He had little patience for idle speculation. When a student pressed him about serving the ghosts of ancestors and about what follows death, Confucius turned the matter around: a man who does not yet understand life is in no position to understand death, so master the duties of this life first. Yet beauty could overwhelm him. In the state of Qi he heard the Shao, an old piece of ritual music, and was so moved that for three months he did not notice the taste of meat. He treated music as moral training, not mere amusement.

His one real chance at power came in Lu, where he held office and meant to set the state right. Neighbouring Qi feared a strong, well-run Lu and sent a gift designed to rot the court: a troupe of dancing girls, chosen for their beauty. The chief minister Ji Huan took them in, the duke held no court for three days, and Confucius judged the place hopeless and left, around 498 BC. For years he wandered through Wei and Song, Chen, Cai and Chu, searching for a ruler willing to govern by his teaching, and he never found one. Between Chen and Cai his band ran out of food, and his blunt disciple Zilu demanded whether even a superior man had to suffer like this. Confucius answered that the superior man may have to endure want, but he bears it without breaking, while a lesser man in want throws off all restraint. Hardship does not spare good character; it reveals it.

Then came grief. His favourite student, Yan Hui, a poor, modest and brilliant young man, died at about twenty-nine, and the old master wept without restraint. When others said his mourning went too far, he asked whom he should ever mourn bitterly, if not a man like this.

ren-humaneness.context_blurb:
Ren is the Chinese word for the highest virtue in the sayings of Confucius, and no English word captures it cleanly: humaneness, benevolence and co-humanity have all been tried. Ren pulls the lesser virtues, loyalty, propriety, courage and honesty, into working order. Confucius almost never defined it. He answered questions about it with small scenes that came out differently each time, as though a student had to learn to recognize it rather than memorize a formula.

When Confucius returned from court and heard that his stables had burned, he faced a costly loss, since horses were worth a small fortune and the grooms were humble servants. Yet his first question was "Was anyone hurt?" He did not ask about the horses, because humaneness puts people above property. His favorite student, Yan Hui, lived in a shabby back alley on a little rice and water, in poverty others could not have borne, yet nothing ever dimmed his joy, and Confucius praised him twice over for it. When the disciple Zhonggong asked for one rule to practice toward everyone, every day, Confucius framed it as a thing to avoid: never impose on another what you would hate to have done to you. Scholars call it his silver rule, the Golden Rule stated in the negative.

The humane person shows himself when he wants to get ahead. Wishing to rise, he raises others along with himself, and wishing to succeed, he helps others succeed. Pressed by Yan Hui on the road to humaneness, Confucius answered in two parts: master your own selfishness, then go back to right conduct. Manage it for one day, he said, and everyone under heaven would turn to goodness, and the work depends on you, not on anyone else. Humaneness can cost a life. A person of high ideals will not cling to life at the price of betraying what is right, Confucius taught, and sometimes he will die rather than live on dishonored.

The disciple Zigong tried to raise humaneness to its peak: surely a man who enriched all the people and saved the masses from misery would be humane? Confucius reset the scale. Such a world-saving deed would stand far above humaneness, he said, at the height of a sage, a rare level that even the legendary sage-kings Yao and Shun would find hard to reach. Humaneness itself is the reachable, everyday virtue.

li-ritual-propriety.context_blurb:
Li is the Confucian word for the right forms of conduct: the manners, ceremonies, greetings and rituals by which civilized people treat one another. It can sound like mere etiquette, a matter of which fork to use. Confucius, the teacher of ancient China whose sayings fill the Analects, took this everyday stuff seriously as moral training, because small rites done well slowly shape the kind of adult a person becomes.

Is feeding your aged parents enough? Confucius said no, since people feed their dogs and horses too. What separates honoring a parent from keeping livestock is the reverence in the way you serve, the respectful manner that carries a love the food alone cannot. Form and feeling belong together. That is why three men disgusted him: an official who handed out rations strictly by the book, a mourner who made every proper gesture of grief, and a leader who finished the whole ceremony. His complaint was not that they were showing off. Each went through the outward motions while the feeling the rite should carry, the reverence or the sorrow, had died inside him.

Watching people lavish money on ceremonial gifts, Confucius burst out that ritual must be more than jade and silk, and music more than bells and drums. The meaning of a rite lives in the reverence of the person performing it and the care with which the act is done, not in the costly objects. Rites also discipline good qualities. Caution with no ritual to guide it sours into timidity, frankness turns hurtful, and boldness erupts into disorder. Ritual, the proper ways of acting, channels a virtue so that it lands rightly, as courage rather than recklessness.

Once his student Zixia quoted a love poem about a pretty, dimpled smile, and Confucius answered that the painting is laid on only after the plain silk is ready. Zixia caught the point and asked whether ritual, too, comes afterward. Real feeling and character come first, like the plain silk, and ritual follows to give that feeling a fitting form; it decorates genuine feeling and can never manufacture it. Confucius was delighted. Meeting his son Boyu crossing the courtyard, Confucius asked whether the boy had studied ritual yet, and warned that without it a person has no ground on which to take his stand. Ritual is the footing that lets a person hold steady and act rightly when a situation is murky and no rule spells out what to do.

the-confucian-golden-rule-negative-form.context_blurb:
The Golden Rule, treat others as you would be treated, has been rediscovered again and again across the ancient world. Western readers know it from Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount. The Chinese teacher Confucius, who lived from 551 to 479 BCE, taught a version with one small change of wording, and that change carves out a slightly different ethic. Thinkers still argue over which form is better.

Confucius gathered his teaching into one word, shu, and spelled it out: never do to others what you would hate to have done to you. A boy who hates his sister reading his notebook, and who then finds her diary lying open, has his answer: he leaves it shut, because he would hate the same thing done to him. The rule is a restraint. It tells you what harm to hold back from, but it never orders you out to perform some good deed, which is why some call it the Silver Rule. Confucius taught it about five hundred years before Jesus gave the positive form recorded in Matthew. In between, the Jewish sage Hillel taught a negative version of his own.

The rule sounds simple, but living it is hard. When his quick-tongued student Zigong boasted of having mastered it, Confucius replied, calling him by his personal name, Si, that this was something still far beyond him. Another student, Zengzi, said the Master's whole Way ran on one thread of two ideas. Shu holds you back from harm. Its partner, zhong, is the giving side: to offer others your whole self and do your utmost to help and serve them.

Critics such as Jan Tullberg say the negative rule falls short in one case, when someone has already wronged you. It lets you simply walk away without harming him. The rule Jesus gave asks more, because it requires you to go out of your way to do that wrongdoer an active kindness. Defenders answer that "first, do no harm" is exactly the right place to start, and the debate stays open.

filial-piety-xiao.context_blurb:
Filial piety, xiao in Chinese, is the Confucian virtue of honoring one's parents, elders and ancestors. For some two and a half thousand years the Confucian tradition has treated it as the root from which the other virtues grow, the place where a young person first learns to care for someone else. Later China filled whole books with legends of devoted children, and readers find them inspiring, melodramatic or unsettling by turns.

The most famous collection, The Twenty-four Filial Exemplars, compiled by Guo Jujing, is full of extravagant devotion. A boy named Wang Xiang has a stepmother who dislikes him, yet when she longs for fresh fish in midwinter, he stretches out on the frozen river so his body heat will thaw it, and two carp spring out of the water to him. The duty to a parent does not depend on the parent deserving it. Lao Laizi, already about seventy, sees that his even older parents are saddened by his gray hair, so he puts on a child's brightly colored clothes and rolls around playing with toys like an infant. In these tales, filial piety means guarding a parent's happiness, not just meeting needs.

Confucius himself, around 500 BC, insisted that care alone is not enough. When his student Ziyou took filial piety to mean feeding one's parents, Confucius pointed out that even dogs and horses get fed. What turns care into honor is reverence, real respect felt from within. Legend's hardest case is the sage-emperor Shun, whose blind father and stepmother plotted his death over and over. He kept on loving them, and the story says Heaven rewarded him: wild elephants arrived to drag his plow and flocks of birds to weed his crops.

Confucius taught his pupil Zengzi that every virtue springs from a single root, and the Classic of Filial Piety makes the point plain: the respect a child first learns toward his own mother and father is where virtue takes root, before law, study or friendship. When his disciple Zai Wo argued that one year of mourning for a dead parent was plenty, not three, Confucius pointed to infancy. For its first three years a child lives in its parents' arms, so three years of grief repays three years of being carried.

The sharpest test is a clash with public duty. The Duke of She bragged about a man in his realm, Gong, who gave evidence that his father had stolen a sheep. Confucius did not praise him. In his own country, he replied, uprightness lies in a father who covers for his son's misdeeds and a son who covers for his father's, because the bond between parent and child is part of uprightness, not its enemy. Whether family loyalty can outweigh a public duty is still argued.

the-junzi-the-cultivated-person.context_blurb:
In Confucius's day the Chinese word junzi meant a lord's son, a nobleman by birth. Confucius took the word apart and gave it a radical new meaning: a fully grown human being whose character has been shaped, by patient practice over years, into something steady, honest and generous. Again and again he set the junzi against the xiaoren, the small or petty person, who may hold wealth or office but has never done the inner work.

The difference shows in the first question each man asks. Offered a chance of easy money, the junzi asks whether it is right, while the petty man asks what he will gain. When a plan falls apart, the junzi turns his eyes on himself, asking where he fell short, while the petty man looks around for someone else to blame. Through hard times the junzi remains calm and composed, unhurried and broad of spirit, while the petty man frets without end.

Confucius's quiet revolution was in who could qualify. A junzi was no longer made by bloodline; anyone of any birth could become one by cultivating his own character, which later scholars called an aristocracy of merit. Such a person leads by example rather than terror. When a ruler asked about putting wicked men to death to frighten the rest into goodness, Confucius told him to become good himself, because the character of those above is like the wind and that of the people like grass, which bends whichever way the wind blows.

A junzi draws out the best in others and helps it come to completion, while the petty man feeds their worst. He carries himself with dignity and ease, but without arrogance; the petty man has arrogance without ease. In a group making a hard decision, both men may nod along, but only the junzi builds real harmony: he says plainly where he still disagrees and works with the others anyway, while the petty man simply echoes the room. Confucius added one more test. The junzi may not show himself in small matters, but you may hand him your weightiest responsibility. The petty man may do well at little tasks but cannot be trusted with anything that truly matters.

the-rectification-of-names.context_blurb:
Around 500 BC the Chinese sage Confucius made a strange-sounding claim: a healthy state begins with getting names right. The Chinese term is zhengming, the rectification of names. A role-name such as ruler, minister, father or son is really a job description. It carries duties inside it, and when the word and the reality drift apart, something worse than a vocabulary problem follows.

Imagine a man who no longer provides for, guides or shields his children, yet still goes by the name of their father. In Confucius's eyes he has not merely failed in private. He has made his own title false: he keeps the name and abandons the duties it pledges.

So when his disciple Zilu asked what he would do first if he were handed a state to govern, Confucius surprised everyone. Before armies or treasuries, his first task would be to correct the names, so that every title fits the duties it really carries. He did not mean editing a dictionary. The fix is to change the man to fit his name, not the name to fit the man: each person must live up to the title he already holds, starting with the ruler himself.

Confucius told Duke Jing of Qi that good government means each man truly being what his title names, from ruler and minister down to father and son. Delighted, the duke added a grim joke of his own. If the names came undone, though his granaries overflowed, he might not get to eat his own supper, because the whole order that grows, gathers and serves his food would collapse.

Confucius once held a gu, a bronze ritual wine-cup prized for its sharp corners. This one had been worn smooth, yet it kept its name, and he exclaimed that it was a gu that was no gu at all. He was really mourning a ruler who keeps the title after losing everything that made him a ruler.

Confucius's idea was tested by real events in Wei, the very state Zilu had asked about. Kuaikui, the heir of Wei, had been banished, and at the old duke's death the crown went to Kuaikui's son instead, so a father and a son each claimed to be the one true ruler. On Confucius's logic, when one name is claimed by two men, the name is at war with itself, and the men who hold it must go to war too. In 480 BC Kuaikui came back by force and threw out his own son, and Zilu was killed in the upheaval.

the-five-relationships-and-social-harmon.context_blurb:
Confucius, the great teacher of ancient China who lived around 500 BC, taught that human life is lived inside a handful of basic bonds. His followers listed five of them, the wulun, and claimed that a society in order is simply those five bonds in order. Every bond carries duties running both ways, and readers still argue over how much of this hierarchical, but not merely authoritarian, scheme fits a society of equals.

The five bonds pair a parent with a child, a ruler with a subject, a husband with a wife, an older with a younger sibling, and one friend with another. Harmony, the Confucians claimed, follows when each side of each bond does its part, and it starts at home. Confucius's student Youzi observed that a person gentle toward his father, mother and elder brothers is seldom the one who rises against his rulers. He called that family devotion the root from which humaneness grows.

People often hear these bonds as pure obedience flowing upward, but an ancient text, the Book of Rites, lists ten matched duties that bind the superior too. A son owes devotion to his father, and the father in turn owes the son kindness and care; the ruler owes benevolence, and the subject owes loyalty. When Duke Jing of Qi asked about good government, Confucius told him that a ruler must truly rule and a father truly be a father, and likewise for subject and son. Order comes when each person really does what his role demands, not when he merely holds the title.

The philosopher Mencius pressed the two-way point on King Xuan of Qi. A minister, he said, mirrors back his ruler's regard. Handle ministers like livestock and they will think of you as a stranger; trample them like weeds and they will think of you as a bandit and a foe. A prince who values his ministers like his own hands and feet, though, will be cherished by them like their own belly and heart. Mencius also gave each bond its guiding virtue: affection between father and son, righteousness between ruler and minister, order between old and young, faithfulness between friends. Husband and wife alone he marked by distinction, attention to their separate functions, by custom the wife ruling inside the home and the husband outside it.

mencius-human-nature-is-good.context_blurb:
Mencius, or Mengzi, "Master Meng," was a Chinese philosopher of the fourth century BCE and the most important follower of Confucius in the generations after the master died. He armed Confucius's teaching with one bold argument, that human nature is good, and his vivid thought experiments still make readers notice something in themselves. His great rival within the tradition, Xunzi, held the opposite.

Legends about his boyhood are lessons about growth. His mother first lived beside a graveyard, and little Mencius played at funerals; when she moved near the marketplace, he imitated the merchants. Only when she moved next to a school did he take to his books, so there she stayed, because a child grows into whatever surrounds him. Once he skipped his lessons, and without a word she took her scissors and cut through the cloth on her loom. Giving up on study halfway, she meant, wastes all the work already done, just like a half-woven cloth cut loose. Mencius told his own growth story, about a farmer of Song who thought his rice was too slow and tugged every shoot upward to help it along. He went home proud of himself, but every plant he had helped soon withered and died. Virtue, like a sprout, cannot be forced.

His most famous thought experiment asks you to imagine anyone who suddenly sees a toddler about to tumble into a well. Before thinking at all, that person feels a jolt of alarm and pity. Mencius took the instant pang as proof that goodness is already inside us, since nobody chose it or learned it. Yet the pang is not a finished virtue. Mencius compared it to a sprout just pushing up through the soil, real but tiny, which must be watered and sheltered the way a farmer tends a shoot through a whole season before it becomes a dependable plant.

He stripped away every selfish explanation of that pang. The onlooker is not trying to win the parents' favor, earn the neighbors' praise or escape being called heartless, and since no reward explains the feeling, it must be native to the heart. He counted four such sprouts: compassion grows into benevolence, shame into righteousness, the urge to defer into propriety, and the sense that tells right from wrong into wisdom. People have these four as surely as they have four limbs, so a man who claims he simply cannot feel compassion or shame is not handicapped; he is stealing from himself something he already owns. The politics followed. If people are good by birth, a cruel tyrant betrays both his own nature and theirs, and Mencius ranked the realm bluntly: the common people come first in worth, and the ruler last.

Mencius defended his view against rivals. Gaozi said human nature is like water: open a ditch eastward and the water runs east, open one westward and it runs west, so nature leans neither way. Mencius agreed that water does not care about east or west, but it does care about up and down: it always flows downward, wherever you dig, and human nature leans toward good the same way. Gaozi tried again, calling nature a willow and morality the cups a craftsman carves from it. You must hack a willow to make cups, Mencius replied, and a doctrine that makes goodness mean hacking at people would set the whole world to wrecking what is naturally human. To those who point at a truly wicked man as proof that people are not good at all, he told of Ox Mountain. Axes felled its lovely woods, and herds of cattle and sheep nibbled away each fresh shoot, until people who saw the bald slopes assumed no forest had ever grown there. A wicked man is a stripped mountain, his goodness worn away rather than missing from the start. Against Yang Zhu, who taught each man to look out for himself, and Mozi, who taught equal love for all, Mencius held that real virtue grows from cultivating the moral seeds that each of us carries from birth.

xunzi-human-nature-is-crooked.context_blurb:
Xunzi, Master Xun, was a Chinese Confucian philosopher of the third century BC and the great rival of Mencius inside the Confucian school. Mencius held that human nature is good, with small sprouts of virtue that need only shelter to grow. Xunzi held that human nature is crooked and must be straightened. The quarrel is still unsettled, and Xunzi deserves a hearing on his own terms.

He liked to teach from the carpenter's shop. Warped wood left alone stays warped; only steaming and a straightening press make it straight, as only a whetstone makes metal sharp. People are the same, he said: goodness is not something we are born with; training has to put it into us from the outside. Even the tools prove it. Nobody would ever invent a straightening board or a plumb line unless wood came out crooked, so the tool's very existence betrays the bend in the material.

Xunzi named his rival and broke with him openly. Mencius said learning reveals the goodness already in our nature; Xunzi said this is not so. Where Mencius pictured learning as a gardener tending a seedling, Xunzi's picture was a carpenter clamping a warped plank to a frame until it lay straight. A potter at the wheel makes the same point. The pot exists because the potter worked the clay; the clay never held a pot inside it, ready to emerge.

He offered everyday evidence. When a starving boy gives his older brother the first helping, he goes against his own hunger, and Xunzi read that as a mark left by teaching, not by instinct. And if human nature were already good, it would be a mystery why every people goes to the effort of creating laws, teachers and rituals that good-natured humans would never need.

Nor would Heaven help. For Xunzi, Heaven was simply the workings of nature, uncaring. If rain follows a prayer for rain, why did it fall? For no particular reason, he said: the sky is only nature, and it does not care about us. So the whole work of straightening human nature falls to people.

Yet he was no pessimist. Any ordinary person, Xunzi insisted, could become a Yu, the sage-king of legend who mastered the great floods. The route is effort heaped on effort over a lifetime, never stopping, because crooked wood is still wood and patient work can bend it straight.

the-mandate-of-heaven.context_blurb:
The Mandate of Heaven, tianming, is one of the oldest political ideas in Chinese history, older than Confucius himself. The Zhou kings were already using it in the 11th century BC to justify overthrowing the dynasty before them. It is a theory of rightful rule and, pushed to its end, a theory of rightful revolt: the right to govern is a license from Heaven, held only on condition. The philosopher Mencius later drew out its most radical consequences.

The condition is just rule. While a king rules justly, Heaven supports him; if he turns cruel, Heaven withdraws its backing and the people gain the right to overthrow him. Nature itself was thought to report on him. Famines, floods, droughts and earthquakes were taken as Heaven's verdict rather than misfortune, warnings that Heaven was angry and the mandate might be slipping away. Legend made Di Xin, final king of the Shang, the model of a ruler who lost it. His appetites, the stories say, built a pool of wine on his palace grounds, with trees hung with roasted meat, where he floated in canoes and drank; in 1999 diggers at Yanshi uncovered a great stone pool matching the tale.

How does Heaven, which never speaks aloud, announce its verdict? Mencius cited an ancient saying from the Book of Documents: Heaven sees as the people see and hears as the people hear. The people's suffering and anger are Heaven's voice. In about 1046 BC, at Muye, King Wu led a smaller Zhou army against the Shang. Many of Di Xin's soldiers were slaves and conscripts, about 170,000 of them, who hated their king, and as the hosts met they turned their spears upside down and went over to the enemy, opening the road to the capital. Cornered, Di Xin put on his finest jewels, climbed the Deer Terrace where his riches were stored, set it alight and burned himself alive among his treasures.

Mencius ranked the parts of a state in an order that startled kings: the people count most, the altars of grain and soil next, and the ruler least. Cruelty, he argued, defeats itself. Like water seeking low ground, people flow down to a kind ruler, and a tyrant drives them into a rival's arms as an otter drives fish into deep water. Such ideas frightened rulers. In 1394 Zhu Yuanzhang, the peasant rebel who founded the Ming dynasty, had Mencius's spirit-tablet removed from the Confucian temple and some 85 dangerous passages cut from his book, though the full text outlived the censorship.

Mencius's boldest answers came when kings pressed him. King Xuan of Qi asked whether Tang and Wu had not committed a monstrous crime in slaying their sovereigns, the tyrants Jie and Zhou. Mencius replied that a man who outrages goodness and righteousness is no king but a mere robber and ruffian; he had heard of the cutting off of the fellow Zhou, but not of the killing of a sovereign. Asked whether Yao, the sage-king, had handed the empire to Shun as a personal gift, Mencius said no: Heaven gave it to Shun, and the people gave it to him, for a throne is a trust and never a private gift.

laozi-and-the-dao-de-jing.context_blurb:
Laozi is the half-legendary sage at the root of Daoism, one of the great traditions of Chinese thought, and the reputed author of one slim book of riddling sayings about the Way that runs through all things. Almost nothing about his life is certain. The story Chinese readers have told about him for two thousand years is a small parable of its own, about a weary old scholar who wanted only to disappear.

As the Zhou kingdom decayed, the story goes, its old keeper of archives mounted an ox and headed west, meaning never to come back. At the frontier pass the gatekeeper, Yinxi, realized who was riding by and saw that this man's wisdom was about to vanish from the world. Yinxi did not bar the road for good. He pleaded with the traveler and named one price for passing: the gate would open only after the old man had set his teaching down in writing. Laozi wrote it all out at one sitting, gave the pages to the gatekeeper and rode off into the west, never to be seen again. Those pages became the Dao De Jing, the Classic of the Way and Virtue, and few books on earth have been translated more often.

The great Han historian Sima Qian gives the archivist's real name as Li Er. Hardly anyone used it. People called him Laozi, a fond title meaning Old Master, and the nickname stuck so firmly that it buried his name. One famous riddle in his book says the Way does nothing and yet nothing is left undone. This is not a recipe for laziness. It is the practice called wu wei, effortless action: letting things take their course instead of shoving against them, and working with the natural flow of a situation rather than against its grain.

The book's very first line undercuts itself. Any Way that can be put into words, it says, is not the eternal Way, and any name you can speak is not the lasting Name, so the most important thing in the book is the one thing words cannot pin down. A later chapter gave the world a motivational poster slogan about a journey of a thousand miles. The Chinese measures the distance in li, and it says the long road begins beneath your own feet, right where you already stand. Legend also says the orderly young Confucius once visited Laozi and came away shaken. A running beast can be trapped, he told his students, a fish netted and a bird shot down, but Laozi was like a dragon that rides the clouds up into heaven, beyond the reach of any snare.

A general would say the hard crushes the soft. The book insists on the reverse, and its emblem is flowing water: nothing in the world is softer or weaker, yet nothing is better at wearing down the hard, and in time it carves stone. The book also ranks rulers. A hated ruler is worst, a feared ruler a little better, a loved and praised ruler better still. The best ruler governs with so light a hand that, when the work is done and the land thrives, his people never think of him at all and say, "We did it ourselves." Modern scholars doubt the tidy legend of one author. The book reads like a scrapbook of brief sayings whose styles clash, and their leading account is a compilation by many hands, older sayings gathered and edited across generations, roughly in the fourth and third centuries BCE.

wu-wei-effortless-action.context_blurb:
Wu wei is a central idea of Daoism, the Chinese tradition of Laozi's Daodejing and the book of Zhuangzi. Word for word it means non-doing, which is almost perfectly misleading. It never meant laziness. It means acting with natural ease, never straining or pushing, going with the grain of things instead of fighting it.

So a teenager who decides that wu wei lets him skip his chores has fallen into the translation trap. From the outside, an idler on a couch and a Daoist master resting in a garden may look the same. Call on them to act and the difference appears: the master moves skilfully and without strain, while the idler stays idle.

Laozi's favourite image is water. Nothing is softer, yet given time it wears rock to sand, because it flows around the stone and never fights it head-on. In the Zhuangzi, Confucius watches a man leap into a torrent so wild that not even fish survive there, and fears he means to die. Downstream the man walks out singing. He has no method, he says: he sinks with the swirling eddies and lets the upwelling water carry him back up, following the water's way and never thinking of himself.

The Confucian Mencius told the opposite story. A farmer of Song, impatient with his slow-growing grain, went down every row pulling each shoot a little higher, then boasted of his hard day. Next morning his son found that every stalk he had pulled had withered and died. Forcing growth kills it.

The most famous picture is Cook Ding, whose carving of an ox for Lord Wenhui moved like a dance. He had used one knife for nineteen years and thousands of oxen, yet it was as sharp as new, because he let the edge pass through the spaces that already exist between the joints and never hacked at bone. Effortless does not mean careless. At a knotted place where the joints locked tight, he went very slowly, watching closely, and the knife scarcely moved, until the piece fell apart like crumbling earth. Such skill lives in the hand. An old wheelwright told Duke Huan that his chisel must go neither too slow nor too fast, a feel he could not put into words; after seventy years he could not teach it to his son, nor could his son learn it from him.

Laozi applied the same idea to ruling. The Dao does nothing, he wrote, yet nothing is left undone: if a ruler stops meddling, things complete themselves. He ranked rulers from the despised to the feared to the loved and praised, and above them all the ruler the people hardly notice. When the work is done, his people say they did it all themselves.

the-dao-the-way.context_blurb:
The Dao, usually translated as the Way, is the central word of Daoist philosophy, the tradition of ancient China linked to the sage Laozi and his book, the Daodejing. The first thing a Daoist text tells you about the Dao is that it cannot really be put into words. That sounds like a dodge, but it hides a serious question about the limits of language, and Daoist writers answer it with images and parables instead of definitions.

The Daodejing opens by saying that the Way that can be spoken is not the lasting Way. In the 1950s the philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein made a similar point at Cambridge. He challenged his students to define the word game so that it fitted hide-and-seek, chess and solitaire alike; each definition failed, either leaving out some game or letting in something that is no game at all. A fixed label can quietly shrink a large, living idea, fencing off part of the whole and losing the rest. To picture natural wholeness, the old Daoist teachers chose a plain image: pu, the uncarved block, a piece of wood no one has yet shaped.

Chapter 32 of the Daodejing says what happens once the block is cut up. Each cut marks off one more separate thing and pins a name to it, so carving stands for naming the world, and the text warns that such names are only provisional. The Way does not bark orders either. Scholars describe it as more like a map than a rulebook: it shows the open routes through the land, which you find and walk yourself.

Most people think power lies with whatever is hardest. The Daodejing crowns something soft instead: water, which takes the shape of whatever holds it, yet given time wears away the hardest stone. The thinker Zhuangzi pressed the doubt about labels further. He once dreamed of being a butterfly, flitting about content, then woke and could not say for sure whether Zhuangzi the man had dreamed of a butterfly's life, or a butterfly was dreaming, at that very moment, of being Zhuangzi. The tale aims at our comfortable belief that the neat boxes we sort the world into, man in one and butterfly in another, hold firm no matter what we find.

zhuangzis-butterfly-dream.context_blurb:
Zhuangzi, Master Zhuang, was a Chinese Daoist philosopher of the 4th century BC and one of the funniest and strangest writers of the ancient world. His most famous story is a single paragraph about a dream, and it raises a serious question about what we can know from inside our own experience, long before Descartes's demon or the brain in a vat.

Zhuang Zhou once fell asleep and became, in his dream, a butterfly flitting about, content with itself. Inside the dream he did not know he was Zhuang Zhou at all; he was wholly the butterfly and had forgotten the man. Then he woke, solid and unmistakably himself. Was he a man who had dreamed of being a butterfly, or a butterfly now dreaming it was a man?

Someone might object that he can surely tell he is awake now. Yet the sense of certainty settles nothing, since the butterfly had exactly the same confidence inside the dream. Zhuangzi pressed further: a man may dream of drinking wine and weep in the morning, or dream of weeping and go hunting cheerfully. From the inside, a dream seems just as real and your thinking just as clear as when you are awake; you can even interpret a dream inside a dream. Lady Li, taken captive from her father's border post, cried until her clothes were drenched, yet once settled in the palace's luxury she could not see why she had grieved. Zhuangzi asks whether the dead, likewise, might be puzzled that they ever held on to life. Certainty that some condition will be terrible is worthless until you have actually been there.

The dream ends the book's second chapter, which notes that the same log looks enormous to an ant and small to an ox: bigness and smallness are drawn by the viewer, not carried by the log. The dream stretches that move to its limit: even the line between real and dreamed is drawn by the viewer, not by the world. Zhuangzi does not settle the riddle. Instead he gives the event a name, the Transformation of Things, and leaves the question deliberately unanswered. He even says that when he calls you dreaming, he is dreaming too, and he labels his own words the Supreme Swindle. So he exempts himself from nothing; he claims no firm footing that he refuses to everyone else.

Zhuangzi lived the spirit of his writing. Fishing by the Pu River, he was offered the government of the state of Chu. Without looking up from his rod, he answered that he would rather be a tortoise alive and dragging its tail in the mud than a sacred one kept dead in a temple.

Descartes raised the same doubt two thousand years later in order to defeat it and rebuild certainty. Zhuangzi settled into the doubt and stayed there, taking the shifting state between as the truth of things, not a problem needing a fix. Scholars still divide: some read the story as a lesson in doubt, others as a lesson in flowing transformation. Since the text supports both, a fair teacher treats them as genuine rivals, and neither camp is plainly wrong.

cook-ding-and-the-ox.context_blurb:
Cook Ding is the butcher in one of the best-loved parables of the Zhuangzi, a Daoist classic from ancient China. Called to carve an ox while Lord Wenhui watches, he turns a bloody chore into a lesson about mastery and about wu wei, acting without forcing. The scene is short, almost cinematic, and its real point hides behind the carving.

As Ding worked, his hand, shoulder, foot and knee all moved as one, and the blade went zip and zoop in perfect rhythm, so smoothly that the watchers were reminded of a graceful dance kept in time with music. Then Ding explained what separates butchers. A clumsy one hacks at bone and needs a new knife every month, and a good one cuts and needs a new knife once a year. His own knife had cut up thousands of oxen in nineteen years, and its edge was still as keen as if it had just left the grindstone.

The lord asked how. There are spaces between the joints, Ding said, and a blade's edge has almost no thickness, so a knife that slides into those gaps has room to spare. He followed the natural grain of the ox and never struck bone, which is why the edge never wore down. His way of seeing had changed as well. When he began, he saw only the whole ox in front of him; three years on, the whole animal had vanished from his sight; and in the end he worked by spirit and no longer looked with his eyes, his ordinary perception at rest while spirit moved where it wanted.

Even the master meets knots. At a tangled spot, Ding said, he sized up the trouble, slowed right down, kept his eyes on the work and moved the knife with the greatest care, until the whole joint fell apart like a clod of earth. Effortless action is not carelessness; the hard places get more attention, not more force. And when the lord cried out at such dazzling skill, Ding laid his knife down and corrected him. What he cared about, he said, was the Way, which goes beyond skill, and the carving was only its visible surface. The lord said he had learned how to care for life.

the-useless-tree.context_blurb:
The Daoist teacher Zhuangzi, of ancient China, filled his book with strange, funny tales that turn common sense upside down. Several of them praise uselessness, a thought that upends the usual talk about living a useful life.

A carpenter named Shih passes a gigantic old oak whose wood is so twisted that no one could make a boat, a coffin or a roof beam from it, and he tells his apprentice it is worthless. That night the oak visits him in a dream. Fruit trees, it points out, have their branches torn off precisely because their fruit is good. Had its wood been worth cutting, it would have fallen to the axe long ago; being good for nothing is exactly how it lived long enough to grow so huge.

Zhuangzi also tells of Crippled Shu, whose body is so twisted that his chin sits against his belly. When the army comes to drag off every able-bodied man, Shu wanders among the recruiters unharmed, since they pass him over as useless to anyone, and he even collects the grain handed out to the disabled.

His friend, the logician Hui Tzu, once mocked Zhuangzi's ideas as a huge, knotted stink-tree, big and good for nothing. Zhuangzi answered with two animals. The quick, clever wildcat springs after its prey and dies in a hunter's trap, while the enormous yak, too big to catch even a mouse, comes to no harm. The wildcat's skill is what leads it into the snare, and the yak's huge uselessness is what protects it.

the-happiness-of-fish.context_blurb:
The happiness of the fish is a short, witty exchange from the Zhuangzi, one of the great books of Daoist philosophy in ancient China. It is one of the earliest entries in the long debate over what philosophers now call the problem of other minds: how can anyone know what another creature feels?

Zhuangzi and his friend Huizi, the sharpest logician of their day, are strolling by the Hao River. Zhuangzi points to the minnows darting about and says that this is what fish enjoy. Huizi objects that Zhuangzi is not a fish, so he cannot know what fish enjoy. Thomas Nagel raised the same worry in 1974 when he asked what it is like to be a bat.

Zhuangzi offers no evidence about the fish. Instead he turns Huizi's own rule around: Huizi is not Zhuangzi, so how can Huizi know that Zhuangzi does not know what fish enjoy? If no mind can ever know another, the skeptic's rule defeats itself.

Huizi presses once more, and Zhuangzi wins with a pun. Huizi's word for how can also mean from where. So Zhuangzi treats "How do you know?" as "From where do you know?", and answers that he knows it from right here, standing above the Hao.

mohism-and-mozi-impartial-care.context_blurb:
Mozi, whose name means Master Mo, was a Chinese thinker who lived from about 470 to 391 BC, in the generations after Confucius. He founded the only school of his age to rival the Confucians, a disciplined band of pacifists who were also experts at defending besieged cities. Then his movement vanished from Chinese thought for two thousand years.

By tradition, Mozi came from the craftsman class and first studied under followers of Confucius, then turned against his teachers and started the first organized rival to the Confucian school. When the engineer Gongshu Ban designed new siege engines to help mighty Chu swallow little Song, Mozi challenged him to fight the siege out on a tabletop. For the city wall, Mozi unbuckled his leather belt and laid it flat. Gongshu Ban tried nine machines of attack, and Mozi beat back all nine.

Mozi measured everything by its cost to ordinary people. He granted that the lords' giant bronze bells and court music sounded pleasant, yet he condemned them. Every bell was paid for with food and cloth taken from the people, ploughmen were dragged from their fields, and the women hired to play had to abandon their spinning and weaving. War got the same plain test. Kill one innocent man and you die a criminal; slaughter ten thousand in an aggressive war and later ages call you great. A rule that punishes the small crime while praising the enormous one, Mozi argued, cannot tell right from wrong at all.

Mozi traced the world's harms, the powerful crushing the weak and the wealthy sneering at the poor, to a single cause: partiality, people caring far more for their own. His cure was jian ai, impartial care, which asks you to regard another man's household as your own household and another man's person as your own self. Old customs got no free pass: a funeral rite, a court ritual or a war had to prove that it actually helped the ordinary people who bore its weight.

His critic Wumazi answered with a confession: he cared more for his neighbors in the next district than for strangers in a far province, more for his own district than the next, and most of all for his family. Wumazi offered this not as a flaw but as the natural and rightful shape of love, strongest for those nearest and fading with distance. Mencius, a Confucian, pressed harder: a love that denies the special duty a son owes his father, he charged, leaves a man no better than a beast.

legalism-and-han-feizi.context_blurb:
Han Fei, a prince of the state of Han in the third century BCE, gave the fullest shape to the Chinese school later called Legalism. The Legalists doubted that moral teaching could make people reliably good, so they built the state on clear laws, rewards and punishments instead. The state of Qin used their methods to conquer its rivals and found China's first empire in 221 BCE.

Han Fei argued in stories. A farmer saw a rabbit run into a stump and break its neck, then quit plowing to wait by the stump for another while his fields went to weeds. The moral is not about trusting luck: Han Fei's target was the ruler who governs today's people with the methods of the long-dead sage-kings, waiting for a golden age that will never return. A market trader once boasted that nothing could get through his shields and that his spears went through anything. Both boasts cannot be true at once, so the Chinese word for a contradiction, maodun, literally means "spear-shield."

Before Shang Yang imposed his harsh code on Qin, he offered gold to anyone who would move a tall pole from the market's south gate to its north gate. Nobody believed so easy a job could pay so well, until he raised the prize and paid the one man who did it, in full, before the crowd. Only then did he post his laws, because rewards and punishments work only when people trust the state to deliver exactly what it promises.

A ruler, Han Fei taught, must keep two handles in his own grip, punishment and reward, since a minister who controls either one can buy the loyalty owed to the ruler. In one story Marquis Zhao of Han nodded off in his hall, and the servant whose one duty was his hat covered him with a robe. The marquis punished the robe-keeper for neglect and the kindly hat-keeper too, for doing a job that was not his. In a Legalist state overstepping your duty is as criminal as shirking it, because it blurs who answers for what.

Han Fei's end was bitter. At Qin's court his old fellow student Li Si, now chief minister, feared being outshone and warned the king that a prince of Han would always favor Han, since that is human nature. It was Han Fei's own teaching, that people act from self-interest rather than loyalty, turned against its author. He was jailed and given poison, and the king's pardon came too late.

the-buddha-and-the-four-sights.context_blurb:
Siddhartha Gautama was a prince of a small kingdom on the plains of northern India, in the sixth or fifth century BCE, who gave up his palace to search for a way out of suffering. His followers came to call him the Buddha, the awakened one, and his teaching became the root of one of the world's great religious and philosophical traditions. The story of his youth is one of Asia's great hero tales.

When the prince was a newborn, the aged hermit Asita visited the palace, read the marks on the infant's body, and burst into tears. His father was alarmed, but Asita's tears were for himself: he saw the boy would become a Buddha, and he knew that he would die, too old, before the child grew up to teach. By legend the marks meant the boy would become either a world-conquering king or a Buddha. King Suddhodana wanted an heir for his throne, so he raised his son in three pleasure palaces, one for each season, with a white parasol held over him day and night. His one great rule was that the boy must never see suffering of any kind: no old age, no sickness, no death. At twenty-nine the prince rode out and met four sights. A stooped old man, a man racked by fever and a dead body borne off to be burned all told him the same thing: this is your fate too. The fourth, a calm wandering holy man, told him something new. It gave him hope: perhaps there was a way out of that fate. On the night he chose to leave, he paused at Yasodhara's doorway. His wife was sleeping, one hand on the head of their baby son, Rahula. He did not wake them, silently vowed to return only after he had awakened, and rode away into the night. Years later, sitting beneath a fig tree at Bodh Gaya, he vowed he would not get up until awakening came, and he kept that vow.

The truth had reached him in stages. On those first rides his charioteer Channa held nothing back: whenever the prince pointed at a strange sight, Channa told him plainly that he too would grow old, fall sick and die. Late one night the prince woke to find the palace dancers sprawled asleep, slack and drooling, and the lovely hall suddenly looked like a house of corpses; all that beauty seemed only a thin mask over decay. He rode out on his horse Kanthaka with Channa beside him, and at the river Anoma he gave up his jewels and robes, drew his sword and with one stroke cut off his own hair and beard, turning prince into wanderer. Then he tried the harshest road he could find. Six years of starving and punishing his body left his limbs like withered reeds and brought him to death's door, yet he was no nearer awakening than on the day he started. Long after, the Buddha taught the lesson of those years to a monk named Sona, who had paced until his feet bled. Sona had once played the lute, so the Buddha asked how its strings must be tuned. Too tight and a string snaps; too loose and it will not play. Effort on the path must be tuned the same way, neither strained nor slack.

His starving had taught him nothing, just as the palace pleasures had taught him nothing, and he saw that the two were one mistake: each chased an extreme, while the truth lay in between. This became the Middle Way. When he began to eat again, his five fellow ascetics abandoned him in disgust. Scholars add a twist. In the oldest Buddhist texts the four roadside encounters are told of an earlier, mythical Buddha named Vipassi, while the historical Siddhartha simply reflects on age, sickness and death. So the famous chariot rides are a later legend rather than sober history, and telling legend from core is part of taking the story seriously.

the-four-noble-truths-and-the-eightfold-.context_blurb:
The Four Noble Truths are the core of what the Buddha taught after his awakening, and nearly every later Buddhist school, from Sri Lanka to Japan, reads as commentary on them. They are shaped like a doctor's diagnosis: what is wrong, what causes it, whether it can be cured, and the treatment. The treatment is the Eightfold Path, and the tradition holds that this small handful of ideas can carry a whole life.

At Sarnath, in a park where deer grazed, the Buddha preached his first sermon. He first turned his back on two dead ends, the hunt for pleasure and the punishing of one's own body, which he had tried as a starving ascetic. Between them he set the Middle Way. The first truth is dukkha, the hardship woven through life. He meant birth, aging, sickness and death, but also troubles of the heart: not getting what you want, being stuck with what you dislike, and separation from those you love. Much of that suffering, he taught, we add ourselves. A man who stubs his foot on a stone is hit by one arrow, the pain; if he spends the day fuming over it, he is hit by a second arrow of his own making. A wise man struck by that same stone suffers far less, because he will not pile new misery on top of a pain that is already over.

The second truth locates the cause. The world is fleeting, and everything we love will change or end, but the Buddha did not blame the world. He blamed our own grasping and clinging, which he called tanha, thirst. The third truth is that suffering can end. Nirvana means a blowing out, like snuffing a candle, but what goes out is not your life; it is the burning of craving, hatred and delusion. The fourth truth, the path, is practical. Right Speech rules out lying, words that turn people against each other, cruel talk, and also empty chatter and gossip that serves no purpose. Right Livelihood forbids five trades that profit from harm: trading in arms, in human beings, in poison, in meat animals and in intoxicants such as liquor.

The Buddha named three kinds of craving: for pleasures, for becoming someone more, and, most surprisingly, for not existing at all, the wish to be wiped out, which he called the same trapping thirst in another mask. The word translated as right throughout the path is the Pali samma, which does not mean morally approved; it means complete, the most effective way to do the thing. When the monk Malunkyaputta demanded answers to grand questions, such as whether the universe is eternal, the Buddha told of a man struck by a poisoned arrow who will not let the surgeon touch it until someone tells him who shot it, what wood the bow was made of and which bird gave the feathers. He will be dead long before his questions are answered. Pull out the arrow first; the grand questions can wait.

anatta-and-the-chariot-no-self.context_blurb:
Anatta is the Buddhist teaching of "no-self." Most people assume that at the core of each of us sits one lasting thing, the real me, that owns my life from birth to death. Buddhism denies it. Its most famous argument comes from The Questions of King Milinda, an ancient record of a debate in northwest India, and versions of the same argument run all the way into modern philosophy.

The king was Menander, a Greek-speaking ruler whose lands ran from Afghanistan into India; Indian writers called him Milinda. His opponent in the battle of wits was a Buddhist monk, Nagasena, who met every challenge. When the king politely asked his name, the monk answered that "Nagasena" was only a word in common use, because no lasting person could be found behind it. The king struck back hard. If no real person exists, who receives the monks' gifts of food, who keeps the rules, and who would be the victim if someone killed you? Without a person, merit, duty and guilt all fall apart, so the whole moral order collapses, and the king called the monk a liar. Nagasena answered with the chariot the king had ridden in. He had the king inspect it piece by piece, the pole, the axle, the wheels, the frame, and the king agreed that no single part was the chariot, nor all of them together, nor something apart from them. Then there is no chariot, Nagasena concluded; "chariot" was only ever a name for the parts.

With the cart settled, Nagasena turned the same reasoning on himself. His own name, he said, is a label for an assembly, the many kinds of matter in a body and the five groups of changing parts, with no extra Nagasena underneath. This was aimed squarely at a Hindu teaching of the time, the atman, a soul that never changes and is a person's true identity. The word anatta means without a self, and it says a person is a bundle of five changing parts, body, feeling, perception, mental habits and awareness, with nothing fixed beneath them.

The argument goes back to the Buddha himself. In his second sermon, at the Deer Park outside Varanasi, he offered his five disciples a test of control. If the body were truly your self, you could order it to stay young and well and it would obey; since illness and age arrive whether you allow them or not, it is not a self you own, and the same goes for feelings and mind. Centuries later, the Scottish philosopher David Hume looked inward for his self and found only passing perceptions, a feeling here, a thought there, but never the "I" that was supposed to own them. His bundle of perceptions echoes Nagasena's chariot almost exactly: a heap of parts and no further thing underneath. An older legend gives the chariot to a woman. Mara, the demon who tempts the holy, came to unsettle the nun Vajira while she meditated, asking who had made her being. She calmly answered that a being is a name for a bundle of parts, just as a chariot is, and Mara realized she knew exactly who he was, and he disappeared, sad and defeated.

Is Nagasena contradicting himself, since he happily says he rode a chariot? Buddhists answer with the doctrine of two truths. He is speaking on two levels: in daily life a chariot, or a person, is a handy thing to name, yet at the deepest level only the parts exist, with no separate thing beneath them. Scholars also notice a gap in the Buddha's sermon. He went through the five parts one by one, showed that none is the lasting self, and stopped. One camp hears a flat denial of any self; the other hears a narrower claim, that of these five parts not one is the self, because his test covered those five and left open a self beyond them. The question stays open. In the twentieth century the philosopher Derek Parfit described a person as a chain of connected events in brain, body and mind, and arrived where Nagasena and Hume had. All three keep the connected stream of parts. What each denies is a separate self that exists over and above the stream.

impermanence-karma-samsara-and-nirvana.context_blurb:
Four Buddhist ideas fit together into one picture: impermanence (anicca), karma, samsara and nirvana. Each is easily mistranslated. In popular English, karma has drifted into a cosmic scoreboard, samsara gets sold as simple reincarnation, and nirvana arrives loaded with images of heaven. The Buddha's own pictures for these ideas are quieter, more surprising and sometimes unsettling.

Impermanence came first, even at the very end. On his deathbed at Kushinagar, with his monks around him, the Buddha left them no secret, only a lesson and a command: all compounded things are impermanent, so press on with diligence. Samsara, Sanskrit for wandering on, is the round of birth, craving, death and rebirth. No god or judge assigns the next life; what keeps the round turning is the being's own clinging, together with ignorance and karma.

At the hub of the painted Wheel of Life, three creatures circle, each with the next one's tail in its jaws: a pig, which is ignorance; a snake, which is hatred; and a rooster standing for greed and grasping. These three poisons drive the whole wheel. Nirvana is no destination for a departing soul. The word means blowing out, and the Buddha's picture for it is a fire that dies when it has nothing left to burn, because craving, hatred and confusion fade once nothing feeds them. Karma is no scoreboard either. It is intention, the Buddha said, that I call action. Shoving a stranger on purpose makes karma and knocking him over by accident does not, because what makes an act karma is the will behind it, and past karma never locks a person's fate.

The whole wheel, with every realm of gods, humans and animals, is clutched in the jaws and talons of Yama, the death-lord, who embodies impermanence; outside his grip the Buddha points at the moon to show there is a way out. When a wanderer named Vacchagotta asked what becomes of an awakened one once he dies, the Buddha pointed to a burning fire and asked which direction it would travel when it went out. An extinguished fire, of course, has traveled in no direction whatever, and asking where a freed being goes is just as confused.

nagarjuna-and-emptiness.context_blurb:
Nagarjuna was a Buddhist monk of southern India, around the second century, whom later Buddhists honored as second only to the Buddha. He founded the Madhyamaka, or Middle Way, school, which steers between two mistakes: treating the world as a cast of self-contained objects, and collapsing it into nothing at all. Tibetan monasteries still treat his thought as the summit of a monk's training, and rival schools still dispute it.

Almost nothing about his life is certain, so the best-known tale of him is a legend. It says he dove beneath the sea to the realm of the nagas, serpent-beings who guarded the lost scriptures of the Perfection of Wisdom, and brought those scriptures back. His teaching starts from something plain. Call a stick long; then place an even longer one next to it, and suddenly the first is short, though no one laid a finger on it. Its longness was never something it owned by itself, because it was long only in comparison with something shorter. That is emptiness: things lack any essence of their own and are what they are only in relation to other things.

His tradition puts a chariot to the same test. Take it apart, lay out the wheels, axle, pole and frame, and search the pile: the chariot is not any one part, not the mere heap, and not some extra thing over and above them. Yet chariots carry riders daily, and the word causes no confusion. So the word names no hidden chariot-essence; it is a convenient label for the parts when they are assembled and doing their job.

Nagarjuna warned that emptiness is dangerous in clumsy hands, like grabbing a viper by the wrong end or bungling a magic spell. The ruinous misreading takes emptiness to mean that nothing is real and nothing counts, and sinks into despair. Emptiness means lacking an independent essence, not lacking existence. In his most quoted verse he welds three ideas into one: coming into being only through causes and conditions, which Buddhists call dependent origination, is the very same thing as emptiness, and both are the Middle Way. A critic charged that if nothing has a fixed nature, suffering has nothing real to work on and freedom from it is impossible. Nagarjuna turned the charge around: emptiness is exactly what lets the path work. If suffering had a fixed essence it could neither arise nor cease, so only things without fixed natures can change, and only what can change can be healed.

the-upanishads-atman-is-brahman.context_blurb:
The Upanishads are the philosophical poems that close the ancient Indian Vedas, composed by unnamed teachers in forest retreats between roughly 800 and 300 BC. Many centuries later the German philosopher Schopenhauer called them the solace of his life. Their great claim is about what lies beneath the many things we see, and it was always one serious position among rivals.

Even the name tells how the teaching travelled. Upanishad is built from three Sanskrit pieces, upa, ni and sad, which together mean sitting down near, the picture of a student settled close to his teacher to receive a secret doctrine.

The most famous lesson comes from the Chandogya Upanishad. Svetaketu returns home at twenty-four after twelve years studying the Vedas, very pleased with himself. His father, Uddalaka Aruni, asks whether he ever sought the teaching by which the unheard is heard and the unknown known. He had not. For all his study, he had missed the single piece of knowledge that unlocks all the rest, the way knowing clay lets you understand every pot made of it.

So Uddalaka teaches him with ordinary things. He has his son drop salt into water overnight. In the morning the salt cannot be found, yet every sip, from the top, the middle and the bottom, tastes of it. The salt is everywhere in the water though no one can see it, and in the same way one subtle essence runs hidden through everything. After each example, the salt, rivers merging nameless into the ocean, the unseen sap of a tree, Uddalaka repeats three words: tat tvam asi, which means you are that. Your innermost self, Atman, is the same as Brahman, the ground of all being.

The Mundaka Upanishad pictures two birds with lovely wings perched on one tree. One eats the fruit; the other eats nothing and only watches. They are two sides of you: the self that is caught up in pleasure and pain, and the witnessing Self that nothing touches.

The teaching reached Europe by a dramatic road. Dara Shikoh, a Mughal prince and the heir of Shah Jahan, builder of the Taj Mahal, had fifty Upanishads put into Persian around 1657 under the title the Greatest Secret. His younger brother Aurangzeb took power soon after and executed him for heresy, for pursuing forbidden ideas.

Ancient Indian schools argued fiercely over what a person is. The Buddhists, for one, denied any permanent self. The Upanishads gave their own answer: behind all the many individuals stands one Self, and every one of us is that Self.

shankara-and-the-rope-mistaken-for-a-sna.context_blurb:
Shankara was an Indian philosopher of the 8th century who lived only about thirty-two years, yet reshaped Hindu thought. Legend has him walking across India, founding monasteries and beating rival teachers in public debates. He was the great defender of Advaita, or non-dualism: the teaching that the many separate things we see are not what they seem. Serious thinkers still dispute his view.

His best-known teaching begins on a dim path at dusk. You stop dead, because a snake lies coiled at your feet. Then someone brings a lamp, and the light shows nothing but a coiled rope lying still. The snake did not slither off or die; it was never there at all. The lamp only revealed the rope. What actually set you free was knowing the truth, since once you know it is a rope there is nothing left to fight or run from, and that is why Advaita teaches that freedom comes through knowledge rather than action. A student might scoff that your fright was foolish. Shankara disagreed: the racing heart and the leap backward were genuine and even sensible, and only the thing they answered to was unreal. That is how ignorance causes real suffering.

Shankara gathered a family of such mistakes. A clear crystal looks red because a red flower stands just behind it; a mirror's scratch looks like a spot on your own face; a rope becomes a snake. Each time the same error is at work: you borrow something real from somewhere else and lay it over what is actually in front of you. His word for it was adhyasa, superimposition. Legend also tells of his debate with Mandana Mishra, a great master of ritual, over whether sacred action or knowledge frees the soul. The judge was Mandana's own wife, Ubhaya Bharati. She hung a fresh flower garland on each man and declared that whoever's garland wilted first had lost. Mandana's withered, and he became Shankara's disciple.

A skeptic demands to know whether the snake was real or nothing at all. Advaita refuses both. The snake was not real, yet it differed from an impossible nothing such as a square circle, because you truly saw it and it leaned on a real rope, while a square circle leans on nothing. The everyday world, Shankara held, has this same borrowed reality, leaning wholly on the one reality, Brahman. He began his greatest work by turning the error inward. Each of us takes the "I", the deathless witness within, for the body and mind that are born and die, and every fear of death flows from that one confusion.

jainism-ahimsa-and-the-blind-men-and-the.context_blurb:
Jainism is one of India's ancient religious and philosophical traditions, as old as Buddhism. Its great reformer Mahavira, in the sixth century BC, handed down a radical ethic of harmlessness toward every living thing, pursued so seriously that a devout monk's whole day is arranged around not hurting anything by accident. Its philosophical centerpiece is a parable about blind men and an elephant.

Ahimsa, non-harm, is the first and supreme Jain vow. A monk carries a soft broom and sweeps the ground ahead of his feet so that he will not crush a tiny insect he cannot see. The parable gathers several blind men around an elephant. One feels its flank and calls it a wall, one handles the trunk and decides it must be a serpent, and one grabs the tail and insists on rope. Each has honestly grasped his own piece, though none has grasped the elephant.

Non-harm reaches the dinner table. A devout Jain family eats no meat, fish or eggs, and it also refuses onions, garlic and potatoes, because uprooting a bulb or tuber destroys the entire plant, along with small creatures in the soil. The blind men's endless quarrel could be settled at once if each man stepped past his own grip to feel what his neighbors were touching. Jain thinkers built a logic on that move, anekantavada, the doctrine of many-sidedness: any single standpoint catches only one face of reality, so truth comes from gathering the standpoints rather than crowning one.

The poet Saxe retold the parable in verse and aimed its final stanza at the debaters of religion and philosophy. In his telling, each side circles one and the same reality while insisting the others are mistaken, all of them talking about an elephant none of them has seen. Jainism also ranks harms. Every killing is wrong, yet its gravity depends on the number of senses a creature possesses. A plant has only touch, a worm adds taste, an ant smell and a bee sight, while animals and humans have all five, so harming a worm weighs more than uprooting a plant.

the-bhagavad-gita-arjunas-dilemma.context_blurb:
The Bhagavad Gita is a short, intense dialogue of about seven hundred verses set inside the vast Indian epic, the Mahabharata, and it has been read and argued over for some two thousand years. On the eve of a war between two branches of one family, the great archer Arjuna talks with his charioteer Krishna, who turns out to be a god. Their conversation is a classic clash between duty and conscience that has never been settled.

At Kurukshetra, Arjuna leads the Pandavas against their cousins, the Kauravas. Before the first arrow flies, he has Krishna drive the chariot into the open ground between the armies so that he can look long at the faces of the men he must kill. That look breaks him. On both sides he sees fathers and grandfathers, teachers and cousins; his limbs give way, his mouth goes dry, and his bow, the Gandiva, slips from his hand. The first chapter ends with him throwing aside his bow and arrows and sinking down in his chariot, refusing to fight.

Arjuna was born a kshatriya, a member of the warrior caste, and his sacred duty, his sva-dharma, commands him to hold his place and fight, because a warrior's first duty is the one he was born to, not the one that feels gentler. Yet across the field stand Bhishma and Drona, the elders and teachers he reveres most. Arjuna puts his refusal into words: he would rather live by begging than slay such great-souled teachers, since any kingdom won that way would be stained with their blood.

Krishna answers in two famous moves. First he teaches desireless action: you have a right to your deeds but never to their fruits, so do your duty and let go of how it turns out. Second, he turns from the body to the deathless self inside it, which weapons cannot cut and fire cannot burn; that self is never born and never dies, so in the deepest sense no one kills and no one is killed. Critics note what keeps the poem a living debate. The Gita treats Arjuna's mercy as a genuine, honourable instinct, and Krishna overrides it rather than proving it wrong.

mohandas-gandhi-and-satyagraha.context_blurb:
Mohandas Gandhi, later called Mahatma, "great-souled," led India's long campaign against British rule until his assassination in 1948. He took an ancient Indian ideal, ahimsa, the refusal to harm, and turned it into a political method he called satyagraha, "truth-force": break an unjust law openly, never strike back, and accept the penalty. Martin Luther King Jr. later carried the method into the American civil rights movement.

In 1930 the British taxed the salt every Indian family used, though salt lay free on the shore. Gandhi walked about 240 miles to the sea at Dandi, setting out with 78 volunteers as crowds swelled behind him. On the beach he simply stooped and picked up a lump of natural salt, a quiet act that broke the law without destroying or seizing anything. Weeks later, at the Dharasana Salt Works, some 2,500 marchers advanced in columns on police armed with steel-tipped clubs. Not one of them raised an arm to ward off the blows; they took the beating without resisting and fell, in one reporter's words, like ten-pins.

Critics dismissed the movement as "passive resistance," a phrase that made it sound limp and easy. Gandhi rejected the label and called satyagraha a weapon of the strong, because standing unarmed before the clubs without hitting back takes more nerve than fighting does. In his teaching, the satyagrahi proves the truth by bearing suffering himself, not by inflicting it on his opponent.

the-six-orthodox-schools-darshanas.context_blurb:
Classical India was not a land of wordless mystics. Its six orthodox schools, the darshanas, argued for centuries over logic, matter, the self and what counts as a valid proof, and some of their arguments stand beside the best Greek work. Which school won any given argument is still debated.

The Vaisheshika school, founded by the sage Kanada, whose name means grain-eater, asked what a pot, a tree or a mountain is made of at bottom. Its answer was atoms: tiny particles that can be neither divided nor destroyed, so that one visible thing differs from another only in how many atoms it holds and how they are arranged.

The Nyaya school, whose name means method of reasoning, taught its students to reason from what they can see to what they cannot. See haze rising from a distant peak, and you know there is fire up there, because smoke never appears without fire. A kitchen hearth shows the two together, and a lake shows neither, so the link holds.

The Samkhya thinkers honoured the Vedas yet argued that no creator God is needed. One reason cut deep: a God who is perfect and never changes could not be the source of a world that changes without end.
