the-house-of-wisdom-and-the-translation-.context_blurb:
In the 800s, under the Abbasid caliphs in Baghdad, scholars set out to recover and extend Greek learning, translating Aristotle, Euclid, Galen and Ptolemy into Arabic and arguing with them rather than merely admiring them. The work went on for about two centuries and drew talent and manuscripts from across the medieval world. Its story shows that ideas are kept alive by whoever argues with them, not owned by any one people.

Once Rome's western empire collapsed, Europe lost most of Aristotle's writings for centuries. When Europeans finally got him back, he came by a roundabout road: Baghdad's scholars had put his works into Arabic, and centuries later European scholars rendered that Arabic into Latin. The master translator was Hunayn ibn Ishaq, who rendered about 129 works of the physician Galen alone. The medieval biographer Ibn Abi Usaybi'a reports that the caliph paid Hunayn in gold equal to the weight of each finished book, a story historians treat as testimony rather than hard fact.

The movement belonged to no single people. Hunayn was a Christian, Thabit ibn Qurra a pagan from a star-worshipping sect, and their patrons Muslim caliphs; learning passed between strangers and rivals rather than down one people's bloodline. Thabit was discovered in the town of Harran working as a money-changer by Muhammad, the eldest of three rich brothers called the Banu Musa, who noticed his command of Syriac, Greek and Arabic and brought him to Baghdad. The Banu Musa paid their scholars around 500 dinars a month and sent agents deep into Byzantine lands to buy up old Greek manuscripts.

The story has its tangles. For centuries Arabic and then European scholars studied a book called the Theology of Aristotle, but it was not by Aristotle at all; it was a reworked piece of the later pagan philosopher Plotinus. The famous House of Wisdom, the Bayt al-Hikma, is often pictured as a grand university full of translators, yet the Yale scholar Dimitri Gutas argues it was more likely a palace library or records office, while the real translating went on in a scattered network of homes and patrons. Legend tells that al-Ma'mun began it all after Aristotle visited him in a dream. Historians credit something less tidy: decades of broad demand and the money of many rival patrons, which kept the work going long after al-Ma'mun died in 833.

avicennas-floating-man.context_blurb:
Ibn Sina, called Avicenna in the Latin West, was an eleventh-century Persian doctor and philosopher whose textbook of medicine was used in European universities for some five hundred years. His most famous thought experiment strips away every ordinary reason to think you are a body, then asks what is left. It anticipated a move Descartes made six hundred years later, and it remains one serious position in a live argument about what the self is.

He dreamed it up in a cell. After the death of Shams al-Dawla, the ruler who protected him, a hostile vizier charged him with siding with a rival and jailed him in a castle for some four months. There he imagined a grown man brought into being all at once, suspended in the air, with no sensation of any kind. The passage became one page in his vast encyclopedia, the Book of Healing, which old accounts say he wrote at a rate of fifty pages or so every day, a tale best taken as legend.

Picture that man in still air that is neither warm nor cold, eyes covered, hearing and smelling nothing, his limbs held apart so that nothing touches him. Though he is stripped of every sense and every memory, one certainty survives: that he himself exists. Yet he has no idea whether he has any body at all, not a hand, not a heart, not a brain. Avicenna adds that you were sure you existed long before anyone told you what lies inside your skull; most people find out that a heart and a brain are in there only by seeing bodies cut open.

From that gap Avicenna drew his conclusion. If the self and the body were one and the same, being sure of one would mean being sure of the other; since the floating man is certain of his self but not of his body, the self must be something other than the body. A thinker who holds that you simply are your brain would reject the step, but that is where Avicenna landed. The man also troubles a tidy rule many thinkers have held, that nothing reaches the mind except through the five senses. Not one sense was feeding him anything, and still he knew he existed. Why, then, does it feel as if we are our bodies? Avicenna compares our limbs to clothes we have worn so long that we forget we could take them off. And he treats knowing yourself as unlike any other knowing. To know a tree, something must travel to you; the self reaches itself directly, with nothing passing in between, which later thinkers called knowledge by presence.

Modern scholars such as Jon McGinnis, Jari Kaukua and Peter Adamson doubt that Avicenna meant a watertight proof at all. He spoke of the floating man as a way to alert you, and on their reading it works more like a nudge that wakes you up to an awareness of yourself that has been there all along. The view Avicenna drew from it, that the self is something real and not the body, was later called dualism, and thinkers still dispute whether it is true.

avicenna-on-necessary-vs-contingent-bein.context_blurb:
Ibn Sina, called Avicenna in Latin, was a Persian Muslim philosopher of around the year 1000. His sharpest argument asks whether the ordinary existence of things explains itself. Most things we meet could just as well never have existed; Avicenna argued that this points to something that cannot be like that. His reasoning later fed Thomas Aquinas's proofs, and the question remains disputed.

He began with the self. Picture a man who springs into being already adult, eyes covered, hanging in the air so that he touches nothing and senses no limbs. He still could not doubt that he himself exists, so the self can be grasped apart from the body, some six hundred years before Descartes. Avicenna then separated what a thing is from the fact that it is. Anyone can tell you what a unicorn is, a horse with a single twisted horn, though none has ever lived. Knowing what a thing is tells you nothing about whether it exists, so in everything but one being, existence comes as an extra, laid over what a thing is rather than built into its definition.

Any tree or star might never have been. Avicenna's name for this condition is "possible in itself." On its own such a thing leans neither toward being nor toward not being, so only something outside it can tip the balance and bring it into being. But the chain of borrowed existence points, he argued, to a being of a wholly different kind, the Necessary Existent, which needs no cause and cannot fail to exist. In every ordinary thing there is a gap between what it is and that it is; in this being there is none, for existence is not something it owns; existence is what it is. Aristotle had argued his way to a first cause from motion. Avicenna's own version, which he called the Proof of the Truthful and judged more solid and nobler, begins from reflection on existence alone, on what it is for anything to be.

His sharpest move concerns an endless chain. Picture a line in which each thing owes its being to the one before, with no first link. Avicenna granted that such a line might run back without end and still argued it leaves something unexplained. Every link is merely possible in itself, so the whole collection is merely possible too, and the entire line still needs a cause from outside it, one that is necessary rather than one more borrower. He did not need to prove that the world had a beginning in time.

al-ghazalis-crisis-of-doubt.context_blurb:
Al-Ghazali was the most honored Islamic scholar of the eleventh century, holder of the top teaching chair in Baghdad. At the height of his fame he gave it all up in a crisis of certainty, and later told the story in a short book, Deliverance from Error. It asks how far reason alone can carry a seeker, centuries before Descartes asked the same.

A legend tells how bandits robbed the young student of his bag of notes, and when he begged their chief to return them, the robber mocked a knowledge so easy to steal, then gave the bag back. Al-Ghazali spent the next three years memorizing his notes, so that nothing he knew could ever be taken from him again. By 1095 he was lecturing to hundreds in Baghdad, but when he searched his heart he found that his learning served fame, and he feared it had brought him to the brink of Hellfire. So he walked away from the chair, gave away his fortune except what his children needed, and slipped out of the city, announcing a pilgrimage to Mecca while secretly planning to settle in Syria.

Before he left, the crisis seized his body. For days he could swallow neither bread nor water. One morning he climbed to his chair before a packed hall, and no words would come; the most celebrated lecturer of the age sat there silent, his tongue as if chained. His doctors could find no bodily cause, and in the end gave a diagnosis straight out of his own teaching: the trouble was in his heart, and from the heart it had sickened his whole body.

Deeper still was the doubt he describes in the book. He set out to doubt everything he believed, starting with his senses and then turning on reason itself. Dreams gave him his sharpest weapon, because a dream feels completely real until you wake and call it fancy. So how can you be sure that waking life is not itself a dream, which some higher state, a mystic's vision or even death, might one day expose as illusion? He saw he could not argue his way out, because no proof can prove that proofs can be trusted. When certainty finally returned, he insisted it came from no chain of arguments but as a light that God sent into his heart. He offered this as a serious account of knowledge, not a retreat from thinking: reason has limits, and direct knowledge of God is a path of its own.

al-ghazali-on-causation-the-fire-and-the.context_blurb:
Al-Ghazali was an eleventh-century Persian scholar who taught at Baghdad, then a great center of Islamic learning. In The Incoherence of the Philosophers he took aim at a word everyone uses without a second thought: cause. When a flame touches cotton and the cotton burns, what do we actually know? His answer remains one real contender in a long and still-open argument.

His claim is startling. Fire, he wrote, is lifeless and does nothing; it is God who creates the blackness in the cotton and turns it to ash, directly or through His angels. His reason is about what we can witness. Watch as closely as you like and you see the flame and the burning arrive together, but you never see the fire forcing the cotton to burn. The link we call necessary is really a habit God keeps. Some 650 years later the Scottish philosopher David Hume made the same move, calling cause and effect a constant conjunction.

So he challenged the philosophers who called fire the true agent of burning to prove it. Their only evidence, he said, was watching the burning happen at the moment the cotton meets the flame, and seeing one thing follow another is not seeing one thing produce another. His motive was to make room for miracles. The Quran tells how Abraham was thrown into a fire that God commanded to be cool and safe for him. If fire had to burn by its own nature, that could never happen; on Al-Ghazali's reading, God, on that one occasion, held back the burning He creates every other time.

The reply came from the philosopher Averroes, who titled his rebuttal The Incoherence of the Incoherence, a jab aimed straight back at Al-Ghazali. Take away fire's power to burn, he argued, and you have erased it, not explained it, because fire robbed of its burning has stopped being fire; a thing's powers are part of what it is. Denying real causes, he added, would wreck knowledge itself, since to know a thing is to know its causes. Scholars today still split over how far Al-Ghazali meant to go. Some read him as denying created things any real power, so that only God acts. The rival camp holds that he wanted only to defend miracles, and may have let fire keep a real power to burn, given by God and never able to bind God's hands.

averroes-and-the-defense-of-reason.context_blurb:
Averroes, known in Arabic as Ibn Rushd, was a twelfth-century judge, doctor and philosopher in Muslim Spain. He believed philosophy had been attacked unfairly by the theologian al-Ghazali and spent his life defending it, both as a careful judge of the law and as the greatest reader of Aristotle in his age. Christian scholars in Paris later studied him obsessively.

His career began with a scare. Summoned by Abu Yaqub Yusuf, the caliph, the young scholar was asked whether the philosophers thought the heavens were created or eternal. Fearing a deadly trap, Averroes began making excuses and even claimed he had never had anything to do with philosophy. Only when the caliph showed his own deep learning did Averroes relax, and that meeting launched his life's work, for the caliph commissioned him to explain Aristotle. He did, at three depths, from short summaries to great line-by-line commentaries, and Latin Europe came to call him simply the Commentator, just as Aristotle was the Philosopher. Dante later honored him in Limbo, naming him by that title.

Al-Ghazali had attacked philosophers in a book called The Incoherence of the Philosophers. Averroes answered it passage by passage and doubled the title, so that the attack was met by a book on the Incoherence of that Incoherence: the muddled thinker, it said, was al-Ghazali himself. On causation he defended plain sense. Al-Ghazali held that a flame does not really burn cotton, since God alone does the burning. Averroes replied that fire burns because burning is what fire is; every thing has its own real nature, and without one a thing would have no name or definition, and all things would be one. His Decisive Treatise met the fear that a philosopher's proof might contradict scripture. A real proof and true scripture can never truly clash, he argued, because truth does not oppose truth but agrees with it and bears witness to it.

Averroes also saw a hidden cost in denying causes. If nothing truly causes anything, then nothing can truly be known, because to know a thing is to know its causes, and science, definition and law would all collapse together. Deny cause, he warned, and you deny all knowledge.

the-mutazila-vs-the-ashari.context_blurb:
In the first centuries of Islam, Muslim theologians argued over a question as old as Plato's Euthyphro: is an act good because God commands it, or does God command it because it is good? Two great schools took opposite sides, the rationalist Mu'tazila and the Ash'ari tradition that rose against them. Each had serious thinkers and real reasons, and the question between them is still argued.

The rationalists got their name from a walkout. In the 700s Wasil ibn Ata, a student of the preacher al-Hasan al-Basri, quarrelled with his teacher over how to judge a believer who commits a grave sin, and he started a rival circle. Al-Hasan remarked that Wasil had withdrawn from us, and the name stuck: Mu'tazila means those who withdraw.

The school trusted reason. Its thinker Ibrahim al-Nazzam insisted God could never punish a child, since punishing the blameless would make Him an oppressor. Asked how he could be sure, he gave the school's defining answer: the human mind can see by itself, before any scripture, that hurting the innocent is wrong, and a just God will not do what reason already condemns. The school also taught that the Quran was created rather than eternal. In 833 the caliph al-Ma'mun made scholars swear to that doctrine. The jurist Ibn Hanbal refused; he was jailed and flogged, and he held out until a later caliph, al-Mutawakkil, reversed the policy.

Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari grew up inside the rationalist school and trained under al-Jubba'i, its leader at Basra. Legend says he broke with it over three brothers. One died pious and went to Paradise, one died wicked and went to Hell, and one died young. Why, the child asks, was I never allowed to grow up? Al-Jubba'i's reply was that God knew the boy would have sinned, so an early death was best for him. Then, al-Ash'ari asked, may the brother in Hell not cry out: why did You not take me as a child too, before I could sin? Al-Jubba'i had no answer. Around the age of forty, al-Ash'ari renounced the school publicly and founded the tradition that became its fiercest rival and, in time, mainstream Sunni theology.

The Ash'ari answer is not mere stubbornness. If right and wrong were a standard standing over God's will, God would stop being the author of right and become merely its subject, answering to a law like any creature, and His power would meet a limit outside Himself. So for al-Ash'ari, whatever God decrees is just because He decrees it.

Put the hardest case to both schools. Suppose God ordered a believer to burn an innocent man alive. Would obedience then be right? The Ash'ari says yes, since the command itself would make the act good. The Mu'tazili refuses, and his refusal commits him to a claim about morality itself: right and wrong are fixed in the nature of acts, and a human mind can know them by its own light. Neither school has conceded, and the fork is Plato's Euthyphro in Islamic dress.

ibn-khalduns-asabiyyah-and-the-cycle-of-.context_blurb:
Ibn Khaldun was a fourteenth-century North African scholar, judge and statesman from Tunis who lived through civil wars, plague and the fall of one dynasty after another. Late in life he wrote the Muqaddimah, the introduction to a universal history, to find the laws behind what he had watched. It is often called the first work of social science, because it studies society the way an astronomer studies the planets.

His search began in grief. In 1348, when he was about seventeen, the Black Death tore through Tunis and killed his father and mother along with several of his teachers. The boy who survived grew up asking why civilizations rise and rot. At the center of his answer stands one bond he called asabiyyah, usually translated as group feeling: a solidarity so strong that it makes men act as one body and put the group ahead of their own comfort. A shared faith can strengthen it, but the bond itself is solidarity, and it is what lifts a hardy, struggling clan to the throne. Once the clan has won, the bond begins to fade. No dynasty, he claimed, usually lasts beyond three generations, roughly 120 years: the founder conquers, his son keeps what he inherited, and the grandson, born into privilege and never tested in battle, squanders it, until a new hungry tribe rides out of the desert.

What kills the bond? Ibn Khaldun's startling answer was comfort itself: the hard life that forged discipline and loyalty vanishes once success brings ease, and the ease eats away at a people from the inside. Civilizations fall, on his account, not because people turn wicked but because their way of life changes. He knew he was doing something new. He called his discovery 'ilm al-'umran, the science of human society and civilization, and wrote that if other scholars had explored the subject before him, their work had never reached him. His own life supplied drama enough. In 1401 the conqueror Timur, also called Tamerlane, besieged Damascus with the aging scholar shut inside its walls. Rather than wait for the slaughter, Ibn Khaldun had himself let down over the city wall on ropes and walked into Timur's camp. He stayed for weeks, talking with the terrifying conqueror about the lands of North Africa and about asabiyyah itself.

Ibn Khaldun pictured the whole cycle as a road from the desert to the city. Out in the desert, tribes scraping by on a hard life keep a fierce loyalty but have few crafts, while settled city dwellers enjoy rich arts and sciences but let their loyalty go soft. The city is the desert's luxurious destination, and its grave. He traced a dynasty through five stages: conquest, the ruler's full control, leisure, contented imitation of what the founders built, and finally ruin. In that last stage a spendthrift generation wastes everything the others gathered, and the dynasty falls apart. Once a people prize comfort above all and put their own interests ahead of others, he warned, the group feeling does more than loosen: it decays into individualism and factionalism, with each man looking out only for himself, and is destroyed. Even the treasury follows the curve. Early rulers raise a large revenue from light taxes, but late rulers who push the rates far higher end up with a smaller total than the light taxes once delivered, a pattern economists would rediscover six centuries later.

maimonides-and-the-guide-for-the-perplex.context_blurb:
Moses Maimonides, called Rambam in Jewish tradition, was the towering Jewish philosopher of medieval times, as well as a rabbi and a physician. His Guide for the Perplexed speaks to believers torn between the Torah and Aristotle, and it asks what human words can truly say about God.

In 1148, when Maimonides was about thirteen, the Almohads seized his home city of Córdoba in Spain and offered its Jews conversion, flight or death. His family fled, and the boy's youth became long years as a refugee, moving through Spain and North Africa before the family finally settled in Old Cairo. Maimonides refused ever to be paid for teaching Torah, so the household depended on David, his younger brother, who traded in jewels. Around 1171 David drowned when his ship went down in the Indian Ocean, taking the family fortune with it. Maimonides mourned and lay ill for almost a year; then he took up medicine and earned his living as a physician for the rest of his days.

Scripture speaks of God's hand and face, His throne and His anger, while Aristotle's reasoning says God has no body and never changes. Maimonides argued there is no real war between them: the conflict comes only from taking those word-pictures literally, and once they are read as figures of speech the perplexity dissolves. How, then, can anyone know God? Maimonides told of a man who has heard of ships but never seen one, and learns nothing about them except denials: no plant, no mineral, not flat, not round, not solid. Our knowledge of God works the same way, he held. We can never say what God is, but each true denial carries us a real step nearer, rather than merely clearing away an error and leaving us where we stood.

Scripture calls God merciful and at times angry, but feelings would mean that God changes, so Maimonides read such words as describing actions. One fire softens wax and hardens clay without being soft or hard itself. Calling God merciful means that God brings about the very things a merciful person would bring about, an effect in the world rather than a feeling inside God. He also pictured a king deep in his palace, with his subjects ranged from outside the city walls to the inner court. What decides how near anyone stands is how deeply he understands what God is, not how strictly he keeps the law.

Maimonides held that even good and wise, said of God, can only deny: God lacks no goodness and no wisdom, because any genuine resemblance to our goodness would shrink God to human size. A century later Thomas Aquinas agreed that crude literal descriptions fail, but he rejected bare denial. For Aquinas the words fit God by analogy, a real likeness between goodness in people and goodness in God, though never an equal one. Both answers remain serious positions.

augustine-of-hippo-the-restless-youth-an.context_blurb:
Augustine grew up in the 300s in what was then Roman North Africa, the son of a devout Christian mother, Monica, and a pagan father. Trained in the best schools of rhetoric, he chased pleasure and a brilliant career before a dramatic conversion in a garden in Milan. Years later, as bishop of Hippo, he told the whole story in his Confessions, with an honesty that still startles readers sixteen centuries on.

As a teenager Augustine and a pack of friends raided a neighbor's pear tree one night and picked it clean. They had better pears at home and hardly tasted the stolen ones; they threw the whole haul to the pigs. He stole, he later admitted, only because it was forbidden. In the same restless years he wanted God with half his heart and his pleasures with the other half, so he prayed a famously honest prayer: make me chaste, Lord, only not yet. He was afraid God might answer too quickly. The turning point came in Milan in 386, in a garden, where he lay crying beneath a fig tree. From a house nearby a child's voice kept chanting the same words, "Take up and read," and he heard in it an order from God.

Looking back, Augustine saw what had pulled him into the theft. Alone he would never have done it; the thrill was the gang. When friends say "let's do it," he wrote, we go along because we are ashamed not to be shameless, ashamed of looking timid in front of them. Monica, his mother, cried and prayed over him for years. She once pleaded with a bishop to talk her son out of his mistakes; he would not, but he gave her a promise she held onto as if heaven had spoken it: it could not be that the son of so many tears would be lost. In the garden, after years of promising to change tomorrow, Augustine finally cried out the question everything turns on: why not now? Then, at the child's chant, he hurried back to the book he had left nearby, the apostle Paul's letters, let it fall open and read a verse urging him to give up drunkenness and lust and put on Christ. In that instant his doubts were gone.

In later life Augustine was haunted by the fact that the theft had served no purpose, neither hunger nor profit. He had loved the wrongdoing itself, and that raised a disturbing question: why does a person enjoy doing wrong simply because it is wrong? His deeper search had started at about eighteen. He was a star student of rhetoric, trained to argue any side and win over a crowd, when Cicero's Hortensius, a book by the great Roman orator, changed what he longed for. Winning was no longer enough; he hungered to find what is actually true, a love of wisdom that is the very meaning of the word philosophy. In Milan a visitor named Ponticianus told him about Antony, an Egyptian monk who went alone into the desert to seek God, and of two officials of the emperor who, after reading the monk's life, abandoned their careers at once. Augustine felt shame, because he already knew the truth and still would not act on it. And beside him in the garden sat his friend Alypius. When Augustine finished his verse, Alypius took the book, read one line further, about welcoming the one who is weak in faith, and gave his own life to God on the spot, at his friend's side.

the-confessions-as-the-first-autobiograp.context_blurb:
Augustine of Hippo, a North African bishop of the late Roman world, finished his Confessions in about AD 397, and many readers count it as the West's first real autobiography. Earlier Greek and Roman writers had recorded their deeds and defended their careers; Caesar wrote about his campaigns and Cicero answered his enemies. Augustine did something the ancient world had no name for.

Old memoirs looked outward at battles won and offices held. Augustine turned his book inward, making his own soul, with all its twists and turnings, the subject. What freed him to set down private doubts, lusts, shames and ambitions was his listener. The whole book is spoken to God, as one long prayer, not to a human reader whose good opinion he needed.

Classical philosophy had sorted people from the outside into tidy lists of virtues and vices. Looking within, Augustine found a puzzle instead, and he asked his own soul why it was so downcast and troubled. The self he discovered was a tangle of contrary impulses that its owner could not master.

augustine-on-the-puzzle-of-time.context_blurb:
Augustine, the North African bishop, wrote his Confessions around 397 AD, and Book 11 holds one of philosophy's most honest puzzles. He asks what time is, a thing he uses every day, and finds the question slipping away the harder he looks. The answer he reaches, that time has its home in the mind, is one serious contender among several, set against Aristotle before him and the block-universe physicists long after.

He begins with a confession. If no one asks him what time is, he knows; the moment someone asks him to explain it, he does not. Then he tests the three times. The past is finished and the future has not arrived, so only the present can truly be said to exist. People also liked to needle him: what had God been up to before creating the world? One wit answered that God was preparing hell for people who pry into mysteries. Augustine will not take shelter in the quip. Perceiving is one thing and laughing another, he says, and he treats the question seriously. In the middle of this hard thinking he even stops and prays, telling God that his soul yearns to know this most tangled riddle and begging for light. For him the puzzle is no dry exercise.

Next he tries to catch the present and look at it. Any present that lasts can be split into a part already past and a part still to come, so the true present shrinks to a sliver with no thickness at all, a knife-edge that has flown into the past before you can grasp it. As for the question about God before creation, he dissolves it. God made time itself along with the world, so before creation there was no then at all to ask about. Time is one of God's creatures. Then he moves all three times into the mind, as three ways of being present. The present lives in attention, the future in expectation, and the past in memory, which holds on to what is over.

Greek thinkers tied time to motion, the turning of the heavens or the swing of a weight, and Aristotle called time the number of motion, something real and out in the world. Augustine grants that moving things help us keep track, but he puts the measuring itself inside the soul, which keeps an imprint of each passing thing and weighs it there. His example is a psalm he has memorized. Before he utters a word, all of it lies ahead in his expectation; as he speaks, each piece passes through his attention and settles into memory, until the whole psalm has crossed over. The same, he says, is true of a single word or a whole life.

His boldest claim follows. Judge that something long gone took a long time, and you face a puzzle: the event no longer exists, so what is your ruler measuring? Augustine answers: the impression the event left on your mind, a trace that stays and can be weighed. He wonders whether time might be the mind itself drawn out, a distension of the soul between memory and expectation. The image came from Plotinus, an earlier philosopher, but Augustine gave it his own meaning. Compared with God, for whom everything is present at once, this scattered, stretched mind is for Augustine a painful fall away from God's timeless eternity. And after all this brilliant work, he ends where he began. He admits to God that he remains ignorant of what time is, though he knows he says all this within time. The puzzle ends in wonder, and rival views remain live.

evil-as-privation-the-absence-of-good.context_blurb:
How could a wholly good creator be responsible for a world full of cruelty, disease and suffering? Augustine, who led the church at Hippo on the African coast about 1,600 years ago, attacked the puzzle by asking what evil actually is. His answer reframed the whole problem and has shaped Christian thinking about evil ever since, though it still has serious critics as well as defenders.

Start with a blind grandmother and a boy who keeps his healthy eyes shut in a dark room. Neither can make out the picture hanging there, but only the grandmother has lost a power, for nothing she does can make her eyes work, while the boy simply declines to use a power he still has. Blindness is not a thing a person carries around; it is sight that is missing. The lack must also be a lack of something that belongs there. A stone cannot see either, but that is just how stones are. A hawk that has lost its sight is the true case of something gone wrong, because a hawk is the kind of creature that is meant to see. Augustine applied the idea to the body. When a doctor heals a wound, the wound does not travel off somewhere else. It simply ceases to be, since a wound was never a substance in its own right, only a gap where health should be.

Corruption works the same way. Rust needs iron and rot needs wood, so decay has nothing to feed on unless something good and whole is already there for it to spoil and consume; the more thoroughly a thing is eaten, the less of it remains. So when someone asks how evil got into a world made wholly by a good God, Augustine's settled answer is that evil has no being of its own. It is the absence or decay of a good, a damage done to something that really exists. Asking who made it is like asking who manufactured the hole in a doughnut.

He reached that answer the hard way. As a young man Augustine spent nine years among the Manichees, a sect that pictured evil as a realm of Darkness forever fighting the Light. His friend Nebridius asked a question that haunted him: if the Darkness is a true rival that God must battle forever and can never defeat, then God is not almighty, because a genuine rival power would set limits on what he can do. Calling evil a mere lack removes the rival. It also yields a striking thought experiment. Peel the good out of a thing bit by bit, hoping to end with pure evil, and at the moment the last good goes you would be holding nothing, since whatever loses every good has also lost its very existence.

Critics push back. Bertrand Russell called the theory too rosy, insisting that pain is positively real, with its own raw, stabbing feel, far more than pleasure gone missing; later philosophers such as Todd Calder sharpened the point, and the dispute stays open. Nor did Augustine invent the idea. Around 386 he read the books of the Platonists, and the pagan Neoplatonist Plotinus had already treated evil as a privation, linking it to shapeless matter and the drift toward nothingness. A pagan philosopher supplied the bones of a Christian answer.

free-will-and-the-origin-of-evil.context_blurb:
Augustine's account of evil as a lack of good explained what evil is, but a sharper question followed: if God made everything good, how did evil get into the world without God being responsible for it? His answer, worked out in his dialogue On the Free Choice of the Will, became one of the great moves on the problem, echoing down to the modern philosopher Alvin Plantinga. It also has a famous pressure point that philosophers still debate.

For Augustine the question was personal. As a teenager, he and a pack of friends stole pears from a neighbor's tree one night, tasted a few and fed the rest to the pigs, though he had better fruit at home. Looking back, he said what he loved was the wrong itself; he stole for the sake of being bad. What lured him in was the sheer company of his friends, for alone, he wrote, he would never have done it. As a restless young man he even begged God to make him chaste and self-controlled, only not yet. That prayer shows how one and the same will can desire the good and push it away in a single breath. Evil, for him, often looks less like a monster than a divided heart.

The Manichees, whom Augustine had once followed, made evil a second eternal power at war with the good. Augustine answered that evil has no stuff of its own; it is the spoiling of something good, so God created no evil thing. When an accuser asks whether God is to blame for handing out so dangerous a gift as free will, Augustine replies that those who abuse the gift deserve condemnation, not the giver. Free will is like a hand or an eye, which stays good even when someone turns it to a shameful act, and everyone who does evil is the cause of his own evildoing.

A challenger pressed further: if God foresees every sin before you are born, is he not its real author? Augustine replied that God's foreknowledge of a sin does not make him its cause, and the will stays free even though it is perfectly foreseen.

The defense still draws fire. J. L. Mackie argued in 1955 that nothing is logically impossible about a free person who always chooses well, so an almighty God could have created a world of free beings without sin. Plantinga answered that not even an all-powerful God can make sure that a truly free creature never chooses evil, since guaranteeing it would remove the freedom. The quarrel turns on whether real freedom needs a live chance of choosing wrong, and it remains open. Augustine's early book later came back to bite him. Decades on, after he had come to stress how badly people need God's grace, followers of Pelagius turned the book against its author, citing it as proof that a person can reach salvation by free will without God's help. Augustine protested that they had read him out of context.

the-city-of-god-vs-the-city-of-man.context_blurb:
In 410 CE Alaric's Visigoths sacked Rome, the first time an invader had taken the city in nearly eight hundred years. Pagans blamed the Christians for neglecting the old gods. Augustine, bishop of Hippo in North Africa, answered with The City of God, the longest book of his life, written over the next thirteen years. It reads history as two communities mingled together and sorted only at the end.

Augustine began with the sack itself. Alaric, himself a Christian, ordered that anyone who fled into the great churches of Saint Peter and Saint Paul, pagan or Christian, be left untouched. To Augustine this showed that the old gods had never protected Rome, while the name of Christ sheltered everyone who ran to His churches.

The two cities, he wrote, are not nations on a map; a Roman or a Goth might be a citizen of either. Two loves built them. The earthly city grows from love of self that reaches even to contempt of God, and the heavenly city from love of God that reaches even to contempt of self.

Some Christians hoped for a plain judgment that their side had won. Augustine pointed instead to the parable in which Jesus lets wheat and weeds grow side by side until the harvest. Worldly success proves nothing about a soul, he concluded, and no empire, not even the visible Church, is yet purely the City of God.

boethius-and-the-consolation-of-philosop.context_blurb:
Boethius was a Roman statesman of the early 500s who rose to the top of government under the Ostrogothic king Theodoric, then fell, was jailed and awaited execution. In his cell, around 524 AD, he wrote The Consolation of Philosophy, a dialogue in which a majestic woman, Lady Philosophy, reasons him back toward calm. For a thousand years it was one of the most-read books in Europe.

At the start, the Muses of poetry gather round the weeping prisoner and feed him mournful verses. Lady Philosophy drives them out, calling them sirens whose sweetness does not last. The book itself mixes the two voices she sorts out: its careful prose arguments keep breaking off for passages of verse poetry before the reasoning resumes. She will not simply pity him. His chains do not settle how wretched he is; his own judgment does, for nothing is miserable unless he thinks it so. And she warns him with the book's most famous image, Fortune's wheel, which carries men to the top and then hurls them down.

His fall was real. Boethius had been consul, then head of the whole government, and his proudest moment came when his two boys became consuls on the same day. When a fellow senator, Albinus, faced a charge of treason, Boethius rose to defend him, declaring that if Albinus had done it, then so had he and every senator, and the accuser turned the charge on him. In prison he finds that the memory of past happiness is what hurts most; the worst sting of misery is to have once been happy. Lady Philosophy even lets Fortune speak for herself. Fortune admits she raised him high and cast him down, yet denies any wrong, because spinning is simply what she does, and she never promised anyone that his place would last. Lady Philosophy herself is strange to look at. Her eyes burn with more than human keenness, and her height keeps changing, now ordinary, now towering until her head pierces the heavens. He had dreamed of putting all of Plato's and Aristotle's writings into Latin, a task his death cut short, but the translations of Aristotle's logic that he did finish were nearly the only way the West met that logic for roughly six centuries.

Her robe is stitched with a Pi near the hem and a Theta near the neck, with steps running between them, a picture of the climb of thought from practical skill to the loftiest truths. Her central argument turns his grief around. He had staked everything on office, money and reputation, all things Fortune could take. Real happiness, she argues, must be built on the one thing chance cannot strip away, his own virtue and reason. In the last book Boethius asks how his choices can be free if God already knows what he will do tomorrow. Her answer reframes how God knows: He stands outside time and sees all of it at once, past, present and future, in a single eternal now, rather than foreseeing it step by step as we would. Boethius was executed at Pavia and later honored as a saint, and centuries afterward Dante set his soul in Paradise, glowing among the wise in the Heaven of the Sun.

boethius-on-foreknowledge-and-free-will.context_blurb:
If God already knows what you will choose tomorrow, is tomorrow's choice really yours? The Roman statesman Boethius pressed that puzzle in the fifth book of his Consolation of Philosophy, written around 524 AD. His answer is bold and ambitious, it still has defenders and critics, and modern philosophers such as Linda Zagzebski have spent whole careers on the same problem.

Boethius had served at the very top of King Theodoric's government until a charge of treason, earned by defending a fellow senator, brought him down. He wrote the Consolation in prison, a condemned man awaiting his death: a man with no future left, arguing that the future is still free. As the book opens, the Muses of poetry sit by the weeping prisoner, feeding his self-pity with sad verses, until a towering, stately woman sends them packing and sits down in their place. She is Lady Philosophy, and her medicine is reason.

In Book V the prisoner states the worry that drives everything. If God foresees all things and can never be mistaken, then whatever he has foreseen about tomorrow is certain to happen, and your power to act freely, rather than following a script written in advance, seems crushed. Boethius then tightens the trap himself. Someone might hope that a free act could surprise God. But real knowledge cannot turn out wrong, so a foreknowledge your act could overturn would sink to shaky opinion, not real knowledge at all.

Lady Philosophy rejects the picture of God squinting into tomorrow like a fortune-teller. God sees your choice as present. Just as watching a stranger walk past right now does not force his steps, God's seeing your act does not make you do it. What is foreknown to us is simply present to him.

That rests on Boethius's famous definition of eternity. Lasting forever is not the same as being eternal. Something that existed endlessly in time would only be perpetual, its present always flowing on from past to future. God is eternal because his entire unbounded life is his all together, in a single present that never passes. Boethius also distinguished two kinds of must. That all men are mortal is a must locked in whatever anyone does. If you see a man walking, he has to be walking, but that must is softer, true only because and while you see him, and he chose to walk. God's foreknowledge lays only the softer, man-walking must on your act, so it stays free. Later thinkers still argue over it. Critics reply that a God beyond time has still known your choice from eternity, so the trap is only moved. A genuinely rival exit, one Boethius refused, holds that a choice not yet made has no settled truth, so not even God can know it in advance. That buys freedom by giving up the divine knowledge he fought to keep.

thomas-aquinas-the-dumb-ox.context_blurb:
Thomas Aquinas was a thirteenth-century Italian friar who wrote one of the longest and most tightly argued books in Western thought, the Summa Theologiae. He was quiet, courteous and absorbed, and his life ran from a family that fought his calling by force to a strange, silent ending.

Son of wealthy southern Italian nobles, born around 1225, he was groomed to become abbot of the great monastery of Monte Cassino, which his great-uncle had once ruled. As a teenager he chose the Dominicans instead, a young order of friars who lived by begging. His furious brothers seized him on the road and locked him in a tower of the family castle for about a year to break his will. Legend adds that they paid a woman to slip into his chamber and tempt him. Thomas snatched a blazing log off the hearth and drove her out.

As a student in Cologne around 1245 he was enormous and hardly spoke, so the sharper-tongued boys took him for a dullard and nicknamed him the dumb ox. Their teacher, Albert the Great, overheard and answered that this ox would one day give a bellow heard throughout the whole world.

Albert was right. Thomas had first met the newly translated works of Aristotle at the University of Naples when he was about fourteen, and he built his thought around Aristotle, whom he simply called the Philosopher, arguing that reason and faith cannot truly conflict. He wrote his vast Summa as a textbook for beginners just starting theology, and he never finished it, breaking off in the middle of the section on the sacraments. His mind never rested. Dining with King Louis IX of France, he fell silent, then crashed his fist on the table and cried out that this argument would settle the Manichees, an old heresy he had been fighting in his head. The king sent for a scribe. When the Church needed hymns for a newly created feast, Thomas wrote them, among them Pange Lingua and Tantum Ergo, and they are still sung today. He was declared a saint in 1323, and the Church honours him as the Angelic Doctor.

Late in life, an old story says, a voice from a crucifix asked what reward he wanted for writing so well, and Thomas asked for nothing but God himself. On 6 December 1273, at Mass, he was overwhelmed by something he never fully described, and he never wrote again. Reginald, his secretary, pleaded with him to complete the Summa, but Thomas answered that all he had written now seemed like straw to him.

In 1274, riding to a church council, his head hit the branch of a fallen tree; a 2025 medical study blamed the blow for his death soon after at Fossanova Abbey. Afraid that his Dominican brothers would carry his body off as relics, the Cistercian monks there boiled the corpse until only the bones were left, and kept them. The quarrel over his remains dragged on for almost a century.

aquinass-five-ways.context_blurb:
Thomas Aquinas was an Italian friar who taught in Paris in the 1200s and wrote the Summa Theologiae, a huge guide to Christian thought. Near its start he offers five short arguments, the Five Ways, claiming that reason alone, without scripture, can reach a first cause that people call God. Each way has serious defenders and serious critics, and the question remains genuinely open.

All five together take up roughly a page, one brief article written as a primer for beginning students, and that brevity is one reason they are so often misread. The First Way starts from motion with a homely picture: a stick pushing a stone. The stick does push, but none of the push is its own; it moves only because a hand is moving it. It is a borrowed mover, and Aquinas argues that if you trace the borrowing back, you must reach a first mover that nothing else moves.

His premise that every moving thing is moved by something else is not about sliding from place to place. Motion, for him, means any shift from what a thing could be to what it actually is, as a cold pot becomes hot or a seed becomes a tree. The Second Way turns to causes. Nothing can make itself, Aquinas argued, because to do the making it would have to exist before it existed, which is impossible. Nor did he invent every argument. The contingency argument came to him from a Muslim philosopher, Avicenna, and a Jewish one, Maimonides, while the motion argument goes back to the Greek Aristotle. The Fifth Way starts from nature's goal-seeking: things without minds, like an acorn growing into an oak, steadily reach their ends. Something with a mind must be guiding them, Aquinas said, as an arrow flies to its mark because an archer aimed it.

The Third Way reasons about maybe-things, things that might not have existed, like a tree that could burn. Suppose nothing but maybe-things existed: over endless past time each would already have failed, and there must once have been a moment with nothing whatever in existence, from which nothing could ever start again. So something must exist by necessity. The Fourth Way looks at qualities that come in degrees and claims each has a single highest source that the lesser cases borrow from. Aquinas used the science of his day: fire, the hottest thing, is the cause of all heat, a premise that makes this Way the most disputed. Bertrand Russell rejected the whole search for a cause of the universe. The universe, he said, is simply there, a brute fact, and that is all; we learn about causes from things inside the world, so asking for a cause of the whole is a mistake.

Defenders answer the objection that causes might run back forever with a distinction. A line of grandfathers, fathers and sons could in principle stretch back endlessly, since a grandfather can be long dead while his grandson lives. But in a hand pushing a stick pushing a stone, each member depends on the one before it acting right now, all at once, and such a chain needs a first member. David Hume objected that once each thing is explained by an earlier thing, the whole collection is explained too. William Rowe granted the point about the parts but said one question remains: why any dependent things exist in the first place instead of none. In 1969 Anthony Kenny argued that Newton's law of inertia wrecks the First Way. Aquinas, following Aristotle, took for granted that motion needs a mover pushing all the while, but inertia says a body in motion stays in motion with no mover at all until something halts it. Defenders such as Edward Feser reply that Aquinas's motion means potential becoming actual, which inertia leaves untouched. Finally, each Way ends modestly, saying only that this is what everyone calls God. Critics from Kant onward pounce on that seam: a bare first cause is still far short of the loving, personal God people worship.

anselms-ontological-argument.context_blurb:
Anselm was an eleventh-century Christian monk at the Abbey of Bec in Normandy who later became Archbishop of Canterbury. In a short book, the Proslogion, he tried to prove that God exists by pure reason alone: no scripture, no evidence from the world, just a definition and logic. Philosophers have attacked and defended his argument for nearly a thousand years, and they still disagree about whether it works.

The legend of its writing is dramatic. Anselm wanted a lone argument that could stand on nothing but itself, and the search cost him food and sleep until he feared it was a temptation from the Devil. Then one night, during the monks' prayers, the answer came to him clear and bright. He scratched it onto wax tablets, but the first set vanished and the second was found smashed on the floor. Only when he wrote it out a third time, on durable parchment, did the book survive.

Anselm already believed before he wrote a word. His motto was that he believed so that he might understand, and the book's first title meant faith seeking understanding. He was not reasoning his way into faith; he wanted to see why what he already held is true. He aimed the argument at the fool of the Psalms, who says in his heart that there is no God. Anselm's first move is a clever foothold: the fool cannot deny that greatest conceivable being without first having the idea of it in his own mind, so the idea is already there.

The argument begins with a definition: God is that than which nothing greater can be conceived. From that alone, Anselm claimed, it follows that such a being must really exist. Everything rests on one ranking he thought too obvious to defend. A thing that exists in reality is greater than the same thing existing only in the mind, just as a picture a painter has actually painted is more than the one he has only planned. So if the greatest conceivable being existed only as an idea, you could conceive a greater one, the same being existing for real, and that contradicts the definition. Centuries later Immanuel Kant attacked exactly this step, insisting that existence is not a real property added to a thing's description.

A fellow monk, Gaunilo, answered in a reply called On Behalf of the Fool. He ran the same reasoning on an island lost somewhere in the ocean, more excellent than every other land, so fine that no island could be better. By Anselm's logic it would have to exist, which is absurd, so the logic must be broken. Anselm's defenders reply that the parody mixes two different kinds of thing. An island's good qualities have no top limit, since you can always imagine more fruit and more beaches, so the greatest possible island makes no sense. God's great qualities do have a ceiling: knowledge tops out at knowing everything, power at all-power, goodness at perfect goodness. Gaunilo's side answers that the parody still lands, and the dispute remains open.

natural-law.context_blurb:
Natural law is the claim that a real moral order is built into human nature itself, open to human reason without any special revelation. The Stoics made it central to their ethics and ancient playwrights put it in the mouths of their heroines, but the medieval theologian Thomas Aquinas gave it its most careful form. It still shapes real legal arguments, and it faces serious rivals who deserve a fair hearing.

Its oldest dramatic champion is Antigone in Sophocles' tragedy. King Creon of Thebes decrees that her brother Polynices, a traitor, must lie unburied on pain of death. Antigone buries him anyway and tells the king that his decree cannot override the unwritten, unchanging laws of the gods, and Creon punishes her by walling her up alive in a tomb. More than two thousand years later Martin Luther King Jr., jailed in Birmingham in 1963 for leading civil-rights marches, drew on the same tradition to defend his defiance of segregation. His test was simple: a law that uplifts human personality is just, and a law that degrades it is unjust. To critics who find a moral law in human nature too fuzzy to use, natural-law thinkers point to concrete goods that people plainly pursue: staying alive, raising children, friendship, and knowing the truth rather than staying in ignorance.

Aquinas, following Augustine, gave the tradition its sharpest slogan: an unjust law is no law at all. A plainly unjust rule that was voted through, published and enforced has, on his view, failed to be a true law, a perversion of law rather than merely a bad one. Legal positivists answer that a wicked law is still a valid law, and the fork between the camps remains live. The judges at Nuremberg after World War Two stood on the natural-law side when Nazi defendants pleaded that they had only obeyed their state's law and followed orders. The court held that an order can be lawful and still void against a higher moral law, so obeying a criminal command is no excuse.

Aquinas arranged human drives in three levels, according to which creatures share them. Self-preservation links us to every existing thing, even stones, and mating and rearing offspring link us to the beasts. The highest level belongs to rational creatures alone: the longing to know the truth and the urge to live with others in a community. The most direct rival denies natural law at its root, holding that morality is whatever an authority decrees, so that before the command there is no right or wrong at all. That view faces an ancient problem from Plato's Euthyphro, where Socrates asks whether the gods' command makes a thing good, or whether they command it because it already is. Choose the first answer, and a divine order to be cruel would make cruelty good; Aquinas replied that goodness is rooted in God's own nature, not in bare will. The 19th-century English jurist John Austin built the other great rival, legal positivism, on one idea: whether a law exists is one question, and whether it is good is a separate one.

faith-and-reason-aristotle-baptized.context_blurb:
In the thirteenth century the full works of Aristotle reached the Latin West, much of them through Arabic and Hebrew commentators, and Christian scholars suddenly faced a towering pagan system. The Italian friar Thomas Aquinas answered with a synthesis often called the baptism of Aristotle: a precise claim about how human reasoning and revealed faith fit together. Critics on both sides have pushed back ever since.

As a heavy, silent student at Cologne, Aquinas was mocked by his classmates as the Dumb Ox. His teacher Albert the Great, who had himself launched the recovery of Aristotle, had heard the young man argue a difficult thesis and turned the insult around. An ox bellows, and this ox's bellowing in doctrine, Albert predicted, would one day be heard across the whole world.

Many thinkers of his day treated faith and reason as natural enemies. Aquinas called them two different roads arriving at one truth. Because all truth comes from God, the two can never really contradict, and an argument that clashes with faith is, he said, an abuse of philosophy rather than philosophy. He packed the idea into a Latin maxim in his Summa Theologiae. In Latin it runs gratia non tollit naturam, sed perficit: grace does not abolish nature but completes it, so human reason is taken up and finished by faith, never erased.

He did not pretend that reason proves everything. Most Christian teachings, such as the Trinity, rest on revelation alone, but a few, which he called the preambles of faith, reason can demonstrate by itself, and his showcase was the existence of God, the source of everything. Nor are the two roads equals. When a careful argument seems to collide with a revealed truth, reason is the one that yields; it may come up short or reach no verdict, yet it can never defeat a truth God has revealed. He also refused to fake proofs to make faith look stronger. Aristotle held that the world had no beginning, while Scripture tells of a creation in time. Like Moses Maimonides, the great Jewish philosopher he called Rabbi Moses, Aquinas judged that the arguments end in a draw, so that the world had a beginning is known by faith, not proved.

the-problem-of-universals.context_blurb:
An apple, a London bus and a ruby have little in common, yet we call each of them red. Do they share one real redness, or do we just use one word for many separate things? This is the problem of universals. Medieval thinkers fought over it for centuries, sometimes with charges of heresy at stake, and careful philosophers still defend both sides.

The quarrel is not about shades of colour or where the word red should stop. It is about whether redness is a real feature that all three things genuinely share, the realist view, or only a name we attach to many separate red things, the nominalist view. The same fork hits humanity: is there one real human nature in every person, or only individual people?

The fuse was lit around 270 AD. Porphyry, in an introduction to Aristotle's logic, asked whether general kinds truly exist or are mere thoughts, whether they have bodies, and whether they sit inside things or apart from them. Then he declined to answer, calling the matter too deep for an introductory book, and medieval readers chased it for nine centuries.

Around 1100 the French teacher Roscelin of Compiègne took the hardest nominalist line. Split the word man into its letters and no hidden humanity falls out. A universal, he said, is nothing but a breath of the voice, a puff of air made in speaking. Roscelin turned this on the Trinity. Without real shared natures, the one divine essence of Father, Son and Spirit becomes a mere name, so the three Persons are three separate beings, and if custom allowed, one could truly say there are three Gods. A church council at Soissons made him recant in 1093.

The realist William of Champeaux taught in Paris that the whole nature man is fully present in every human at once. Around 1108 his young student Peter Abelard took him on in public debate and won so thoroughly that William had to revise his theory, while most of William's students went over to Abelard.

In the early 1300s the English friar William of Ockham swept away any ghostly redness standing behind red things with a rule of thinking that now bears his name: never multiply things past what you need to explain what you observe. Individual red things and a concept in the mind, he argued, already explain everything.

ockhams-razor.context_blurb:
William of Ockham was an English Franciscan friar and philosopher of the early 1300s, named for his home village of Ockham in Surrey, "Oak Hamlet." His name is fixed to one of the most used tools of reasoning, a principle about simplicity in explanation. He lived a rough life: his ideas were condemned while he lived, and he ended in exile after a quarrel with a pope.

Here is the razor at work. A thump wakes you at midnight. Perhaps your cat knocked something down, or perhaps a silent burglar slipped in through the roof and out again, taking nothing. Both fit the thump, so begin with the cat; the burglar tale smuggles in a stranger, an entry and a reason, none of which you have any evidence for. At Oxford, Ockham earned an odd nickname, the Venerable Beginner. He was cleared to start as a master of theology yet never completed that last stage, so he stayed, forever, the beginner.

The razor grew from Ockham's view of reality, called nominalism. Beyond every particular dog, is there also a real, invisible Dogness that they all partake of? Ockham said no. Nothing exists but the particular dogs, and Dogness is just a word the mind coins for their likeness. Rival philosophers then and now defend real universals, and the dispute remains open. The popular version of the razor, that the simplest explanation is always true, is a corruption of it. Only when rival explanations match the evidence equally and forecast the same results does the razor act, choosing the one that assumes less.

Misused, it becomes a bludgeon. For decades cigarette makers denied that smoking causes cancer, insisting a plainer story should win over a complicated causal chain. That turns the tool upside down, because the razor only chooses between accounts that match the facts equally and gives no power to dismiss an account the evidence backs. Ockham turned the razor on Aristotle's ten categories of being, such as place, time and relation. He trimmed them to two, substance and quality, holding that a body's size is nothing extra: it just has parts lying outside other parts.

The razor's most famous Latin wording, the warning against multiplying entities without need, is not in Ockham's works at all. It first appears in 1639, in the work of the Irish friar John Punch, nearly three centuries after Ockham died, and Punch himself called it a saying the scholars already shared. Ockham's own life ended in conflict. Summoned to the papal court at Avignon in 1324, he backed the Franciscans who held that Christ and the apostles owned nothing and that friars should do the same. When Pope John XXII condemned that teaching as heretical, Ockham turned the charge around: the Pope was the heretic, and Christians were released from obeying him. In 1328 he fled the papal court.

duns-scotus-the-subtle-doctor.context_blurb:
John Duns Scotus was a Scottish Franciscan philosopher of the late thirteenth century who died in his early forties. Admirers called him the Subtle Doctor for the precision of his distinctions. He defended the realist side of a medieval quarrel that William of Ockham would soon attack, and his name went on to a very strange afterlife.

His followers were known as Dunsmen or Dunses. When Renaissance humanists turned against scholastic hair-splitting, they made his name an insult, and by the sixteenth century dunce had become English for a slow-witted person who cannot be taught; the dunce's cap followed later. The subtlest thinker of his age gave the language its word for the dullest.

His own great puzzle was what makes you uniquely you. Name everything true of Socrates, that he is a rational, mortal human, and every one of those traits fits Plato as well, so no description, however full, picks out Socrates alone. Scotus answered that beyond all qualities there must be a further principle, a bare thisness, that fixes Socrates as this particular man; his followers later coined the Latin word haecceitas for it. Behind this lay his stand on universals, the question of whether the humanity that Socrates and Plato share is something real or only a word. For Scotus the common nature truly exists, and it exists inside each individual thing, narrowed down to one person by his thisness. Ockham and the nominalists replied that only individuals exist, and that fork is still open.

abelard-and-heloise.context_blurb:
Peter Abelard was the most dazzling teacher in twelfth-century Paris: proud, cheerful about his own gifts, and so good at public argument that students followed him across France. Heloise was the brilliant young niece of Fulbert, a powerful Paris churchman. Their secret love affair became one of the most retold stories of the Middle Ages, and it ended in catastrophe.

The affair began with a scheme. In his own autobiography, the Historia Calamitatum, Abelard confesses that he paid Fulbert to take him in as a lodger and offered to tutor Heloise for one reason: to be alone with her and seduce her. When Heloise bore a son, the couple gave him a startling name, Astrolabe, after the scientific instrument used to chart the stars and to find a traveler's position on the earth. The lovers married in secret, but Fulbert believed the marriage did nothing to mend his family's disgrace. His kinsmen bribed a servant, crept into Abelard's room at night, and castrated him in his sleep.

Abelard's other legacy was a book, Sic et Non, whose Latin title translates as Yes and No. For 158 hard questions of faith he gathered passages from Scripture and the Church Fathers that seemed to clash, and then refused to settle a single contradiction himself. By leaving the saints in open disagreement, Abelard forced the student to stop accepting a claim just because a great authority had made it and to work out the answer by his own reason. That habit became the engine of the scholastic method, which ran the medieval universities for centuries.

The book's preface gave the questioning mind its motto: by doubting we are led to inquire, and by inquiring we reach the truth. For Abelard, doubt was not the enemy of faith but its doorway. Heloise had a mind every bit as independent. Before the secret wedding, when Abelard offered to marry her to calm Fulbert's rage, she argued hard against a match that was meant to protect her good name. A wife and a household, she warned, would wreck the calling of a great philosopher, and love freely given was worth more than any legal tie. She would rather be called Abelard's mistress, she wrote, than the Emperor's empress.

the-problem-of-evil.context_blurb:
The problem of evil is as old as philosophy: if God is all-good and all-powerful, why is there suffering? The puzzle has a logical form, which asks whether evil and such a God flatly contradict each other, and an evidential form, which asks whether the suffering we see makes that God unlikely. Serious thinkers stand on both sides, and the attacks and the defenses both have real strength.

Philosophers first split suffering in two: moral evil is harm that people choose, like a thief's beating, while natural evil, like a house falling in an earthquake, comes from blind nature and was chosen by no one, which makes it the harder case. Dostoevsky gave the problem its most painful scene, in The Brothers Karamazov. There Ivan describes to his brother Alyosha a five-year-old girl whom her own parents beat and then shut overnight in a freezing outhouse. Ivan refuses to accept that any final, perfect harmony could repay her suffering: no paradise, he says, is worth the tears of that one tortured child.

The oldest form of the attack is a trap known as the Epicurean paradox. If God wants to prevent evil but cannot, He lacks power; if He can but will not, He lacks goodness. And if He both can and will, the trap closes with its sharpest question: then whence comes evil, and from where does it arise? Leibniz replied that God weighed every possible world before creating, and claimed not that nothing here is bad but that among all the worlds God could have made, none was better overall: this is the best of all possible worlds. Voltaire's Candide mocked the idea through Dr. Pangloss, who calls everything for the best while catastrophes pile up. The free will defense, used by Augustine and in our own era by Alvin Plantinga, holds that goodness forced on a person would not be his own choice, so even an all-powerful God cannot make people freely choose only good, and a world of free people can be better than a world of puppets. William Rowe answered with an image: a fawn trapped by a lightning fire deep in a forest, burned and suffering for days where no one will ever know, and he asked what greater good such pain could possibly serve.

John Hick, drawing on the second-century bishop Irenaeus, replied with soul-making: courage grows only by facing danger and kindness only by facing real suffering, so a God who rescued us from every hardship would leave us moral infants, never able to win virtue for ourselves. Augustine had argued that evil has no existence of its own but is a lack of good, as rust is iron eaten away and blindness is sight gone missing; critics reply that a torturer's cruelty is no mere gap but something horribly active and present, so calling it an absence makes it sound far milder than it is. Ivan Karamazov, for his part, refuses heaven on such terms. It is not God he rejects, he tells Alyosha; he only most respectfully returns Him the ticket.

J. L. Mackie pressed the logical problem in 1955, arguing that evil and a God of perfect goodness and power could not coexist, but Plantinga's reply only had to show that a world with free creatures and some evil was possible. In 1982 Mackie himself conceded that the free will defense succeeds in showing there is no outright contradiction, admitting that the strongest form of his attack had failed, though he still held the problem was far from settled. So the fight moved to the evidential problem, which says evil makes God not impossible but unlikely, and its sharpest version rests on pain that seems to serve no purpose whatsoever, like Rowe's fawn. Stephen Wykstra answered with his "noseeum" argument: our minds are to an infinite mind as a one-month-old baby's are to its parents' plans, so the fact that we spot no reason for some suffering proves almost nothing, because a reason beyond our sight is exactly what we should expect. Even the famous trap is not quite what it seems: Epicurus' own surviving works never state it, and we have it only because the Christian writer Lactantius quoted it precisely in order to argue against it.

theodicy-the-free-will-and-soul-making-d.context_blurb:
If God is all-good and all-powerful, why is there suffering? A defence of God's goodness in the face of evil is called a theodicy. Two modern answers are the best developed: Alvin Plantinga's free-will defence and John Hick's soul-making theodicy. Each has serious defenders and sharp critics, and the question remains open.

The Australian philosopher J. L. Mackie pressed the problem in 1955. Grant that freedom is worth having, he said: could God not have created people who are fully free and yet in fact always choose rightly? Plantinga answered that this is no task an all-powerful being failed at, because it is no task at all. A choice God brings about is not a free choice, so not even omnipotence can guarantee people who are free and also never do wrong.

Plantinga went further. Imagine a person who, in every possible world where he exists and is truly free, goes wrong on at least one choice. Plantinga calls this transworld depravity. If it is even possible that every possible person suffers from it, then no matter which free beings God sets out to make, He cannot obtain a world that has moral good without any moral evil. Plantinga claims only that this is possible, not that it is true. Critics then asked about earthquakes and childhood cancer, which nobody chooses. Drawing on Augustine, Plantinga raised a possibility: such evils might come from the free choices of nonhuman persons, such as Satan and fallen angels.

Hick took another road. In an 1819 letter, the poet John Keats told his brother that the world is no vale of tears but the vale of Soul-making, a schoolroom whose troubles turn a raw intelligence into a soul. Hick borrowed the phrase. He argued that the world's hardness is deliberate, because goodness earned slowly through real moral struggle has a value in God's eyes that ready-made goodness lacks. His view follows Irenaeus, an early bishop of Lyon. Augustine pictured the first humans as perfect in Eden before their fall. Irenaeus put perfection at the end of the story: humans began immature and are still growing toward a perfection that lies ahead.

Marilyn McCord Adams pressed both answers with horrors such as a fawn burning slowly to death in a forest fire no one sees. Outweighing such pain with goods enjoyed by others elsewhere is not enough, she argued. God must defeat the horror inside the victim's own story, folding it into a life that turns out good for that very creature.

the-euthyphro-dilemma-applied.context_blurb:
Plato's dialogue the Euthyphro poses a question that has outlived every empire since: do God or the gods command what is good because it is good, or is it good because it is commanded? The question does not depend on which god you have in mind. It returns in Christian debates about divine command and in a great dispute within Islam, and serious believers and skeptics stand on both sides.

The scene is an Athenian court. Socrates waits there as the accused, charged with impiety and corrupting the young. Euthyphro has come as a prosecutor in a murder case, and the shock is whom he is prosecuting: his own father, over a labourer who died bound in a ditch. Socrates asks him what holiness is, and every answer slips loose. Socrates jokes that his words behave like the statues of his legendary ancestor Daedalus, which came to life and ran away. Pressed one final time, Euthyphro suddenly remembers that he must be somewhere else and hurries away.

Philosophers since have pressed each branch of the fork. On the first branch, God's command is the whole of goodness, with no reason standing behind it. Then God could have made cruelty good simply by ordering it. Gottfried Leibniz added that calling God good would then say nothing, since the word would fit whatever God willed; why praise him, if the opposite would have earned equal praise? On the second branch, God orders what is good because it is good already. Then goodness seems to stand above God, as a standard he must consult like a rulebook, and he becomes its follower rather than its source.

Some refuse the fork. Robert Adams located goodness in God's own loving nature, so a command to be cruel is not a real possibility, because it would contradict who God is. Others bit the first horn hard. William of Ockham held that God's will is bound by nothing except the rule against contradiction, so even hatred of God himself would be good, indeed required, if God commanded it. Muslim theologians had already split over the same fork centuries earlier. The Mu'tazila held that good and evil are real and knowable by reason. The Ash'aris, whose view largely won in Sunni theology, held that an act is good only because God commanded it, and that nothing about the act makes it good beforehand.

the-cosmological-argument.context_blurb:
The cosmological argument is one of the oldest routes to the conclusion that something must stand behind the universe. It starts from plain facts: things change, things come into being, things depend on other things. Thomas Aquinas, Islamic philosophers and the modern defender William Lane Craig have all built versions, and critics have attacked each one. Whether God exists stays an open question.

Underneath lies an old rule, in Latin ex nihilo nihil fit: nothing comes from nothing. A magician only seems to pull a rabbit from an empty hat; a real rabbit was hidden somewhere. Aquinas argued in his First Way that whatever moves is moved by something else, as a walking staff moves only when a hand shoves it, and that the chain of movers cannot stretch back forever, so something must have started the motion without being moved itself. Gottfried Leibniz saw the deepest question behind it all, why there is something rather than nothing, and answered with his principle that nothing exists without a sufficient reason.

During a radio debate in 1948, the Jesuit Frederick Copleston urged Bertrand Russell to grant that the universe requires an outside cause. Russell refused, replying that the universe is simply there, and that's all there is to say. Most first-time hearers ask what caused God. Defenders reply that the argument never said everything has a cause. In the kalam version, only what begins to exist needs a cause, so a being without a beginning falls outside the rule. Physics gave the debate a twist. In the late 1920s the Belgian priest and physicist Georges Lemaitre proposed that the universe grew from a tiny primeval atom, the seed of the Big Bang theory. Many hurried to say his physics proved creation, but Lemaitre warned that finding a starting point in the mathematics does not, on its own, show that anyone created it.

Russell pressed a sharper point. Each person has a mother, yet humanity as a whole does not. To argue that because each thing in the universe has a cause the universe itself must have one is to treat a property of every part as if it must belong to the whole, the fallacy of composition. Craig, defending the kalam, answers that the past cannot stretch back forever, because an actual infinity breeds absurdities. His favourite is Hilbert's Hotel, with infinitely many rooms and every one full. When a new guest arrives, the manager moves each guest up one room and leaves room 1 free. Critics reply that this is simply how infinite sets behave, not a true contradiction.
