the-design-argument-paleys-watch.context_blurb:
William Paley was an 18th-century English clergyman whose book Natural Theology opens with one of the most famous scenes in English philosophy: a walk across a heath and a watch lying in the grass. The design argument is far older than Paley, but his version made it famous and set it up to meet Charles Darwin's answer. The dispute is still live, with serious positions on each side.

Kick a stone on the heath, Paley says, and if you are asked where it came from, you could fairly answer that it has lain there forever. Find a watch, and that answer will not do, because its parts have been shaped and fitted to one another for a task. Complexity alone is not the mark, Paley insisted; the mark of a made thing is that its several parts work together to bring about one result, here pointing out the hour. From that, the inference is unavoidable. We need not know the craftsman's name or where his workshop stood; we reason from the evident workmanship in front of us to a workman we have never met. Paley then turned to the eye. It is built on the same laws of light, the bending of rays through lenses, as a telescope, so it carries exactly the same proof of having been made for seeing. The young Charles Darwin, while still a student, loved the book, which delighted him as much as Euclid; he accepted its premises without question and was won over completely, charmed and convinced.

Paley met objections in advance. A watch that runs badly, with sticking hands and parts whose use no one can see, is still obviously the product of design, flaws and all. Stranger still, imagine a watch that could make another watch like itself, carrying the moulds and tools inside. That would not remove the need for a maker; the design of the first watch would remain wholly unexplained. Richard Dawkins answered Paley in 1986 with a book titled The Blind Watchmaker. Dawkins agreed that creatures truly seem engineered for their tasks, but he said the building is done by the process Darwin found, which keeps whatever happens to work and scraps the rest, with no aim in view. It is neither a planner nor luck but a blind, cumulative filter.

Paley also rejected a clever dodge: that the watch is just one of the many shapes matter can fall into, produced by the workings of the laws of metal or by a principle of order. Naming such a law, he said, merely relabels the ordered thing we set out to explain. Darwin, in later life, decided that Paley's argument had failed after all. A clam's lovely hinge, he wrote, no longer demands an intelligent maker as a door's hinge does, because natural selection can shape well-fitted parts without any designer. Even before Paley wrote, David Hume had pressed another difference. We may infer a watchmaker from a watch because we have seen watches made many times over, but no one has ever watched a world being made, so there is no track record to reason from.

humes-reply-to-design.context_blurb:
David Hume's Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion appeared in 1779, after his death, because he knew they would stir controversy. In them the skeptic Philo presses objection after objection against Cleanthes, who defends the watchmaker argument that the world's order points to a designer. Hume kept his own final view ambiguous. Philo's lesson travels anywhere two things are compared on thin evidence, and his objections have real replies.

The engine of Philo's case is a rule about comparison: the more closely two things resemble each other, the more one's history tells you about the other. A girl whose bike matches her friend's in brand, model and year can fairly expect it to last as long, while her brother's scooter, which shares little beyond wheels, predicts almost nothing. Every step away from similarity, Philo said, weakens the evidence in proportion. He granted that a house surely had a builder, because we have seen builders put up house after house, but nobody has ever seen a universe being made. The universe is also one of a kind. Judging that something was made means comparing it with things we have watched being made, and a one-of-a-kind object has nothing to be compared with, whether it is a strange humming device with no maker's mark or the cosmos itself.

Philo also offered rival comparisons. In his view the world looks more like a living creature or a vegetable than like a watch, which would suggest it grew rather than being manufactured. And if loose resemblances count, why not a legend of the Brahmins, in which an infinite spider spun everything there is from his own belly? It is hard to say, Philo jabbed, why an ordered system could not come from a belly as well as from a brain.

Even granting the machine comparison, it does not deliver what Cleanthes wants. Great human projects such as ships and cities are built by crowds of workers laboring at once, so the analogy fits a committee of gods as well as a single one. Nor does a flawed world tell us much. Even if the order of things hints at a maker, it cannot vouch for his perfection, his skill, or even whether he is still alive. Perhaps, Philo mused, this world is the botched work of some lesser deity, or of an aged god now dead. That is not atheism, and it answers the friend who says suffering proves there was no maker.

Philo even revived the account of the Greek atomist Epicurus: over endless time matter tumbles through every possible arrangement, and only the self-sustaining ones last, so order needs no intention behind it. Scholars see in it a foreshadowing of natural selection. Yet when Philo finally gives his own verdict, he neither denies nor affirms a maker. A total suspense of judgment, he says, is our only reasonable course, since so feeble an analogy can decide the question neither way.

the-ontological-argument-and-its-critics.context_blurb:
Around 1078 Anselm, an Italian-born monk who later became Archbishop of Canterbury, wrote one of the strangest arguments in Western thought: a proof that God exists, worked out entirely in the head without a single glance at the world. Critics answered almost at once, and again six centuries later. The argument still has defenders as well as attackers, and the dispute is open.

Anselm already believed fully before he wrote a line. For him the proof was devotion, faith seeking understanding, and his motto put belief first and understanding second: he believed in order to understand. He would not argue from stars or living things. He started instead from one definition: God is the greatest thing anyone could conceive, that than which nothing greater can be thought.

His target was the fool of the Psalms, who tells himself privately that God does not exist. Even the fool understands the phrase when he hears it, Anselm said, and that act alone puts the being into his mind as an idea he now holds. Then the trap closes. Compare that idea with a rival: the very same being, except that it exists out in reality as well. The rival is greater, so a being that lived only in the mind would not be the greatest after all, and it must exist in reality too.

Anselm went further. A rock or a star exists, but you can easily picture it gone, and whatever you can picture as gone might really be gone. So the greatest being must be one that cannot even be thought of as absent.

A fellow monk, Gaunilo, replied on behalf of the fool. Imagine the most perfect island anyone could dream up, he said, and apply Anselm's steps to it. The same steps prove that the perfect island is real. Since that is absurd, the reasoning itself must be broken.

Some six centuries later Immanuel Kant pressed a deeper objection. A hundred real coins and a hundred imagined coins have exactly the same description; the real ones do not contain one coin more. The difference lies in what the real coins let you do, since only they can be spent. So existence is not a feature in the way that knowing everything is. To say a thing exists adds nothing to what it is like; it only says that the thing so described is actually there. Anselm, Kant concluded, had slipped existence into a list of perfections where it does not belong.

pascals-wager.context_blurb:
Blaise Pascal was a 17th-century French mathematician, inventor and devout Catholic thinker. Having helped build the mathematics of chance, he turned it on the largest question there is, and the result, Pascal's Wager, is often called the first serious argument in decision theory. Believers and skeptics have argued over it ever since, and it leaves the existence of God itself an open question.

Proofs and disproofs of God are common; Pascal did something odder. He granted at the start that reason cannot settle whether God is real, so his subject is how to act when you cannot find out, not whether God is there. And he insisted that everyone must choose. A friend who says he will stay neutral until the evidence comes in has already chosen, because the way he lives while waiting already places one of the two wagers; there is no seat on the fence. Denis Diderot answered that a Muslim cleric could run the very same reasoning for his own faith. The bet works for any religion that promises an endless reward, so it recommends all of them equally and picks out no one god. Pascal never finished or published the argument. It survives only as an unsorted scrap discovered in his papers after his death in 1662, later printed in his Pensées.

In 1654, in letters with Pierre de Fermat, Pascal solved an old gambler's puzzle, how to split the stakes fairly when a game of chance is broken off partway, and so launched probability theory. That November he lived through an overwhelming religious experience and jotted down a record that opens with one word, "Fire." He stitched the parchment inside his coat and kept it on him for the rest of his life, and no one knew of it until he died. His table of bets leans on one case. If you wager on God, living a life of faith and self-denial, and there turns out to be no God, what have you lost? Hardly anything, he said, just a few limited worldly pleasures, staked against an infinite prize; his critics reply that he waves away real costs too quickly. A man once told him the Wager convinced him but he still could not make himself believe. Pascal's startling advice was to behave as believers behave, using holy water and having Masses said, and belief would grow out of the habit.

Later thinkers sharpened the math and then turned it around. Ian Hacking set out its strongest form, which holds even for someone who rates the odds of God at one in a million. Multiply even the slimmest odds by an infinite reward and the expected value stays infinite, beating every finite alternative. Alan Hájek turned that engine against Pascal. If even a small chance of coming to believe is enough to collect the infinite reward, then tossing a coin to decide, or living as you please while keeping a faint possibility of converting at the end, earns the same infinite score, and wholehearted faith can no longer beat it. Voltaire and others found it unseemly to believe in God for a payoff, and Richard Dawkins made that objection bite on the table itself. An all-knowing God might reward sincere doubt over belief put on for profit, so wagering on God might cost you everything rather than nothing.

hume-on-miracles.context_blurb:
David Hume's essay on miracles, a short, surgical section of his first Enquiry, asks how much weight to give testimony that a miracle happened. Its lesson travels anywhere a surprising claim meets an uncertain source. Hume does not claim to prove that miracles never happen; he sets out how to weigh a report, and the answer tends to come out skeptical. His critics' replies deserve their say too.

The essay runs on one line: a wise man proportions his belief to the evidence. If a friend swears he saw a stone float up into the sky, set your confidence by how much evidence supports the claim, after subtracting whatever evidence tells against it. For Hume a miracle meant a violation of nature's laws, such as a resurrection or water becoming wine. A single report of such a break lands on a scale already loaded on the other side with all the experience that established the law to begin with. So when a man claimed to have watched the dead return to life, Hume asked whether it was more likely that the witness was lying or deceived, or that a corpse truly lived again. He treated the witness's error as a lesser marvel in its own right, set on the scale against the greater, and rejected whichever was the bigger stretch.

Hence his strict rule: no testimony can establish a miracle unless its being false would be even more miraculous than the event it reports. He tried the rule on the strongest pagan wonder-story he knew. Tacitus records that Vespasian, while in Alexandria, cured two sufferers, restoring a blind man's sight using his own saliva and healing a lame man with the touch of his foot. The witnesses were good and had no motive to lie, and Hume still rejected the report.

His hardest case was the healings claimed in the 1730s at the grave of the Abbé Paris, vouched for by judges of good name and never disproved. Against that cloud of witnesses, Hume admitted, he could set only the plain impossibility of what they described, which is exactly where critics say he begs the question. In 1777 Richard Price argued that Hume had rigged his scales. Never having seen a dead man rise is only an empty space in our experience, yet Hume treated it as though it were a failed test, proof against the event. In 1837 Charles Babbage answered with arithmetic. If witnesses usually tell the truth and report independently, a large enough number of them can outweigh the improbability, so that testimony could in principle win, which turns Hume's own balancing test against his never. John Earman later pressed the same point.

the-hiddenness-of-god.context_blurb:
The hiddenness argument is one of the sharpest modern arguments against the existence of a loving God, set out by the Canadian philosopher J. L. Schellenberg in 1993. The complaint that God cannot be found is as old as the Psalms, but Schellenberg gave it new force. The replies are serious, and the contest is still open.

His signature picture is a small child lost in a dark forest, crying for her mother. A loving mother who hears and is able to come will come; only something beyond her power could keep her silent. Nothing is beyond the power of an all-powerful God, so His silence toward a sincere seeker has no such excuse. Schellenberg also points to the map of belief. A child born in Thailand usually grows up Buddhist, one born in Saudi Arabia Muslim, and millions in the secular West believe nothing. What people end up believing, he argues, tracks where they grew up, not how honestly they searched.

The ache itself is ancient. The prophet Isaiah cried that God is a God who hides himself, Martin Luther came back to the hidden God again and again, and mystics wrote of the dark night of the soul. Schellenberg's new move was to turn that old cry of longing into a precise, step-by-step argument.

Defenders reply that God stays hidden deliberately, so that faith, humility and longing have room to grow. Schellenberg grants these are real goods, but he answers that none of them seems weighty enough to leave a sincere seeker entirely shut out of the relationship that was the whole point. He is no scornful atheist. He calls his outlook skeptical religion and holds that his argument refutes only the personal, loving God of theism, leaving open some impersonal Ultimate. His steps run roughly so: perfect love would keep God always open to a relationship with any willing person; no one can knowingly relate to a being he does not believe in; yet some honest seekers never come to believe; so there is no perfectly loving God. Critics seldom deny that sincere nonbelievers exist. The step they dispute is whether perfect love really must make belief available to every sincere seeker.

william-james-and-the-will-to-believe.context_blurb:
William James was an American psychologist and philosopher of the late 1800s, a founder of pragmatism. His essay The Will to Believe answers a strict rule laid down by the mathematician W. K. Clifford: never believe anything on insufficient evidence. James argued that in certain special cases we may believe before the evidence is in. Neither side has settled the matter.

Clifford began with a ship's owner who privately doubts that his ageing emigrant vessel can still cross the ocean safely. He smothers his doubts, recalling her many safe voyages, and waves her off cheerfully; she sinks with everyone aboard. The guilt, said Clifford, came before she ever sailed: the wrong lay in how he arrived at his comfortable belief that she was safe, a belief his evidence never entitled him to.

James's own life had shown him another side. Around 1870, aged about twenty-eight, he sank into years of despair, fearing that his will was an illusion. After reading Charles Renouvier, he vowed in his diary that the opening use of his free will would be the decision to believe in it, and he later credited that vow with his recovery.

James answered Clifford that a thinker has two duties: to know the truth and to avoid error. Clifford obeys only the second. Yet turning down every belief that carries risk is a choice too, and it can lose you a truth you might have had. Some facts come true only if people believe in them in advance. A few highwaymen can rob a whole train car of brave passengers, because each fears he will be shot if he moves first. If every rider trusted that the whole car would rise together, it would, and the robbery would never happen.

James limited this right to believe to genuine options the evidence cannot settle. One condition is that each side must be live, a real and tempting possibility for the person facing it. For his New England audience, agnostic or Christian was live; theosophist or Muslim was not. That is why his argument is not Pascal's wager. Pascal bets on an infinite reward; James notes that a Muslim leader could press the same bet on Western readers and it would fall flat. James's case applies only where the option already has a hold on the person.

In his Edinburgh lectures of 1901 and 1902, James studied religion as lived experience. He sorted believers into the healthy-minded, at ease in life's goodness, and the sick souls, who must pass through despair. Far from calling the sick soul merely gloomier, he held that the sick soul sees a wider range of life, bitter truths included, that cheerful people overlook.

faith-vs-evidence-kierkegaards-leap.context_blurb:
Søren Kierkegaard was a Danish writer of the 1800s, often counted among the founders of existentialism, whose work wrestles with what it means to be a Christian for real rather than for show. His leap of faith is one side of a sharp fork. On the other side stands the English mathematician W. K. Clifford, who held that every belief must be earned by evidence. Each side has serious defenders, and the dispute is unresolved.

Clifford's case begins with a shipowner who doubts that his old emigrant ship is still seaworthy. He smothers the doubt with fond memories of earlier voyages, never orders a survey of her hull, and lets her sail; every soul on board drowns. His wrong, Clifford said, was that he trusted the ship without having earned that trust through patient, honest investigation; he got his confidence by stifling his doubts. Clifford spoke from inside science, not against it. A gifted mathematician, dead of tuberculosis at thirty-three, he proposed decades before Einstein that gravity could simply be space itself curving. Kierkegaard's own life held a leap. In 1840 he became engaged to Regine Olsen, then decided he must give her up for his calling as a writer. He played the part of a cold, cruel cad on purpose, so that she would be the one to end it.

Clifford added a hard twist. Had the same ship, trusted in the same careless way, happened to come home safe, the owner would be just as guilty: the wrong was done when he formed the belief dishonestly, and no stroke of luck afterward can undo it. Nor is belief a private affair. Every belief spills over into what we say and do, so one man's careless believing loosens the whole community's grip on truth. Believing on too little evidence, Clifford concluded, is wrong always, everywhere and for anyone. Kierkegaard pictured faith the opposite way, not as standing on solid ground but as staying joyful while suspended above water seventy thousand fathoms deep. Faith, for him, is an objective uncertainty held fast with the most passionate inner conviction. Without risk, he said, there is no faith.

In Fear and Trembling (1843) Kierkegaard turned to Abraham, who travels for three days ready to give up his son Isaac at God's command, against the plain moral law. Kierkegaard claimed that faith can raise one individual, for a time, above the moral rules that bind everyone, a move he called the teleological suspension of the ethical. Evidentialists find this monstrous; Kierkegaard found it the purest faith, and scholars read the book as his own story of giving up Regine. He even held that proving God like a theorem would destroy faith, because faith means staking your trust exactly where no certainty can be had. William James answered Clifford in 1896. Holding out for proof, James argued, can cost a person truths as surely as believing too fast can fool him. Still, he let the passions decide only when a choice is live, forced and momentous: both sides are real possibilities for you, refusing to choose is itself a choice, and the stakes are serious.

bacons-four-idols-of-the-mind.context_blurb:
Francis Bacon was an English philosopher, lawyer and statesman who rose to Lord Chancellor in the early 1600s. In the Novum Organum, the New Instrument, published in 1620, he listed four Idols, four traps the human mind walks into without noticing. He meant them as a portable checklist, something to catch yourself in during ordinary life, and each has its own cause and cure.

The Idols of the Tribe are flaws built into every human mind. Bacon said the mind is not a clean, flat mirror but an uneven one, which blends its own nature into what it reflects, so the image comes back bent. Wishful thinking is one of these flaws. A boy who instantly trusts the sunny forecast over the rainy one before a beach trip is believing what he would rather were true, and he cannot see his own wanting. The Idols of the Marketplace come from words, which people mint in everyday talk. Two friends who argue for an hour over whether a movie monster is a real dragon, yet would draw the same creature, have let a slippery word take the wheel, steering the argument instead of serving it; Bacon called these the most troublesome traps of all. The Idols of the Cave come from your own private world, your upbringing and pet obsessions. A scholar who has studied only bees for thirty years and drags every dinner topic back to bees has made his narrow specialty the lens for every question.

The Tribe has deeper habits too. The mind loves neatness and imagines more pattern in the world than nature actually put there, which is why astronomers kept forcing perfect circles onto lopsided planetary orbits long after the measurements refused to fit. Even the senses mislead. Bacon compared them to an enchanted glass that bends whatever passes through it, which is exactly why he demanded instruments and controlled experiments to correct the mistakes the unaided senses make. The fourth trap, the Idols of the Theatre, comes from the grand philosophical systems students were taught to admire. Each is like a play on a stage: a made-up world that seems real while you sit in the theater and has never faced the world outside. Bacon's sharpest charge was that nobody who holds such a system worked it out for himself; he was given a finished script and accepted it.

Bacon meant the four as a checklist to run on yourself. A man certain that his own family's holidays and table manners are simply the right way to live, with everyone else in error, is caught in the Cave: he mistakes the private world he grew up in for the plain way things are. In the Marketplace, the worst word-trap is a name for something that does not exist. Learned men of his day argued at length over Fortune, as if it were a power, and over an Element of Fire supposed to sit above the air; such words point at nothing, yet they summon a ghost that the mind then argues about in earnest. Bacon also sorted the four by origin. The Tribe and the Cave are inborn, part of human nature, so they can only be watched and checked. The Marketplace and the Theatre come in from outside, through language and through doctrines handed down, so in principle they can be cleared away.

Bacon did not flinch from naming giants. Among the Theatre's systems he called the superstitious kind the worst, and he accused Pythagoras, along with Plato and Plato's followers, of tangling the study of nature up with religion and mystical lore, so that faith nobody had tested passed itself off as knowledge. The list was only the opening move of a larger plan. The Novum Organum was meant to replace Aristotle's logic, and the Idols had to be cleared away before any building could start, because a mind stuffed with false images cannot take in new knowledge built up patiently from evidence. You cannot fill a cup that is already full of phantoms.

knowledge-is-power-and-the-experimental-.context_blurb:
Francis Bacon was an English statesman and philosopher who rose to Lord Chancellor under King James I before falling in a bribery scandal in 1621. He became the loud prophet of a new way of knowing, a break from the medieval habit of answering every question about the natural world by citing Aristotle. His slogan still echoes: knowledge rightly gained is power over nature. Critics still argue whether science really works the way he described.

The scholars of his day reasoned from authority about how nature ought to behave. Bacon said real knowledge starts with gathering many particular observations firsthand and only then, carefully, drawing general conclusions. He distrusted the unaided senses too, calling them an enchanted glass. The same instinct shows in his essay Of Studies, which compares reading to eating: a reader should merely taste some books, swallow others, and chew and digest only a few, weighing what he reads rather than gulping it down on trust. His death was a test of his own method. In late March 1626, crossing snowy Highgate by coach, he wondered whether cold could keep meat fresh, so he bought a hen and stuffed it with snow himself. He caught a chill that turned to pneumonia, and he was dead within days.

Dying, he dictated a last letter comparing himself to Pliny the Elder, who lost his life studying the eruption of Vesuvius, and he reported that as for the experiment itself, it had worked excellently well. That devotion matched his creed. Human knowledge and human power meet in one, he wrote, because no one can produce an effect without knowing its cause. Hence his paradox that nature, to be commanded, must be obeyed: mastery comes from submitting to nature's real workings first and only then turning them to human use.

Bacon mocked two failed kinds of thinker with insects. The ant merely hoards facts; the spider weaves webs of theory from its own insides. The true natural philosopher is a bee: it collects material from the flowers of observation and then transforms it by reason, letting the world correct the mind. He showed the method on heat. He drew up tables of things that are hot, of similar things that stay cold, such as moonlight, and of cases where heat rises and falls, then crossed off every candidate that failed. Light was struck off, for instance, because it can occur without heat. He concluded that heat is a swift motion of the tiny particles inside a body, remarkably close to the modern view.

galileo-authority-vs-observation.context_blurb:
Galileo Galilei was a seventeenth-century Italian mathematician and astronomer who turned an improved spyglass on the sky and saw things no one had ever seen. Later the Roman Inquisition tried him for defending Copernicus's sun-centered picture of the heavens. The real story is messier than brave scientist against wicked church, but the question he left behind endures: when careful observation collides with an authoritative text, which one wins?

The telescope was a Dutch invention; Galileo learned of it secondhand and improved the lenses until his instrument enlarged things twenty or thirty times. In August 1609 he climbed the campanile of St. Mark's with the rulers of Venice and sold them on its military use, promising it would let them sight hostile fleets long before they reached port. The Senate rewarded him with a professorship at Padua for life. Merchants kept their spyglasses trained on the horizon; Galileo pointed his upward, at the stars. On January 7, 1610, he noticed three small points of light beside Jupiter that no chart showed, and after a week of watching he understood they were moons circling Jupiter itself, the first clear proof that not everything in the sky goes around the Earth.

Aristotle had taught that everything beyond the Earth was flawless and changeless. Through the telescope the Moon proved to be a battered landscape of peaks and pits; Galileo's training in the painter's art of light and shadow let him read its moving shadows as real mountains and valleys. He named Jupiter's moons the Medicean Stars after the Medici, who ruled Florence, a calculated bid for a patron, and the Grand Duke made him his court mathematician and philosopher.

Late in 1610 he watched Venus for months, showing every phase from slender crescent to almost full disk, and growing and shrinking as it changed. The Earth-centered system could never produce that, so the only explanation was that Venus circles the Sun, the first physical evidence for Copernicus. Saturn baffled him, since his crude telescope showed its rings as two bumps. He mailed fellow astronomers a scrambled line of letters, an anagram of the Latin for I have observed the highest planet to be three-bodied: the jumble let him prove later that he had seen it first, without exposing the claim before he was sure.

His downfall was no simple clash of church and science. Pope Urban VIII had once admired him and permitted him to discuss Copernicus's system in print, provided he gave both systems an even hearing. In his 1632 Dialogue, Galileo put Urban's own favorite argument into the mouth of Simplicio, the dim-witted character, and the Pope felt mocked; a powerful friend became an enemy. At his 1633 trial, under threat of torture, Galileo knelt and renounced his teaching, and his sentence was house arrest at his villa near Florence, where he lived on, going blind, until 1642. Legend says he muttered eppur si muove, and yet it moves, but the line first appeared in print more than a century later. Another favorite tale, of priests who refused to look through his telescope, is mostly wrong too. The two men who would not look were academic rivals, the philosophers Cesare Cremonini and Giulio Libri, not clergymen, while the Jesuit astronomers Christopher Clavius and Christopher Grienberger looked and confirmed what he saw.

the-copernican-revolution-and-cosmic-hum.context_blurb:
Nicolaus Copernicus was a Polish canon of the Catholic Church who spent decades on an astronomy manuscript and published it only as he lay dying, in the early 1500s. For over a thousand years European scholars, following Ptolemy and Aristotle, had set the Earth at the fixed center of the cosmos. Copernicus moved it, and the aftershocks reached philosophy and theology as well as astronomy.

One of his showpieces was the strange backward loop of Mars. Night after night the planet drifts one way, then for some weeks it halts and creeps in reverse. Ptolemy's system explained this with circles bolted onto circles. Copernicus made it a trick of perspective: faster Earth, racing round on the inner track, overtakes slower Mars, which then appears to slide backward as we go by, the way a slow car seems to drift back when a fast one passes it. Critics had a serious objection. Aristotle argued that if the Earth spun east, a stone let fall from a high tower ought to strike the ground well to the west. Galileo answered with a ship. Let a ball fall from the top of a ship's mast while the ship glides smoothly along, and it lands at the foot of the mast, because the ball is already moving with the ship and carries that motion down with it.

Copernicus's real leap was about where we stand. The ground beneath our feet is not the still hub of everything; it is one ordinary planet among many, itself moving around the Sun. Careful astronomers resisted with real evidence. If Earth circles the Sun, nearby stars should seem to shift back and forth over a year as we view them from different places, a shift called parallax. No one could see it. A careful skeptic was left with two choices that both seemed absurd: either Earth does not move, or the stars lie at unimaginably vast distances.

The usual moral is that Copernicus humbled humanity by knocking us out of the place of honour. The historian Dennis Danielson points out that medieval thinkers did not see the center that way. To Pico della Mirandola the middle of the Earth was the world's filthy dregs, and Dante placed Hell there. Read in that light, the Copernican move was a promotion, lifting Earth out of the cosmic basement to join the circling heavens. Proof that Earth moves took nearly three hundred years. In 1838 Friedrich Bessel finally measured the parallax of the star 61 Cygni: about 0.31 arcseconds, roughly a third of an arcsecond, like the width of a coin seen from miles away, which put the star about ten light-years off. The skeptics' absurd option had been right all along: the stars really are that far away, and Earth really does move.

newtons-clockwork-universe.context_blurb:
Isaac Newton, the solitary English mathematician of the late 1600s, published his Principia in 1687. Its three laws of motion and its law of universal gravitation let the same equations govern a falling stone and a wheeling planet. The orderly cosmos his physics suggested raised hard questions for the next two centuries, about God, about scientific method and about human choice.

The apple legend is half true. No apple ever struck Newton's head. But in 1726 he told his friend William Stukeley over dinner that, sitting in the orchard at Woolsthorpe, he had watched an apple fall and wondered why it always dropped straight to the ground, never off to the side or upward. Push Newton's lawful universe to an extreme, called hard determinism, and each event, down to a single nerve impulse, is fixed by whatever came just before. Picture a girl raising her hand in class. The clockwork leaves her motion untouched; what it threatens is the claim that she could truly have done otherwise, and philosophers still divide over whether free choice survives.

His boldest idea was that heaven and earth run on a single set of laws. To test it, Newton asked whether the force that pulls an apple down, thinned out by distance, could also keep the Moon circling the Earth once a month. It could: one force, weakening with the square of the distance, drops the apple and bends the Moon's path, where earlier scholars had assumed earthly and heavenly things ran on different principles.

Critics demanded the deeper cause behind gravity. In 1713 Newton answered with a famous line, "I frame no hypotheses": he would describe the pattern he could measure, but he would not pass off an untested story about what lies behind gravity as established fact. Other thinkers drew a theology from his tidy cosmos that was not his own. The Deists pictured God as a watchmaker who assembles the cosmos like a clock, sets it ticking with a single winding and leaves it alone.

The twist is that Newton himself denied the clock was self-running. In his view the planets' small irregularities would pile up unless God now and then set the system right. Gottfried Leibniz pounced: a God who must keep mending His own work is an unskilled craftsman, because a fine maker builds a clock that never needs fixing. Newton's friend Samuel Clarke replied that a world running with no help from God is the very picture of materialism and fate. Pierre-Simon Laplace pushed the clockwork to its limit in 1814, imagining an intellect that knew the position and motion of every particle. For such a mind nothing would be uncertain, and the future would lie before it as plainly as the past.

pascals-thinking-reed.context_blurb:
Blaise Pascal was a 17th-century French mathematician and physicist who, with Fermat, laid the foundations of probability, proved that air has weight with a famous barometer test on a mountain, and built one of the first calculating machines. After a religious experience in 1654 he began a defense of the Christian faith that he never finished. His scattered notes became the Pensées, full of startling lines about being human under the vast new sky that Copernicus and Galileo had opened.

Pascal felt the enlarged universe as something that could unsettle a thinking person, not merely dazzle one. What frightened him in those infinite spaces was not their size but their endless silence: a vastness that never replies. Yet he turned the dread into dignity. A man is a reed, the feeblest thing in nature, which a vapor or a drop of water can kill, but he is a thinking reed. If the whole universe crushed him, he would still be nobler than what killed him, because he knows that he dies, while the universe has no idea of it. Pascal also urged his reader to gaze outward to the endless reaches beyond the stars, then inward into a tiny mite, with worlds nested inside worlds and no end to the smallness. A man hangs between the two abysses: nothing compared with the infinite, all compared with nothingness.

bacons-death-by-snow.context_blurb:
Francis Bacon was the great prophet of the experimental method in early-1600s England: stop settling questions about nature by argument and start settling them by trial. The story of his last days, told by the gossipy biographer John Aubrey some fifty years later and probably polished along the way, packs his whole method into one scene.

One freezing day in 1626, riding near Highgate, Bacon wondered whether snow could keep meat fresh the way salt does. He climbed out of his coach, bought a hen from a woman nearby, had her gut it and helped stuff the body full of snow with his own hands, an old statesman kneeling on an icy road.

He caught a chill and was dead within days. Dying, he wrote to the Earl of Arundel that the experiment itself had succeeded excellently well. The snow preserved the hen, but the cold he braved to test it was killing him: the method won and the man lost.

In the same letter Bacon reached for an ancient comfort. He said he had nearly shared the fortune of Pliny the Elder, the Roman scholar who died trying to study the eruption of Mount Vesuvius. Both men were killed by the very thing they went out to study, a fitting end for a life spent insisting that we go and check.

descartes-methodic-doubt-and-the-evil-de.context_blurb:
René Descartes was a seventeenth-century French mathematician and soldier-turned-philosopher, the inventor of the coordinate geometry still named for him and the figure usually counted as the opening act of modern philosophy. In his Meditations on First Philosophy, published in 1641, he set himself a ruthless task: to doubt everything that could possibly be doubted, and see what was left standing.

His new way of thinking, he later wrote, began on a November day in 1619, when winter stranded him near Ulm and he spent the whole day shut up alone in a small room warmed by a stove, free to talk with himself about his own thoughts. His rule was harsh: any belief with the slightest room for doubt would be treated as false. The point was not despair. He wanted to learn whether any belief at all could withstand every doubt, a bedrock to build on. He began gently, with the senses. A distant tower can look round and prove square when you walk up to it, so the senses sometimes deceive us and cannot be fully trusted. To push doubt to its limit, he imagined a malicious demon of supreme power and cunning, a being that spends all its energy deceiving him about everything. It is the nightmare of the film The Matrix, three and a half centuries early: the fear that everything you experience could be a flawless forgery piped in from outside. Later philosophers such as Gilbert Harman and Hilary Putnam retold the same worry as the brain in a vat.

Dreams sharpened the doubt. Descartes seemed to be sitting by the fire in his dressing gown with a page in his hand, yet he had often dreamed such plain scenes and believed them completely. Since no sure sign marks waking off from dreaming, even this moment might be a dream. So he treated his beliefs like a basket of apples hiding a few rotten ones. One rotten belief left in the basket can spoil the rest, and picking through them one at a time would let the rot spread, so he tipped the whole basket out and put back only the apples he could see were sound.

Even in a dream, though, two plus three still comes to five, and squares still have just four sides. If even arithmetic stood undoubted, his tearing down was not yet total, so Descartes gave his imagined deceiver one more staggering power. The demon might corrupt his reasoning itself, making him err every time he added two and three, something no dream could do. The first Meditation ends in dread, not triumph. Descartes compares himself to a prisoner enjoying a dream of freedom who starts to realize it is a dream and dreads waking, fearing that waking would drop him out of this light into a darkness he could never escape.

Then he found the one crack the deceiver could never reach. Let the demon fool him as much as it liked, it could never make him nothing while he thought he was something. Anyone who is being deceived must exist in order to be fooled. Archimedes boasted that he could move the earth if only he had one fixed point to stand on, and Descartes now had his: his own thinking, the one thing he could not doubt while he was doing it. Even the deceiver's name was chosen with care. He called it genius malignus in Latin, the malicious genius, and he wrote just after the Inquisition condemned Galileo in 1633. Church doctrine held that God cannot deceive, yet an all-powerful liar might look like God himself, so pinning the deception on a demon spared Descartes the charge of casting God as the arch-deceiver.

i-think-therefore-i-am-the-cogito.context_blurb:
Having pushed doubt as far as it could go, René Descartes looked for anything that would survive it. The Latin tag cogito ergo sum, usually translated as I think, therefore I am, is the line most people remember from that search, though his Meditations reaches the conclusion without the catchphrase. What matters is the move's strange shape: the harder you push against your own existence, the more the pushing proves it. The cornerstone has been attacked and defended ever since.

The story begins in 1619, when Descartes was a young soldier wintering near Ulm. One freezing day he withdrew by himself into a small chamber warmed by a tiled stove, a poêle, thought all day, then had three vivid dreams he later read as a calling. The heart of the cogito is simple. Try to doubt that you exist and you fail, because every act of doubting requires someone who doubts, so the doubter must exist.

Against an all-powerful deceiver, Descartes flung a bold boast: however hard the demon tries, it can never make him nothing so long as he thinks himself something. The thought first appeared in print not in Latin but in French, je pense, donc je suis, in his Discourse on Method of 1637, written in the everyday language to reach readers beyond the scholars; the Latin form came in 1644. Once sure that he existed, he asked what this I is. Stripping away everything he could still doubt, he concluded that he is a thing that thinks: one that doubts, understands, affirms and wills, and also imagines and senses. His body and brain were still open to doubt.

In the Meditations he wrote only I am, I exist, leaving out the word therefore, because he did not reach it by deduction at all; he grasped it, he said, by a simple intuition, a truth seen at once. Readers soon pointed out that Augustine, in The City of God around 410, had turned the skeptics' favorite worry back on them. He argued that if he was deceived, then he existed, since what does not exist cannot be fooled. About six hundred years before Descartes, the Persian philosopher Avicenna had imagined a man created floating in midair with no senses at all, who would still be sure that he himself exists. When Pierre Gassendi mocked the argument with I walk, therefore I am, Descartes had an answer. In a dream you seem to walk while your legs lie still, so walking proves anything only through your being aware of it, and that awareness is a thought.

Descartes was careful about how much the certainty covered. I exist is guaranteed only while the thinking is actually happening; should he cease from thinking altogether, he said, he might cease to exist. Even the fear that he is dreaming cannot touch it, since a seeming still needs someone to whom things seem. Right after the proof, he confessed that he still lacked a clear grasp of what this I might be. That gap invited the sharpest objection. We say it rains without imagining a rainer, Georg Lichtenberg noted, so perhaps we should say only that it thinks. On that view the thinking shows only that thought is happening, not that a single lasting self is its owner.

the-dream-argument.context_blurb:
Before he imagined an evil deceiver, the French philosopher Rene Descartes opened his Meditations with a gentler worry that anyone can test. Vivid dreams feel exactly as real from the inside as waking life does. If nothing in experience marks a moment as waking rather than dreaming, then everything the senses report might be dream-stuff. The worry is ancient, and it keeps returning in new costumes.

A boy who pinches his arm to prove he is awake proves nothing, because a dreamed pinch can sting every bit as much. A girl who simply knows she is awake is no better off. Inside a dream you feel exactly that sure, so the certainty cannot tell waking from dreaming. Descartes met the doubt while sitting by his fire in a winter gown, holding a sheet of paper. He recalled nights when he had felt equally certain of sitting there, yet had in fact been asleep in bed, so this very moment might be one of those dreams. Centuries earlier and a world away, the Chinese sage Zhuangzi dreamed of life as a butterfly, happily drifting from bloom to bloom, then woke as a man and wondered whether he might really be a butterfly now dreaming of being a man.

Descartes aimed the dream at a bigger target. If no sure sign separates waking from sleeping, then nothing the senses report can be fully trusted, because any sight, sound or touch might belong to a dream. Yet the doubt has a limit. Asleep or awake, two and three make five and a square has four sides: truths of arithmetic and geometry hold whether or not any object is real. The modern heir is the brain in a vat, made famous by Hilary Putnam and put on screen by The Matrix. A brain wired to a computer would live a fed-in life that felt from the inside just like the real one, so it could never tell the difference.

mind-body-dualism-and-the-pineal-gland.context_blurb:
René Descartes, the 17th-century French philosopher, split the human being in two. The mind, he held, has no size, shape or location, while the body is matter spread out in space like a stone or a clock. That neat split raised a famous puzzle, pressed hard in his own lifetime, and every later philosophy of mind has had to answer it. The position is still contested: modern materialists reject it, and some religious traditions defend a form of it.

Descartes said reality holds two utterly different kinds of stuff. Mind is defined by thinking and takes up no space; body is defined by taking up space and does no thinking. Because their defining features are opposites, he argued, mind and body are two separate substances, each able to exist without the other. That left a question physicians had long debated: where does the soul meet the body? Descartes chose a tiny organ in the middle of the brain, the pineal gland, as the one spot where the soul does its work.

Critics seized on the snag at once. Moving a solid object takes a push, and a push takes contact between surfaces. A mind with no size and no place has no surface at all, so how could it ever shove solid matter? This is the interaction problem. Descartes himself pointed to a fact that sits uneasily with his split. A ship's captain can see a hole in his hull without feeling any pain, because he merely rides in the ship. Yet when injury or hunger strikes your own body, you feel the pain and the hunger as your own, which showed Descartes that mind and body are mixed together into a single whole, not merely lodged side by side like a pilot in his vessel. The pineal gland, once biologists understood it, proved far humbler than a seat of the soul. It releases the hormone melatonin in darkness, and it sets the body's daily rhythm of sleeping and waking.

Descartes' account of the machinery was vivid. Nerves, he thought, were hollow tubes carrying animal spirits, a swift, fiery breeze of tiny particles. The soul could not heave an arm itself; it merely nudged the gland, and the slightest nudge steered the breeze into particular tubes, inflating those muscles so that they pulled. He modeled the body on the moving fountain statues of the king's gardens at Saint-Germain-en-Laye, whose limbs were driven by water forced through hidden pipes. The soul at the gland, he wrote, works like a fountain-keeper posted at the water tanks from which the pipes run. Critics struck back. The anatomist Thomas Willis found the same gland, large and healthy, in beasts that seemed to have almost no imagination or memory, sheep among them; if a sheep has one, it cannot be the seat of a soul only humans possess. Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia, aged twenty-four, wrote Descartes a letter in 1643 now regarded as the earliest sharp framing of the mind-body puzzle. She turned his own picture of the soul against him: a thing that only thinks, with no extension, could never set a body moving, since causing motion seems to need contact.

That June Elisabeth went further. She told him it would be easier for her to grant the soul matter and extension, size and place like a body, than to believe that a thing with neither could move a body or be moved by one. In 1669 the anatomist Nicolas Steno dissected the gland to test Descartes' claim that it dangled freely, ready to rock like a little lever. He found it firmly anchored and surrounded by veins, not the arteries Descartes had described, so it could not tilt the way the theory required.

the-wax-argument.context_blurb:
In his second Meditation, published in 1641, René Descartes pauses for a small household experiment with a piece of beeswax. He uses it to pull apart two ideas of what knowing a physical thing means: the reports of the senses, or a deeper power of the mind. The empiricists John Locke and David Hume later read the same melting wax very differently.

Fresh from the comb, the wax has a flowery scent and a honey taste; it is hard and cold, and it rings when tapped. Descartes holds it near the fire. Its scent and flavour disappear, its colour alters, its shape slumps into a hot liquid, and tapping it gives no sound. Every quality his senses reported has changed. Yet, Descartes insists, the puddle is the very same wax he began with; no one denies it.

What held on to the wax through the change? Not the eyes, the tongue or the fingers, since each of them reported something different after the melting. It was his understanding, a power of mind the senses cannot supply. Nor can imagination do the job, because the wax can take on countless shapes, more than any picture in the head can hold, so only the pure intellect grasps it. Strip away everything the fire changed and what remains is the wax's real nature: something extended, spread out in length, breadth and depth.

Descartes found the same lesson at a window. Looking down at the street, he says he sees men, but what his eyes actually catch is hats and coats that might hide clockwork machines. The real work, which he had been giving his eyes credit for, is done by his judgment, concluding that men are wearing the coats.

The wax was never really about wax. Every judgment Descartes makes about it shows him something even more certainly than the wax itself: that he exists as a thinking thing. The mind, he concludes, is better known than any body.

spinoza-god-or-nature-excommunicated-and.context_blurb:
Baruch Spinoza was a 17th-century Dutch Jew of Portuguese descent who became one of the most radical thinkers in Western philosophy. His Amsterdam community cast him out at twenty-three, and he spent the rest of his short life in rented rooms, earning his living by hand and writing in Latin. Jewish, Christian and atheist readers still argue over his God, agreeing only on how startling it is.

In the summer of 1656 the rabbis declared a cherem against him, a solemn ban and curse. The community had banned others before, but Spinoza's ban was the harshest it ever issued, and unlike all the rest it was never lifted. No one was to speak to him, trade with him or read his words. He answered quietly. His Hebrew name Baruch means blessed, and from then on he signed himself Benedictus, the Latin name with the same meaning. He also took care. After a fanatic tried to stab him, his letters carried a seal showing a thorny rose and one Latin word, Caute: be careful. Turning down fame, he earned his bread by grinding optical lenses for microscopes and telescopes. Years of breathing fine glass dust probably scarred his lungs, and he died of consumption in 1677, aged forty-four.

The idea that got him cast out was partly about God, and he built his whole philosophy on it. His phrase Deus sive Natura, God or Nature, says that God and Nature are one and the same, with no separate creator standing outside the world. Only one thing truly exists in its own right, needing nothing else: a single infinite, eternal substance. Every rock, mind and person is a mode of it: not a thing standing on its own, but a passing modification of the one substance. He set all this out in the Ethics, written like Euclid's geometry, with each step closed by Q.E.D. His aim was not disguise but force: anyone who granted his few opening self-evident truths would be compelled, step by logical step, to grant everything that followed.

When Heidelberg's university invited him in 1673 to take its chair of philosophy, the letter promised wide freedom to teach, with one proviso: the prince was confident he would not misuse it to unsettle the state's religion. Spinoza politely declined. He saw that the single condition quietly took back the very freedom the offer granted. He preferred his craft, and he practised it superbly. In 1665 the famous astronomer Christiaan Huygens, a lens grinder himself, spent a night beside Spinoza as the two men aimed a thirty-foot telescope at the planet Jupiter.

For Spinoza nothing is merely possible: everything that happens flows from God-or-Nature with the same necessity by which a triangle's angles are fixed by its definition. That rules out miracles in the strict sense. His claim is not just that a seeming miracle has a natural cause we have yet to find; it is that nothing whatever can run contrary to Nature, so a true miracle cannot happen at all. He also dissolved an old puzzle about how a choice can lift a hand, or how an injury can grieve the mind. Mind and body, for Spinoza, are one single reality described in two ways, so neither ever pushes the other. The highest human good, he wrote, is the intellectual love of God, the delight a mind takes in truly understanding Nature. As its ideas come to mirror the eternal order of things, such a mind shares in eternity itself.

spinozas-ethics-laid-out-like-geometry.context_blurb:
Spinoza's masterpiece, the Ethics, was published only after his death and was soon banned in several places. It is one of the strangest-looking great books in philosophy, because Spinoza wrote a guide to living in the form of a geometry textbook. Whether it succeeds is still argued, but the confidence of the attempt startles readers four centuries on.

He copied the structure of Euclid exactly. Each of the five parts opens with definitions and axioms, truths taken as self-evident, and then proves a chain of propositions, each one only from what has already been established. The full Latin title says it plainly: Ethics, Demonstrated in Geometrical Order. Every proof closes with Q.E.D., the Latin shorthand a geometer writes when what had to be shown has been shown. Putting that mark under a claim about God, just as under a claim about a triangle, announced something daring: reason alone had reached the conclusion, with no appeal to scripture, authority or revelation.

In the third part he turned the method on love, hatred, jealousy and fear, promising to treat them as if he were studying lines, planes and solids. He meant to understand human feelings, not to mock or condemn them. Passions, on this view, follow from their own causes by strict necessity, so they can be explained like any other effect in nature.

leibnizs-monads.context_blurb:
Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz was a German polymath of the late 1600s who invented calculus alongside Newton and served the court of Hanover. He asked what the universe is made of at bottom, and his answer was not bits of matter but an infinite swarm of simple, partless, mind-like points he called monads, each reflecting the whole universe from its own point of view. Strange as it sounds, he believed strong arguments drove him there.

Leibniz insisted that no two things in nature are ever perfectly identical. Around 1695, in the gardens at Hanover, Princess Sophie challenged one of her courtiers to find two leaves that matched exactly. The courtier failed, because however closely two leaves resembled each other, he could always find some small way they differed. Two things that shared every property, Leibniz reasoned, would be one thing, not two. He also asked you to imagine a thinking machine swollen to the size of a mill you could tour. Inside you would find only cogs and levers shoving one another and never a thought or a feeling, so perception must belong to something simple, without parts. We also sense far more than we notice. The roar of the sea that reaches you as one sound is really built from countless tiny sounds of single waves, each too faint to pick out alone, and Leibniz called such hidden inputs small perceptions.

His most famous line says that monads have no windows through which anything could come in or go out. A thing without parts has nothing inside to rearrange, so no outside cause can push on it: no monad can act on another or be changed by one.

Sealed as it is, a monad is not cut off from reality, because its inner states express every other thing that exists. Leibniz called each monad a mirror of the universe, a living one that reflects the whole cosmos perpetually, though dimly, and most clearly what lies nearest. Monads are never idle; their work is perceiving, and that holds even for the monads in a rock. To make this sensible, Leibniz split perception, a monad's passing inner state, from apperception, a word he coined for being aware that you perceive. A rock's monads perceive without ever noticing that they do, because having a perception and being aware of it are two different things.

That leaves a puzzle. If no monad can affect another, how do they all stay in step, like musicians who never hear one another yet keep perfect time? Leibniz's answer is pre-established harmony: God designed every monad at creation, fitting each one to all the others, so their agreement was built in once and for all. He rejected the rival view of Malebranche, in which God resets things at every moment, as a perpetual miracle. Pre-established harmony remains one powerful and still-contested account of mind and world.

pre-established-harmony-and-sufficient-r.context_blurb:
Gottfried Leibniz built his universe out of countless simple points that cannot act on one another, so he owed an answer to an obvious question: why does my decision to raise my arm seem to raise it? His answer, a direct rival to Descartes, rests on a principle he used almost everywhere, and together they led him to bold conclusions about God, freedom and space that Newton's camp fought hard.

In Leibniz's favorite image, soul and body are a pair of clocks that agree to the second, year after year. His explanation, called pre-established harmony, is that God made each one so perfect from the outset that it runs true without help, so mind and body stay in step though neither ever acts on the other. Behind it sits the Principle of Sufficient Reason, which he applied to everything from a fallen tree to a war to the color of a coat. Nothing just happens to be so without a ground: behind every fact lies something explaining why things stand thus and not otherwise, even when we cannot find it.

Leibniz's monads are sealed, with no window through which any influence could pass, yet each is forever changing. The change comes from within, as each monad unrolls what was packed inside it from the start, rather than being pushed from outside. The principle also answers an old puzzle about a perfectly rational donkey set midway between two identical bales of hay, which supposedly starves for lack of any reason to choose. Leibniz said it never starves, because perfect symmetry never really occurs. Some slight difference too small to notice, a faint perception below awareness, always sways it toward one side. He also rejected Malebranche's view that God steps in at every moment, moving your arm the instant you will it. Leibniz argued that a creation that runs by its own laws shows a better craftsman than one needing constant repair, and endless intervention would be a perpetual miracle unworthy of a perfect maker.

He turned the principle on Newton's idea that space is a real, standing container in which things sit. In letters to Newton's defender Samuel Clarke, he imagined God setting every object in the mirror-opposite place, east swapped for west, with every distance kept the same. Since God could have no grounds for preferring one layout to its mirror image, Leibniz concluded that the two worlds would not truly differ at all, and so space cannot be a real thing standing by itself. The same principle shaped his most famous conclusion. Because a perfectly wise God must have a reason for creating this world rather than any other, ours must be the best of all possible worlds. Voltaire mocked the claim in Candide through Dr. Pangloss, a cheerful professor who repeats it amid earthquake and disaster, and Leibniz's argument and Voltaire's objection from real suffering still face each other.

the-best-of-all-possible-worlds.context_blurb:
Gottfried Leibniz, the German philosopher and mathematician, took on one of the oldest problems about God: if God is perfectly powerful and good, why did He make a world so full of suffering? His answer became a famous slogan, and later an infamous one. Whether God chose well, chose at all, or exists in the way Leibniz needed is still honestly argued.

Leibniz's tool was the Principle of Sufficient Reason: nothing is so without a reason why it is so and not otherwise. A perfect God, facing endless possible worlds, needed a reason to create this one. For a being supremely good and wise, the only deciding reason is that no other world offers as much reason to prefer it: the world of greatest perfection. Faced with the obvious objection, that God could always have made a better one, Leibniz turned it around. If there were no single best world, a perfect God would have had no reason to prefer any, and so would have created nothing at all. That anything exists shows a best was found.

In 1759 Voltaire replied with Candide, a short novel that drags its hero through floggings, a shipwreck and the burning of men after the Lisbon earthquake. Surrounded by the carnage, Candide wonders aloud that if this is the best world there could be, what must the other worlds be like?

the-empiricist-wager-all-knowledge-from-.context_blurb:
While Descartes, Spinoza and Leibniz insisted that the deepest truths are reached by pure reason, a rival movement grew in the British Isles. Its great wager, carried by John Locke, George Berkeley and David Hume, was that whatever is in the mind came in first through the senses, with no stock of ideas we are born holding. That wager set up a lasting collision with the rationalists, and the argument still goes on.

The empiricist test is simple: trace an idea back to something you actually saw, heard or touched. A boy has never laid eyes on the back of his head, yet he can know there is hair there, because he has felt it with his hands and seen it in a mirror. Reasoning that it must be so, or that everyone says so, does not trace back to experience. Locke, in his Essay Concerning Human Understanding of 1690, pictured a newborn's mind as white paper with no marks on it. Where does it get all its later materials of reason and knowledge? His one-word answer was experience. So when a girl insists she can clearly picture a colour no one has ever seen, the empiricist asks whether she can trace it back to some particular thing she once sensed. If she cannot, the idea is empty, however vivid it feels.

The rationalists pushed back. Descartes pointed to the idea of a perfect triangle. Every triangle you have ever seen is a little crooked, yet you understand the perfect shape well enough, so that idea, he concluded, was already in the mind, not copied from anything seen. Locke answered thinkers who said certain truths, such as that a thing cannot at once exist and not exist, are stamped on every mind at birth. Young children, he observed, show not the least grasp of such truths, so they cannot be inborn in everyone. Hume sharpened the test. He split the mind's contents into impressions, the lively first-hand feelings of seeing or hearing, and ideas, their fainter copies in memory. To check a hazy idea, look for the first-hand impression behind it, and if you can find none, the idea is empty.

lockes-blank-slate-tabula-rasa.context_blurb:
John Locke was a 17th-century English physician and philosopher whose Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690) opened the British tradition of empiricism, the view that knowledge comes from experience. Locke lived through civil war and revolution, and he believed the question of where ideas come from mattered for politics and religion as much as for philosophy. His target was the claim that some truths are stamped into us before birth.

Locke asked us to picture the newborn mind as a sheet of white paper with no writing on it, waiting for life to fill it in. Later readers nicknamed the image the blank slate, in Latin tabula rasa, though Locke himself never wrote that phrase. Where does all the writing come from? Locke's answer was one word, experience: everything a person lives through supplies the ideas, and all our knowledge is founded on it. To check claims of inborn truths, such as the logical rule that nothing can at once exist and not exist, he devised a simple test. If some truth were stamped on every soul from birth, it ought to shine most plainly in babies and the unschooled, whose minds are least cluttered by lessons, yet ask an infant about it and you get a blank stare.

Experience, Locke said, flows from two fountains. Sensation brings in the outside world: color, sound, smell. Reflection is the mind turning its gaze inward and noticing its own work, its perceiving, thinking, doubting and willing, and since that too is experience, it breaks no rule. In 1688 William Molyneux mailed Locke a riddle. A man born blind has learned by touch to tell a metal globe from a metal cube; then his eyes are healed, and the globe and the cube sit in front of him, untouched. Could his eyes alone tell which is which? Both men said no, because sight would be a brand-new sense, and his mind would not yet have learned to connect what he sees with what he once felt.

Locke carried the attack into morality. If any moral rule were stamped on every heart, surely it would be the rule against killing your own child. Yet he pointed to peoples in history who, he reported, exposed their infants in the wild and felt no remorse, and concluded that not even that rule can be inborn, since a whole people could ignore it. That is Locke's argument, not a settled verdict; Leibniz and later Kant held that morality springs from something inborn. Leibniz answered the blank page with an image of his own, a block of veined marble whose grain already traces the figure of Hercules. Experience is only the chisel that frees the statue the stone was leaning toward, because for Leibniz we are born not with finished facts but with leanings, built to grasp what experience then draws out. The dispute between the two pictures is still alive.

primary-vs-secondary-qualities.context_blurb:
In his Essay Concerning Human Understanding, John Locke asked whether all the properties of an apple, its redness, roundness, coldness, sweetness and weight, sit in the apple in the same way. He split them in two. Primary qualities, such as shape, size and motion, really belong to the object; secondary qualities, such as color, taste, warmth and sound, are only powers in the object to produce sensations in us. George Berkeley later turned the split against Locke.

Locke's most famous test takes two minutes. Put one hand in icy water and the other in hot, then put both into a bowl of lukewarm water. The same water feels hot to one hand and cold to the other, and since it cannot be both, the warmth you feel must live in your hands, not in the water. Fire teaches the same lesson. Near a campfire you feel warmth; move closer and the same fire gives pain. No one thinks the pain was waiting inside the fire, and Locke presses the point: the warmth, like the pain, is in you, a sensation the fire has the power to produce. Now picture a snowball left in a dark, empty room. Several of its qualities depend on whoever returns to look, touch or squeeze it, but its roundness stays true of the snowball itself, because shape is primary.

Locke's example was porphyry, a red-and-white streaked stone. In total darkness the colors vanish, and they come back with the light, so all the stone genuinely has, day or night, is an arrangement of its tiny parts able to cause the sensation of color in a viewer. Galileo had reached the idea first, in 1623. A feather drawn across a marble statue does nothing, while the same feather on a living person tickles, so the tickle belongs to us. Wipe out every creature with ears, tongue and nose, Galileo wrote, and all tastes, sounds and smells would be annihilated, while the shape and motion of bodies would remain.

Locke clinched the point with an almond. Grind a sweet white almond with a pestle, and its color turns dirty and its taste turns oily. Yet a pestle can change nothing but the texture, the way the parts are arranged. So the whiteness and sweetness had never been in the nut as such; they were powers that depended on the arrangement of its particles. A sharp enough eye, Locke thought, would see even the yellow of gold dissolve into an arrangement of parts. Blood looks evenly red, but under a good microscope, he reported, it proves to be just a scattering of red globules swimming in a transparent fluid.

locke-on-personal-identity-the-prince-an.context_blurb:
The English philosopher John Locke asked, in his Essay Concerning Human Understanding, what makes you the same person you were ten years ago, when your body and your opinions have both changed. His answer, and the strange stories he told to test it, began a puzzle every philosophy class still argues over. Rival thinkers tie identity to the body, to a soul, or to nothing lasting at all, and the question remains open.

In Locke's most famous story, a prince's memories and awareness wake up one day in the body of a cobbler, and the cobbler's own self has vanished. The town sees its familiar cobbler, but Locke says the person in that bed is the prince, answerable for the prince's deeds, because the self goes wherever the memories go, not wherever the body goes. Locke kept the man, the living human animal, apart from the person. What fixes the person over time is consciousness, the thread of awareness you can follow back through your own remembered past, so the self reaches exactly as far back as you can remember being. Picture Socrates asleep and dreaming, then awake with no memory of the sleeper's thoughts. One living man runs unbroken through that gap, Locke says, but the person is split in two by it, which is why punishing the waking Socrates for the sleeper's doings would be unjust.

Why count any being as a person, rather than as a creature that merely feels, like a dog? Locke's definition is a reflective power: a person is a thinking, reasoning being that can consider itself as itself, the same thinking thing at different times and places. He then raised a hard case against his own rule. Suppose a man drinks himself into a blackout, breaks the law and wakes with no memory of it. Locke's rule seems to say the man who wakes is not the one who acted, yet Locke defends the court that convicts him. His reason is evidence: no human judge can look into another man's consciousness, so a court has to go by the outward act it can prove. The final weighing of what the man was truly aware of, Locke reserved for the Day of Judgment, when every heart lies open.

Locke pushed his rule to wild extremes to show that it rests on consciousness and nothing else. If your consciousness somehow traveled off with a cut-off little finger, leaving the rest of the body behind, the finger would be you. Picture one body run in shifts by a day-mind and a night-mind, neither remembering the other. Locke called them two persons, as distinct as Socrates and Plato, and went further still: even if both minds belonged to one shared soul, they would remain two persons. Why does it matter so much? Locke called person a forensic term, a word for the courtroom. Getting the same person right means settling who rightly owns a past deed, and so who has earned praise or blame for it.

Two critics struck back. Thomas Reid told of a boy flogged for robbing an orchard, who becomes a young officer who seizes an enemy flag and still remembers the flogging, and then an old general who remembers the flag but has forgotten the orchard entirely. By Locke's rule the general is the officer and the officer is the boy, so the general is the boy; yet the general remembers nothing of the boy, so by the same rule he is not. Identity built from overlapping memories forms a chain, and a chain of overlaps does not always join its two far ends. Bishop Joseph Butler called the theory a wonderful mistake. Knowledge can reveal a truth but never makes it true, and memory works the same way: remembering a deed already assumes it was you who did it, so memory can report that you are the same person but cannot be what makes you so.

berkeleys-idealism-to-be-is-to-be-percei.context_blurb:
George Berkeley was an Anglo-Irish philosopher, later an Anglican bishop, whose central claim has struck first-time readers as impossible for three hundred years: the world contains only minds and their ideas, and no mindless matter at all. He was no skeptic about tables and trees, and his view is still defended as a serious option in philosophy today.

His famous puzzle is a tree standing alone in a deserted courtyard, unseen and unheard. For an ordinary object, Berkeley argued, being real is simply a matter of being perceived, by some mind or other; his Latin slogan was esse est percipi, to be is to be perceived. So what keeps the unwatched tree in being? A famous limerick pokes fun at that worry, and an anonymous reply answers it: the writer is always about in the Quad, so the tree goes on existing, observed by "Yours faithfully," God himself. The joke captures Berkeley's real answer, that God perceives everything always. Most people are surprised to learn that he wrote both of his world-upending books, the Principles of Human Knowledge in 1710 and the Three Dialogues in 1713, while still in his twenties; he became a bishop only decades later. In 1763 James Boswell told Samuel Johnson that Berkeley's claim could not be refuted by reason. Johnson drove his foot against a big stone with such force that he rebounded, and declared that he refuted it thus. Philosophers point out that the kick missed the target, since Berkeley never denied that stones are hard and real, only that hidden matter lies behind the hardness we feel.

In Berkeley's world there are only two sorts of thing: spirits, which perceive, will and act, and ideas, which are colors, shapes and sounds taken in by a mind. An idea is wholly passive, and it can never cause anything, which is why he denied that mindless matter could produce our sensations. He saw himself as common sense's rescuer, not its enemy. The real threat, he argued, came from believing in a matter that nobody has ever sensed, because if real things lie behind our ideas, we can never check our ideas against them, and skepticism about whether any outside world is there follows at once. Strangely, his bestseller in his own lifetime had nothing to do with any of this. Siris, in 1744, set off a craze across Europe for tar-water, made by soaking pine tar in water, which he praised as a remedy for nearly everything.

If everything is ideas, how does a real fire differ from an imagined one? Berkeley's answer: the ideas of a real fire are vivid, orderly and lawful, and they come whether you will them or not, so the fire burns you whether you like it or not, while an imagined fire is faint and bends to your whim. He also laid down a challenge. Try to conceive of a tree existing wholly unperceived, and he would give up his whole philosophy. It is a trap, he said, because the moment you imagine the unseen tree, your own mind is perceiving it.

His deepest argument answers materialists who granted that we directly experience only our own ideas but claimed those ideas resemble a hidden matter behind them. Berkeley answered that ideas can only ever look like other ideas: colors can match only colors, and shapes only shapes. So our ideas could never resemble matter, which makes the very notion of matter empty, a word that names nothing we could ever compare with anything.
