why-obey-consent-tacit-consent-and-the-p.context_blurb:
Social-contract theory says government rests on the consent of the governed. But you never signed anything. So what obliges you to obey the law at all? Thinkers have answered with consent, fair play and gratitude, and each answer has serious defenders and sharp critics. The question remains open.

The oldest answer comes from Plato's Crito. Socrates sits in prison awaiting execution, and his friends offer him escape. He imagines the Laws of Athens speaking to him: a grown citizen who knows the city's ways and remains there of his own will has thereby agreed to obey whatever the city lawfully commands. So Socrates stays.

John Locke separated two kinds of consent. Express consent is an oath that makes a man a full member for life. Tacit consent comes merely from using a country, even walking its highways. That quiet duty lasts only as long as the use, so when a road-using stranger leaves for good, his duty lapses as soon as he no longer enjoys the country's benefits.

In 1748 David Hume attacked the idea that staying means agreeing. Could a poor labourer who knows no other language and lives from one day's small wage to the next really choose to emigrate? Poverty ties such a man to his home; he has no genuine freedom to leave. It is as if someone had been brought onto a ship in his sleep and could get away from the captain only by jumping into the sea to drown. A choice whose only way out is death is no free choice.

Other grounds fared no better with their critics. Some say that if you benefit from a shared scheme, fairness obliges you to do your part. Robert Nozick imagined a neighbourhood that runs a loudspeaker playing music all day, giving every household a turn of one day a year at the controls. You never joined, though you sometimes enjoyed the songs through an open window. Nozick concluded you owe nothing: simply enjoying the fruits of a scheme you never joined puts you under no obligation. Others appeal to gratitude, as a child owes a parent. A. John Simmons replied that gratitude is owed for a freely made sacrifice, but public officials draw salaries and public services are bought with the citizen's own taxes, so the state sacrifices nothing.

Simmons tested every ground in turn and found that none binds the ordinary citizen. His conclusion was careful, and he did not urge revolt. There can be good reasons to do what the law says, but the bare fact that it is the law is not one of them.

the-leviathan-frontispiece.context_blurb:
In 1651 the English philosopher Thomas Hobbes published Leviathan, named after the biblical sea monster, which argued that the only escape from civil war is one undivided sovereign power. Its first edition carried one of the most famous images in philosophy, an engraving credited to the Paris artist Abraham Bosse and worked out with Hobbes himself. The picture is an argument in its own right.

A crowned giant towers over a quiet town and countryside. Peer closer and his body turns out to be built from some three hundred little human figures, pressed together like the scales of a fish. The image answers, before a word is read, where the ruler's power comes from: it springs from the people, who create their ruler by uniting into one body.

One hand grips a sword; the other holds a bishop's hooked staff, the crosier. Hobbes meant that the sovereign alone commands both earthly and spiritual authority, leaving no church able to rival the king; the panels below match castle with church and cannon with the thunderbolts of excommunication. Hobbes also had a handwritten vellum copy made for Charles II before he took the throne. In ordinary printed copies the little figures show us their backs as they gaze up at the crown, but in the king's copy the body is made of faces, every one looking straight out at the viewer.

mills-harm-principle.context_blurb:
John Stuart Mill was a 19th-century English philosopher whose father raised him as an experiment in genius; he read Greek at three and suffered a breakdown at twenty. His 1859 book On Liberty is one of the great defenses of individual freedom in English, and it turns on a single rule, the harm principle: the only reason society may rightly use force against one of its members, against his will, is to prevent harm to others.

Picture a quiet man who drinks himself sick each night, yet owes no one money and harms nobody. Mill says the town may not stop him. His own good, physical or moral, is not enough to justify force, so a ruin with no victim but himself remains his own business. Freedom worthy of the name, Mill wrote, means pursuing your own good in your own way, so long as you do not block others from pursuing theirs. A boy who longs to spend his life building strange clocks is free exactly when he can chase that dream his own way while harming no one.

In his most quoted sentence, Mill made each individual sovereign over his own body and mind, so the final say over choices that touch no one else belongs to the man himself. Mill sorted all conduct with one question: does this act affect other people, or only the person who does it? The part of a life that concerns others answers to society; in the part that concerns only himself, a man's independence is absolute. Neighbors are not powerless before a private vice. They may reason with the man, plead with him and try to persuade him, but they may never compel him or punish him for refusing, and a penalty such as shunning him until shame breaks him counts as compulsion too.

Is grabbing someone always coercion? Mill imagined an officer who sees a man heading onto a bridge that is about to give way, too far off to be warned. Seizing him and pulling him back is no real breach of his liberty, because liberty means doing what you desire, and the man has no desire to fall into the river. Drink can also cross the line. Drunkenness by itself concerns nobody else, but a soldier or a policeman drunk on duty may rightly be punished, because he is failing a duty owed to the people who rely on him. Mill feared the dead hand of habit, which he named the despotism of custom, and he saw protected private choice as what drives humanity forward. Protected liberty lets people try different experiments of living, and everyone can learn from the results.

Speech has its edge too. Mill would let a pamphlet call corn-dealers starvers of the poor and leave the printed words alone. But yell the same charge at a furious crowd massed in front of a corn-dealer's home, and it may justly be punished, because now it puts a real man in danger. Mill also drew one hard line through choices that concern only oneself: no one may contract himself into slavery, however freely he signs. A man who sells himself gives up all his future freedom, and being allowed to throw freedom away is not freedom. Critics press a harder objection, and Mill admits it has force. Trace any private vice far enough, a wrecked liver, a squandered fortune, a bad example, and it reaches family and neighbors, so hardly any act is truly a man's own business alone. Mill granted the difficulty without abandoning the principle, and the edges of his line are still argued over.

the-marketplace-of-ideas.context_blurb:
The marketplace of ideas is the modern name for an argument that comes mainly from John Stuart Mill's On Liberty, published in 1859. Mill did not defend free speech simply as a right to say what you please. He argued that among fallible people, truth gets established only through open challenge, so silencing even a wrong opinion costs something. It remains one of the strongest cases for free discussion ever written.

Mill framed his whole book with one rule. The only reason a society may use force against a grown person's will is to prevent harm to others. Offending people or upsetting them is not harm in that sense, so a council that bans a pamphlet because it upsets residents oversteps. Majorities get no special license either. If all mankind but one held one opinion, Mill wrote, mankind would have no more right to silence that one person than he would have to silence mankind. He admired a custom of the Catholic Church: before naming a saint, it appointed an official whose whole job was to argue against the candidate, the devil's advocate, so even the highest claims faced a chosen opponent.

Mill's most surprising claim is that even a false opinion is worth hearing. A falsehood argued in the open makes the truth defend itself, and that keeps the truth's meaning vivid and well understood. A truth that no one ever challenges goes soft; it stiffens into dead dogma, recited by people who could no longer defend it. The famous phrase itself has a twist. The words are usually pinned on Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes, whose 1919 dissent praised the competition of the market as the best test of truth. Yet Holmes never wrote the exact words; later judges coined the marketplace of ideas decades afterward.

Mill saw a hidden flaw in every act of censorship. Anyone who bans an opinion because it is false, Mill argued, must be assuming that he himself cannot possibly be wrong, a certainty no person or government has. History shows the danger. Mill reminded readers of Socrates, sentenced by his own city, and of the man crucified on Calvary. Those who condemned them were not monsters but decent, respected men who honestly thought they were in the right, which is exactly why suppression is so dangerous.

the-tyranny-of-the-majority.context_blurb:
Tyranny of the majority names a danger inside democracy itself. The French observer Alexis de Tocqueville sharpened it after touring the young United States in the 1830s, and John Stuart Mill, the English philosopher, took it up. The worry is not that democracy is bad, but that a free people can oppress one another with no king required, through law and, more quietly, through social pressure.

Suppose a class picks its year-end trip by vote. Nobody breaks a rule and nobody punishes the lone boy who voted for another place, yet for weeks the rest freeze him out until he regrets standing apart. A teacher might insist that since no law was broken, nobody forced him. The better answer: no rule was used against him, but being shunned weighed on him as heavily as any penalty. Mill said protection against rulers is not enough; people also need protection against the tyranny of prevailing opinion. He even judged that social tyranny can be worse than political oppression, because there are fewer ways to escape it, and it reaches into every small corner of everyday life.

Mill drew a line for the law as well. In On Liberty, published in 1859, his harm principle says the community may override a person's freedom for one purpose only: to stop him from harming others. A town that merely dislikes how a quiet man spends his evenings at home has no right to force him to stop.

Tocqueville showed how a democratic majority can silence a dissenter without any jail. It tells him he is free to think differently, but from now on he will be a stranger among his own people, shunned by all; it spares his life, but leaves him an existence far worse than death. Its quieter power reaches even those who never rebel, because it hands people ready-made opinions and spares them the work of thinking for themselves.

Some argued that a free people can never tyrannize itself, so a majority's power may grow without limit. Tocqueville refused. Unlimited power is dangerous in itself, he held: what makes such power perilous is how much of it there is, not who holds it, and a majority of millions is no safer with it than a single despot. He also foresaw a softer ruin, a vast, mild power wrapping people in a fine net of small rules until the nation becomes a flock of timid, hardworking animals with the government as its shepherd.

higher-and-lower-pleasures.context_blurb:
Jeremy Bentham, who founded utilitarianism in the late 1700s, held that the right act produces the greatest sum of pleasure, and he treated all pleasures as one kind of thing measured on one scale. His godson John Stuart Mill kept the framework but could not swallow that flattening. He argued that some pleasures are higher in kind, and he searched for a fair test to tell which. Critics still ask whether his repair holds.

Mill granted that a thoughtful person suffers more than a contented simple one, and still sided with the thinker in a famous line. A dissatisfied human being, he wrote, is better off than a satisfied pig; Socrates dissatisfied is better than a fool satisfied. Bentham had taken the opposite line on purpose. He set push-pin, a trivial children's game, beside great verse and held that only the quantity of pleasure counts, so if the pin game delights as much as the poem, it is worth just as much.

Mill broke with Bentham on exactly this point. In his view, pleasures come in different kinds as well as different sizes, and some kinds are simply of higher quality, so they cannot be totaled like coins. Defending utilitarianism in 1861 against the jibe that it was a philosophy fit for pigs, he offered one test for ranking two pleasures: only those who know both pleasures firsthand get a vote, and their settled preference decides. From their verdict, he said, there is no appeal.

Mill admitted that the richer mind feels sharper pains and harder wants, yet such a person would refuse to drop to a simpler, more comfortable life. What holds him back, Mill said, is a sense of dignity, which he would never sell, so much a part of his happiness that nothing at odds with it could tempt him for long. Critics press on the weak joint. Mill also says pleasure is the only good. But to rank one pleasure above another by quality, Mill must appeal to some standard other than how good it feels, and then pleasure is no longer his only measure. If Socrates' life is better for a reason other than feeling better, the standard has quietly changed.

berlins-two-concepts-of-liberty.context_blurb:
Isaiah Berlin was an Oxford philosopher, born in Riga to a Jewish family that fled the Russian Revolution. In a 1958 lecture, Two Concepts of Liberty, he argued that the one word liberty hides two different ideas, each a real good with its own dangers. One asks how many doors stand open to you; the other asks who is steering your life.

The first is negative liberty, freedom from interference. For a boy who counts himself free when no locked gate, no grabbing brother and no rule is in his way, freedom means that nobody stands in the way of the routes open to him: the more doors open, the freer he is. Berlin drew a sharp line here. Only deliberate human interference makes you unfree, not mere inability. A girl too short to reach the cookie jar is not unfree because of her height, but she is unfree when her brother blocks the kitchen door, because another person is choosing to bar a way she could otherwise take.

The second is positive liberty, freedom to be your own master. A young man who says open doors are not enough, because habits and cravings he never chose push him around like the tide pushes a cork, wants to govern himself, so that his own reason steers his life. Poverty tests the line between the two. A boy who wants a bicycle in a shop window faces no law against owning it; he simply lacks the money. Is he unfree or merely unable? Berlin said it depends on whether his poverty was caused by other people.

Berlin's fear of what freedom-talk can become began when he was seven. In Petrograd in 1917, as revolution broke out, he saw a mob crying for freedom haul away a policeman of the Tsar, pale with fear, to be killed, and the scene left him with a horror of violence for life. Positive liberty, he warned, hides a quiet trap. Self-mastery requires splitting the self into a higher, reasoning part that knows your true good and a lower self of passing desires, and you count as free only when the reasoning part governs the wanting part. Once some people are judged more rational than others, they can claim to know what you really want.

Next the true self is stretched beyond the person into a nation, a race, a church or the State, which forces its single goal on everyone and names that obedience their freedom. Your real will, it announces, resides in the State, so whatever the State commands is what you yourself want, and crushing you becomes you obeying yourself. Berlin linked this to Rousseau's notorious paradox: such rulers claim the right to force people to be free, for their own real good. Yet Berlin did not make the leave-me-alone kind of freedom absolute either. He borrowed an image from R. H. Tawney: total freedom for the pike means death for the minnows. Unlimited liberty for the strong can destroy the weak, so some basic needs, like security and food, can outrank liberty.

It is easy to read Berlin as hating self-mastery and loving only being left alone, but he insisted that self-government is a real human need, one value among many that any free society requires. He feared the way that ideal could be bent into a disguise for despots. Behind both liberties sat his deepest claim. Liberty, equality, mercy and justice are all genuine goods, yet they cannot all be had in full at once; more of one can mean less of another. So clashes between real goods, sometimes tragic ones, can never be wholly removed from human life.

negative-vs-positive-rights.context_blurb:
When someone claims a right, what is he asking of other people: to leave him alone, or to do or supply something for him? Political philosophers call the first kind a negative right and the second a positive right. Isaiah Berlin and Robert Nozick sharpened the distinction in the 20th century, and the quarrel over how far positive rights reach is still alive.

An old saying captures the negative kind: your freedom to swing your fist stops at the tip of the other fellow's nose. A right like that obliges everyone else simply to stay off you, and beyond that it asks nothing of them. In one classroom, Mia claims a right not to be pushed around, and Theo claims a right to have lunch handed to him. Mia's claim is met the moment people leave her alone, but Theo's can be met only if some person actually provides the food. A whole nation can leave everyone alone at once, at no cost, but pledging a house to every household runs into arithmetic, because houses have to be built from real materials and real labor, and both are limited. The French economist Frédéric Bastiat, in The Law, an 1850 pamphlet, offered a blunt test for spotting when law turns into what he called plunder. Ask one question: does the law strip one person of what is his in order to hand it to someone else?

The legal theorist Wesley Hohfeld gave a sharp test for any claimed right to something: find out exactly who is obliged to deliver it. A genuine claim-right always names someone who owes you. A negative right asks everyone to hold back, while a positive right pins a duty on a specific person to hand over work or goods. The strongest case for positive rights came from Franklin Roosevelt. In January 1944, ill with the flu, he proposed what he called a Second Bill of Rights, guaranteeing jobs, food, homes, medical care and schooling, on one blunt ground: necessitous men are not free men. Someone crushed by need, on this view, is not truly free, since the right to speak or to sign a contract is a cruel formality to a man who is starving. In 1948 Eleanor Roosevelt led the drafting of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, whose Article 25 promised food, clothing, housing and medical care. The fiercest resistance she had to overcome came from her own government's State Department, wary of economic rights.

Bastiat held that the true order runs the other way from what lawmakers assume: people's liberty and property come first, and law is made afterward only to protect them. That is why critics distrust any claimed right to another person's labor. Bastiat named two forces that twist law into plunder. One is plain selfishness; the other he called false philanthropy, kindness that is forced on a bystander, who is made to foot the bill. Charity freely given is a high virtue, but compelled from an uninvolved person, Bastiat argued, it becomes plunder. Senator Rand Paul, a physician, pressed the point at a 2011 Senate hearing, asking whether a right to health care meant a patient could send the police to drag him off to treat her. A right to be given a doctor's labor, he argued, amounts to a claim to own the doctor himself. Critics noted that a doctor may simply quit medicine.

Nozick's 1974 book Anarchy, State, and Utopia went furthest. Taxing what people earn to pay for such rights, he argued, is on a par with forced labor, because seizing the fruits of your work is the same in kind as seizing hours of your life and directing how you spend them. Others reject the comparison, and the dispute stays open. Henry Shue's Basic Rights, published in 1980, challenges the split itself. Even the plain right not to be killed, Shue argued, depends on a costly standing force of police, courts and armies, so every real right asks others both to hold back and to provide. Berlin's 1958 Oxford lecture, "Two Concepts of Liberty," distinguished freedom from interference and the freedom of self-mastery, without ranking them. His warning was that the two ideas respond to different questions and can come into fierce conflict, and that the second has often been twisted into forcing people to be free.

tocquevilles-soft-despotism.context_blurb:
Alexis de Tocqueville, a French aristocrat, toured the young United States in 1831 and wrote Democracy in America, still one of the deepest books about democratic life. In its second volume, published in 1840, he imagined a new kind of unfreedom that no ancient tyranny resembled: no secret police and no fear in the streets, only prosperous, busy citizens tended by a mild power that manages everything. Readers across the political spectrum have found the picture uncomfortably familiar.

Tocqueville drew a sharp contrast. A good parent raises a child to stand on his own one day. This soft power works the other way on purpose: its goal is to hold its citizens in a childhood that never ends, so that they can never do without it. Looking at the gentle habits and small wants of his age, he wrote that such a people would be governed not by tyrants but by schoolmasters, endlessly grading and correcting them.

It needs no chains. Instead it spreads over society a fine mesh of petty, intricate regulations, tiny and uniform for everyone, which the most original minds cannot break through to rise above the crowd. It seldom forces anyone to act. Rather, it softens, bends and guides the will: it keeps holding people back from acting, so that their choices die before they are ever made. Little by little it dulls a whole nation until the people become a flock of timid, hard-working animals, with the government as their shepherd.

Why would free people accept this? Each man lets himself be led on leading-strings, the cords once used to keep toddlers from falling, because the hand at the far end of his chain belongs to no single person or class but to the whole people. Even voting fits the pattern. Under such a system, Tocqueville wrote, people throw off their dependence for just the moment it takes to pick their master, and then sink back into it.

wollstonecraft-and-equity-feminism.context_blurb:
Mary Wollstonecraft was an English writer who in 1792, with the French Revolution fresh news, published her Vindication, a book-length defence of women's rights and one of the first sustained arguments in English for treating women as full moral and intellectual beings. Her case rests on Enlightenment reason, not grievance, and it is aimed as much at women who had accepted a narrow life as at the men who kept them there. It is often called equity feminism: fair treatment, without pretending the sexes are interchangeable.

She begged her readers' pardon for one choice. The usual writers spoke to women as pretty pets stuck in an endless childhood. She would speak to them instead as rational grown-ups answerable for their own lives.

Her central claim was about cause. Men of her day treated women's thin reading as evidence of naturally feebler minds. Wollstonecraft answered that the lack of learning showed nothing but that they had never been properly taught; the fault lay in the schooling, not the mind. She also exposed the flattering word used to defend that schooling. Calling a girl's ignorance innocence gives a deprivation forced on her the flattering look of a virtue.

She showed what such an upbringing does. Raise a girl to believe her looks are her only power, and her mind bends itself to fit her body, until it wants to decorate its cage rather than escape it. Like a flower planted in soil too rich, she is admired for a season while her true abilities waste away before she ever grows into them.

Why would anyone want women kept ignorant? Power, she argued, always seeks blind obedience. A tyrant wants slaves and a sensualist wants a plaything, and a woman who reasons for herself slips out of both their grips. When Rousseau warned that educated women would lose their power over men, she agreed that this was the point. She did not want women to have power over men, but over themselves.

Critics feared that an educated woman would abandon her home. Wollstonecraft answered that reason would make her a better wife and mother, one her family is the stronger for.

fdrs-second-bill-of-rights.context_blurb:
In his State of the Union message of January 1944, during the last full year of the Second World War, President Franklin Delano Roosevelt proposed a Second Bill of Rights. The first, from 1791, protected people from their government: free speech, assembly, security against unreasonable searches. Roosevelt argued that such liberties were not enough on their own and called for guaranteed jobs, homes, food and medical care. His case is the strongest form of a serious argument, and critics meet it with hard questions.

The seed was planted in a 1941 speech to Congress, before America had entered the war, when Roosevelt named four freedoms the world should rest on: speech, worship, freedom from fear, and freedom from want. That last, economic freedom grew into his 1944 list. When the 1944 message came, Roosevelt was just back from conferences at Cairo and Tehran and sick with the flu, so he sent the text to Congress and read it to the nation by radio. No film of the whole address survives. Its famous lines exist on camera only because he re-recorded the key passages for the newsreels afterward.

His case rested on one old line, that needy men are not free men. Steel-manned, it says a man may enjoy every political liberty written on paper and still lack real freedom, because desperation will make him submit to whatever terms the powerful offer, so his choices are not truly his own. Roosevelt did not coin the phrase. He borrowed it from the English judge Lord Henley, who in a 1762 mortgage case, Vernon v Bethell, was protecting a desperate borrower who had put up his land as security on harsh terms.

Critics press two questions. The first is what kind of right this is. Free speech requires nothing of others except that they not interfere. Medical care is another matter: it lays a claim on a doctor, whose work must be provided whenever the sick man calls on it. A right of the first kind costs others only restraint, while a right of the second kind obliges someone to supply his labor. The second question is whether any guaranteed pattern of wealth can be kept at all. Robert Nozick imagined starting from whatever distribution you think perfectly fair, then letting a million fans gladly hand the basketball star Wilt Chamberlain a quarter apiece to see him play, leaving him $250,000 richer and the distribution lopsided, though every payment was voluntary. To hold any chosen pattern of wealth in place, Nozick concluded, the state would have to keep stepping in to stop people spending their own money as they please. Liberty, as he put it, upsets patterns.

power-tends-to-corrupt-acton.context_blurb:
Lord Acton (John Dalberg-Acton, 1834-1902) was a Victorian English Catholic historian who spent his life studying how liberty is won and lost. In a private letter of 5 April 1887 to the bishop and historian Mandell Creighton, he objected to his fellow historians' habit of going easy on the wrongs of kings and popes. That letter holds the sentence by which almost everyone now knows him.

Give one ruler command of all the laws, the courts and the army, and Acton warns what follows: power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely. The more a person holds, the more it bends and corrupts him, which is why power must be limited and divided rather than trusted to anyone in full. Most people forget the very next sentence, that great men are almost always bad men. The celebrated and powerful turn out bad far more often than good, so a crowd's admiration is no reason to hand them still more power. Acton drew a rule from this. Instead of giving the powerful the benefit of the doubt, our suspicion of wrongdoing should grow as their power grows. And though he was a devout Catholic who loved his Church, he insisted that kings and popes alike be held to exactly the standard that would condemn an ordinary man for the same deed. As he put it, there is no worse heresy than the belief that the office makes its holder holy.

adam-smith-and-the-invisible-hand.context_blurb:
Adam Smith was a Scottish moral philosopher who taught at the University of Glasgow. In 1776, the year the American colonies declared independence, he published The Wealth of Nations, the founding book of economics. His great insight was that a working society does not need everyone to aim at the common good: under the right rules, strangers chasing their own ends weave a vast order of cooperation.

Smith started with dinner. You do not eat because the butcher, brewer and baker out of pity or goodwill. They feed you because it serves their own interest, since selling you meat, beer and bread is how they earn a living, and that motive is steadier than kindness. Next he looked inside a small pin factory. A lone, untrained worker could scarcely finish one pin a day, yet ten men who each did one small step, instead of each making whole pins, turned out about 48,000 between them. Behind all this splitting of work, Smith saw one human quirk, the urge to "truck, barter, and exchange." No other animal has it: nobody, he wrote, ever saw a dog fairly swap one bone for another with a second dog.

The same logic tells you how to shop. Begging a shopkeeper with how badly you need something gets you nowhere; Smith's advice is to show him what he himself stands to gain, because a deal moves when each side gets what it wants. Back in the pin factory he counted about eighteen separate steps, from drawing out the wire to sharpening the point, each done by different hands. Once everyone specializes like that, no one lives on his own work alone: the baker cannot eat only bread, so he sells it, and in Smith's phrase every man becomes in some measure a merchant. For all his grand vision, Smith was famously absent-minded. One morning, lost in thought, he dropped bread and butter into the teapot, brewed himself tea from it, and complained that it tasted awful.

People remember Smith for self-interest and forget his first book. In The Theory of Moral Sentiments, published in 1759, he built ethics on sympathy: we naturally share the feelings of others by imagining ourselves in their place. Since we all take our own side, Smith proposed a test anyone can run in his head to judge his own conduct fairly. Picture how a calm, well-informed stranger would see what you did; Smith called this inner judge the impartial spectator, the man within the breast. In The Wealth of Nations he gave the market its most famous phrase. A merchant who aims only at his own profit is led by an invisible hand to promote the public good, an end that was no part of his intention.

Smith first used the invisible hand years earlier, and not about markets at all. In his 1759 book he pictured a proud landlord gazing over his fields and dreaming that he alone will eat the whole harvest. The dream collapses on one plain fact: his belly can hold no more food than a poor peasant's, so he must hand the rest to the workers who grow and cook it, feeding them without meaning to. Smith's own life ended in irony. The great champion of free trade, whose book armed merchants against tariffs, was appointed a Commissioner of Customs in Scotland in 1778 and spent his last years collecting the very duties he had argued against.

hayek-and-the-knowledge-problem.context_blurb:
Friedrich Hayek was a twentieth-century Austrian-born economist and philosopher who taught in Vienna, London, Chicago and Freiburg. Best known for his 1944 warning The Road to Serfdom, he made his deepest contribution in a short 1945 article, The Use of Knowledge in Society. Its question is not whether planners mean well, but whether anyone could hold the knowledge a modern economy needs, and how a society runs on knowledge no single mind has.

Leonard Read's 1958 essay I, Pencil makes the point with a plain wooden pencil. It traces its cedar, graphite, paint, rubber and metal band to people around the world, then declares that no one alive could make it alone, because no one knows how. Hayek's favorite example was tin. If tin grows scarce somewhere, users scattered across the world, strangers to one another, soon start using less, though nobody orders them to and few know why. Tin's price went up, and each user, finding it more expensive, economized. Small, urgent choices that turn on facts changing by the hour, a flooded field or a half-loaded truck, must be left, Hayek argued, to the man on the spot, who sees the passing circumstances with his own eyes.

What should astonish us, he wrote, is that tens of thousands of people no investigation could even identify all adjust the right way, with no boss and no known cause. Each producer is like an engineer watching a few dials: he keeps his eye on how the prices of his inputs and products move. His last book, The Fatal Conceit (1988), attacked the belief that a clever mind can redesign society like a blank page. That belief is deadly, not merely wrong, because the knowledge a society lives on is spread across millions of people, and no planner's mind can ever gather it. His 1974 Nobel prize was split down the middle with Gunnar Myrdal, the Swedish socialist and architect of the planned welfare state.

Hayek added a sad note: had the price system been deliberately invented, it would be hailed as one of the mind's greatest triumphs, but since it was never invented by anyone, no inventor gets the applause. The debate had begun in 1920, when Ludwig von Mises argued that if the state owns every factory and machine, they are never traded and so carry no real market prices, so planners have no way to tell whether building a railway from steel or from aluminum squanders resources. They are left groping in the dark. Hayek distinguished a made order, like an army in battle array, from a grown order, like a language, the common law or the market, which arises from people following rules yet was planned by nobody. The fatal error is trying to direct a grown order by command, as if it were a made one. He even disliked calling the market an economy, a word from the Greek for managing one household, and coined catallaxy from a Greek verb that meant to exchange, but it also meant to welcome someone into the community and to change a foe into a friend.

Oskar Lange, a socialist economist, replied to Mises during the 1930s with a planning board that would set prices by trial and error. He began with a half-mocking tribute, proposing that Mises be honored with a statue in the great hall of the central planning ministry for forcing socialists to take calculation seriously. Hayek replied that by the time a board resets its prices, the fleeting local facts have moved on. He closed his Nobel lecture with a warning: the man who believes he can steer society becomes a tyrant over his fellows, and may become the destroyer of a civilization that no mind designed, grown from the free efforts of millions.

bastiats-broken-window-the-seen-and-the-.context_blurb:
Frédéric Bastiat was a French economist and journalist who died young, of tuberculosis, in 1850. His essay on what is seen and what is not seen opens with a tiny parable about a broken window that may be the most retold story in economics. His method is to pause the story just as the crowd finishes its argument and ask what the crowd forgot to count.

A shopkeeper's boy carelessly breaks a pane of glass, and a crowd gathers to console the father: glaziers, after all, need broken windows to live. The good they can see is real. The glazier gets a new job and is paid six francs to put in fresh glass. But Bastiat asks about the cost no one counts. Had the window stayed whole, the shopkeeper would have spent those six francs on something else, a new pair of shoes, say, and now he quietly goes without them. So the accident has created nothing. The six francs have merely changed hands, going to the glazier instead of the cobbler, and the town has lost a window. In Bastiat's phrase, destruction is not profit.

The person who suffers is invisible. The shopkeeper's loss is plain to see, but the shoemaker never learns that a sale was coming, so he never misses it aloud; his loss is as real as the glazier's gain, and invisible. For Bastiat this is what separates poor economists from good ones. The poor one sees only the visible effect, the glazier pocketing his francs. The good one also reckons the effects nobody can see. A boy who thinks that throwing a rock through his neighbor's window helps the economy, because the repairman gets paid, has missed the same thing. The repairman's wages are just the neighbor's money, which he would have spent elsewhere anyway, so the rock adds nothing and destroys a good window.

Henry Hazlitt's 1946 bestseller Economics in One Lesson retold the parable with the shopkeeper saving up for a new suit. The glass money is the suit money, so the tailor misses an order he never knew he had, and the suit never gets sewn. The same logic answers anyone who says a hurricane or a war will be good for the economy because of all the rebuilding jobs. The rebuilding is seen. Unseen are the new homes, factories and goods those same workers and that same money would have built if they were not busy replacing what was destroyed. Even respected experts fall for it. After the 2011 Fukushima earthquake, the economist Paul Krugman suggested the rebuilding might act as a stimulus. Bastiat's readers answer that we notice the repair bills only because they replace riches that vanished without a sound, and no credential exempts anyone from counting the unseen.

Tuberculosis had wrecked Bastiat's throat, so he could no longer speak in France's National Assembly, and he poured his last strength into writing. When death came in Rome on December 24, 1850, he is reported to have repeated one word at the end: "Truth."

bastiats-candlemakers-petition.context_blurb:
In 1845 the French economist Frédéric Bastiat wrote a fake petition to France's lawmakers, signed in the name of everyone who makes candles, lamps, wicks and tallow. It is a satire that pushes the ordinary protectionist argument of his day, shield home producers from cheap foreign goods, to its logical limit, so the reader can feel the argument's shape for the first time.

The petitioners complain of a ruthless foreign rival who sells light so cheaply that no shop can compete. The rival turns out to be the sun, which lights every home for nothing from dawn to dusk. The complaint protectionists make about cheap imports sounds mad the instant the cheap competitor is sunlight.

So the candlemakers ask for a law, drafted in dead-serious detail. Parliament should order every window, skylight, dormer and shutter in France closed, every hole and chink through which daylight might creep. Imagine a nation boarding up its windows at noon to sell candles: that is the protectionist logic followed to its end.

Bastiat ends by springing the trap. French law already barred coal, iron and wheat from abroad for the sake of French producers, and the cheaper an import got, the harder it was barred. The sun's light costs nothing at all. Refusing a completely free gift is just the extreme case of refusing a cheaper import, so shutting out the sun is the same move as shutting out any cheap foreign product, only pushed further, and whatever condemns the one condemns the other. Bastiat does not lecture about trade policy; he lets the argument's own shape do the work.

public-choice-buchanan-and-tullock.context_blurb:
James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock, American economists of the 1950s and 1960s, founded the school called public choice, and Buchanan won the 1986 Nobel Prize in economics for it. Their insight was simple. Textbooks assumed that people in markets respond to incentives but treated people in government as selfless servants of the public good. Public choice drops that double standard and turns the same economic lens on politicians, bureaucrats, lobbyists and voters.

Buchanan's motto was politics without romance. To forecast how officials will actually behave, assume they pursue their own goals, such as re-election, bigger budgets and status, the way a shopper chases a bargain: the same human being in a different arena. That explains how a sugar quota can hand a few hundred growers millions a year while adding only pennies to each shopper's grocery bill, and survive in Congress for decades, though the shoppers' combined loss exceeds the growers' gain. For the growers the stakes are enormous, so they fight hard; for each shopper the loss is trivial, so he shrugs. Economists call this concentrated benefits and dispersed costs.

Lobbying wastes more than it moves. Suppose a steel company pays lawyers and lobbyists a million dollars to get a tariff on foreign steel, and a rival spends a million on a faster, cheaper furnace. The lobbying buys a special favor and produces nothing, while the furnace money turns into steel people can use. Tullock exposed this waste in 1967, and Anne Krueger later named it rent-seeking. Voters, meanwhile, often stay uninformed for a reason. Anthony Downs argued in 1957 that one voter's studying would almost never change the outcome, so it is hardly worth his time, and he called this rational ignorance; it lets narrow lobbies slip favors past an inattentive public. In the Senate, a farm-state senator and a textile-state senator, each with a subsidy the rest would reject, can each vote for the other's subsidy so that both pass together, a trade called logrolling. A saying often credited to H. L. Mencken calls such democracy two foxes and a chicken voting on lunch. Because a majority can lawfully help itself to a minority's goods, public-choice thinkers conclude that a free society needs constitutional limits that shield certain property from any vote.

Public choice also explains why reforms disappoint. Throw the rascals out of a corrupt agency and put honest people in, and little changes, because the new officials face exactly the pressures the old ones did, so what must change is the incentives and rules, not the faces. Tullock's transitional gains trap shows how a privilege locks itself in. New York capped the number of taxi medallions, licenses every cab must own, and the first owners grew rich as the badges turned scarce. A driver who bought one later paid the full market price and earns no special profit, yet he fights abolition harder than anyone, since he paid a fortune for a badge that abolition would make worthless, and he could never recover that money. When ride-hailing arrived, medallions that had peaked near 1.3 million dollars in 2013 crashed to about 150,000, leaving many drivers buried in debt.

sowell-trade-offs-and-compared-to-what.context_blurb:
Thomas Sowell is an American economist, the son of a North Carolina sharecropping family, a Marine veteran and a longtime scholar at Stanford's Hoover Institution. He is famous less for one theorem than for a style of thinking, packed into short phrases readers carry for life. Each phrase is a move for catching a common mistake in arguments about policy.

Sowell's own road was hard. He was born in the segregated South in 1930, lost his father before birth, grew up in Harlem, left high school, and took photographs for the Marine Corps before he got to Harvard. As a young man he was a committed Marxist, a belief he would spend his career taking apart. His best-known line holds that there are no solutions, only trade-offs. So when a friend promises that a new rule will fix the litter in the park, the Sowell question is who pays, because every choice spends something, and part of the price usually falls on people nobody sees or counts. His second tool is a three-word question: compared to what? A bus plan with real flaws is no failure just because it falls short of perfection. It should be measured against the best actual alternative the town could pick instead, since a messy plan can still beat every real rival.

In Applied Economics, published in 2003, Sowell warns against stopping at Stage One, the first visible result of a policy, which politicians who think only to the next election seldom see past. Follow a policy on to its later effects, he urges, because they can run opposite to the first one. Raise taxes on a business and at first the state collects more money; later the company builds its new factories in other states, and revenue can end up lower than before. Sowell learned to look this way in 1960, as a young Marxist interning at the federal Labor Department. Looking at Puerto Rico's sugar industry, he found that each rise in the minimum wage cut jobs. What shook him more was the agency. Running the minimum wage paid for much of the department's budget and staff, so it had little reason to discover the harm the program did.

Sowell kept a demanding definition of the word solution: a solution exists only when nothing has to be traded away. Almost no real choice clears that bar, because picking any option still means bearing a real cost somewhere to gain something elsewhere; what people call a solution is usually a trade-off in disguise.

In his 1987 book A Conflict of Visions, Sowell sorted political thinkers by how they explain evil. Thinkers like Jean-Jacques Rousseau blame it on bad institutions and foolish choices, all of which could be fixed; Sowell called this the unconstrained vision. The other camp, the constrained vision of Adam Smith and Edmund Burke, traces evil to limits of mind and morals that are built into every human being and never go away. On that view nothing will cure evil for good, and the most anyone can hope for is a prudent trade-off.

friedman-results-not-intentions.context_blurb:
Milton Friedman was a twentieth-century American economist at the University of Chicago, winner of the Nobel Prize in 1976 and a gifted popular writer, known for books such as Capitalism and Freedom and the television series Free to Choose. His signature habit of mind was simple: to judge a policy, do not stop at what it was meant to do. Follow it out to what it actually produced.

The most retold parable comes from colonial Delhi. British officials paid a bounty for dead cobras, locals began breeding cobras for the reward, and when the bounty was scrapped the breeders freed their snakes, leaving the city worse off. Historians find no records of the breeding, so treat it as a parable, but the lesson holds: judge the bounty by its real effects, not by how sensible its goal sounded. A joke often put in Friedman's mouth says that if the government ran the Sahara Desert, within five years there would be a shortage of sand; the line was in print by 1951, before Friedman used the theme. When the talk-show host Phil Donahue asked him in 1979 whether capitalism simply feeds on greed, Friedman turned it around, asking him to name any society that is not driven by greed, and so shifted the question from motives to results.

Friedman and George Stigler tested rent control with newspaper ads in San Francisco. Under wartime rent control in 1946, ads from would-be renters outnumbered offers many times over. In 1906, weeks after the earthquake and fire left 225,000 people homeless, rents were free to climb, and the paper carried roughly 64 ads offering homes against just 5 from people looking for one, with no mention of a shortage. The same move fits a case with no Friedman quote at all. A law meant to save the rare red-cockaded woodpecker, a bird that needs old Southern pines to nest, restricted logging wherever the bird turned up. When Dean Lueck and Jeffrey Michael, two economists, studied timber owners in North Carolina, they found that landowners near known colonies cut their pines prematurely, harvesting young trees so their land would never grow old enough to attract the birds.

Friedman applied the test to the minimum wage. When the federal minimum rose in 1956 from three quarters to one dollar, teenagers of both races had been jobless at about the same rate. Within two years, he reported, the jobless rate for black teenage boys had leapt to about 24 percent, against about 14 for white boys, and he judged the law most harmful to black teenagers in its effect, whatever its intent. Readers can weigh his reading of the cause; the habit is to go and look at the number. He explained why results drift from intentions in a single sentence: no one is as careful with another person's money as he is with his own.

i-pencil-spontaneous-coordination.context_blurb:
In 1958 Leonard Read published a short essay, I, Pencil, narrated by an ordinary wooden pencil reciting its own family tree: loggers, graphite miners, chemists, sailors and railwaymen, all strangers to one another. Its quiet punchline is a large one about how a modern economy works, and it pairs naturally with the ideas of Adam Smith and Friedrich Hayek.

The pencil's cedar is felled by loggers in a distant camp, and the pencil boasts that untold thousands of people, growers, shippers and roasters who never met, had a hand in every cup of coffee those loggers drink. If one cup takes that many, the pencil takes vastly more.

The essay reached millions in 1980, when Milton Friedman held up a pencil on his television series Free to Choose, and so its author is often forgotten. It was Leonard Read, who had founded a free-market institute, the Foundation for Economic Education, and printed the essay in its magazine, The Freeman.

Millions of people help make the pencil, yet not one of them could make it alone. Then the pencil names a fact it finds more astounding still: there is no master mind dictating or steering any of these countless acts. No chief, planner or committee designs the pencil, yet it turns up everywhere, cheap and plentiful, an order with no master plan.

spontaneous-order-vs-designed-order.context_blurb:
Some orderly patterns are made on purpose, like a watch, an army or a cathedral. Others arise from many people chasing their own small aims with no one in charge, and still come out orderly and useful. Adam Smith, Friedrich Hayek and the thinkers who followed them taught people to tell these two kinds of order apart, because confusing them is the mistake a planner most easily makes.

Watch a campus lawn where the paved walk bends around a corner. Soon a bare dirt track cuts straight across the grass. Planners call it a desire path, and nobody designed it: it was worn down step by step, each walker taking the quickest line, and once a faint track shows, others follow it. Language works the same way. No council ever wrote the rules of English and handed them out; its grammar grew up by itself over the centuries as people spoke and made themselves understood, which is why Hayek loved language as his favourite example of order without an inventor.

Designed languages do exist. In 1887 the eye doctor L. L. Zamenhof built one from scratch, with only sixteen grammar rules, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, one who hopes. Most invented languages die unspoken, but Esperanto became the most successful language anyone has ever made up, and even it began to grow on its own once real people used it. Money grew too. Barter runs into a wall, because each trader must want what the other has. Carl Menger argued that no king or committee invented money. Each trader kept accepting whatever good was easiest to pass on, everyone drifted to the same one, and it quietly became money.

The Scottish thinker Adam Ferguson, in Edinburgh in 1767, wondered how a nation ends up with its laws, customs and prices. His answer planted the whole notion of unplanned order: such institutions are the result of human action, but they carry out no human design. From it comes a simple habit of mind. Faced with any custom, keep three possible answers open at once: someone designed it, it grew with no designer, or it was blind chance. The mistake is to assume design the moment you see order. Hayek drew the line with two Greek words, taxis for a made order and kosmos for a grown one. Asking the purpose of an army makes good sense, because a commander built it to win battles. Ask the same of a market and you are misled, because nobody built the market, so it has no aim of its own, however useful it is to the people inside it.

karl-marx-and-the-communist-manifesto.context_blurb:
Karl Marx was a nineteenth-century German philosopher and journalist, expelled from Prussia, France and Belgium, who settled in London and spent decades in poverty writing Das Kapital. His closest friend and backer, Friedrich Engels, came from an industrial fortune. In 1848, as revolutions broke out across Europe, the two published a short, fiery pamphlet, The Communist Manifesto, that carried their names into the next two centuries.

The Manifesto's first words are famous: a spectre is haunting Europe, the spectre of communism. It closes with a rallying cry, telling the workers that they have nothing to lose but their chains and a world to win, so workers of every country should unite. Years later, too poor to rent a study, Marx wrote Das Kapital day after day in the free reading room of the British Museum, beneath its great dome; the first volume appeared in 1867.

Its central argument is enormous: the history of every society so far is the history of class struggles. The pamphlet was no lonely burst of inspiration. In 1847 the Communist League, a band of German workers in London, commissioned Marx and Engels to write the movement's official statement of aims, due in December; Marx, then 29, drafted it in January 1848, and it appeared without the authors' names just weeks before revolution broke out in France that February. For twenty years Engels supported the Marx family with money from his wealthy family's cotton mill in Manchester, the very kind of business Marx attacked. Engels sent an estimated 3,000 to 4,000 pounds over those years, and the Marx household nicknamed him the General. Even so, the Marxes suffered. In the 1850s the family lived in two wretched rooms in Soho's Dean Street, where creditors once seized the furniture and even the baby's cradle, and amid that hunger and cold several of their small children died, among them baby Franziska and young Edgar. Jenny Marx remembered the place as the frightful rooms that held all their joy and all their pain.

For years Marx wrote in agony, covered in boils called carbuncles, and he turned even that into a dig at the ruling class. To Engels he called it a truly proletarian disease, hoping the bourgeoisie would remember his carbuncles until their dying day. He died in 1883, and only about a dozen mourners stood at his grave in Highgate Cemetery. Engels opened his speech by announcing the hour at which the greatest living thinker stopped thinking. Marx's tomb bears his demand on philosophy: philosophers have only explained the world in one way or another, but the point is to change it. He wrote that line in Brussels in 1845, and it was published only after his death; the front of the tomb repeats the Manifesto's call for workers of all lands to unite.

alienation-the-worker-estranged-from-his.context_blurb:
In 1844 Karl Marx, a German writer of twenty-six living in Paris, filled a set of notebooks now called the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts. He was not yet calling for revolution; he was trying to name what had gone wrong in the lives of factory workers. His word for it was alienation, or estrangement: a man cut off from his work, his products, himself and other men.

Marx began with a bitter contrast. The worker's labour builds palaces, but he goes home to a hovel; it creates beauty for the rich man's world and ruin and poverty for the man who does it. Worse, Marx argued, the arithmetic runs backward. The more goods the worker turns out, the cheaper he himself becomes, so the world of things rises in value exactly as the world of men falls. Then Marx asked when the worker feels like himself. Away from work, he answered; the minute the shift begins, that feeling is gone. That shows the work is not freely chosen but forced, something he does only because he must. Marx even offered a test: remove every pressure, boss, threat and need, and see what happens. In the factory, the worker flees at once and shuns the work like the plague, proof that it was never really his.

The strangest break is with the thing he makes. He pours his strength and hours into an object, and once it is carried off to be sold, it turns on him like a stranger with power over him, something he made that now rules him. Marx drew a haunting reversal from this. Creating should be the most human act, yet the factory worker feels free only in his animal moments, when he eats, drinks and rests, while at the workbench, where a human should be most himself, he feels like a beast. A fourth break follows by logic. If what I make is not mine, it belongs to someone else, a man who never made it, so the worker's own toil creates the owner's power over him; his labour forges his master.

Underneath sits Marx's picture of what a human being is. A bee shaping its comb, Marx said, simply is that activity. A person can hold his own activity before his mind, step back from it, plan it and freely choose how to work. Animals build when need compels them and always to their species' set design; a free human makes things even when nothing compels him, and shapes them by the laws of beauty, finer than need requires. Then came the move that startled even friendly readers. The common view blames the boss's ownership for the worker's misery. Marx reversed it: alienated labour comes first, in the act of work itself, and private property is its result, not its cause.

Decades later Henry Ford's assembly line looked to many like Marx's nightmare made real, and writers still argue whether warehouse and gig jobs fit the picture. Marx's complaint was never mainly pay or hours. It was the man who does one tiny piece of the job forever, with no hand in the whole or in its design.

historical-materialism-and-class-struggl.context_blurb:
Historical materialism is the name later given to Karl Marx's lens for reading history. Its bold claim is that the engine of every great change is not ideas, religion or great men but something concrete: who owns the tools, the land and the factories, and how those who own nothing must work to eat. Marx and Friedrich Engels built a whole account of law, art and morality on that move, and the philosopher Karl Popper raised the hardest question about it.

The lens works like a detective's rule: follow the money. Britain's Corn Laws put a tax on foreign grain, which propped up the price of British grain; the landed gentry who grew it defended the tax, and the factory owners campaigned to scrap it until it fell in 1846. Knowing a man's trade told you his side, because each camp simply supported the law that served its own purse. In 1848 Marx wrote that the new capitalist class had stripped the old halo of respect from physicians, lawyers, priests, poets and scholars, turning all of them into hired hands paid wages, like any laborer. At Marx's grave in 1883, Engels compared him to Darwin and summed up the theory in one plain law: people need food, drink, a roof and clothes before they can do anything else, whether politics, art, science or religion.

Marx saw modern society splitting into two hostile camps. On one side stood the bourgeoisie, the owners of factories, land and capital; on the other stood the proletariat, laborers whose only property was their ability to work. He pictured society as a building. Its foundation is the economy, the way goods get made and who controls the tools for making them, and on top rises a superstructure of law, government, religion and art. In his picture, the economic base molds the legal and religious superstructure built upon it.

Marx pushed the point all the way inside the mind. It is not people's consciousness that determines their existence, he wrote, but their social existence that determines their consciousness, so a man's place in the economy reaches into his very sense of what is true and right. In Capital he told how a working class gets made. English landlords fenced off the common fields and turned farmland into sheep pasture, evicting the peasants who had always farmed there. With no way left to grow his own food, the evicted man had to hire himself out for daily wages to a mill owner.

The theory's reach delighted its admirers. Popper called that same reach its undoing: a lens that can explain any strike, war or law by pointing to class interest could never be proved wrong by any event, and a theory that nothing could refute is not doing the work of science. Defenders reply that a lens which reliably uncovers hidden interests can still be a real insight, even if it makes no testable prediction.

commodity-fetishism-and-religion-is-the-.context_blurb:
Karl Marx, the German thinker of the 1800s, left two images that are quoted far more often than they are read. One comes from Capital, his enormous study of the market, where he wrote of the fetishism of the commodity. The other, from an essay of the 1840s, now rides on bumper stickers: religion as the opium of the people.

Marx noticed how naturally a shopper says a coat is worth two shirts, as if the price belonged to the cloth like its color. He argued that a price only looks like a property of the object. What it really measures is human labor: the work poured into each item, and the ties between the people who did it, disguised as a relation among things. He borrowed the word fetish, a charm, to picture people bowing to things they had made.

The opium line now sounds like a sneer at believers. But in the 1840s opium and laudanum were ordinary legal painkillers that a household kept for real pain, so to Marx's first readers the comparison meant relief, not poison. Read whole, the passage calls faith the sigh of the oppressed creature, the heart of a heartless world.

That reading shaped his cure. Plenty of his later followers set out to crush faith by force, but Marx aimed elsewhere. For him the painkiller was not the disease, so the real task was to heal the misery underneath until the comfort was no longer wanted.

the-labor-theory-of-value-and-the-margin.context_blurb:
Two serious economic positions meet here. The labor theory of value, which Karl Marx inherited from Adam Smith and David Ricardo, holds that labor is what gives goods their value, and Marx used it in Capital to argue that profit is unpaid labor skimmed from the worker. The marginalist revolution of the 1870s, begun independently by Carl Menger, William Stanley Jevons and Leon Walras, reframed how value is set in a working market, and the Austrian Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk turned it directly against Marx.

The puzzle began with Smith in 1776. Water is vital to life but sells for next to nothing, whereas a diamond is nearly useless but fetches a fortune. Smith separated a good's value in use, how useful it is, from its value in exchange, what it will trade for, but he could not explain the gap. In 1871 Carl Menger did. What you pay tracks the worth of one more unit, not of the whole supply. Since water is everywhere, an extra glass is worth almost nothing; diamonds are scarce, so one more is worth a great deal. Robert Nozick, in Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), drove the point home. A craftsman who spends weeks shaping huge, beautiful mud pies that nobody wants has made nothing valuable, while a hiker who stoops to pick up a diamond holds a fortune. Effort is neither necessary nor sufficient for value; what buyers want decides it.

Marx had already closed one gap in his theory. Does a slow, idle worker who takes all day make a more valuable shirt? No, Marx said: only socially necessary labor counts, the time an average worker needs at the normal skill and pace of the day. His vision of the factory was dark. Capital, he wrote in Das Kapital (1867), is dead labor that feeds like a vampire on living labor, growing stronger the more it sucks. In 1896 Bohm-Bawerk likened Marx to a man who, wanting to be sure of pulling out a white ball, puts nothing but white balls into the urn. Marx, he charged, had defined value as labor at the outset and then presented the conclusion that value comes from labor as a discovery.

the-communist-record-what-actually-happe.context_blurb:
Marx's ideas have a real place in the history of philosophy, but in the 20th century actual states tried to put his program into practice: the Soviet Union under Lenin and Stalin, China under Mao, Cambodia under the Khmer Rouge and others. When the Soviet archives opened after 1991, historians could document what had happened on a scale they had never been able to measure before. The honest task is to look at the record plainly.

The most-quoted count comes from a volume of French historians edited by Stephane Courtois, published in English in 1999 under the title Black Book of Communism. In its introduction Courtois put the toll of communist regimes at 85 to 100 million deaths. Among the worst single crimes was a famine in Soviet Ukraine. Stalin's regime stripped Ukraine's villages of grain in 1932 and 1933, trapped the hungry farmers in the countryside, away from city food, and went on selling grain abroad as millions starved. Ukrainians call it the Holodomor, joining their words for hunger and extermination. In Cambodia, the Khmer Rouge captured Phnom Penh on 17 April 1975 and declared Year Zero. Within three days they drove all two million of the city's people, even hospital patients, out into the countryside to farm, chasing a forced peasant utopia.

Courtois broke the total down by regime: about 20 million in the Soviet Union, two million each in Cambodia and North Korea, and roughly 65 million in China alone, more than all the others put together. Much of China's toll came from the famine of Mao's Great Leap Forward. After years digging through state archives, the journalist Yang Jisheng put its starvation deaths at about 36 million in his book Tombstone. Beijing never challenged his figures; it simply banned the book in mainland China. The Khmer Rouge went furthest of all against markets, private property and trade: Cambodia became the only country ever to abolish money outright, and the regime blew up the National Bank in Phnom Penh to make the point.

Honest counting also means policing your own side's numbers. Two of the book's own chapter writers, Nicolas Werth and his colleague Jean-Louis Margolin, objected in public to their editor's headline figure. Margolin protested that he had never put Vietnam's dead at a million, and he accused Courtois of piling up charges in the service of a cause. Their quarrel was over careful arithmetic, not over whether the crimes happened.

rawls-and-the-veil-of-ignorance.context_blurb:
John Rawls, a Harvard philosopher who had fought as an infantryman in the Pacific, spent some twenty-five years on one old question: how should a society's basic structure be arranged if we take seriously that free people are equals? His answer, A Theory of Justice (1971), is probably the most influential work of political philosophy in English since the Second World War. It rests on one thought experiment, and the debate it began is still open.

The question had roots in his childhood. At seven, in 1928, Rawls fell ill with diphtheria, and his little brother Bobby caught it from him and died; the following winter Rawls had pneumonia, which killed his brother Tommy as well. Rawls traced his lifelong stammer to those losses, and he spent his life asking what we owe those dealt a harsh fate through no fault of their own. His thought experiment asks you to design a society's rules before you know who you will be in it. Behind what he called a veil of ignorance you do not know your future wealth, race or sex, or how talented you will turn out to be, though you keep all general knowledge of economics and human behavior. Since you could land anywhere, the rational choice is rules you could bear even from the lowest place in society. Rawls named the whole view justice as fairness: a rule is just because all would accept it before learning which person each of them will be, not because the powerful like it or tradition hallowed it.

From behind the veil, Rawls argued, come two principles in strict order. The first gives every person, equally, the same basic liberties, and no bargain may sacrifice it, not even one that brings greater wealth all round. The second, the difference principle, permits gaps in wealth on one test. An inequality such as a chief executive's huge salary is just only if the system that allows it does more for the poorest group than any alternative could.

Why play it so safe? Rawls called the reasoning maximin, maximize the minimum. Offered one society with glittering heights and cruel depths and another plainer but with a tolerable floor, you look only at the worst position in each and take the society whose worst is least terrible, because you might be the one at the bottom. Rawls also held that the luck of the draw in talents and upbringing is morally arbitrary, since nobody chose or earned his gifts. Those born gifted may gain from that luck, but only under arrangements that benefit the less fortunate too. Robert Nozick answered with a basketball star. Begin with any distribution you call fair, let a million fans each pay an extra quarter to see Wilt Chamberlain, every payment voluntary, and the fair pattern is gone. Freedom keeps disturbing any fixed distribution, Nozick argued, so a society must choose between holding the pattern and letting people decide.

Nozick's rival theory looked to history: anything reached from a just starting point by just steps is just as well. From it he drew a sharp claim, that taxing wages to fund redistribution is equal to forced labor, because taking what you earn takes hours of your life. Other critics kept the veil but rejected Rawls's caution. The economist John Harsanyi said someone who calmly weighs the odds would not be gripped by dread of the worst place; he would aim for the highest average welfare, which is the utilitarian answer. Michael Sandel attacked the veil itself. Strip a person of race, faith, loyalties and history, and what remains has no commitments or aims left, so it is not a self capable of choosing anything. Rawls replied that the veil is a device for reasoning, not a portrait of real people, and the contest remains open.

nozick-the-wilt-chamberlain-argument-and.context_blurb:
Robert Nozick taught down the hall from John Rawls at Harvard, and in 1974, three years after Rawls's A Theory of Justice, he published Anarchy, State, and Utopia, a playful libertarian reply that became the other classic of modern justice. His target was the hidden assumption that you can judge whether wealth is justly spread from a snapshot of who ends up with what. The book offers a move to recognize, and Rawlsians still answer it.

Nozick starts from persons. Every person is distinct and has a single life to live, so nobody may be treated merely as an instrument for others. Rights are therefore side constraints: fixed limits on what anyone may do to you, never goals to be maximized, not even for a good cause. Justice in holdings is historical. The test of a just holding is how its owner came to get it, not whether the final spread matches a chart of who deserves what. Then comes his famous story. Begin with wealth divided equally, an arrangement everyone calls fair. Wilt Chamberlain, the basketball star, signs a deal giving him a cut of every ticket, and all season fans happily pay a quarter extra to see him, until he is far richer than anyone. Nozick's question is blunt: can anyone call the lopsided outcome unjust? He also imagined a machine that could pipe in any blissful life you liked, so convincing that every triumph and friendship inside it would feel genuine. Most people, he guessed, would refuse to plug in for good, which shows we care about really doing things and really being a certain kind of person, not just the sensation of it.

Nozick's answer rests on three principles: acquisition, how unclaimed things first come to be owned; rectification, how old injustices are repaired; and transfer. A transfer is just when it is voluntary, free of theft, force and fraud. If the equal start was just and every quarter changed hands by a free choice that wronged no one, then the lopsided result must be just as well, because nothing but free choices brought it about. Any fixed pattern, equal shares or shares by merit or need, is upset the moment people may trade, so a society that insists on its pattern has two options forever: forbid the exchanges that upset it, or keep confiscating and reshuffling people's earnings without end. Nozick concluded that only a minimal state, the night-watchman state, can be justified, and its only work is to protect people from violence, theft and fraud and hold them to their contracts. His Tale of the Slave walks one man through nine arrangements, from a master who beats him whenever he likes to a system where his single vote among ten thousand counts only when the others are evenly split. Nozick ends by asking where along the way the slave stopped being a slave.

His most shocking charge is that taxing what people earn by working is equal in kind to forced labor. Defenders of redistribution answer that a taxpayer keeps his job and his freedom. Nozick replies that taking the fruits of hours you worked conscripts that labor, and an automatic claim on it hands others partial ownership of you. Rawls's rule permits inequality only if it does the most for the worst-off. Nozick never called that goal heartless; his objection was that it turns gifted people into a common pool for others' benefit, ignoring that each is a separate person with one life. He parodied Marx's famous call to take from each by ability and give to each by need with a slogan of his own: from each as he chooses, to each as he is chosen. The line covers every free way property moves, from a sale to a gift to a lost poker hand. Finally he recast the minimal state as a framework for utopia. Because it forces no single blueprint on anyone, people can found countless competing communities, move into whichever they like and walk out of any that disappoints them. The contest with Rawls remains open.

rawls-vs-nozick-fairness-or-liberty.context_blurb:
In the 1970s two Harvard philosophers, working down the hall from each other, gave modern political philosophy its two most durable pictures of justice. John Rawls imagined designing a society for people who do not yet know their place in it, and found rules that favor the worst-off. Robert Nozick insisted that justice depends on how people came by their holdings, through free exchange and gift. Both are serious positions, and the argument between them is still open.

Rawls's war marked him. As a foot soldier in the Pacific war, he was decorated with a Bronze Star for service in New Guinea, was busted back to private for refusing an order to punish a fellow soldier, and in the autumn of 1945 toured bombed-out Hiroshima. Many biographers trace his concern for society's most vulnerable to what he saw. His thought experiment puts you behind a veil of ignorance, choosing rules before you know your wealth, race, sex, talents or even your idea of a good life. Since you might wake up as anyone, a clear-headed chooser would raise the lowest place in society as high as it can go. Nozick countered with Wilt Chamberlain. Begin with wealth shared perfectly fairly, then let a million fans each gladly pay the star an extra 25 cents, with no one forced or cheated, until by season's end he towers over everyone in wealth. Keeping wealth in any fixed shape, Nozick concluded, would require a free society to keep cancelling people's willing exchanges. The philosopher G. A. Cohen replied that no one consented to the lopsided result.

Rawls ranks his two principles in strict order. Suppose a government proposes that every citizen surrender a single freedom, such as free speech, in return for making even the poorest richer. Rawls's framework forbids the deal, because liberty ranks above wealth and cannot be bartered for it, so the trade fails at the first principle before wealth is ever weighed. Nozick's entitlement theory judges by history, not by snapshots. Picture two societies with the same vast gap between rich and poor, one where every fortune grew from fair beginnings through willing exchange and gifts, the other built on conquest and theft. On Nozick's theory only the first is just, since identical holdings cannot wash clean a fortune won by plunder. And when the state taxes the earnings of your work to hand them to others, Nozick wrote, it has claimed a piece of your hours, which he declared on a par with forced labor.

Rawls's boldest claim is that no one earned the hand he was dealt at birth, not his intelligence, his strength or even a sunny temperament. He called these gifts the outcome of a natural lottery, morally arbitrary, and concluded that gifted people may gain from their talents, provided the rules that let them also improve the lot of the poorest. Defenders of desert, Nozick among them, reject that premise. Yet Nozick himself later softened. In The Examined Life, published in 1989, he wrote that the libertarian position he once propounded now seemed to him seriously inadequate, chiefly because it neglected the cooperative things a community does together. He never declared his old arguments refuted, and neither man settled the dispute.
