marys-room-the-knowledge-argument.context_blurb:
In a 1982 essay the Australian philosopher Frank Jackson imagined Mary, a brilliant scientist who has lived her whole life among black and white and has never seen a color. She has mastered every physical fact about color vision, every wavelength and every firing neuron. Then the door opens and she sees a ripe tomato. Does she learn something? The puzzle, called the knowledge argument, is a famous test of physicalism, the view that everything is physical, and the debate remains open.

The stakes are simple. Mary had all the physical facts before she stepped out, so if seeing red teaches her anything new, there was some fact about the world that was not a physical fact she already had. Jackson warmed up with Fred, a man whose color vision outdid everyone's: where the rest of us see a single red, Fred saw two distinct reds and coined the names red1 and red2 for them. No physics of Fred's eyes, Jackson argued, tells you what his extra red looks like. Thomas Nagel had made a cousin of the point in 1974 with a bat, which steers by shrieking and listening for echoes. A full physical account of its brain, Nagel said, would still not tell you what it is like, from the inside, to be that bat. All three cases circle what philosophers call qualia: the felt quality of an experience, the redness of red or what a sunset is actually like to see, which a list of wavelengths and firing cells seems to leave out.

Jackson set out the argument as a chain. Inside the room Mary has the complete physical story of color; on seeing red she plainly learns something; so she lacked a fact even though she had every physical one, and the physical facts are not all the facts there are.

Physicalists answered in different ways. David Lewis argued that Mary gains no new fact, only new abilities: the power to recognize red, to picture it and to call it back to mind, which is know-how rather than know-that, like learning to ride a bike. His test question was about tasting Vegemite, the salty Australian spread people either love or loathe: knowing what that is like, he said, means having abilities, not storing a fact. Daniel Dennett went further and denied she learns anything, since someone who truly knew every physical fact would already know what red looks like. In his version, her captors try to dazzle her with her first colored object, a banana painted blue. Mary snaps at once that they tried to trick her, because bananas are yellow and this one is blue.

Another reply, often called the old-fact-new-guise view, says Mary held the physical fact all along, though only in the dry terms of science, and seeing red simply gives her a new, felt way of thinking about that same old fact. The textbook picture is the discovery that Bruce Wayne is Batman: one man, two ways of thinking about him, and no extra person in the world. The last twist belongs to Jackson himself. After defending his argument for about fifteen years, he turned against it and accepted physicalism after all. Part of his reason was that seeing red makes Mary exclaim, so her experience has physical effects, which his old view had denied. He announced the reversal in three blunt words: "I have capitulated."

the-chinese-room.context_blurb:
In 1980 the American philosopher John Searle published a paper, Minds, Brains, and Programs, built around a strange locked room. It attacks one claim about artificial intelligence: that running the right program is all it takes to have a mind. Searle's slogan is that shuffling symbols is not the same as grasping what they mean. Critics have argued back for decades, and the question remains open.

The room had a real target. In the late 1970s Searle was invited to speak at Yale's artificial intelligence lab, where Roger Schank's team showed off a story-reading program that, its builders claimed, truly understood the tales it was quizzed on. Told that a man stormed out of a restaurant without paying because his hamburger came burned, the program correctly said he had not eaten it. Searle was unmoved: producing the correct reply is one thing, and understanding the story is another. So he imagined himself shut in a room with an English rulebook and boxes full of Chinese characters, the rules telling him which squiggle goes beside which squoggle. He knows no Chinese, yet by following the rules he passes out replies so fluent that native speakers outside believe the room understands them. In truth he is only matching shapes by rule, with no idea what any of them mean. The room is aimed at one claim, which Searle called Strong AI: that a properly programmed computer literally has a mind and really understands. The milder claim, that a computer merely imitates thinking, he could accept.

His keystone point is that shuffling symbols by their shape, however flawlessly and for however long, never gives the shuffler the faintest idea what the symbols refer to. In his words, syntax is not enough for semantics. That is his reply to Alan Turing, who proposed in 1950 that a machine able to converse as well as a human should count as thinking. Searle's room would pass that test without a single slip and still understand nothing, so acting just like a mind falls short of being one. Nor does the material help. Build the same program out of beer cans dangling from strings, or toilet rolls and stones, and it is plain that a correct pattern built from the wrong stuff understands nothing at all; only something with the causal powers of a brain could understand.

Critics struck back. The most famous rebuttal, the Systems Reply, pressed early by Ned Block, concedes that the person in the room knows no Chinese; he is merely the engine, like one chip in a computer. The understanding, they say, lives in the whole room, man, rulebook and baskets together, taken as one system. Others offered the Robot Reply: give the program a robot body with cameras for eyes, and its symbols will connect to the world. Searle answered that the camera's signals would reach the man as one more tape of numbers, and he would not even know where they came from. The trouble, he argued, is not a missing list matching words to sights: more symbols are still only symbols, never their meaning.

Searle had sharp answers to both. Suppose, he said, the man learns the entire rulebook and all the symbols by heart, runs every step mentally, and strolls around outside conversing in Chinese. Now he contains the entire system, and he still understands nothing. To those who wanted a program copying a Chinese speaker's brain neuron by neuron, he offered a man working a vast network of water pipes, one valve per synapse, mirroring every firing. The water copies the firing exactly, yet neither the man nor the pipes understand a word; copying a brain is not having one. Paul and Patricia Churchland turned his style of argument against him. Wave a magnet about in the dark and no glow appears, yet the physicist James Clerk Maxwell was right that light is an electromagnetic wave. A lone neuron grasps no English, yet a whole brain does. Searle's mistake, they charged, is trusting a gut feeling that quietly breaks down when a process is very slow or very large.

nagels-what-is-it-like-to-be-a-bat.context_blurb:
In 1974 the American philosopher Thomas Nagel published a short essay, "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?", that handed the study of consciousness one of its most lasting puzzles. Even a perfect physical description of a bat's brain, Nagel argued, would leave out what the world is like from the bat's own point of view.

The choice of creature was deliberate. A bat is a mammal, close enough to us that we are confident it has experiences at all, yet it finds its way by sonar, firing rapid shrieks and reading the echoes, a sense humans entirely lack. We are sure there is an inner life there, and we have no way in. Nagel then said something surprising about that inner life. There genuinely is a way things seem to the bat, and those facts are real and fixed whether or not anyone studies them. Yet they may stay permanently out of reach of human concepts, the way the facts of color may stay out of reach for someone blind from birth.

Readers often file the bat under proofs that the mind must be more than the brain, and Nagel called that a misreading. His claim is more modest: not that materialism is false (the view that thinking is simply brain activity), but that we cannot yet see how it could be true. We lack the concepts to understand it, which leaves it a mystery rather than a refuted doctrine. The essay is a close cousin of Frank Jackson's Mary's room, and its exact lesson is still debated.

the-mind-body-problem-the-framing-fork.context_blurb:
How does a mind fit into a body? Three families of answer have argued for centuries. Dualists say mind and body are two different things. Identity theorists say the mind simply is the brain. Functionalists say a mind is defined by what it does. The dispute is still open.

Start with a humble tool. A snapping bar, a sticky pad, a box that tips over and poison bait share no parts and no workings, yet each one counts as a mousetrap for one reason: it catches mice, whatever it is made of. Functionalists say minds work the same way. Pain is whatever state an injury causes that makes a creature flinch and guard the hurt, whether in a human, an alien or a robot.

In 1949 the Oxford philosopher Gilbert Ryle attacked the dualist picture with a little story. A visitor is shown every college, library and playing field of a university, then asks where the university itself is. His blunder is to hunt for the university as one more thing standing beside its parts, when it simply is those parts working together. Ryle called this a category mistake and said Descartes made the same error by picturing the mind as a ghost in the machine.

Identity theorists such as the Australian J.J.C. Smart met the obvious objection, that a toothache feels nothing like firing cells, with an astronomer's discovery. The bright Morning Star seen before sunrise and the Evening Star seen after sunset look like two lights, yet both are one planet, Venus. Two descriptions can name a single thing.

Descartes himself reached dualism by doubting. A deceiver might fool him into thinking he had a body, but nothing could make him doubt his own existence while he was busy doubting. From that gap he concluded that mind and body are two entirely different kinds of thing: a thing that thinks and a thing that takes up space. He added a second argument. Any body can be cut in half, then in quarters, then smaller still, but you could never split a mind, since there is no such thing as half a self, and what can be divided cannot be the same as what cannot.

U.T. Place, writing in 1956, argued that a sensation simply is a brain process, one event described in two ways, not a separate effect of it. Science has found such identities before, he said: lightning turned out to be nothing but a flow of electric charge. We learned it by investigation, and the same might hold for mind and brain.

The dualist's sharpest critic came early. In 1643 Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia, aged twenty-four, accepted Descartes's picture and asked one question. In the world of mechanics a body moves only when something pushes it, and pushing takes contact and size. So how could a soul with no size at all ever set a body moving? Descartes pointed to the tiny pineal gland as the soul's seat, but he never explained how something without extension could nudge it.

Hilary Putnam struck at the identity theory in 1967. Suppose pain were exactly one brain state, one particular set of fibres firing. An octopus has a body and brain laid out nothing like ours, yet it recoils from injury and shields the wound. Humans, birds, reptiles and octopuses all seem to feel pain with very different brains, so no one fixed brain state could be what pain is.

philosophical-zombies-and-the-hard-probl.context_blurb:
In the mid-1990s the Australian philosopher David Chalmers made famous a strange creature, the philosophical zombie: a being identical to you atom for atom, behaving exactly as you do, but with no inner experience at all, nothing it is like to be it from the inside. The zombie is a weapon in the fiercest dispute in philosophy of mind, over whether felt experience is anything beyond physical facts, and serious thinkers stand on every side.

Picture a perfect copy of you that flinches and cries out when pricked, yet feels nothing. Chalmers holds that this copy is coherently imaginable, and many of his rivals agree; they differ over what follows. Chalmers's own conclusion is that, because such a copy can be imagined, experience must be something further, not fixed by the physical facts at all. Rival thinkers grant the same picture and draw other conclusions.

Two earlier thought experiments point the same way. In 1974 Thomas Nagel asked what it is like to be a bat, a creature that steers by squeaking and reading the echoes. Learn everything objective about its brain and its sonar, and you still could not reach the bat's own point of view on its world, since that subjective standpoint is exactly what outside data leave out. Frank Jackson's Mary knows all the physics of color yet has lived among only black and white, until one day she sees a ripe red tomato. Jackson asked whether that first sight of red gives her a fact she truly lacked.

Chalmers divided consciousness research into easy problems, like explaining how the brain processes and reports sensory information, and one hard problem that would remain after every easy one was solved: why all that processing should come with any inner feeling whatever. The hard problem is not why experience lands in this brain rather than another; it is why there is experience at all. The word zombie came from horror films. In 1974 Robert Kirk brought it into serious philosophy as a weapon against physicalism, the thesis that once all the physical facts are settled, every mental fact is settled too.

Chalmers's argument moves from imagining to possibility: if zombies can be conceived, they could exist, and if they could exist, physical facts do not settle everything. Critics attack the move from conceiving to possibility with water. Before chemistry, a thinker could easily picture water made of something other than hydrogen and oxygen, yet experiment showed what water must be. Being able to imagine something vividly does not show it could really be, so imagining zombies may prove nothing. Defenders answer in turn, and the dispute is far from settled. Even Jackson changed sides, deciding that Mary picks up no new fact, just a new way of being acquainted with something she already knew.

leibnizs-mill.context_blurb:
Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, the German co-inventor of calculus, slipped a striking thought experiment into his short 1714 work, the Monadology. Imagine a machine built to think and to feel, then enlarged until you could walk inside it as you would a windmill, hunting for its thoughts.

Inside you meet only parts pushing other parts. Leibniz did not conclude that the thought was hiding in some piece too tiny to see. Perception, he argued, is simply not the kind of thing that could ever turn up as one more piece of the works, so he looked for it in a simple substance with no parts at all.

Materialists answer with water: no one drop is wet, yet the glassful is. On their reply, called emergence, thinking is a new property of the whole machine once its gears run together, not a faint scrap held by each gear. Critics answer that the felt quality of experience still seems left over. In 1980 John Searle imagined a lone man in a room matching Chinese characters by a rulebook without understanding a word, and scholars call the mill its ancestor. Both arguments make the same move: they examine the mechanism one piece at a time, find no mind in any piece, and conclude that no mind is there.

the-inverted-spectrum.context_blurb:
The inverted spectrum is one of the strangest puzzles in the philosophy of mind. What if the inner experience you have when you see red is the one I have when I see green? We would still both call tomatoes red and stop at red lights, and no test of behaviour would seem able to reveal the swap. The puzzle presses on theories that identify an experience with the role it plays, and it remains a live dispute.

John Locke raised the first clear version in 1689. He imagined that one person's experience of a violet might be another's experience of a marigold. His verdict was that no one could ever detect such a swap, since no one can pass into another person's mind to compare, and so he thought it changed nothing about how we talk or live.

Later thinkers found a crack. Our colour space is lopsided rather than a neat mirror. Darken yellow and it becomes brown, a quite different colour, while darkened blue stays blue. A person whose colours were truly flipped would report brown where others did not, so the swap might show itself after all. The philosophers of the Vienna Circle took a harder line still. A difference that no observation could ever detect, they held, is no difference at all, so the suggestion that your red might be my green only looks like a claim, and underneath there is no fact to be right or wrong about.

the-ship-of-the-self-the-brain-transplan.context_blurb:
What makes you the same person over time: your memories, your body or something else? In the 1600s the English philosopher John Locke posed the question with a prince and a cobbler, and modern philosophers have sharpened it with imagined brain transplants. Each answer has serious defenders, and none has won.

Locke imagined a prince's mind waking inside a cobbler's body. Everyone would say this man must answer for what the prince did, not for the cobbler's doings, because what crossed over was the prince's memory. For Locke you are whoever's past life you can remember living. The body settles which man you are; consciousness settles which person. That is why he called person a word for courts. Blaming a man for an act his own consciousness cannot reach or own would be no fairer than punishing one twin for his brother's crime.

In 1963 Sydney Shoemaker brought the puzzle into the operating room. A surgical team bungles a double operation, and Robinson's body ends up housing Brown's brain. Waking, this Brownson recalls Brown's life and carries on Brown's plans, and most people feel sure he is Brown, because the person seems to travel with the brain that remembers.

Bernard Williams pushed back. You are a living animal, he argued, so having your brain moved into a fresh skull is no different from giving your liver to someone else. The organ leaves; you stay behind with the emptied head. He also told one story two ways. Described as a swap between two strangers, a mind moving into another body sounds cheerful, and we side with the mind. Now tell the same story to you: tomorrow you will be tortured, after your memories are wiped and rewritten. The dread does not lift, which hints that you are still the body.

Then comes fission. Split your brain and put each half into a new head. Each of the two, Lefty and Righty, remembers your whole life and has your character. By the memory rule each of them is you, yet they are plainly two people, and one person cannot be two at once. Derek Parfit concluded that identity is not what matters in survival; continuity is.

the-trolley-problem.context_blurb:
In 1967 the Oxford philosopher Philippa Foot imagined a runaway tram heading for five workmen. In 1985 the American philosopher Judith Jarvis Thomson built a whole family of cases around it. The aim is to find the exact moral line that splits cases with the same arithmetic but opposite verdicts. Rival explanations are still argued, and the debate is wide open.

Start with the switch. Left alone, the tram kills five men; turned onto a side track, it kills one. Nearly everyone answers that you should turn it, because losing one life is less bad than losing five. Now stand on a footbridge beside a very large stranger. Shoving him onto the track would stop the trolley and save the five. The trade is the same, one for five, yet surveys find that while about nine in ten people would throw the switch, a clear majority refuse to push. That recoil shows that two acts with identical outcomes can still differ in whether they are permitted. A surgeon's case points the same way. Five patients will die without new organs, and a healthy visitor matches all five, yet nearly everyone says the surgeon may not cut him up. Saving five at the price of one is not always allowed, so the body count cannot settle it alone.

Foot paired her tram with a judge. A mob will slaughter part of a town unless someone hangs for a crime, and the judge could frame one innocent man. The driver may turn; the judge may not. The difference is that the driver steers away a harm already loose, while the judge creates a new death out of nothing. Foot's third figure, a pilot whose doomed airliner will crash whatever he does, may aim it at an emptier district. Driver and pilot both redirect a harm already on its way; the surgeon and the pusher use a person's body to absorb it. From these pairs Foot drew her rule: actively causing harm is, as a rule, worse than letting it happen, so the duty not to kill weighs more than the duty to rescue.

Thomson moved the hero. In her version you are a mere passer-by beside the lever, with no special duty as driver, and people still think you may turn the trolley. So the driver's job was never the point; what people accept is the act of redirecting itself. Thomson also offered a sharp test. Imagine the victim vanishing a moment before you act. If the man on the footbridge vanishes, your plan fails, so his death is your means of saving the five. If the workman on the side track vanishes, you are only glad, so his death is merely a foreseen side effect.

The tidy lines keep wobbling. Suppose the heavy stranger is in fact the villain who tied the five down, and many who would not push an innocent stranger now say push him. So the original reluctance was never just counting; whether the victim deserved the harm was shaping the verdict all along. In Thomson's loop case, the side track curves back to rejoin the main line, and only the lone workman's body stops the trolley from circling round to the five. Now his being struck is what saves them, so pulling the lever works through his death, not past it, just as the push does. Her own answer turned on rights: redirecting a danger onto fewer people is allowed only if it violates nobody's rights, and pushing a man plainly violates his. Then she pressed her answer hard. If turning even a plain trolley onto one man violates his right, then the fact that five need saving cannot strip the surgeon's victim of his right either.

Brain scans added a new angle. In 2001 Joshua Greene found that the switch case mostly engaged the brain's calm reasoning regions, while the footbridge set off its emotional alarms. He traced the alarm to one feature of the push: it is up close and personal, your own hands shoving a living body. That describes what the brain does; it does not say which choice is right.

consequentialism-utilitarianism-the-move.context_blurb:
Consequentialism is the view that an action is right or wrong because of its results and nothing else. Its best-known form, utilitarianism, took shape in England with the reformer Jeremy Bentham in the late 1700s and his godson John Stuart Mill, whose book Utilitarianism appeared in 1861. Its pull is strong: it refuses to hide cruelty behind rules and counts everyone's welfare. Its critics press just as hard.

The basic move is simple. Suppose a new well can go in a village of 300 thirsty people or in a hamlet of 12. The results-thinker drills in the big village, because the right choice is whatever brings the greatest good to the greatest number. The same move strips rules of any weight of their own. If a boy promised his sister the last slice of cake and four hungry friends arrive, the strict results-thinker says the promise carries no force by itself; it binds only so far as keeping it does the most good. Thinkers who judge by duty answer that a promise binds whatever the count, and that dispute is still alive.

Critics built cases to test the move. In 1967 Philippa Foot pictured a runaway trolley bearing down on five people, with a lever that can send it down a side line toward just one, and most people would pull the lever. In 1976 Judith Jarvis Thomson kept the arithmetic but changed the act: now the only way to stop the trolley is to push a heavy stranger off a bridge so that his body blocks it. Almost no one agrees to that. Same sum, opposite gut. Sharper still is a surgeon whose five patients will die without new organs while a healthy visitor waits for a routine exam. The count says carving up one saves five, yet nearly everyone recoils, because maximizing the total would demand using an innocent person as raw material. That clash between the tally and the prohibition is where critics push hardest, and defenders answer it in several ways.

In the first lines of his 1789 book on morals and law, Bentham announced that nature has placed mankind under two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure, which rule both what we do and what we ought to do. All value reduces to them, so the source of a pleasure is irrelevant and only its amount counts. He drove the point home with push-pin, a trivial pub game: if push-pin gives more pleasure than poetry, he wrote, then it is worth more. The same arithmetic is radically equal. When a utilitarian adds up what a law will bring, a duke's joy weighs exactly as much as a stable-boy's, and Mill credited Bentham with the rule that everybody counts for one and nobody for more than one. But Mill could not accept that the kind of pleasure makes no difference. Anyone who has tasted both the higher and the lower pleasures will not trade down, he argued, so a dissatisfied Socrates is better off than a fool who is satisfied.

Bentham even hoped to put pleasure on a measuring scale. His felicific calculus scored each pleasure on seven counts: its intensity, its duration, its certainty, its nearness in time, its purity from pain, its extent across people, and, most surprising, its fecundity, the chance that it will breed still more pleasures. Mill needed a different tool for quality, since no ruler says whether a poem outranks a feast. His test was to ask the people who have deeply known both and see which they prefer, even at some cost in discontent. The famous slogan about the greatest happiness of the greatest number is not even Bentham's. Francis Hutcheson used it in 1725, in his inquiry into moral good and evil, decades before Bentham believed he had found it in the writings of Joseph Priestley. Nor did either man expect a shopper to tally every option's happiness before buying milk. Bentham said his calculus need not be run before every judgment, and Mill called that charge a misunderstanding; for both men the calculus defines what makes an act right, but nobody has to work it out at every turn.

deontology-duty-the-move.context_blurb:
Deontology is the great rival to judging acts by their results, and its most famous champion was the eighteenth-century German philosopher Immanuel Kant. Its move is that some acts are simply wrong in themselves, so no balance of good outcomes can make them right: you keep the promise and refuse the lie because of what the act is. Critics press it hard, and the clash between duty and results still frames much of modern ethics.

Picture a vow to a dying grandfather to carry his ashes to his favorite lake. Nobody else knows of it, and burying the ashes in the yard would be far easier. The pull to make the trip anyway is the duty move: a promise keeps its grip on you even when nobody remains to hold you to it. Judging only by results struggles to explain why a secret promise to the dead should matter at all. The same move divides two friends arguing about a riot. Mara would frame one innocent man if it would calm a deadly mob, since for her the outcome is all that counts. Tomas refuses, standing on the principle that certain acts are off-limits in themselves, however much good they might buy.

The duty move blocks the arithmetic even at five to one. In Judith Jarvis Thomson's transplant case, a surgeon could save five dying patients by carving up one healthy visitor whose organs match them all, yet almost everyone says he must not, because killing an innocent man for his parts is forbidden even when it would save a greater number. Kant took the hardest case he could find. In a 1797 essay answering Benjamin Constant, he imagined a killer at your door asking where your friend is hiding. Kant held that you still must not lie, because the deliberate lie is wrong in its very nature, no matter what good it might win.

So why do people who would switch a runaway trolley from five onto one refuse the surgeon? Defenders of duty point to how the death figures in the plan. In the transplant the man's body is the rescue itself, so harming him is the means; on the track the lone worker's death is an unwanted side effect of turning the trolley. Whether that difference carries real moral weight is itself debated. Critics have a sharper challenge: if murder is bad, should you not commit one murder to stop two others? The duty view refuses, holding that you answer for the murder you commit yourself, not for keeping down the total of other people's crimes, a refusal its critics count as a real cost. Bernard Williams pressed a related worry in 1973. In his story, Jim comes upon a soldier named Pedro who is ready to execute twenty prisoners and offers to spare nineteen if Jim will shoot one. The numbers favor shooting, yet Williams argued that firing would make Jim himself the author of a killing he finds monstrous, where otherwise the deaths would be Pedro's work.

virtue-ethics-the-move.context_blurb:
Ethics has three great moves. Rule-based thinking asks which rule to follow, and results-based thinking asks which outcome is best. Virtue ethics, rooted in Aristotle and Thomas Aquinas, asks something simpler and stranger: what would a good person do here? Character does the work, not calculation.

Mara finds a fat wallet stuffed with cash, and no one is watching. Torn, she uses her grandmother's trick: she asks herself how a truly good person would act in her place. The question points at the kind of person acting, not at a rule or a tally.

Motive matters as much as the deed. A man visits a sick friend in hospital, and her smile fades when he admits he came only because it was his duty. To a virtue ethicist the confession spoils the visit, because friendship means showing up out of care for the person herself, not out of obedience to a rule. In the same way, a merchant who never cheats but says honesty is simply good for business, and that he will drop it the day it stops paying, is not an honest man. His fairness is only a strategy, and the wholehearted commitment that makes honesty a virtue is missing.

How do you get such a character? Aristotle's answer was plain: by doing brave things again and again until courage becomes a habit, the way a musician grows skilled by practice. He also placed each virtue between two faults. Courage has two opposites, not one: cowardice on one side and, on the other, recklessness, charging into every danger with too little fear.

The approach shines in hard cases. A killer bangs on your door hunting a friend you are hiding. A strict rule-follower says never lie; a calculator weighs a lie against a life. The virtue ethicist pictures a person who is honest to the core and also full of compassion, and most land on the protective lie, because honesty, as a trait of good character, was never a promise to hand innocents to their killers. Defenders of the strict rule still disagree.

nozicks-experience-machine.context_blurb:
In his 1974 book Anarchy, State, and Utopia, the American philosopher Robert Nozick slipped in a thought experiment that still troubles anyone who thinks pleasure is all that matters. Picture a machine that could feed you a whole lifetime of experiences of your choosing, any triumph, love or adventure, as vivid as reality, while your body floats in a tank, wired to a computer. Would you plug in for life?

Nozick added one clever rule: plugging in wipes away the memory of choosing it, so the life inside never feels fake, and knowing it was fake can never spoil a single moment. The film The Matrix stages the choice. Cypher, a man who has learned that his world is a computer simulation, sits over a steak he knows is not real and agrees to return to the simulation and have his memory wiped, trading the real world for a comfortable illusion. Viewers find him unsettling because most would choose otherwise.

Most people, Nozick found, refuse the machine, and he offered reasons. First, we want to do certain things, not just have the experience of doing them. Inside the tank you could stand on the summit of Everest and never doubt it, but what would be missing is the feat itself, really hauling yourself up the mountain, rather than a feeling of it made to order. Second, we want to be a certain kind of person, brave or kind or witty, and someone floating in a tank is none of these, just an indeterminate blob. So Nozick called plugging in a kind of suicide: you would not die, but the self you had been would simply end.

Critics pushed back. In 2010 the philosopher Felipe De Brigard turned the question inside out, telling volunteers that their entire lives so far had been lived inside such a machine and asking whether they wanted to unplug into reality. Barely half did, and when told their outside life was a prisoner's, only about one in eight chose to leave. The refusal, he suggested, may come less from a special love of reality than from a pull toward whatever life we are already living. Nozick had anticipated the being and doing objections with two more devices: a transformation machine that really remakes your character, and a result machine that really brings about whatever you would have achieved. People would refuse those too, he argued, because what we most want is to live our lives ourselves, as doers, in touch with what is real.

the-utility-monster-and-the-repugnant-co.context_blurb:
Two famous thought experiments test the utilitarian rule that we should always maximize total happiness. Robert Nozick built the first in his 1974 book Anarchy, State, and Utopia; Derek Parfit built the second in Reasons and Persons in 1984. Neither is a knockout of utilitarianism, but both are hard tests its defenders still have to answer.

Nozick imagined a utility monster, a creature that wrings a hundred units of pleasure from an apple that would give anyone else a single unit. If the rule is to produce the biggest possible total, the arithmetic demands that every apple and every other resource go to the monster while everyone else goes without. Nozick's grim phrase was that everyone else must be sacrificed in the monster's maw for the sake of a bigger total. The monster also exposes a promise. Utilitarians say each person counts for one, but the slogan turns into this: the best converter of resources into pleasure takes everything, and everyone else counts for nothing.

Parfit's trap starts from a flourishing world. Bring into being an extra population, apart from the first, whose lives are still worth living, then even everything out into a larger world, and repeat. Step by step the world grows more crowded and its lives grow poorer. Mozart's music disappears, then Haydn's, then Venice, until all that remains in the final world is muzak and potatoes, billions of lives barely worth living. Yet that world holds more total happiness. Parfit called this the Repugnant Conclusion. Critics keep searching for the broken link, but each move on its own looks defensible, so no single link can be cleanly cut; the trouble lies in the whole chain.

Some philosophers try to dodge it by maximizing average happiness instead. That fix breeds a monster too. The average rule would prefer a single blissful person, just a hair happier than each of ten billion very happy people, to all ten billion of them.

the-doctrine-of-double-effect.context_blurb:
The doctrine of double effect goes back to Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century Dominican friar. It applies when one act has two foreseeable results, one good and one bad, and it holds that it matters morally whether the bad result is intended as a means or merely foreseen as a side effect. The line still shapes debates in medicine and war, and critics argue that it is too thin to bear such weight.

Consider a soldier who throws himself on a grenade to save his sleeping comrades. Like a suicide, he brings about his own death knowingly. But he does not seek his death; if any way of shielding his friends had let him survive, he would have taken it gladly, and that is what makes him a hero rather than a suicide. Two wartime pilots kill the same number of civilians. One aims at a crowded neighbourhood to break the enemy's will; the other destroys a munitions plant, and the houses beside it fall too. For the first pilot the dead are the very thing his plan runs on, while for the second they are wreckage his plan passes over. The death toll is the same, but the intention splits the verdict.

Aquinas first stated the idea while defending a man attacked by a murderer. One act, he wrote, can have two effects, only one of which is intended. The man means to save his own life; his attacker's death lies outside his intention, a cost he accepts but would gladly have spared if he safely could. Aquinas added a brake at once: the defender must keep his force within what the danger demands, for violence beyond that turns a lawful defense unlawful. Medicine gives the doctrine its modern home. A doctor who raises the morphine dose to quiet unbearable pain, knowing it may hasten death, wants the suffering gone and accepts the risk; a doctor who gives a dose meant to kill wants the patient gone. Many palliative doctors add that well-judged morphine seldom shortens life at all.

The hardest test came from a grim pair of cases in childbirth. Crushing an unborn child's skull to save the mother was called forbidden, but taking out a womb riddled with cancer, which the child could not survive, was allowed. Critics such as Jonathan Bennett objected that a surgeon could claim to intend only the crushing and not the death, so the line between intending and foreseeing is drawn too finely to be real. The objection is still unresolved.

singers-drowning-child.context_blurb:
Peter Singer is an Australian philosopher whose short 1972 essay Famine, Affluence, and Morality changed how many people think about charity. It begins with a child drowning in a shallow pond and ends at your wallet. The argument is powerful at full strength, and the replies to it, that it demands too much and that love for those near us comes first, have become major positions of their own.

Imagine passing a shallow pond where a small child is drowning. Wading in will ruin your clothes, and cost you nothing else. Almost everyone sees at once that you must go in, because muddy clothes count for nothing against a child's life, and Singer builds his whole case on that shared gut reaction. He wrote the essay in November 1971, while famine drove nine million refugees from Bangladesh toward starvation. Singer set rich countries' aid beside their luxuries: Australia had spent twelve times as much building the Sydney Opera House as it gave the refugees. To him the comparison showed the rich world putting its own comforts ahead of distant lives, which is exactly the wrong way round.

From the pond Singer draws a general principle: if it is in your power to stop something bad from happening without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, you ought to do it. A new shirt is not as important as a child's life, so the shirt money is owed to a child dying of a preventable disease far away. Distance, Singer insists, makes no moral difference; the faraway child is just as savable, and the only thing that fades with the miles is how strongly you feel, which is no excuse. Nor do other people's failures help you. If twenty bystanders all refuse to wade in, your duty does not shrink to a twentieth share, because the child still dies and you could still have saved it.

Pushed to its end, the logic turns severe. Singer would have you keep giving up to the point where the next gift costs you as much as it does the receiver good, and he concedes that this means living nearly as poorly as the refugees. In a 1982 essay called Moral Saints, Susan Wolf answered that a morality this total demands more than any real human being can live up to; it leaves no space for an ordinary good life and is fit only for saints. Other critics notice who is missing from the pond: parents. A father who spends his spare money on shoes, braces and swimming lessons for his own children instead of a malaria charity is honouring a duty he owes first to the children he has taken into his care. Distance may not matter, these critics grant, but relationship does. Bernard Williams sharpened the point with a man who sees two people drowning and has time to rescue just one, his wife among them. If the husband stops to reason that saving one's wife is morally permitted, Williams said, he has had one thought too many; a loving husband simply dives, and pausing to justify the choice already betrays the love a little.

one-thought-too-many-williams.context_blurb:
The British philosopher Bernard Williams gave moral philosophy one of its sharpest images in a 1981 essay, "Persons, Character and Morality." The essay is the most famous defense of partiality, the view that a husband for a wife or a parent for a child rightly acts from love without first running an impartial check. It stands squarely against Peter Singer's demand for impartial duty, and the two views are still argued side by side.

A man can rescue only one of two people in the water, a stranger and his wife, and he saves his wife; for Williams, nothing more is needed to justify it. But suppose he first thinks: this is my wife, and in cases like this saving one's wife is allowed. That extra step is one thought too many. It makes his love wait on a rule's approval, when loving her ought to have been all the reason he needed. His wife of almost two decades, Shirley Williams, served Britain as a Labour cabinet minister, a life of impartial public service.

Marcia Baron, defending Kant, said Williams had attacked a strawman. When her Kantian husband plunges in, love moves him, and duty stands only as an outer fence that his love never comes near. He does not wait for duty to sign off first, which would itself be Williams's one thought too many. Williams also took aim at utilitarianism, the view that we should always produce the best outcome. He imagined George, an out-of-work chemist who abhors chemical weapons and is offered a post at a weapons lab; if he refuses, a zealot will take the job and push the research harder. Counting outcomes alone, George should accept. Williams objected that a theory giving that order turns George into a builder of weapons because of what someone else would otherwise do, severing him from the deep commitments that make his life his own, which Williams called his integrity. In another story the botanist Jim is invited to shoot one of twenty captives so the rest go free. Williams never claimed the arithmetic gave the wrong answer. What it leaves out, he said, is that the hand on the trigger would be Jim's own.

Peter Railton replied for the consequentialists with his sophisticated agent, who produces the best outcomes precisely by not calculating in the moment: she simply loves, acting from attachment and approving of those habits on reflection because they generally turn out well. Williams's error, on Railton's view, was that he ran together what makes an act right and how a good person goes about choosing. The quarrel remains open.

moral-luck.context_blurb:
In 1976 the American philosopher Thomas Nagel and the British philosopher Bernard Williams each gave a paper called "Moral Luck," opening one of the most awkward puzzles in ethics. We like to think people are blamed only for what they control, yet luck, which no one chooses, seems to change how guilty we hold them.

Nagel imagines a motorist who neglected to have his brakes checked, though nothing seemed wrong. When a child runs out and the neglected brakes give way, the child is killed. Such a man does more than feel awful; he blames himself for the death. Had no child run out, he would be an ordinary driver. Williams adds a truck driver, wholly blameless, who kills a child who darted in front of him. Unlike any bystander, the driver feels what Williams called agent-regret. It brings an urge to go to the child's family and try to make amends, because the death is bound up with what he did, though it was not his fault.

Two men fire guns meaning to kill, but one target stumbles at the last instant and the bullet goes astray. The law charges the killer with murder and the other with mere attempt, which carries a lighter sentence, though the intent was the same. Nagel and Williams use such pairs to expose an unsettling fact: how guilty we hold someone can turn on luck rather than choice. That describes how we do judge, not whether we should. Williams's signature case is the painter Paul Gauguin, who abandoned his family in 1891 to paint in Tahiti. When he sailed, Williams argued, no reasoning could yet show whether he was right; only the outcome could decide it. If his talent succeeded and the gamble paid off, the desertion was justified by its results, and had his talent failed, the same act would stand condemned.

A follower of Kant holds that an act's moral worth depends solely on the will, and Kant said a good will glows on its own like a gem, whatever comes of it. Shown two equally reckless drivers, one who killed a child and one who found the road empty, the Kantian must call them equally guilty, because the outcome was luck and not will. Nagel follows the rule against blaming people for what they cannot control all the way down. Remove luck in results, then luck in the circumstances life handed you, then luck in the character you were born with, and nothing is left of a self to blame, only a stretch of events to deplore or celebrate. Philosophers who hold that outcomes truly matter are not thereby wrong, and the dispute remains open.

moral-relativism-vs-realism.context_blurb:
Are right and wrong discovered, like truths of mathematics, or invented, so that each society makes its own and none is really better than another? Relativists, from the Greek sophist Protagoras to the modern philosopher Gilbert Harman, point to how widely moral customs differ. Moral realists answer that some acts are wrong everywhere, whatever any society says.

A boy declares that right and wrong are only whatever each family picks. His sister asks whether the neighbors could make cruelty to their cat, done purely for amusement, acceptable just by deciding so, and he falls silent. His hesitation points at the realist's core claim, that certain acts stay wrong whoever declares them acceptable. Realists press it with what philosophers call the Moorean move. I am surer that torturing a child for fun is wrong than I am of any premise in a clever argument to the contrary, so an argument whose conclusion clears such cruelty has thereby shown that one of its own premises is false.

Relativism's oldest evidence comes from the historian Herodotus. King Darius asked some Greeks what payment could persuade them to devour their fathers' corpses, and they were horrified. Then he asked the Callatiae, whose custom was to eat their dead as a mark of honor, what would persuade them to burn their fathers instead, and they were horrified too. Realists grant the story fully: burial customs really do differ, and each seems self-evident to the people who grew up with it. James Rachels showed that leaping from varied customs to no moral truth at all is invalid, using geography: some peoples once thought the earth flat and others round, yet their disagreement never made the earth's shape a matter of opinion. What people believe, however widely they disagree, cannot by itself settle what is actually true. Realism's sharpest weapon is the reformer's dilemma. If "right" simply means "what your society approves," then Frederick Douglass and the abolitionists, who fought the slavery their own society backed, were by definition in the wrong, and moral progress becomes impossible. The abolitionists were plainly right, so the definition that condemns them must be false.

Harman put relativism at its strongest. He argued that if Hitler had grown up wholly outside our moral community, it would sound oddly out of place to say he ought not to have acted as he did, though Harman himself did not think the genocide acceptable. We are far more certain that Hitler ought not to have murdered millions than we could be of any premise concluding that we cannot say so, and a theory that must stay silent about genocide has lost far more than any of its arguments could win.

care-ethics.context_blurb:
Care ethics grew up in the 1980s from the work of the American psychologist Carol Gilligan and the philosopher Nel Noddings. It grounds moral life first in care between actual people, with the bond between mother and child as its model, rather than in impartial rules. It has been influential, and it has drawn serious criticism.

Gilligan's famous example is the Heinz dilemma. Heinz's wife is dying, and the medicine that could cure her costs more than he has; should he steal it? A boy named Jake answered like arithmetic, since a life outranks property. A girl named Amy kept thinking about the people, picturing Heinz in jail and his wife left alone, and proposed something the question never offered: Heinz should return to the druggist and keep reasoning with him until the man understood what the wife was going through. In Noddings' terms there is a "one-caring" who gives and a "cared-for" who receives, and caring is complete only when the cared-for receives it and responds to the giver, as when a baby smiles back.

Gilligan had worked at Harvard as research assistant to Lawrence Kohlberg. Kohlberg's famous ladder of moral growth rested on interviews with 84 boys, and it ranked women one rung down, reading their concern for other people's needs as a sign of immaturity. Gilligan argued that the women were not lagging behind but answering a different question, one about keeping relationships whole, that the scale was never built to hear. Critics press care ethics hardest on its reach. Noddings separated caring-for, personally looking after someone right beside you, from caring-about, such as sending a few dollars to feed the hungry far away, which she called a poor second cousin to caring. Pressed on what she owes a starving stranger, she held that a stranger beyond her reach does not hold the full moral claim on her that a person close at hand does. Critics say such an ethics struggles to reach distant people at all.

The philosopher Claudia Card warned that praising caring as the highest virtue risks honoring relationships in which carers are badly abused, like a battered wife admired for her devotion. A caring relationship, she and others argued, must also be tested for justice, not only for whether caring is present. Joan Tronto pressed another point. The advantaged simply buy care, hiring nannies and aides and then excusing themselves from caring about its quality, a habit she called privileged irresponsibility. Private care for the people around you, she concluded, cannot on its own change the social arrangement that forces some people to do the caring.

what-is-art-duchamps-fountain.context_blurb:
In 1917 Marcel Duchamp, a French artist living in New York, turned an ordinary porcelain urinal on its side, painted the name R. Mutt and the date on it, called it Fountain and entered it in a New York exhibition. The piece asks a simple, difficult question: what makes something art rather than a plumbing fixture? The debate it opened is still unresolved.

The show had promised that anyone who paid could exhibit, with no jury and no rejections, and Duchamp sat on its board. Not knowing the piece was his, the board quietly kept it out of sight and would not show it, and Duchamp resigned in protest. In the argument beforehand, one director asked whether their rule would oblige them to exhibit a heap of horse dung. Walter Arensberg answered bluntly that yes, by their own rules, it would.

An unsigned editorial in their little magazine, The Blind Man, answered the critics. Whether Mr Mutt made the fountain with his own hands did not matter, it said; the creative act was that he chose it. It closed with a jab: the only works of art America had given the world were its plumbing and its bridges.

Duchamp had a name for such things, readymades: everyday objects he chose and titled rather than made, such as a bicycle wheel fixed to a stool and a snow shovel hung on a wall. He said they must be picked with complete visual indifference, free of any good or bad taste, and he warned that staring at one for a fortnight would let its looks seduce you, and the choice would be spoiled. In 1919 he took an inexpensive print of the Mona Lisa, pencilled a moustache and a little goatee onto her face, and gave it a crude title.

The original Fountain was soon lost or thrown away. The only record of it is a single black-and-white photograph that Alfred Stieglitz took in his gallery; every Fountain in a museum is a later copy. Yet in a 2004 survey, 500 people from the British art world named it the most influential work of twentieth-century art, ahead of Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon. The artist Pierre Pinoncelli assaulted one replica on two occasions; after taking a hammer to it in 2006, he told a Paris court the blow was a wink at Dadaism, one Duchamp himself would have enjoyed.

Philosophers took the riddle seriously. Arthur Danto noticed that the same urinal is art in a gallery and not in a hardware store, so what makes it art cannot be a property you could point to in the object. He located it in the atmosphere of art theory and art history around the object. Following Ludwig Wittgenstein, Morris Weitz compared art to the word game, which covers chess, football and patience without any one feature they all share, only a web of family resemblances. On that view, calling a shocking new object art is a decision about whether to extend the word to include it.

beauty-in-the-object-or-the-eye-of-the-b.context_blurb:
Is beauty a real feature of things, the way blue belongs to the sky, or does it live only in the eye of the beholder? Two eighteenth-century philosophers, the Scot David Hume and the German Immanuel Kant, both said beauty is felt rather than measured, yet both refused to conclude that anything goes. The dispute is still open.

Hume's famous essay Of the Standard of Taste, published in 1757, begins by handing the skeptic a big concession. Beauty, he grants, is no quality in things themselves but only a feeling in the mind that views them, so each person may keep his own verdict. Everything after that is his attempt to escape it. From Don Quixote Hume takes the story of two kinsmen, famous wine-judges, who sample a fine old cask, and one detects a hint of leather while the other tastes iron. The neighbors laugh, until the cask is drained and an old key on a leather strap lies at the bottom. A finely tuned palate, Hume concludes, picks up what is truly in the wine, things the careless drinker never notices. Tastes differ, but putting the forgotten scribbler John Ogilby on a level with John Milton is as absurd as claiming a molehill matches a mountain; some judgments of taste are not just unpopular but plainly wrong.

Kant agreed there is no arguing about mere liking. If you love a sweet wine and your friend hates it, each simply has his own taste. Beauty is different, because to call something beautiful is to speak for everyone, claiming that all ought to share your verdict; that is why people argue about beauty and expect to win. A rose in a garden you will never enter pleases you just as much as one you hold, so the pleasure of beauty must be disinterested, a pleasure in just looking, which wants nothing from the flower. Hume's word for a fine judge's gift was delicacy, senses so fine that nothing in the mix slips past them, and he used it for wine and poems alike. The palate that catches leather in a cask and the eye that catches craft in a poem are, for Hume, one and the same fineness of perception.

Who, then, sets the standard? For Hume it is the joint verdict of several true judges: people of strong sense and delicate feeling, practiced, used to comparing, and free of prejudice. Such judges are rare. Hume also trusted the test of time. Fashions fade within a generation, but Homer's poems, two thousand years old and from a lost world, still win admirers in Paris and London, evidence that the beauty lived in the poem itself, not in a fad of one time and place. Kant had to explain how a private feeling can claim everyone. His answer was the free play of imagination and understanding: in beauty the two fall into step freely, with no rule in charge. Because all people carry the same two powers, that harmony is open to anyone.

The two rescues differ at the root. Hume anchors the standard in experience: better judges really exist, and their agreement sets it. Kant anchors it in the structure of the mind, the powers all people carry, which lets a private pleasure speak for everyone. Kant even framed the dispute as two proverbs at war: taste cannot be argued over, yet we argue over it all the time and expect to win. Both hold, he said. A judgment of beauty rests on no provable rule, so no argument can clinch it, yet it reaches for everyone's agreement, so it is worth arguing over; taste is argued but never settled. Even tolerant Hume drew a moral line. Many differences of taste are blameless, as when the young love passionate verse and the old prefer the wise kind. But a poem that praises wicked behavior without any sign of condemning it is truly disfigured. Kant also described beauty's darker twin, the sublime. Facing a huge night sky or a soaring mountain, the imagination tries to hold it all and cannot, and out of that defeat rises a strange lift of the spirit: it shows us our own reason, which can conceive the infinite even when the senses cannot take it in.

the-sublime.context_blurb:
Beauty has a stranger, overwhelming cousin called the sublime: the thrill of a thunderstorm over the sea, or of a sheer cliff that dwarfs you to the size of an ant. It is pleasure braided with awe and even dread. In the eighteenth century Edmund Burke and Immanuel Kant tried to explain why people seek out sights that ought to frighten them.

A pretty flowerbed calms you, but a storm watched from a safe window stirs pleasure and fear together in the face of something huge and overpowering, so it is a different kind of feeling altogether, not just a stronger dose of prettiness. Burke made distance the key. When danger presses too close it is simply terrible, he wrote, but at a safe distance the same force becomes delightful. So a monstrous wave that is pure horror to the sailor it drowns can thrill the painter watching from the headland, because she is in no danger herself.

Burke even drew up two opposed lists: the beautiful is small, smooth, delicate and bright, while the sublime is great, rugged, powerful, obscure and dark, and endlessness is its surest trigger. That idea set Romantic painters and poets free to leave tidy gardens and calm harbors behind and chase storms, cliffs and ruins instead, the scenes that overwhelm.

Kant turned the question back on the watcher. A violent mountain storm seen from safety, he argued, does not humble us but lifts us up, because it reveals in us a fortitude, a greatness of mind that could stand up to nature's seeming omnipotence and that no avalanche can crush. Sheer size works the same way. When you try to picture the whole night sky as one image, your imagination stalls, and the failure feels like defeat. Then reason rescues us: it can still grasp the endless as one complete idea even though no picture can hold it, so the defeat flips into triumph and reveals a power in our own minds greater than nature.

the-paradox-of-fiction.context_blurb:
At a horror film you clutch the armrest as the monster closes in on the heroine, and your heart pounds. Yet you know perfectly well that the monster does not exist. Philosophers call this the paradox of fiction: how can we truly feel for things we are sure are made up? The debate is still open.

The knot is easy to state. You feel fear toward a monster you are completely certain is not real, and yet ordinary fear seems to need the belief that something dangerous is actually there. Three claims each look true: we feel real emotions at the movies, we do not believe the characters exist, and real emotion requires that belief. They cannot all be true at once.

Colin Radford, who opened the modern debate in 1975, refused to explain the puzzle away. Audiences weep when Mercutio dies in Romeo and Juliet, a man they know never lived. Such tears are natural, Radford said, but strictly irrational, because they catch us in a contradiction.

Kendall Walton denied that the feeling is real fear. He imagined Charles, a moviegoer who tenses and clutches his seat as green slime oozes toward the camera. Charles's body is genuinely aroused, but he never once thinks of running from the theatre or phoning the police, as anyone would who believed he was in danger. So, Walton argued, Charles is playing a game of make-believe that adults play, with the screen as his prop; his body reacts inside the pretence, and what he feels is only a quasi-fear.

Noel Carroll objected that a game is something you choose. If horror-fear were a pretend move, we could switch it on and off at will, but it seizes us whether we welcome it or not, and that involuntary grip suggests a real emotion. Carroll and Peter Lamarque defended the thought theory instead: a vivid thought, without any belief, is enough to stir a true feeling, so a reader sobbing over a character's death is genuinely grieving. Each camp escapes by denying a different one of the three claims, and none has won.

the-paradox-of-tragedy.context_blurb:
Why would anyone pay to be made miserable? A great tragedy sends you home red-eyed and wrung out, and glad you went. Thinkers have puzzled over this for more than two thousand years, from Aristotle in ancient Athens to David Hume in eighteenth-century Scotland, and their rival answers are still debated.

Aristotle gave the oldest answer in his Poetics. A tragedy deliberately rouses pity and fear, then purges them: the play drains those feelings off inside the theatre, so you walk out lighter than you came in. He called this catharsis, a cleansing.

Hume, in his 1757 essay Of Tragedy, sharpened the puzzle. Crowds pay to weep and shudder, and the oddest part is that the more a play moves and afflicts us, the more we enjoy it. His answer lay in the artistry. A clumsy telling of a sad story is merely depressing, but beautiful writing does more than outweigh the pain: it converts the painful feeling itself into delight.

Centuries earlier, Saint Augustine recalled with unease his youthful love of the theatre in Carthage. He found it absurd that a crowd applauded an actor most when he made the audience cry hardest, so that grief itself became the pleasure.

Edmund Burke, an Irish writer, published his book on the sublime in the same year as Hume's essay. Storms, cliffs and battles can thrill us, he wrote, but only on one condition. Danger delights only when it reaches us from a safe distance, never close enough to do real harm; pressed too near, it is simply terrifying.

Susan Feagin took another route in 1983. Perhaps we do not enjoy the grief at all. Instead a second, quieter pleasure rests on top of it: we discover that we are the sort of people who recoil hard from cruelty and injustice, and that discovery pleases us.

the-intentional-fallacy.context_blurb:
In 1946 the American critics W. K. Wimsatt and Monroe Beardsley published an essay arguing that once a poem is out in the world, what its author meant to say is neither available to us nor decisive about what it means. The meaning lives in the words and their shared conventions. Treating the maker's stated aim as the last word became known as the intentional fallacy, and the dispute is still genuinely open.

Beardsley offered a test case. Imagine a carved twist of teak whose maker declares it a symbol of Human Destiny, though viewers see only handsome wood. If declaring were enough, anyone could make anything mean anything; a maker's words cannot pour into a work a meaning the work itself will not carry. His cleanest example was the poet A. E. Housman, who denied an irony that a critic found in one of his poems. Beardsley held that a poem's meaning rests in the public conventions of the language we share, which can hold more than its maker intended.

Defenders of intention answer with Daniel Defoe's 1702 pamphlet urging the shortest way with Dissenters. Its straight-faced plan for stamping out religious dissenters read to some as an earnest proposal and to others as a savage joke. Philosophers such as E. D. Hirsch argue that telling the sincere from the ironic can depend on the author's aim, so intention may help fix meaning after all.

tolstoy-art-as-the-transmission-of-feeli.context_blurb:
Late in life the Russian novelist Leo Tolstoy, author of the giant novels War and Peace and, later, Anna Karenina, gave a startling answer to the question of what art is. In his 1897 book What Is Art? he rejected beauty and technical skill as the test. His view gives art a strongly moral edge, and it remains one serious rival among several.

His example is a frightened boy who once came face to face with a wolf and later describes the encounter so vividly that his listeners feel his fear. That, for Tolstoy, is art: handing on to other people a feeling the artist has really lived, so that they catch it as well.

He applied the test without mercy. He called Beethoven's Ninth Symphony bad art, because it was long, confused and artificial, beyond the grasp of ordinary listeners. He even turned the test on himself, branding his own great novels bad art, products of upper-class vanity that united no one in shared feeling.

the-meaning-of-life.context_blurb:
What is a human life for? Most people first meet that question in a dark hour, not a classroom. Here three writers stare it down: the Russian novelist Leo Tolstoy, the French-Algerian writer Albert Camus and the American philosopher Thomas Nagel. Two later philosophers, Richard Taylor and Susan Wolf, then argue over where meaning could come from. Each reached a different answer, and the dispute is still open.

In the late 1870s Tolstoy had everything: fame from War and Peace and Anna Karenina, a loving wife, children, a great estate and the strength to mow hay alongside his peasants. Nothing had been taken from him. What broke him was a single question: does my life hold any meaning that my coming death will not wipe out? He could not answer it, and the despair grew so deep that each night he carried the rope out of his room, so that he would not hang himself from a beam. In his book A Confession he retold an old Eastern fable to show the mood. A traveller dangles from a bush inside a well with a dragon waiting below, while a white mouse and a black mouse, day and night, chew through the branch. Even so, he reaches out with his tongue to lick drops of honey from the leaves. The honey is life's small comforts, and once Tolstoy had seen the dragon, the honey lost its sweetness.

In occupied France, Camus wrote his essay The Myth of Sisyphus during World War II and opened it bluntly. The one truly serious problem in philosophy, he said, is suicide: whether life is worth living at all. Everything else waits until you have decided to go on living.

His hero was a Greek king. Legend says Sisyphus cheated death twice. Thanatos, the god of death, came for him at Zeus's order, and Sisyphus chained Death up himself; while Death sat bound, no one on earth could die, until the war god Ares set him free. When Sisyphus was finally hauled below, he had one more trick ready. He had told his wife to leave his body lying unburied in the public square. Then he complained to Persephone, queen of the dead, about the insult, won leave to go back up and scold his wife, and refused to return. For this the gods set him rolling a boulder up a hill forever, only to watch it roll down. Camus cared most about the walk back down, when Sisyphus sees his fate clearly and owns it, and he ended his book by saying we must imagine Sisyphus happy.

Thomas Nagel, in a 1971 essay, traced the absurd to a gap between the weight we give our own lives and how flimsy they look from outside. Everyday embarrassments show it in miniature: declaring undying love into an answering machine, or having your trousers drop at the very moment you are knighted. A mouse is never absurd, Nagel noted, because it cannot step back and judge itself.

The deepest replies answer one another. Camus refused both escapes from the absurd. Suicide surrenders to it, and the leap of faith, which he charged against Kierkegaard, cheats by inventing hope to dodge the problem. His own answer was revolt: keep living fully, with open eyes, holding the clash between our hunger for meaning and a silent universe. Nagel found that heroic stance too romantic. If, seen from eternity, nothing matters, then that does not matter either, so the fitting reply to our absurd lives is irony, not heroism and not despair.

Richard Taylor imagined the gods granting Sisyphus a strange mercy: they do not free him but plant in him a burning wish to roll stones. Nothing outside changes; the rock still rolls back, and the work never adds up to anything. Yet his life is transformed, which shows, Taylor argued, that meaning comes from within a man, from his own will, and is not handed down from outside. Susan Wolf answered that passion alone is not enough. A life spent building the world's biggest ball of string can absorb a person completely and still be empty. Meaning, for Wolf, arrives when real love meets real worth: loving something genuinely worth loving.

ad-hominem-attacking-the-person.context_blurb:
Ad hominem is Latin for "to the man." It is the move of attacking the person who makes a claim instead of the claim itself, one of the oldest tricks in argument, and it works on crowds because people are easier to judge than ideas. The flaw is simple: a liar can tell the truth and a saint can be wrong, so who says a thing never settles whether it is so.

Picture a peasant warning travelers that the river bridge has fallen, and a knight who sneers at his ugly, lowborn face and rides on without a glance at the river. A face, handsome or plain, has nothing to do with whether the timbers lie in the water; only looking at the bridge can settle that. A subtler version is tu quoque, Latin for "you too." When a doctor who smokes tells you to quit, pointing at her cigarette proves she is a hypocrite, but her habit does not change one fact about what smoking does to the body.

A coach tells his team never to skip practice, and a player fires back that the coach skipped all the time in his own playing days. The player has scored a point about the coach and none about practice, since the coach's old habit does not make skipping any less harmful today. Plain insult is the crudest form, called abusive ad hominem. A man who calls the backers of a river cleanup lazy, smelly tree-huggers has offered no reason at all to think the cleanup would fail.

Circumstantial ad hominem points at the speaker's interests. A councilman argues for a convention center downtown, and a rival notes that he owns land nearby and would get rich. That stake is worth knowing, and it is a fair reason to check his claims twice, but the rival still has to show that the center itself is a bad idea on its merits: traffic, cost and need. A cousin of the fallacy is guilt by association. In the 2008 U.S. election, Sarah Palin hammered Barack Obama over his old acquaintance with Bill Ayers, who had been a Weather Underground radical in the 1960s. Even if the link were exactly as she described it, whom a man once knew does not show that his arguments are wrong.

Sometimes the personal charge is true and still beside the point. In a stinging pamphlet in 1764, Voltaire revealed anonymously that Jean-Jacques Rousseau, his great rival and the author of a book urging parents to raise their own children, had handed all five of his own to a Paris foundling hospital. The hypocrisy stained Rousseau the man, but his argument about parenting still had to be judged on its own. A close relative of the fallacy attacks an idea's birthplace instead of its speaker: the genetic fallacy. Sneering that a crackpot cult dreamed up an idea long ago fails, because where an idea first came from has no bearing on whether it is true now.

The label itself has a surprising history. When John Locke made the phrase argumentum ad hominem popular in his 1690 Essay Concerning Human Understanding, he meant no insult but a fair debating move: pressing a man with what follows from his own stated principles. Character can matter, too. The philosopher Douglas Walton pointed out that when you weigh testimony, honesty is part of the evidence. A lawyer who proves that a witness has a long record of lying under oath can soundly conclude that his word should not be trusted, but not that his story must be false; that last leap is the fallacy again.

Everything turns on relevance. Two eyewitnesses claim they saw a robbery at midnight on the far side of a dark street. Proving that the first is badly short-sighted weakens her account, because poor eyesight bears directly on what she says she saw; proving that the second cheated on his wife does not, because his marriage has nothing to do with the street. A man's immoral private conduct tells you nothing about whether his sums about the planets are right, but it is real evidence when the question is whether he is fit for a position of trust, such as a seat leading the city council. The insult is never the point; the link between the flaw and the claim is.

poisoning-the-well-and-circumstantial-ad.context_blurb:
The circumstantial ad hominem is a subtler cousin of the plain insult. Instead of attacking a speaker's character, it points at his interests: of course the merchant says so, he profits from it. Its close relative, poisoning the well, discredits a speaker before he even opens his mouth. Both swap a reason to check a claim for a reason to dismiss it, and the lesson running through both is that bias calls for scrutiny, not dismissal.

A merchant assures travelers that the pass is safe for wagons this year, and a rival shouts that of course he says so, since he lives off the traffic. The motive is real, but a motive for calling the road safe tells you nothing about the road itself. The same holds for hypocrisy. A father who smokes warns his daughter that smoking causes disease, and she cries, "But you smoke too!" She is right about him, yet his habit changes nothing about the medical fact, and rejecting his warning because of it is the "you too" fallacy, called tu quoque. So what should you do when a company's paid spokesman swears its product is safe? Noticing his stake is fair. Then examine his evidence with extra care; his stake earns the claim closer scrutiny, not a verdict.

Poisoning the well is marked by timing. A debater who reminds the crowd that his opponent once sat in jail, before his rival has spoken at all, gets in first, so whatever the rival says next is heard with suspicion. The well can also be poisoned by framing. A councilman who announces that anyone opposing his school-funding plan hates children leaves critics no way to object without seeming to admit they hate children. Guilt by association is a near relative. When a senator called the Secretary of State soft on communism because of the fuzzy-headed liberals at his cocktail parties, he never addressed a single policy, and the guest list is no evidence about what the man's policies are.

Sometimes pointing at a person is fair. The logician Douglas Walton notes a courtroom case: a lawyer who has shown that a witness committed perjury before may urge the jury to weigh it. Here the jury must decide whether to trust what he says, and a record of proven lying is real evidence on exactly that, though it would prove nothing about whether an argument is logically sound. Attacking where a belief came from works the same way. Saying a man holds a view only because his father did is the genetic fallacy, because where a belief came from counts against it only if that source actually shows the belief to be false, and a parent's say-so shows no such thing.

The name comes from a famous quarrel. Charles Kingsley, a clergyman, assailed the famous Catholic convert John Henry Newman in print in 1864, refuting none of his beliefs but telling readers that no defense Newman offered could be believed. In his reply, the Apologia Pro Vita Sua, Newman named the trick. Kingsley had prejudiced readers beforehand, so that any reply Newman made would be doubted before it was even read. Newman called it poisoning the wells, borrowing a dark image from the Black Death, when Jews across Europe were falsely accused of poisoning wells, a lie that set off massacres.
