tu-quoque-and-whataboutism.context_blurb:
Tu quoque is Latin for you too. It is the move of answering a criticism by pointing out that the critic does the same thing, and its political cousin is called whataboutism. Sometimes the critic really is a hypocrite, and that is worth knowing. But a hypocrite can still be right, and the fallacy lies in using you too to avoid answering the charge.

A father tells his son that lying is wrong, and the boy shoots back that his father lied yesterday. He is right about the lie, but that proves nothing about lying itself: don't lie is sound advice no matter who says it. An uncle with a pack-a-day habit tells his nephew never to start. Smoking is deadly or not because of how the world is, not because of who gives the warning. The philosopher Douglas Walton used the same case. A child who tells a smoking parent that the argument collapses because the parent smokes has aimed at the parent's habits and never touched the parent's real reason, that smoking causes disease.

The move works as a distraction. When Ben criticises Mara and she snaps that he does the same thing, everyone turns to stare at Ben. She has got herself off the hook by shifting the spotlight onto her critic, without answering anything. The old sayings about a pot that calls a kettle black, and about two wrongs never adding up to a right, catch the same error: treating someone else's wrongdoing as if it cleared you of your own.

The name came from the stage. In 1611 a London comedy starred the clown Thomas Greene as Bubble, a fool whose reply to every insult was tu quoque, the same to you. Audiences loved it so much that the playhouse renamed the whole play after his catchphrase. The modern word is younger. In 1974 Sean O'Conaill, a teacher of history in Troubles-era Northern Ireland, wrote to a newspaper about partisans who met any accusation by pointing to the crimes of the other side; he called them the Whatabouts.

Whataboutism became a Cold War habit. Throughout the Cold War, Moscow met American complaints about its treatment of dissidents by pointing at American wrongs, and one retort became a decades-long punchline: the charge that Americans were lynching black people. The reflex was older than communism. After a deadly anti-Jewish pogrom at Kishinev in 1903, the Tsarist minister Vyacheslav von Plehve waved it away by comparing the rioters to Americans who lynch.

Not every you too is a dodge. Suppose a critic condemns your government's political prisoners while saying nothing about his ally's. Pointing that out can be fair. What decides it is consistency: are both sides being judged by one standard, or is the subject simply being changed? Even then, exposing the double standard tells you about the critic's motive and bias, and nothing about the facts; his charge against your country could still be true.

the-genetic-fallacy.context_blurb:
The genetic fallacy is judging a claim true or false by where it came from instead of by the evidence for it. "That idea came from a wicked king, so it's false." "You only believe that because of how you were raised." A good idea can have an ugly source and a bad idea a noble one. The fallacy is a close cousin of the personal attack, aimed at an idea's birthplace instead of at the speaker.

A girl stuck for a present opens a fortune cookie, finds a genuinely perfect gift idea, and throws it away because cookies cannot think. Her mistake is judging the idea by its silly source instead of asking whether the idea itself is good. The wedding ring is the textbook case. Someone may claim the ring began as a symbol of the chains that kept wives from running off. Even if that history were right, the meaning a custom had when it began does not fix what a ring says to a couple today. The everyday jab "you only think the earth is round because your parents told you so" misses for the same reason: how a person came to hold a belief tells you nothing about whether the belief is correct.

A scholar who refuses to unroll an old map because a thief drew it should instead test whether the map is accurate; a mapmaker's bad character cannot make a true map false. August Kekule, a chemist, credited a daydream of a snake swallowing its own tail with showing him that benzene's atoms form a ring. A dream proves nothing, but the dream was only how he first got the idea, and experiments later showed the ring to be correct. Apollo's Saturn V Moon rocket descended from the V-2, the missile Wernher von Braun designed for Nazi Germany, assembled by concentration-camp prisoners, thousands of whom died. That is a real moral horror, yet whether the rocket science is sound has nothing to do with who first built it or for what purpose.

Freud traced belief in God to a child's longing for a protecting father and called the belief an illusion. Critics reply on logical grounds alone: even if his account were right, a story about where a belief comes from does not touch the separate question of whether it is true. The objection takes no side on whether God exists, and the move cuts both ways, since unbelief can be explained psychologically too. Origin is not always useless. A careful peer-reviewed study deserves more first trust than an anonymous blog post. The honest rule is that where a claim comes from may raise or lower your trust for now, but it can never stand in for checking the claim itself. The fallacy can also run backward. For thousands of years, in many cultures, the swastika stood for good fortune, until the Nazis adopted it. An honourable origin cannot cleanse the meaning the sign took on under the Nazis, so their banner is not made innocent by its ancient past.

appeal-to-authority-when-its-legitimate-.context_blurb:
Almost everything you know, you took on trust. You never personally rediscovered plate tectonics or the structure of DNA; someone who had done the work told you. Trusting experts is not a mistake. The mistake, which philosophers call the appeal to authority, lies in trusting the wrong authority, trusting a real one too far, or letting a famous name stand in for evidence.

When you are sick and your doctor prescribes a pill, taking it without checking the chemistry yourself is perfectly sensible, because medicine is exactly her field, and nearly all human knowledge reaches us this way, passed along by people who know the subject. A movie star who swears by a brand of vitamins can send sales soaring, but only his fame is doing the persuading, and being famous is not the same as understanding nutrition, so his word adds nothing as evidence. A neighborhood association president may know every street and rule on his block, yet if he declares the lunar surface buried in dust, he is speaking outside his expertise: right person, wrong subject, since the moon belongs to astronomers and geologists. Even a giant can mislead. For centuries students ended arguments with "Aristotle said so," even about things they could have checked by looking. But a brilliant mind can still err, so a great name decides nothing; only looking at the world can.

Real expertise also has edges. A respected doctor who gives stock tips on television is spending authority she does not have, because years of training in disease give her no special knowledge of markets. Even inside the right field, an expert's backing is a good rule of thumb rather than a proof: it makes a claim more likely to be true, but only evidence or sound logic can establish it, because experts make mistakes too. And when experts of equal standing disagree, as nutrition scientists still do about whether salt harms the heart, quoting one of them decides nothing, because the other's word cancels his out. There is a mirror-image mistake as well. A man who answers a climate scientist's evidence by sneering at a small slip she made years ago thinks he has refused to bow to authority, but he has only attacked the person instead of the argument, which is blind obedience turned inside out.

The clearest case of brilliance straying outside its field is Linus Pauling. Pauling collected two Nobel Prizes, each unshared, one for chemistry and one for peace, yet when he claimed late in life that megadoses of vitamin C would ward off colds and even cancer, the prizes gave him no standing, since his genius lay in molecular chemistry and he had no training in clinical nutrition. Pauling himself took about 18 grams of the vitamin every day, roughly the amount in 360 oranges, and defended the habit with a theory of his own, orthomolecular medicine. Laureates who drift outside their field like this have given the problem a nickname: the Nobel disease. The trick of hiding behind famous names is old. John Locke named it in 1690 argumentum ad verecundiam, the appeal to modesty, because it works on the opponent's shame: to dispute a crowd of celebrated thinkers is to look arrogant, so a modest person keeps quiet.

In the end the cure for misplaced authority is evidence, and Galileo is its emblem. A famous story has him dropping two balls of unequal weight from the Leaning Tower of Pisa to prove Aristotle wrong about heavy things falling faster, but historians treat the tower as a legend invented by his student Vincenzo Viviani. What the real Galileo did was let balls roll down gentle ramps, where the shallow slope stretched out the fall enough for him to time it with precision. Measurements, not a famous name, settled the question.

appeal-to-the-people-bandwagon.context_blurb:
The bandwagon fallacy, also called the appeal to the people, says that a belief must be true because so many people hold it. Its flaw is simple: popularity is not evidence. Whole societies have been wrong together, and the psychologist Solomon Asch showed how easily one person bends to a confident crowd. Yet some kinds of agreement really do count, and telling them apart is the skill.

A market trader swears his copper charm wards off fevers because everybody in town wears one. The number of people wearing it tells you nothing about whether it works; that still has to be tested. Advertisers play the same card. An ad that tells you to watch a channel because it is the most-watched in the country has quietly swapped popular for best, claiming the channel is the most worth watching when it has proved only that many people tune in.

In 1951 Asch seated one real student in a room with seven hired actors and asked which of three lines matched a sample. The task was easy; alone, people almost never erred. But when the actors all named the same plainly wrong line first, the student went along and named it too about 37 percent of the time, and roughly three in four caved at least once. The lines never changed, only the crowd. Crowds can empty wallets as well. In the Dutch Republic of the 1630s, families in Amsterdam and Haarlem sold houses and savings to buy what everyone else was buying: flower bulbs. At the peak a single rare tulip bulb cost about six years of a craftsman's wages, until in February 1637 the buyers stopped paying and prices collapsed.

For fifteen centuries nearly all learned people held that the Earth sat still while the heavens wheeled around it, and as late as 1600 just a handful of astronomers, about twelve, had sided with Copernicus. That agreement proved nothing, because a fact does not care how many people deny it, and the Earth was moving all along. One careful method can outweigh centuries of opinion. Around 240 BC Eratosthenes compared a well in Syene, where the noon sun cast no shadow, with a stick in Alexandria that did cast one, and with geometry he calculated how big around our planet is, landing within about 1.4 percent of the true figure. In 1847 Ignaz Semmelweis made the doctors on his Vienna ward wash in a chlorinated lime solution, and deaths from childbed fever fell from 18.3 percent to 2.2. The medical majority still rejected him, and the most uncomfortable reason was pride: to accept his rule, they would have had to admit that their own dirty hands had been killing the mothers in their care.

Some appeals to numbers are honest. When many investigators, working separately, look at the same evidence and land on the same conclusion, their agreement is genuine evidence, because it rests on investigation rather than on catching a belief from one another. And some questions are settled by the count itself. Who won an election is decided by how people vote, with no hidden fact underneath the tally. Snob appeal is the bandwagon turned upside down. A watch ad that says only elite, discerning people wear it makes the same mistake, letting the prestige of the buyers stand in for the quality of the watch.

appeal-to-emotion-and-appeal-to-pity.context_blurb:
An appeal to emotion stirs up a feeling, pity, fear, love or flattery, so strongly that the feeling takes the place of the argument. The appeal to pity is its clearest form. The ancient Greek teachers of speech counted pathos, the stirring of feeling, as a fair part of persuasion, but a motive is not a proof. The lesson is not to become hard-hearted but to notice which question a feeling actually answers.

Picture a squire who has just been unhorsed by three knights, kneeling to beg the judges for the champion's crown because he trained harder than anyone and his dog is sick at home. His effort and his dog are real and deserve sympathy, yet neither one shows that he fought best in the lists today. A girl who tells her father that if he truly loved her he would let her skip her chores, and that it would make her so happy, does the same thing in miniature: she has set a feeling, his love and her joy, where a reason for skipping the chores ought to be.

The classroom version is a student named Max who wants an A on a history quiz since his wrist got broken in the final basketball game. The cast is real and the teacher winces, but a grade measures what he got right on the quiz, not how much sympathy he has earned. A lawyer rolls his client's wheelchair to the front of the courtroom and asks the jury whether a man who cannot walk could really be an embezzler. The case turns on ledgers and bank transfers, and the lawyer is inviting the jury to swap the hard question, who moved the money, for the easy feeling of pity at the wheelchair.

Feelings are not useless, and the line between motive and evidence is the heart of the matter. When Tom, down on his luck, asks his neighbor Ruth for rent money, her sympathy gives her a perfectly good reason to help him. If Tom further insists that his landlord cheated him on the rent, her sympathy settles nothing about that, because it is a separate question of fact. The writer Leo Rosten defined chutzpah, sheer gall, with the most naked case of all: a man kills his mother and father, then begs the court for mercy because he is an orphan. His orphanhood is a wound he made himself, and it says nothing about his guilt. Pity can also be paired with a rush. A buyer who knocks on a widow's door days after the funeral, waving a check and urging her to sign today, is using her sorrow and the hurry together to get her signature before anyone asks whether his price is fair.

Sometimes mercy really is the question. In 1924 the lawyer Clarence Darrow took the case of Leopold and Loeb, young killers who had already admitted murdering a fourteen-year-old boy, Bobby Franks. With their guilt settled, Darrow spoke for twelve hours, never claiming innocence, only begging the court to spare their lives and resting everything on mercy, on their youth and their diseased minds. Because the only question left was the sentence, his emotional plea was on point, and the judge spared them, citing their youth. Socrates, on trial in Athens, refused even that kind of plea. Other defendants wept and paraded their crying children; Socrates had three sons and would not bring them in. The jurors, he said, had sworn to judge by the facts and the argument, not by tears or pity, and he would rather die by his own kind of defense than live by the other.

appeal-to-force-appeal-to-fear.context_blurb:
The appeal to force backs a claim with a threat instead of a reason. Its Latin tag, ad baculum, means "to the stick." Its close cousin, the appeal to fear, inflates a danger to win agreement. A threat can make people go quiet or say yes, but fear can force compliance without ever showing that a claim is true, which is why the move has long been a favorite of tyrants.

A baron tells a villager who called the new harvest tax unjust that the tax is just, and that if he questions it again he will rot in the dungeon. The terrified villager agrees. The threat has changed what the villager says, but it has given no reason at all to think the tax is fair. The test is who delivers the harm. A blacksmith who says the forge will burn your hand is giving advice about what fire does. A bully who says he will burn you with a poker unless you praise his drawing is promising to cause the harm himself in order to force agreement, and that is the giveaway of a threat. The same move hides in plain clothes at work. An employee asks why he must work a weekend he was promised off, and his manager hints that a new employee is easy to find. A threat to the man's job has taken the place of a reason, so his honest "why" is never answered.

History is full of the club. In May 1856, after Senator Charles Sumner gave a long speech against slavery, Congressman Preston Brooks beat him at his Senate desk with a heavy cane, so badly that Sumner could not return for years. Brooks answered none of Sumner's arguments, and the beating proved nothing about slavery: force can silence a man but cannot show that he was wrong. In 1633 the Roman Inquisition showed the elderly Galileo its instruments of torture, and he publicly denied that the Earth circles the Sun. The threat changed what he would say in public. It did nothing to the Earth and Sun, which went on moving exactly as before. Fear works without a club, too. In Wheeling in February 1950, Senator Joseph McCarthy waved a paper he said listed 205 communists in the State Department. He never produced it, and a later inquiry found nothing behind it, yet the crowd was swept along by the dread of hidden traitors, which raced ahead of any proof.

Not every threat is the fallacy. When a robber snarls "your money or your life," he is not reasoning badly, because he is not reasoning at all. Charles Hamblin, a logician, noted that only an argument can be fallacious, and the robber offers only a demand, so there is no argument to be bad. The fallacy needs the threat dressed up as a reason. Nor is every fearful warning a fallacy. Campaigners who oppose an underground nuclear test because it could trigger earthquakes or leak radiation are naming harms the blast could really cause, so the fear bears directly on whether to run the test. The baron's dungeon has nothing to do with whether his tax is fair; it is just a stick.

the-red-herring.context_blurb:
A red herring is a reply that changes the subject while looking like an answer. The name comes from a smoked fish so strong-smelling that it could cover almost any other scent. The test for it is simple and worth remembering: does the reply actually bear on the point that was raised? If not, the question is still open, however good the reply sounds.

A teacher catches a boy cheating on a spelling test. He confesses at once, then wails that his parents will kill him if he fails. He has conceded the charge and veered off to a fear that has no bearing on whether he cheated. A wife lists three complaints, the clutter, the unlocked door and the piling trash, and her husband snaps back that she never parks properly in the driveway. That you-too reply may be true, but it swaps in a fresh complaint about her and answers none of hers.

The dodge often comes with real facts attached. A steward is asked where the lord's grain has gone, and he answers by describing ice-bound roads, starving herds and snow without end. The winter may be real, but the reply never says where the grain went, so the question still stands. An official charged with funnelling city contracts to his wife's business answers with fond stories about her wardrobe, their dog and the youth baseball team he pays for. Those likable details tug at the feelings but never touch the accusation.

Compare two neighbours who receive the same complaint about a barking dog and a falling fence. Greer accuses his neighbour of approving of collapsing fences as long as they look quaint; he stays on the topic but twists it, which is a straw man. Pike asks when his neighbour will repaint that ugly shed; he drops the complaint and walks off to a new topic, which is the red herring. Because it covers any reply unrelated to the point, the red herring is the family's parent, and two of its best-known offspring are the straw man and the appeal to pity. That is why logicians rarely use the broad label and reach for the narrower names instead.

The fish has a story of its own. In 1807 the radical journalist William Cobbett wrote that as a boy he had dragged a red herring on a string for miles across the fields to pull the hounds off a hare's scent. He used the tale to mock London newspapers that had chased a planted rumour. Much later, two word-historians, Gerald Cohen and his colleague Robert Scott Ross, searched for proof, and the Oxford English Dictionary adopted their verdict: there is no sign the practice ever happened. Cobbett's tale was itself a false trail, and it fooled people for two centuries.

Detective writers made the false clue an art. In A Study in Scarlet, the first Sherlock Holmes story, the killer daubs RACHE, German for revenge, in blood on a wall, and the police set off after the wrong man.

appeal-to-ignorance.context_blurb:
The appeal to ignorance, argumentum ad ignorantiam to medieval logicians, treats a gap in our knowledge as if it were an answer. One version says a claim must be true because no one has proved it false; the mirror version says a claim must be false because no one has proved it true. The fix is the burden of proof: whoever makes a claim is the one who must back it up.

A villager declares the town well cursed, and when asked for proof he shrugs that nobody has ever shown it isn't. But a claim nobody has disproved is still a claim nobody has proved; an empty space where evidence should be tells you nothing either way. The move runs in both directions, and both are equally broken. One neighbor says ghosts must be real because no one has shown them fake; another says a distant moon must be lifeless because no one has found life there. Neither argument works, because not knowing whether a claim is true settles nothing about whether it is. And the burden falls on the claimer. When a child insists a monster lives under her bed and dares her father to prove otherwise, the job is hers, because whoever says an unusual thing exists must show that it does.

Courtrooms are built on this rule. If an accused man could be convicted because no one proved he didn't do it, an empty file would become a guilty verdict. Anglo-American criminal law starts from the presumption that the accused is innocent and makes the prosecution carry the whole burden, so a gap in the evidence can never be turned into guilt.

Bertrand Russell made the point with a teapot. Suppose, he said, a little china teapot circles the sun somewhere between Earth and Mars, too tiny for even the best telescope. No one could disprove it, yet anyone who called doubt arrogant here would deserve to be told he was talking nonsense, because the person making the claim owes the evidence, not the doubter. Carl Sagan told of a neighbor with a dragon in his garage. Flour would show no footprints, because the dragon floats; a heat sensor would find nothing, because its fire is heatless; paint would not stick, because it has no body. Each test met a new excuse, and Sagan asked what difference remained between such a dragon and no dragon at all. A claim built so that no test could ever count against it tells you nothing. Senator Joseph McCarthy once said of an accused man that nothing in the files disproved his Communist connections. Logicians quote the sentence because it turns a gap where evidence would be into evidence itself, and puts the burden on a silent file instead of on the accuser.

Does an empty-handed search ever tell against a claim? Yes, but only under a strict condition: the search must be careful and complete, and the thing, if it existed, would have been bound to leave signs in exactly the places searched. That is why the Loch Ness monster differs from Sagan's dragon. A thirty-foot animal living in a lake of fixed size, swept by searchers for decades, should have turned up on sonar by now, so the empty search is a genuine, though not absolute, reason to doubt it. The fallacy is leaping from "nobody checked" to "true." The sound inference is "we checked hard, where it should have shown, and it did not."

the-straw-man-and-steelmanning.context_blurb:
A straw man is a scarecrow stuffed with straw, a fake person who never fights back. In argument, building a straw man means swapping your opponent's real position for a weaker copy and knocking that down instead. The honest opposite is steelmanning: rebuilding the other side's case in its strongest form before you answer it, so that any win you claim is real.

Picture a knight too scared to face his rival. He props up a straw dummy, shouts the rival's name, hacks it apart while a crowd cheers and struts off claiming victory. He has beaten a stand-in, and the real rival stands untouched. Arguments go the same way. Will wants more money for schools and hospitals, and Warren accuses him of hating his country and wanting to gut the army. Will never mentioned the army; Warren attacked a position Will never took because it was easier to hit.

The commonest version inflates a modest claim. A lawmaker proposes background checks before gun sales, and her opponent warns voters that she is coming for every gun they own. He has inflated a small, specific proposal into a sweeping one that is far easier to attack. Another speaker says only that the military budget should not grow any further and hears that he wants the country defenceless against invasion: his opponent seized the worst-case reading instead of what was actually said. Or one speaker urges a town to fix its single cracked bridge, and his rival proves the town could never rebuild every bridge at once. The crowd roars, yet nothing has been won: the rival knocked over a target the first speaker never put up.

Spelled out, the trick looks like this. One person asserts X. The other attacks Y, which only resembles X, and beats it soundly. However perfect the attack on Y, it never touches X, so the real claim survives. Aristotle described the dodge some 2,300 years ago in his Sophistical Refutations: a rebuttal aimed at something the opponent never said decides nothing about what he did say. In 1520 Martin Luther accused his critics of attacking a man of straw, of inventing a flimsy, false Luther and fighting that instead of him.

The sneakiest straw man is no crude lie. The arguer stretches a real position slightly past what was meant, adding an all, a never or the worst possible case, and crushes that. Because the swollen version grows out of words the person really used, it looks fair, and listeners who would catch a plain lie let it pass.

The honest opposite is to repair the other side's case until it is as strong as it can be, and only then to answer it. A writer who blogged as Black Belt Bayesian put it sharply: if you only want to win, you will refute your opponents' arguments, but if you want the truth, you will first fix their arguments for them. The idea has a serious ancestor. Neil Wilson gave it a name in 1959, the principle of charity, and Quine and Davidson later made it a method: take a speaker's words in the most sensible, consistent sense they will bear before you judge them.

Compare two debaters. Mara cuts the other side's case back to its weakest claim and knocks that over. Jonah mends every gap, supplies the best point the other side forgot, and defeats the stronger result. Only Jonah has truly proven his opponent wrong, because he beat the strongest possible version, leaving no better form to retreat to.

the-false-dilemma-false-dichotomy.context_blurb:
The false dilemma, or false dichotomy, forces a choice between two options when more exist. It turns up in politics, in family quarrels and anywhere a speaker wants a quick surrender instead of a careful answer. It is not the same as a genuine either-or, since a switch really is on or off; the trick lies in squeezing a wider field down to two. A careful reasoner learns to look for the quiet third path.

A father tells his son that he either loves him or hates him, and that if he loved him he would eat his broccoli. But love and hate are not the only feelings; a boy can be annoyed, or simply not hungry. When an uncle at a cookout asks whether you want ketchup or mustard, remember that "or" need not mean only those two: you could want both, neither or relish.

A coach who warns a player that it is college or a failed life has crushed a wide range of real roads, a trade, the army, a business of his own, into two extremes. A girl who refuses to join a schoolyard fight and is told she must be with the gang or against it is being denied real options: she can stay neutral, back the goal but not the method, or simply not have chosen yet. A false dilemma can hide inside a loaded survey, too. Asking whether the boss is drunk at work once a week, twice a week or more often leaves no room to disagree, because the honest answer, never, was left off the list.

Famous speeches use the trick on purpose. In 1775 Patrick Henry ended a speech in Richmond, Virginia, crying for liberty or death. A real revolution offered other roads, but the line's bravery comes precisely from slamming every middle road shut: no waiting and no bargaining, only freedom or the grave. In the days after the attacks of September 2001, President George W. Bush told Congress that every nation was either with America or with the terrorists. The philosopher Paul Keeling noted that an airtight version would say "with us or not with us." Bush swapped "not with us" for "with the terrorists," but not joining one side does not tell you whose side, if any, a nation is on. In Joseph Heller's novel Catch-22, Colonel Korn tells the airman Yossarian that he is either for us or against his country. The trick is the slide from "us," just two colonels, to "your country," so that crossing two officers looks like treason.

In Revenge of the Sith, Anakin Skywalker tells Obi-Wan Kenobi that anyone not with him is his enemy. Obi-Wan has a third place to stand, because his loyalty belongs to the Republic, not to Anakin personally. Not every either-or is false. "Will you give twenty dollars or not?" covers every outcome. "Give twenty dollars, or else you want the planet destroyed" counts a simple refusal as a wish to see the planet ruined, and ignores the honest reasons someone might decline, such as being broke or preferring another charity. Likewise, saying a jar contains 10 marbles or some other number is airtight, but saying it contains 10 or 11 quietly drops 2, 17 and every other count.

Logicians name the deep error. Contradictories, such as hot and not hot, cannot both be false. Contraries, such as hot and cold, can both fail, since the day might be warm, so they never cover every case, and a false dilemma dresses contraries up as contradictories. There are three classic escapes from a dilemma: deny the first horn, deny the second, or go between the horns by showing there are more than two options. Only the last defeats a false dilemma, as when a graduate told to take a job or amount to nothing names the trades, start-ups and further study the recruiter left out. The word dilemma comes from Greek for a double proposition, and medieval logicians called the trap a horned argument, because whichever horn you grab, you get gored.

begging-the-question-circular-reasoning.context_blurb:
Begging the question means smuggling your conclusion into one of your premises, so the argument walks in a small circle and ends where it began. Its old Latin name, petitio principii, means asking for the starting point: asking the listener to grant the very thing in dispute. In logic it describes an argument that can persuade only someone who already agreed.

A campaign flyer says a senator can be trusted because she is honest and always tells the truth. Telling the truth is just honesty said again, so it gives a doubting voter nothing new to weigh; anyone who doubts the conclusion doubts the premise just as much. A deli owner claims his are the finest sandwiches around, since nobody else's beat them. Finest and unbeaten are one claim said twice, and no actual reason, better bread or fresher meat, is ever given.

Sometimes the circle is a single line. In a story by the French writer Guy de Maupassant, a villager explains a man's death by saying he died because he died. That sounds like a cause but is only the bare fact repeated as its own explanation. In Spain, the head of a bullfighters' association said women have rights but should not fight bulls, since, he said, bullfighters are men and ought to be. Strip away the bluster and the reason he offers is simply the conclusion he owed us an argument for: women should not, because women should not.

Learned words can hide the same trick. In Molière's 1673 play, doctors quiz a student about what makes opium bring on sleep, and his grave Latin reply is that opium contains a "dormitive virtue," that is, a sleep-making power. All he has done is give the effect a fancy name and then present that name as the reason. Circles can have two steps. A speaker who says a law is illegal because it is immoral, and would not be illegal if it were not immoral, props each half up with the other, and nothing from outside the circle holds either one. Any religion's scripture can be dropped into the same frame: a sacred book must be true since a god wrote it, and we know a god wrote it because the book says he did. A doubter could accept one half only after accepting the other first, so the argument moves him not at all. The fault lies in the structure, not in any particular creed.

Stacking up endorsements does not help if they form a ring. A spokesman who says the President can be trusted on the White House's word, while the White House can be trusted because the President picked its staff, offers a circle in which each witness owes his standing to the very circle he is vouching for. Such an argument can be flawless in form, with the conclusion really following from the premise, and still prove nothing, because nobody can accept the premise without having accepted the conclusion first. One loaded word can carry the whole circle. In "murder is wrong, so abortion is wrong," the word murder already contains the verdict of wrongful killing that the argument was supposed to establish, so the person who needs convincing will not grant it; the flaw is in the logic, whatever one's view of the issue. A cousin of the fallacy is the loaded question, such as demanding a yes or no on whether a man has quit beating his wife, when he never did. Either answer convicts him, because the assumption is buried in how the question is worded, while begging the question buries it in a premise.

The hardest circles to spot are long ones. Claim one supports claim two, which supports claim three, and several steps later the chain loops back to hold up claim one. Each link looks fine alone, but at some point along the chain the conclusion ends up holding up one of its own premises, and only walking the whole ring reveals it. So how can two arguments with identical words differ, one honest and one circular? The test is not the wording but where the premise draws its backing: could someone who doubts the conclusion still have good grounds to accept the premise? If not, the argument has begged the question.

equivocation.context_blurb:
Equivocation is the trick of using one word in two different senses inside a single argument, so that a conclusion only seems to follow because the word changed meaning halfway through. Aristotle listed it in his handbook of sophistical tricks, which makes it one of the oldest named fallacies. The defense is simple: pin down each key word and hold it to one meaning from start to finish.

Jokes make the slide easy to see. One riddle proves that no feather can be black, because feathers are light and light things are never dark. Light first means low in weight and then switches to bright, and a thing's weight says nothing about its color. Another proves that a ham sandwich beats eternal happiness, since nothing beats eternal happiness and a sandwich beats nothing. The first sentence makes happiness the top of the scale, while the second only says a sandwich is better than having no sandwich, so the two make different comparisons. Rivers have banks and banks have vaults, yet rivers hold no vaults: a river's edge and a money bank are two terms hiding in one word. And if Brad is a nobody and nobody is perfect, Brad is still not perfect, because nobody first means a person of no importance and then means not one single person.

Everyday arguments slide the same way. A boy argues that because he is entitled to watch his show, watching it must be the right thing to do instead of his chores. Right first means something he is allowed to do and then means the morally good choice, and having a right to do something does not make it right to do. Noisy children may be a headache, but aspirin will not cure them, because the first headache is a figure of speech for an annoyance and the second is a real pain in the head. An old argument that women cannot be rational, because only man is rational and no woman is a man, collapses once you notice that the first man refers to the whole human species and the second to males only.

In debates about science the slippery word is often theory. A parent who calls evolution just a theory, and then treats a theory as a mere hunch, slides between two senses: the casual sense of a guess and the scientific sense of a well-tested framework that explains the evidence. The flaw lies in the switch, whatever one thinks of evolution. Plato mocked the sophists' word games in his Euthydemus. A sophist gets young Ctesippus to agree that his dog is a father and that the dog is his, then announces that the dog is his father, so Ctesippus beats his own father. Each statement is true alone, but welding the dog being his and the dog being a father into the dog being his father changes what both phrases mean.

Political speech leans on the trick. A spokesman praises his nation's love of freedom, then calls for a ban on every news outlet the state does not run, since official media shield people from foreign falsehoods. Freedom starts as the liberty to choose and ends as being kept safe from something bad, and the persuasion rides on that switch, whatever one thinks of state media. Advertisers do it too. If soil is natural, and whatever is natural must be healthy, then dirt belongs on the dinner menu; but natural first means found in nature and then means safe and healthy, which are not the same. Spotting that switch unmasks a lot of all-natural marketing. Equivocation was once a deadly scandal. The Jesuit Henry Garnet, executed in 1606 in the wake of the Gunpowder Plot, argued at his trial for a doctrine of equivocation. It let a man answer with words that sounded true while holding back their real meaning in his head, so that he misled his questioners without telling a flat lie. In Macbeth, Shakespeare's drunken Porter mocks a man whose double talk could not get him through heaven's gate.

the-loaded-question.context_blurb:
A loaded question is built on an unproven assumption, so any direct yes-or-no answer concedes the assumption just by playing along. Logicians call it the complex question. The defense is almost never to answer yes or no; it is to name the hidden claim out loud and refuse it. The trick works in courtrooms, interviews and debates because it sounds like a polite request for information.

A teacher asks a boy who has never cheated whether he has stopped cheating on his tests. Answer yes or answer no, either way he confesses to having cheated, because the accusation is smuggled into the question before he speaks. When a brother asks his sister, who has never touched his food, whether she has stopped sneaking his snacks, her best reply rejects the hidden premise: she has never touched them at all. In court the same move draws an objection. A prosecutor who asks whether a defendant smirked when he kicked a man takes the kick, which no one has proven, as already settled; lawyers object that the question assumes facts not in evidence.

A loaded question is really several questions crammed into one. An innkeeper who demands to know where a traveler hid the stolen gold is asking at once whether gold was stolen, whether the traveler took it, and where he put it; splitting it up exposes the trick. The oldest recorded escape comes from about 300 BC. The philosopher Alexinus asked Menedemus whether he had stopped beating his father. Menedemus denied both halves together: he had not been beating him, and so he had not left off either.

Loaded questions can spread lies. During the 2000 presidential primary in South Carolina, fake pollsters rang voters and asked if it would change their view of John McCain to learn that he had an illegitimate black child. He had none; the call slipped a smear into voters' minds by dressing a lie up as an established fact. Not every presupposition is a trick, though. Asking whether you enjoyed the cake assumes you ate some, and that is fine. A question turns foul only when it slips in a claim that the person being asked would reject. The tactic also carries a counter-trap. When a mayor refuses to answer whether he will keep wasting taxes and challenges the word wasting, a reporter can tell viewers that he dodged the question, so the correct refusal of the premise gets spun to look like guilty evasion.

no-true-scotsman.context_blurb:
"No true Scotsman" is the trick of saving a sweeping claim by redrawing a group's borders the moment a counterexample turns up. The British philosopher Antony Flew named it after a joke about porridge, and it appears wherever a defender insists that an embarrassing member of a group was never a real member. Logicians separate it carefully from honest definition, because the trick lies in shrinking the category after the awkward case arrives.

In Flew's joke, a Scot declares that no Scotsman sugars his porridge. A friend names an uncle, Scottish born and bred, who sugars his every morning, and the first man replies that no true Scotsman does. He has not answered the counterexample; he has simply bent the meaning of the word to shut the uncle out, sparing himself the admission that he erred. Picture a girl who says no one on her soccer team ever misses practice, hears that one teammate skipped twice last week, and answers that anyone truly devoted to the team would never skip. The honest reply was to retreat to a smaller claim that is actually true, such as "almost nobody on the team skips." Little words such as true, real, genuine and pure do the dirty work, which is why logicians also call this the appeal to purity. When a fan insists that proper fans must hate the new movies, and then, shown lifelong fans who loved them, declares that those people never counted, the word does no describing at all. It simply expels any awkward case from the group by definition.

Sometimes the definition is rigged in reverse. A clubman boasts that his fellow members are all model citizens; told that several are behind bars, he decides they were never true members, though he counted them until that moment. By making good character part of the definition of a member, he guarantees that no convict could ever count against his boast. Timing is the tell. When the preacher Harold Camping's forecast of doomsday in 2011 came and went, many believers announced he had never been a true Christian, without offering any agreed test for what makes one. The badge of false faith appeared only once the prophecy flopped, and its job was to stop his failure from reflecting on other believers.

Some narrowing of a word is honest. "No true vegetarian eats steak" is perfectly fair, because not eating meat is what the word vegetarian has always publicly meant. The porridge sentence has the same shape but is a dodge, since its rule was invented on the spot to escape one case. A single question usually settles which kind you face: was this test for membership on record before the troublesome example appeared, in terms the group itself would accept?

The trick also ruins what it rescues. That every swan is white was once a bold, checkable claim, until Europeans exploring Australia came upon black swans. Fall back on the claim that every genuine swan is white, and the claim boils down to saying that white swans are white: true by definition, and empty of news about actual birds. Flew called such a rescued claim an impotent tautology, one that gains truth at the cost of saying anything.

the-slippery-slope-and-when-its-legitima.context_blurb:
A slippery-slope argument claims that one small step will lead, link by link, to disaster. Logicians call it a fallacy when the links are merely asserted. But the shape alone proves nothing either way, because some slopes are real. The whole skill is learning to test each link.

Start at home. Maya decides that failing one test means failing the class, then failing out of school, then a ruined life. Each jump treats a possibility as a certainty. The cure is to name the weakest link out loud: one bad test does not force a failed class, and the chain stops there. Compare a warning that trash dumped on a sidewalk will pile up into a health hazard. That is a fair argument, because everyday experience backs each step, so the bad outcome really is likely.

Lawyers call the cheating version a parade of horribles. A speaker warns that letting same-sex couples marry will bring demands to marry pets, then furniture, and races to the lurid finish. What he has skipped, without a word, are the middle steps that would force each stage into the next. The famous boiling frog is a slope image that fails even as a fact. When Friedrich Goltz in the 1870s and Victor Hutchison in 2002 actually warmed the water, a normal frog climbed out, struggling to escape once the heat grew uncomfortable. Old fables work the same way. A camel that pokes its nose into a man's tent on a cold night and ends with the whole beast inside makes a vivid picture of the worry, but a story cannot show that any real chain forces the next step.

So shouting that's a slippery slope refutes nothing. The slope shape proves nothing on its own; you have to show that a particular link is weak. T. Edward Damer renamed the fallacy the domino fallacy. Real dominoes topple one after another only when they stand close enough for each one to strike the next, and the bad arguer assumes events are packed that tightly when they may be scattered across the table.

A careful rule measures any chain. Its strength drops with every extra step between the start and the feared end, and grows the harder each link pushes on its neighbour. The legal scholar Eugene Volokh explained how a slope can have real teeth even when the first step is reasonable. One mechanism: the first step makes the next one cheaper, so it becomes easier to take. History also keeps score. In 1895 a cartoonist mocked votes for women by drawing the wild wedding scenes of the year 2001. The cascade of chaos never came.

Eric Lode found the feature that decides whether a slide is real: whether there is a clear place to stop. That gives one blunt test for any slope: what stops us from halting at the very next step? If you can point to a clear, non-arbitrary line, the slide loses its force.

The deepest version is the ancient heap puzzle of Eubulides. One grain is not a heap, and adding a single grain never turns a non-heap into a heap, yet heaps exist. The tempting wrong lesson is that since no single grain makes the difference, a few grains and a full heap are not really different. Being unable to draw a sharp line does not mean there is no real difference, just as a toddler and an adult are plainly different though joined by a chain of single days.

the-continuum-line-drawing-fallacy.context_blurb:
The continuum fallacy, also called the line-drawing fallacy, claims that because no sharp line separates two things, the difference between them is not real. It grows from an ancient Greek puzzle called the sorites, from soros, the word for heap. The fallacy is the leap from "no crisp line" to "no real difference," and it returns whenever someone calls bald, rich, old or adult meaningless.

Nobody can name the second when day turns into night, because dusk slides smoothly from light to dark. That missing cutoff does nothing to erase the plain gap between noon and midnight. In the same way, no single hair's loss turns a man bald, yet Patrick Stewart is clearly bald, while the young Conan O'Brien, with his full head of hair, clearly is not. A word can mark a real difference at its two ends even when its middle is full of borderline cases.

The original puzzle runs like this: one grain of sand is not a heap, and no single added grain can make a heap out of something that was not one, so there are no heaps at all. Every step looks harmless, which is the trick. Tiny differences that each seem to change nothing can still pile up into a genuine change. Philosophers answer the whole family, heap, beard and bald man alike, with one line: a difference of degree is still a difference, and a big enough one becomes a difference of kind.

Chrysippus, the great Stoic, devised an escape from the riddle. When a questioner climbed number by number, asking whether three was many, then four, Chrysippus meant to fall silent and refuse to answer just before the questions reached the fuzzy border; the Greeks called this hesuchazein, keeping quiet. The skeptic Carneades mocked him, in a joke Cicero preserved: rest, even snore if you like, but what good will it do? The next questioner will simply ask about the next number, and the same problem is back.

The fallacy does real damage in public argument. Someone says that because no single day turns a child into an adult, any voting or drinking age is meaningless. But where exactly the line falls is partly a decision, while the difference it marks between a child and an adult is completely real, which is why societies set ages for driving and limits for speed. Medicine labels blood pressure over about 140 over 90 as high, a number people chose, and a reading just under it differs little from one just over. Still, a very high reading harms you whatever number was picked, so an arbitrary line can flag a real danger.

hasty-generalization.context_blurb:
Hasty generalization is the leap from a small or lopsided sample to a sweeping claim about a whole group: one rude knight, and suddenly the whole kingdom is rude. Generalizing is a useful habit; the fallacy lies in overshooting what the evidence can carry. Statisticians sharpen the diagnosis with two questions, how big the sample is and whether it is biased, and the answers often matter more than any vivid example.

A traveler who meets one rude innkeeper at a border inn and declares the whole kingdom rude has made the purest version of the slip, because a single grumpy host tells you nothing about thousands of strangers. An old tale told in Buddhist, Jain, Hindu and Sufi tradition gives the classic picture. Several blind men lay their hands on an elephant: the man at its flank decides it is a kind of wall, the man gripping its trunk a kind of serpent, and the man hugging a leg a kind of pillar. Every man mistakes the patch under his own hands for the entire beast.

Size matters. A man who meets three visitors from China who fear dogs, then announces that most of China's 1.4 billion people fear dogs, has overreached, since three jumpy travelers reveal nothing about the feelings of a billion-odd people. Yet a sample of one can be enough when the thing sampled is uniform. A cook can test one strand of spaghetti but not one sip of soup, because pasta in a rolling boil is evenly done, whereas soup left unstirred varies from layer to layer, so a sip speaks only for the spoonful.

A huge count can still be biased. For fifteen centuries Europe was sure every swan was white; the Romans ranked a black swan with a flying pig. Then Willem de Vlamingh, exploring Western Australia in 1697, found a river swarming with black swans. Europe's birdwatchers had never looked in the southern half of the globe, so their enormous count was blind to an entire population. John Stuart Mill used the case to show that a million white swans cannot prove a rule that one black swan breaks. Statistics can also hide their own setup. A famous gum ad boasted that four dentists in five favored sugarless gum, but the dentists could pick sugarless gum, sugared gum or no gum at all, and the holdout often recommended chewing nothing rather than a competing brand.

In 1936 the Literary Digest mailed 10 million mock ballots, collected 2.4 million and forecast a crushing win for Alf Landon over Roosevelt, who won in a landslide instead. The names came from phone books, car registrations and country-club lists. In the Great Depression only the well-off, people who could afford phones, cars and club dues, ever received a ballot, while the poorer voters who backed Roosevelt went uncounted. George Gallup called the race right with about 50,000 well-chosen replies. The mathematician Abraham Wald saw the same trap in World War II bombers that came back riddled in the wings and body but almost unmarked on the engines. He told the generals to armor the engines. The planes struck in the engine had gone down and never been counted, so the holes on the returning planes marked only the places a plane could be hit and survive. A different slip is generalizing from a freak. A girl whose new turtle dies in two days, and who decides turtles do not outlive tarantulas after all, is building her rule on one freak case, not on too few typical ones, an error logicians call converse accident.

composition-and-division.context_blurb:
Composition and division are mirror-image slips in reasoning about parts and wholes. Composition pushes a trait upward, from each part to the whole the parts make. Division pushes a trait downward, from the whole to each of its parts. Aristotle listed both among the tricks of clever arguers, and they survive because the jump from part to whole hides inside a single word, where almost nobody notices it.

Picture a coach who signs the five top scorers in a league and promises his owner a team nobody can beat. Being a star is true of each player, but the coach assumed that what holds for each player must hold for the team they form. Five players who all want the ball can wreck the passing and the chemistry, and the best individuals can add up to a bad team. Division runs the slip in reverse. A finished wall can be enormously heavy while every brick in it is light, because the wall gets its weight by adding many bricks together, and that trait of the whole does not pass down into any single brick. In the same way, a family famous around town as a learned household need not have a doctorate in every crib. What is true of the family taken together need not be true of each member, down to the baby.

Chemistry shows why the slip matters. Sodium is a metal so fierce it catches fire when it touches water, and chlorine is a poison gas that armies once used, yet when sodium hands an electron to chlorine the pair becomes table salt, which people eat and need to live. Assuming a danger in each element must carry over into the compound gets the chemistry exactly wrong, because bonding changes the properties. Totals mislead the same way going down. A whole class can eat a mountain of ice cream in a year while one boy in it eats almost none, so the class total says nothing about any single child.

Some advantages exist only by comparison. A fan who stands up at a ballgame suddenly sees the whole field, but only because the people around him are still sitting. When the entire stadium stands, his edge vanishes, and everyone is simply standing and uncomfortable. Sometimes a whole even gains something no part had. Neither hydrogen nor oxygen is wet, yet water is; carbon atoms arranged one way make soft graphite and arranged another make hard diamond. Philosophers call this emergence: the whole can show a new trait that none of its parts had by itself. Still, some traits really do add up, such as mass and weight, which is exactly why the slip is so tempting.

Economists catch the same move in policy talk. One student who earns a college degree catches an employer's eye, but his edge came from standing out against people who had none. Hand a degree to everyone and it only raises the baseline, so the gap that made the lone graduate appealing disappears. The paradox of thrift has the same shape. Saving more gives one family a cushion, but if every family saves far more in the same year, the nation as a whole need not be better off, because one household's spending is another household's income. The point is logical, not a policy verdict: a habit that is good for one part need not be good for the whole.

accident-misapplying-a-general-rule.context_blurb:
The fallacy of accident takes a sound general rule and forces it onto a case the rule was never meant to cover. Aristotle named it. The mistake is treating a rule of everyday life as if it had no exceptions, when nearly every honest rule carries unspoken limits.

Take a bird called Tweety. "Birds can fly" is true of birds in general, but it is a rule of thumb, not a law of nature. Tweety is a penguin, the odd case the generalization was never built to reach, so concluding that Tweety flies stretches the rule past its range. The law against slashing people with a blade is aimed at assault in a street fight. A surgeon cuts too, but the operating room is a setting that law was never framed to govern, so calling surgeons criminals misapplies a good rule rather than refuting it. In the Republic, old Cephalus suggests that justice means being truthful and giving back what you borrowed, and Socrates answers with one case: a friend lends you his weapons, then goes mad and wants them back. Handing a sword to a madman is plainly not just, so the rule must have carried an unstated exception all along.

Suppose a neighbor lent you a knife and you swore to bring it back by Friday, but by then he is raving that he will hurt someone. Keeping promises is genuinely good, but arming a maniac is exactly the abnormal case the everyday rule leaves out, so the fault lies in treating a good rule as exceptionless, not in the rule. Aristotle's own example shows the structure underneath. Coriscus differs from Socrates, and Socrates is a man, so the argument concludes that Coriscus, a man himself, differs from a man. It assumes that whatever is true of a thing must also be true of every passing description that thing happens to wear. But one thing wears many descriptions, and a property true under one need not carry through another.

The hardest test came in 1797, when Benjamin Constant challenged Immanuel Kant, who held that lying is always wrong: must you then tell a murderer where your friend is hiding? Constant's deeper point was about who is owed honesty at all. Truth, he argued, is a duty only toward someone with a right to it, and a murderer hunting his victim has forfeited that right. Kant held his ground: answer truthfully even then. Whether "never lie" has a built-in exception is what the two men fought over, and the fight is still open.

the-suppressed-correlative-and-the-defin.context_blurb:
Some arguments win by stretching a word until its opposite disappears. Philosophers call this the suppressed correlative. Every useful word draws a line, and the trick quietly erases the far side of the line while pretending to have discovered a fact.

A story about Abraham Lincoln shows it. Riding in a stagecoach, Lincoln argued that every good deed is secretly selfish. Then he jumped out to rescue a sow's piglets from drowning in a muddy slough, and explained that he did it for his own peace of mind. The philosopher Joel Feinberg spotted the flaw. Lincoln's relief depended on a wish he already had, that the pigs be saved; he aimed at their safety, and the good feeling came only as its result.

A friend who insists that everything is mysterious, even the well-charted flow of blood, makes the same move. A word earns its meaning by drawing a line; stretch mysterious over everything, even the sum of three and four, and it marks off nothing, so it says nothing.

The slipperiest cousin is the persuasive definition. Declare that real freedom means obeying the state's just laws, and a prisoner becomes more free than ever. The word keeps its warm glow while its meaning changes. The conclusion was built into the definition before any argument began; calling obedience freedom decides the question by decree, and no reasoning has been offered at all.

post-hoc-ergo-propter-hoc-after-this-so-.context_blurb:
Post hoc ergo propter hoc, Latin for "after this, therefore because of this," may be the oldest causal fallacy of all: mistaking a sequence in time for a chain of cause. Our minds are built to notice what comes before what, a habit that helps us survive but misleads us when we reason. Much of science's machinery, its control groups, repeated trials and random assignment, exists to guard against this one mistake.

A farm boy hears the rooster crow every morning just before sunrise and decides the crowing raises the sun. But coming first is not the same as causing; dawn would arrive if every rooster on earth stayed silent. A girl blames the black cat that crossed her path for the ankle she sprained that afternoon, yet nothing ties the cat to the fall except their order, and the many black cats followed by no mishap are simply forgotten. A building manager blames the new tenants when the groaning old furnace dies a week after they move in. The move and the breakdown have nothing in common but their dates, since the worn-out boiler was dying anyway. A boy credits his aunt's honey tonic when his cold clears three days later, but colds run their course within days, so he would have mended without a drop of it. The honest check is whether people who skip the tonic recover just as fast.

Sometimes the supposed cause even runs backward. Baby walkers are sold partly on the promise of earlier walking, but when pediatricians in Ireland tested them in the 1980s, babies who used walkers sat up, crawled and walked later than those who did not, because the tray hid their own moving legs. Rituals can ride the seasons. The Hopi danced each year at the end of summer, in late August; the monsoon was due then anyway, so the ritual took credit for rain that would have fallen regardless. When the footballer Pelé slumped after giving away his match shirt, a friend claimed to have found it, and Pelé's form returned, though the friend had really handed him a shirt from his bad stretch. His touch returned by itself, and an irrelevant shirt was given the glory. In 1948 B. F. Skinner fed hungry pigeons on a fixed timer, regardless of what they did, and caught the fallacy forming. Whatever motion a bird was making at the moment of feeding, it repeated, turning in circles or poking a corner, as though its own movement summoned the grain, since grain kept appearing just after it.

The fallacy has worked on a national scale. English subjects long trusted that a royal touch could heal scrofula, a disease that swells the glands of the neck, and Charles II alone touched some 100,000 sufferers. Many felt better, most likely because the disease often fades by itself, and the king's hand, laid on just beforehand, was thanked for it. There are honest tests. John Stuart Mill described taking away a suspected cause and watching what follows. Move the rooster far away and the boy's sun still rises on time: remove the supposed cause, check whether the effect still happens, and here the crowing proves to do nothing. Another guard is to look for a hidden third thing. Sales of ice cream and the number of drownings rise and sink in step, not because cones drown people but because summer heat pushes up both, filling the ice-cream stands and the swimming spots alike.

correlation-vs-causation-the-lurking-thi.context_blurb:
When two things rise and fall together, statisticians call them correlated. The trap is leaping from there to the claim that one causes the other, when a hidden third factor, called a lurking variable or confounder, may be driving both. Real causes often do show up as correlations, so the error lies in the leap, not the noticing. Controlled experiments grew up largely to pry the two apart.

In a beach town, ice cream sales and drownings climb every summer and fall every winter. Banning ice cream would save nobody, because summer heat is behind both: it sells ice cream and it fills the sea with swimmers, and more swimmers means more drownings. A man who wakes with a pounding head whenever he fell asleep in his shoes has the same puzzle. Heavy drinking explains both, since a drunk man is too far gone to undress and wakes up hung over, so taking his shoes off cures nothing.

Across a grade school, children with bigger feet read better. The hidden link is age: older children have bigger feet and more years of practice, and comparing two six-year-olds makes the gap disappear. Sometimes there is no third cause at all. The law student Tyler Vigen collected comic matches, such as cheese eating against deaths by tangled bedsheets, to show that a tight, beautiful graph can be pure coincidence that means nothing whatever.

Passing a math test does not rescue a coincidence. Vigen's graph pairing Nicolas Cage's yearly films with swimming-pool drownings scores a correlation near 0.67, enough to count as statistically significant by the usual rule, and it still proves nothing about cause. A confounder can even point backwards. Across many fires, bigger crews go with bigger damage, because a huge blaze both summons more trucks and burns more, though at any single fire the crew plainly helps. A textbook joke blames loud musicians for the poor cornfields they live beside. Likelier, poor soil made the land cheap enough for struggling musicians to afford, one cause with two effects. That side-by-side blunder is called cum hoc. Its cousin post hoc is about order: a rooster who crows before every sunrise and credits himself with the dawn has mistaken one event following another for one event producing another.

In 2000 the statistician Robert Matthews showed that across 17 European countries, stork numbers tracked birth rates so closely that chance would explain it only once in 125 tries. He titled the paper Storks Deliver Babies, mocking how a tiny p-value can dress up nonsense. The lurking variable was land area, since bigger countries hold more storks and more people having babies. In 1973 Berkeley's graduate school admitted far more of its male applicants than its female ones, yet Peter Bickel, checking department by department, found the bias gone, and in some departments the edge went to women. Women had mostly applied to fiercely competitive departments and men to easier ones, so the department set the odds, a reversal called Simpson's paradox. Doctors also saw fewer heart attacks among women taking hormone replacement, until a randomized trial stopped in 2002 found that the hormones slightly raised the risk. The women who chose them had simply been richer and healthier from the start.

So how do we ever establish a cause? For years the tobacco industry dismissed smoking and lung cancer as mere correlation. Sir Austin Bradford Hill answered that in 1965 with tests for a real cause, and the strongest is dose-response: the more cigarettes a person smokes, the higher his lung cancer risk climbs, step by step, a gradient that coincidence rarely produces. The danger also runs the other way. In 1897 Karl Pearson divided two unrelated measurements by a shared third number and watched a strong link appear from nothing. He named this a spurious correlation, a falsely high figure between measurements that have no true tie.

reversing-cause-and-effect.context_blurb:
Reversing cause and effect means pointing the arrow the wrong way: claiming that A causes B when B actually causes A. Both ends of a real connection are present, and the only mistake is which end is pinned to which. Statisticians call it reverse causation, and it is one big reason scientists run experiments instead of only watching. Its old nickname is putting the cart before the horse.

A child seeing a windmill for the first time watches its sails spin in a gale and announces that the windmill is making the wind. But the gale arrived first and drove the sails, so he has confused what is pushed with what does the pushing. A girl sees umbrellas bloom all along her street whenever the rain begins and wonders whether umbrellas bring the rain. One simple test settles the direction: rain often falls where no umbrella exists, while umbrellas appear only when rain does. And the farm rooster that crows just before sunrise, strutting as if he hauls the sun up, has it backwards; the glow before sunrise is what sets him crowing, so dawn moves the bird rather than the reverse.

Order in time can crack the case, because a cause must come before its effect. In a village with one healer, a rumor spreads that her visits make people ill, since she is always at a sickbed. She simply asks which happens first: the sick summon her once the fever has already struck, so the illness precedes the visit. Medieval Europeans made a real version of the mistake. Noticing that the gravely ill and the dying almost never had lice, many took lice as a sign of health and their loss as a cause of sickness. In fact lice flee a body racked by high fever, so losing them was a sign of serious sickness, not what caused it.

The reversal fools experts too. One health table showed people who had quit smoking dying of lung disease more often than those who still smoked, as if quitting were deadly. But many had stopped smoking because doctors had already found cancer or emphysema, so the illness came first and the quitting followed. A young man who sees that rich men own yachts and spends his savings on a boat has it backwards, since wealth comes first and buys the yacht, so the boat is a product of riches, not a road to them. Not every misread link is a reversal, though. Often a hidden third factor drives both things at once, which is a different mistake. A true reversal keeps the same two things linked but flips the arrow, as when someone concludes that wearing reading glasses ruins eyesight over the years. Weak eyes are what send a person for glasses, so the glasses are the effect, never the cause.

regression-to-the-mean-the-sports-illust.context_blurb:
Regression to the mean is the statistical fact that extreme results, such as a record streak, a career-best season or a freak bad day, tend to be followed by more ordinary ones. The Victorian polymath Francis Galton first measured it. The drift itself is real; the fallacy is blaming it on a cause that did nothing, as fans do with the famous Sports Illustrated cover jinx.

Sports Illustrated's cover in November 1957 hailed Oklahoma, unbeaten in 47 straight games, as unbeatable; days later Notre Dame, an unranked team, won 7-0. Fans blamed the cover, but a freak run that long could not last, and the team simply settled back toward its normal form. The sophomore slump works the same way. A player who wins Rookie of the Year almost certainly had more good luck than bad; the next season his skill is unchanged but the luck does not repeat, so he comes back to earth, and stars at every stage of a career fall off after a personal best. In 2002 Sports Illustrated examined its own 2,456 covers since 1954 and found that featured athletes did slump afterward about 37 percent of the time. It still found no curse, because athletes earned the cover by peaking, and peaks settle.

Daniel Kahneman put it simply: a record day mixes genuine talent with a run of luck. The talent carries over to the next showing, but the luck does not, so the champion returns to earth with no curse required. Believers in the jinx point to tragedies. Pat O'Connor, a racing driver, appeared on the cover ahead of the 1958 Indianapolis 500 and was killed on the first lap, and the figure skater Laurence Owen appeared in 1961 and died weeks later when her plane crashed. The deaths were real, but with thousands of covers printed, chance alone guarantees that a handful will precede a disaster. Galton found the pattern in heights. In 1886 he measured 1,078 English families and saw that very tall parents had tall children, though not quite as tall. The children of very short parents were short too, yet taller than their parents, showing that extremes at either end slide back toward the middle; Galton named the drift regression.

Regression fools sharp observers. A veteran Israeli Air Force instructor told Kahneman that praise backfired and scolding worked: cadets who earned his praise for a superb maneuver did worse on the next try, and those he chewed out for a poor one did better. He had seen correctly, yet an exceptional flight, good or bad, tends to give way to a more typical one whatever the instructor says. Kahneman drew a disturbing lesson. Because we praise people after unusually good performances and punish them after unusually bad ones, we keep learning a false rule: that harshness pays and kindness backfires, when neither made any difference. The same trap inflates miracle cures. Pick the most severely depressed children you can find, give them an energy drink, and they will improve, but anyone chosen at his lowest point is likely to bounce back somewhat anyway. Only a comparison group that got no drink could show whether the drink did anything.

the-gamblers-fallacy-due-for-a-win.context_blurb:
The gambler's fallacy is the belief that past chances change the next one: a fair coin lands heads five times, so tails must be due. It is named for the casinos where it has emptied countless pockets, and it is a first lesson in independence, the idea that one trial's outcome does not tilt the next. Real randomness looks clumpier than our minds expect.

A fair coin has no memory, so after five heads in a row the next toss is still a fifty-fifty bet, and the earlier heads create no debt that tails must repay. The same holds for a lottery machine that tumbles fresh balls every week: each draw stands on its own, so last week's winning numbers are exactly as likely to come up as any other set.

A run of five heads is a rare sight, but that rarity belongs to the whole run, which has already happened; the single flip still to come is a plain even bet, and pinning the run's unlikeliness on it is the mistake. In August 1913, at Monte Carlo, a roulette wheel came up black 26 times in a row, and gamblers who bet fortunes on red to correct the imbalance lost millions of francs, because red was still about as likely as ever on every spin. That night gave the error its other name, the Monte Carlo fallacy.

A roulette wheel is built exactly the same on the twenty-seventh spin as on the first, with no memory and no machinery for evening things out, so a run of black does nothing to make red more likely; even the green zero is only the house's edge. The false belief that chance corrects itself has a grand old name, the doctrine of the maturity of chances. The error also runs backward, as the inverse gambler's fallacy. If a stranger rolls double sixes on her very first throw, it is wrong to assume she has been throwing all night. Double sixes come up one time in thirty-six on any throw, first or hundredth, so a rare result says nothing about how many tries came before it.

The fallacy is centuries old. In 1796 Pierre-Simon Laplace described anxious fathers who, after a month of many boy births, felt certain a daughter was now due, as if nature kept a running tally and owed them a girl, though each birth is independent, in a cradle as in a casino. It bends serious decisions, too. Researchers studying U.S. asylum judges in 2016 found that a judge who had just granted two claims in a row was roughly 5.5 points less willing to approve a third, because a third yes felt like too long a streak. The mirror image is the hot hand, the belief that a streak must continue. A famous 1985 study called it a myth, since basketball players' hits and misses seemed as random as coin tosses. Then Miller and Sanjurjo found a hidden bias in the way such streaks had been counted, and once they corrected it, the 1985 verdict was overturned: the hot-hand edge was real, and large.
