the-base-rate-fallacy-ignoring-how-rare-.context_blurb:
The base-rate fallacy is the mistake of judging a positive test or a confident prediction without asking how rare the thing being tested for really is. Bayes' theorem is the formal tool for keeping that rarity in view, and the psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman made the blind spot famous in the 1970s. It matters wherever medical tests, security screens and search programs sort the many from the few.

Picture a knight checked with a plague test that errs only once in a hundred, when the plague strikes about one person in 10,000. For every sick person there are nearly 10,000 healthy ones, so even a one percent false-alarm rate throws up roughly a hundred false positives for each true one: the healthy crowd is so big that the test's rare mistakes outnumber its few real hits. A breathalyzer that catches every drunk and wrongly beeps for five percent of sober drivers is no different. Calling it 95 percent accurate says nothing about what one beep means until you know how rare drunk driving is among the drivers on that road. If only one in 1,000 is drunk, a beep means roughly a two percent chance.

Experts fall in too. In 1978 Ward Casscells and two colleagues quizzed sixty Harvard Medical School doctors and students about a disease striking one person in 1,000, with a test that falsely flags five percent of healthy people. The true chance that a positive patient is sick is about two percent; 27 of the 60, nearly half, answered 95 percent. Kahneman and Tversky's taxicab puzzle works the same way. In a city where 85 percent of cabs are Green and 15 percent Blue, a witness who is right 80 percent of the time says a hit-and-run cab was Blue. Most people say 80 percent, but because Green cabs so outnumber Blue, her mistaken sightings nearly cancel her correct ones, and the real chance is about 41 percent, less likely than not.

Gerd Gigerenzer found 95 of 100 American doctors putting a woman's chance of cancer after a positive scan at around 75 percent, when cancer affects about 0.8 percent of women screened. Because most positives are false alarms, only about one positive scan in eleven is real, around nine percent. Rarity can even change over time. At an outbreak's peak a rapid test gives mostly true positives; months later, with almost no one infected, the same test gives mostly false ones, because the true cases have nearly vanished and its steady false-alarm rate takes over.

Why do smart people drop the base rate? Kahneman and Tversky's answer was that we quietly swap questions: instead of asking how common a type is, we ask how much a case resembles a typical example of it. They called this the representativeness heuristic. In their Tom W. study, students were first told that about 80 percent of graduate students studied the humanities, then given a sketch of a neat, orderly, rather dull young man. Over 95 percent still guessed computer science; the nerd stereotype beat the number they had just been handed. Gigerenzer found a cure that needed no new mathematics. He rewrote the same cancer problem with every percentage turned into a head-count within one group, for instance 8 of 1,000 women have cancer, so the big healthy crowd became visible, and far more doctors got it right. The habit is stubborn, though. When researchers repeated a Harvard-style question in 2014, 36 years later, roughly three in four of the medical people answering still missed it.

survivorship-bias-the-bullet-holes-that-.context_blurb:
Survivorship bias is the mistake of studying only the things that made it through a filter and forgetting the ones that did not. Its most famous story belongs to Abraham Wald, a Hungarian-born Jewish statistician who helped the Allies in World War II decide where to armor their bombers. The lesson applies anywhere the losers vanish from view.

A museum case of gleaming medieval swords tempts a visitor to decide that every smith of that age was a master. But the badly forged blades snapped in combat or crumbled into rust long ago; only the toughest lasted long enough to reach a display case, so the survivors are no fair sample. The same trap hides in the tale of college dropouts who became billionaires. We hear about the few who struck it rich, while the far larger crowd who left school and struggled never became famous and so leave no trace. A coach who boasts that every athlete he still trains has got faster is counting only survivors too. The honest question is what happened to the athletes who quit or were cut, since the method may have failed exactly them. Wald himself knew about being shut out. Born in 1902 into a devout Jewish family in Kolozsvar, now Cluj in Romania, he was kept out of the local schools because they held classes on Saturday, the Sabbath his family kept as a day of rest.

In 1943 Allied officers studied bombers that had come home from Germany riddled with bullet holes and planned to add armor where the damage was worst. Wald stopped them. The armor, he said, belonged on the engines, the one place the returning planes were nearly clean. Admired medieval ironwork tells a survivor's tale twice over. The flimsy pieces vanished long ago, and when experts examined the survivors up close, they found them quietly corroding from within, like the 13th-century iron rods in Bourges Cathedral, rusting away even under a roof. Wald's own end carried a grim irony. In December 1950, on a lecture tour of southern India at the government's invitation, he and his wife died when their plane crashed into the Nilgiri Mountains.

Why did the engines matter most? Engine hits were the rarest of all, about 1.11 per square foot of engine compared with 1.73 for the fuselage, and most officers took that as good news. Wald reasoned that gunfire must have struck the whole plane fairly evenly. Bombers hit in the engines went down and never came home, so their damage never reached the chart; the gap in the data marked the deadliest spot. He did more than notice the bias. The planes that could prove his point were lost under the sea or strewn across Germany, so he treated the holes on the survivors as a sample and worked backward, square foot by square foot, to how often a hit in each place was fatal. The same filter fooled vets. A 1987 study found that cats falling more than six stories arrived with fewer injuries than cats falling from a few floors. In 1996 a statistician pointed out that cats killed outright by the longest falls were never brought to a vet, so only the high-fall survivors were ever recorded.

Behind the famous story lies a darker one. Wald reached America in 1938, but of nine family members left behind in Europe, all but one died in the gas chambers of Auschwitz, murdered by the Nazis. The bomber tale itself has grown in the retelling, and historians warn that its most dramatic scenes cannot be verified. What is solidly documented is his 1943 report, A Method of Estimating Plane Vulnerability Based on Damage of Survivors, which showed how to judge a plane's weak spots from the damage on the planes that returned. Money shows the bias too. A fund company may boast of growing about 10.8 percent a year after quietly dropping its closed funds from the list. Because companies shut down the funds that do worst, leaving them out lifts the average of the ones that remain; add the failures back and the real return falls to about 8.9 percent.

cherry-picking-and-suppressed-evidence.context_blurb:
Cherry-picking means showing only the evidence that fits a claim and quietly burying the rest. Logicians also call it suppressed evidence, because the trick lies as much in what is hidden as in what is shown. A wall of good examples looks like proof, and the illusion collapses only when someone asks for the full record, every attempt and every failure.

A fortune-teller boasting of three accurate prophecies has shown you nothing yet. Before believing her, you need her whole record, every forecast she ever made, so the misses can be counted beside the hits and you can see whether she beats chance. A seller's page of glowing reviews works the same way. Every review may be true, yet a pile of successes cannot show that a tonic works; you need to know how many took it and how many it did nothing for. The trick can even run inside your own head. A boy who remembers his horoscopes nailing his mood all year is trusting a memory that clings to the lucky matches and lets the misses slip away unnoticed. A written log defeats the trap, because paper cannot forget the failures.

The oldest version hangs in a temple. The Greek freethinker Diagoras of Melos was shown a temple wall hung with pictures dedicated by sailors saved from shipwreck after praying, offered as proof that the gods answer prayer. His reply gutted the display. Where, he asked, were the paintings of the men who prayed and drowned anyway? The wall counted only survivors. Admirers of Nostradamus run the trick backward. They wait for a disaster, then hunt his hundreds of vague verses for one that can be bent to fit. The countless lines that fit nothing are quietly ignored, so one lucky match shows no power to see ahead.

During World War II, military planners looked over the bombers that survived their missions, saw bullet holes peppering the wings and body, and wanted to armor those spots. The statistician Abraham Wald told them to armor the engines instead, where the returning bombers were nearly unmarked. A bomber shot in the engine went down and was never examined, so the untouched places on the planes that returned showed exactly where a hit was fatal. A swindler can manufacture a perfect record the same way. He mails a stock tip to a thousand strangers, half saying up and half saying down, keeps only those who got the right call, and repeats. Because every wrong guess went to someone he then dropped, a handful of people end up, by pure chance, having received only correct calls. Even an accurate chart can lie. When a speaker shows a rising measurement suddenly flat for a decade, the first question is why the line starts in that particular year, since a hand-picked starting point can fake or erase almost any trend.

Not every omission is cheating. A lawyer may skip the day's weather, which tells the jury nothing about guilt; leaving out the single witness who points away from his client is a different matter. The line is relevance and direction: burying evidence that matters and hurts your case is the cheat, while dropping facts that could not change the verdict is not. Sound judgment rests on all the relevant evidence, especially the inconvenient part.

the-texas-sharpshooter-drawing-the-targe.context_blurb:
The Texas sharpshooter fallacy is named after a joke. A gunman who cannot shoot straight fires at a barn wall, then daubs a bullseye around the thickest clump of holes and brags that he never misses. The move is finding a pattern after the fact and presenting it as if it had been predicted. Statisticians count it among the main sources of false discoveries in science.

His trick works because he chose where the target went only once the bullets were already in the wall, so it could fit any pattern at all. A real shooting coach would name the rule he broke: the target has to be set before the first shot, and only a hit you announced beforehand proves anything. The same rule separates real science from fooling yourself.

Swindlers use the trick. A con man mails free stock predictions to thousands of strangers, different people getting different calls, and keeps writing only to those whose calls came out right. The lucky few see a flawless record, because each of them received only the calls that came true, while everyone who got a wrong one was quietly dropped. Fans of Nostradamus do something similar. His hundreds of verses are vague and gloomy, and most match nothing. The fans wait for a disaster, then hunt for a verse to fit it, ignoring the many that foretold nothing.

Chance makes clusters too. In the Second World War, Londoners believed the V-1 flying bombs were steered at certain districts and kept away from others. After the war, in 1946, an actuary named R.D. Clarke split the city into a grid and counted the hits in each square. The clumps matched a purely random scatter almost perfectly; nobody had been aiming. Atul Gawande, a surgeon and writer, described residents who found a handful of cancer cases on their street and blamed something local. Their mistake was to draw the line around the sick houses after finding them, and a line drawn that way will always enclose a cluster.

Checking many things at once multiplies the danger. In 1993 Swedish researchers compared people living near power lines against more than 800 medical conditions, and childhood leukemia looked four times higher. Test that many things and a handful will look alarming by pure luck; the headline simply circled whichever number happened to leap. Later studies found no real link.

Noticing a cluster is not the mistake; treating it as its own proof is. In 1854 the London doctor John Snow saw cholera deaths bunched around a water pump on Broad Street. He did not stop there. He gathered fresh evidence that the cluster could not give, tracing which households drank water from which company, so that new data could confirm or kill his hunch.

misleading-averages-and-statistics-that-.context_blurb:
Some of the most effective lies are built entirely from true numbers. An average, a percentage or a chart is always one summary chosen out of many, and the person choosing can pick whichever one tells his story. The classic field guide is Darrell Huff's 1954 book How to Lie with Statistics, and its lesson is less that numbers lie than that someone always chooses which numbers you see.

Imagine ten drinkers in a tavern, each earning about fifty thousand dollars a year, when the richest man alive sits down at the bar. Add his billion and divide by eleven, and the mean income in the room leaps to around a hundred million. To describe a normal patron, line everyone up by income and report the person in the middle, the median, which still says about fifty thousand. Percentages hide their base. A crier who shouts that assaults have doubled may be telling the truth when the ledger shows one assault last year and two this year, a rise that says almost nothing about real danger. A claim that one in three Johns Hopkins women students had wed a faculty member sounded scandalous until someone checked the raw count: only three women were enrolled, and one had married a professor. Huff's gee-whiz graph keeps every number honest but chops the bottom off the vertical axis, so the scale no longer starts at zero and a one-percent rise climbs like a cliff.

A smoker dismisses the Surgeon General's findings because Uncle Harry puffed away for four decades and still reached ninety in good health. Uncle Harry is real, but a single survivor cannot shift a rate drawn from millions of smokers, since he is exactly the kind of lucky exception the tables have already counted. In 1936 the Literary Digest mailed ten million ballots, got over two million back and forecast a win for Alf Landon over Franklin Roosevelt, who then carried every state but two. The magazine took its names from car registrations and telephone books, and in the Depression those lists held the well-off, who leaned against Roosevelt. George Gallup called it right with fifty thousand people chosen to mirror the country.

Percentages also hide their starting point. Huff described an accountant who honestly tells shareholders that profits rose forty percent and tells the tax board that they fell sixty percent, about the very same year. Each figure compares that year with a different past, one an average of earlier years and the other last year alone, so the same profit is a rise from one and a fall from the other; a percentage means nothing until you know percent of what. After Sally Clark lost two baby sons to sudden crib death, an expert witness told her 1999 jury that the odds of two such deaths in one family were one in seventy-three million, a figure reached by squaring the chance of one crib death. That multiplication works only for independent events, like separate coin tosses. Two deaths in one family are not independent, because shared genes and a shared home make a second death far likelier once the first has happened. The Royal Statistical Society condemned the figure as baseless, and her conviction was quashed.

modus-ponens-the-valid-baseline.context_blurb:
Modus ponens, Latin for "the mode that affirms," is one of the two baseline valid patterns of classical logic, treated as bedrock since Aristotle and the ancient Stoics. An if-then rule is granted, its trigger is confirmed, and the result follows with no gap. It is taught first because its crooked twins, the common fallacies, only stand out once you can see what a valid inference looks like.

Suppose a castle's rule is that whenever the drawbridge is lowered, a mounted knight can cross, and a scout reports that the bridge is down. The captain need not go and watch, because once the rule is accepted and its trigger confirmed, the promised result cannot fail. Since it lets you pull the result loose from the rule once the trigger fires, modus ponens is also called the law of detachment. When the eastern pass is confirmed clear, a general can bark the single word "March!" without restating the rule beside it, because the conclusion is settled and now stands on its own. The rule also runs validly backward from a missing result, a cousin move called modus tollens. If the tower bell always rings before the volcano blows, then a bell that stays silent rules the danger out, since the rule promised a ring whenever the danger was real.

The fallacies run the rule in directions it does not go. Suppose the watchmen fire the war-beacon whenever the enemy marches. A blazing beacon still proves nothing certain, because a beacon can be lit for other reasons, such as a careless watchman or a drill, and arguing from the result back to the trigger is the fallacy of affirming the consequent. A teacher's rule that early finishers may read at their desks permits early finishers to read but never makes them the only readers, so a student still bent over his quiz is not barred by it. Switching off the trigger does not switch off the result, and that mistake is called denying the antecedent. What makes modus ponens airtight is its bare pattern, which holds whatever the subject, so that accepting the two premises while rejecting the conclusion is impossible.

Validity is about form, not real-world truth. Take this argument: every toaster is golden; everything golden can travel through time; so every toaster can travel through time. Its premises are absurd and its conclusion false, yet it is valid, because if the premises were true the conclusion could not fail, and validity demands nothing more. An argument that is valid and also has true premises is called sound; this one is valid but not sound. Lewis Carroll, the author of Alice, showed why the rule itself is special in an 1895 puzzle about the Tortoise and Achilles. The Tortoise accepts both premises of an argument yet refuses the conclusion, and Achilles keeps adding the linking rule as a fresh premise, which the Tortoise keeps accepting while still refusing, forever. Carroll's point was that an inference rule has to be allowed to act, carrying you to the conclusion, because a rule turned into one more premise only starts an endless regress.

affirming-the-consequent-the-sprinkler.context_blurb:
Affirming the consequent is the invalid twin of a valid rule. The rule says that if P is true, Q is true. You notice that Q is true and leap to P. The leap fails because something else may have brought Q about. Logicians have taught it with wet grass for over a century, because the bad shape sits so close to the good one that sharp minds slide right across.

The classic case is a lawn glittering at dawn. Rain makes grass wet, the grass is wet, therefore it rained. But rain is only one road to wet grass: a sprinkler, dew or a burst pipe ends in exactly the same place, so the wet lawn alone cannot tell you which cause showed up. Make the shape silly and it is easy to see. Dogs have four legs, and so does my cat, but four legs is a club with many members, cats and horses and even tables among them, and belonging to the club cannot prove you are the one member called dog. Or take places. Everyone in San Diego lives in California, yet knowing that Joe lives in California leaves his city wide open, because the rule runs only one way, from the small city into the big state, and Joe could just as well be in Los Angeles.

Not every use of the move is worthless. Hearing a woman at a party speak Portuguese, you might guess she is Brazilian. But Portuguese is also spoken in Portugal, Angola and Mozambique, so her fluency shows only that she might be Brazilian: a real clue, never proof. It does not show nothing, either, since the language really does make Brazil more likely.

Why does such a plain mistake fool sharp people? The mind quietly turns the rule around. It swaps the one-way "if P then Q" for its reverse, "if Q then P," and then reasons perfectly well from a reversed rule it never earned. The swap is safe only when both directions happen to be true, and usually they are not. That also marks where a useful hunch turns into an error. Wet grass makes rain likelier and Portuguese makes Brazil likelier; the fallacy begins at the moment a clue is promoted to a proof, when "she might be Brazilian" is treated as if it had shown that she is.

The same shape hides inside science. A scientist reasons that if her theory is true, an experiment will give a certain result; it does; so the theory is true. Karl Popper noticed that this is affirming the consequent, because a rival theory could predict the very same result, so piling up successes never proves a theory. Science advances, he argued, by chasing the failed prediction, the result that kills a theory outright, since that step is logically valid. In medicine the error can be deadly. Many illnesses bring the same aches and fever as the flu, so settling on the first cause that fits is the same backward leap. One teenage girl had a lump on her neck that doctor after doctor blamed on mono for years, until a biopsy finally showed a cancer that had been growing the whole time.

denying-the-antecedent.context_blurb:
Denying the antecedent is a slip in reasoning with if-then rules. The rule says that if P happens, Q follows; P did not happen; so, the reasoner concludes, Q cannot be true either. But the rule only promised what happens when P occurs. It said nothing about the other ways Q might come about, and that silence is exactly where the argument collapses.

A logic teacher announces that anyone trained as a knight carries a sword, so an untrained traveler must be unarmed. A merchant spoils the lesson: though he never trained, he purchased a blade only last week. Knight-training is just one route to owning a sword, and closing that route leaves every other route open. A student makes the same slip when he decides that a man who is not a ski instructor must have no work at all. Teaching skiing is one job among countless others, so ruling it out tells you nothing about the rest.

A single living counterexample can sink such an argument. Every mammal is warm-blooded, but a creature that is no mammal can still be warm-blooded: a bird reaches that warmth by a different road. Alan Turing met the same shape in his 1950 paper on thinking machines. An objector reasoned that a man who lived by fixed rules would be a mere machine, and since men live by no such rules, they cannot be machines. Turing refused the conclusion, because fixed rules are only one way of being machine-like, and ruling them out cannot rule out every other way.

Denying the antecedent has a mirror twin, affirming the consequent. Reasoning from wet pavement to rain fails for the same reason as reasoning from no rain to dry pavement: both forget that some other cause, such as a hose, can soak the pavement, so ruling rain in or out settles nothing. The one denial a rule allows runs against its far end. A guard whose rule links a safe bridge to a dark warning light can trust only one move: when he sees the light shining, he may conclude the bridge is not safe. Logicians call this modus tollens. Even a granted premise cannot rescue a denied antecedent. The creationist author Henry Morris claimed in 1972 that atheism depends on belief in evolution, and inferred that anyone who turns down atheism must turn down evolution as well. A critic granted the first claim and still rejected the conclusion, because many religious believers accept evolution, so leaving atheism behind leaves evolution standing.

modus-tollens-the-valid-contrast.context_blurb:
Modus tollens, Latin for "the mode that denies," is the second baseline valid pattern of classical logic: if a promised result is missing, the trigger it depended on cannot have happened. Logicians pair it with modus ponens to show the two directions an if-then rule really licenses, and it is the heart of what scientists call falsification, where a failed prediction brings down the theory that made it.

In Arthur Conan Doyle's story "Silver Blaze," a racehorse disappears in the night, yet the stable's guard dog, which barks at any stranger, makes no sound at all. Sherlock Holmes reasons backward. Any stranger would have set the dog barking, so the quiet night proves that no stranger came near. The same move works in the chemistry lab. Every acid turns blue litmus paper red, so when your paper stays blue, the liquid is not an acid. Notice what you cannot say: you have learned what the liquid is not, not what it is.

The valid move and its fake twin look almost alike; the difference is which half you deny. Grant that snow always means cold. Mara reasons from a warm day to no snow, and she is airtight. Jonah reasons from a snowless day to no cold, and he is wrong, because cold has causes besides snow. Theo makes Jonah's mistake when he finds his lawn soaked after a rainless night and calls it impossible. Rain is only one way to wet grass, and dew or a sprinkler can soak it too, so ruling out rain does not rule out wet grass; that slip is denying the antecedent. Real modus tollens gives certainty, not a good guess. A knight reasons that a dragon in the cave would scorch the walls black, then finds them cold and damp, and he need not hunt for the beast. If the rule holds, scorching is unavoidable with a dragon present, so cold walls make a dragon flatly impossible, not merely unlikely.

Why is the backward step as strong as the forward one? "Every rose is a flower" says exactly what "anything that fails to be a flower fails to be a rose" says; flip both halves, swap them, and you have the same rule, called the contrapositive. So modus tollens is really modus ponens in disguise, run on the mirror sentence, and reasoning back from a missing result is exactly as airtight as reasoning forward. Karl Popper built his picture of science on this move. A genuine theory has to risk a bold prediction, and if the predicted thing fails to appear, the theory is dead, so science advances not by piling up confirmations but by ruling false theories out. The 1919 eclipse put Einstein's general relativity to such a test: had starlight passing the Sun not bent by the predicted amount, the theory would have fallen, but Eddington's expeditions measured the bending and it survived.

converse-and-inverse-errors-flipping-if-.context_blurb:
An if-then rule runs one way, like a one-way street. "Every wizard wears a robe" does not mean that everyone in a robe is a wizard. Logicians name two common ways of flipping such a rule by accident: the converse error runs it backwards, and the inverse error negates both halves. Ordinary speech is careless about direction, which is why both slips feel natural.

A child who decides that because all thumbs are fingers, all fingers are thumbs has made the converse error, also called illicit conversion. The quickest cure is one counterexample: point to his own index finger, plainly a finger and plainly no thumb. Being a thumb is enough to make something a finger, but being a finger is not enough to make it a thumb. In if-then form the same slip is called affirming the consequent. A man who always feels tired when he is sick cannot conclude from today's tiredness that he is ill, since tiredness has plenty of other causes, such as a hard workout, a short night or plain boredom. The inverse error, denying the antecedent, fails the other way. If barking guarantees a dog, a silent animal may still be one, because a dog that is asleep or cannot bark is still a dog.

Joseph Heller turned the converse error into comedy in his war novel Catch-22. An officer accuses the chaplain of forging letters signed Washington Irving, and his whole proof is that a censored letter shows that name beside the chaplain's own. But a name can sit on a page without its owner writing anything there; in the novel the forger is Yossarian.

Alan Turing met the inverse error in his 1950 paper on thinking machines. An objector argued that a man who followed fixed rules would be nothing more than a machine, and since men follow no such rules, they cannot be machines. Turing rejected the reasoning. The rule ran only from fixed rules to machine, so lacking fixed rules proves nothing, and a man might still be a machine in some other way. The logic settles nothing about minds either way.

The airtight move from "if it rained, the grass is wet" grabs the far end and denies it. If the grass is dry, there was no rain, a pattern logicians call modus tollens. Wet grass, by contrast, proves nothing, since a sprinkler or dew could have soaked it.

the-undistributed-middle.context_blurb:
The undistributed middle is one of the oldest reasoning errors, catalogued in Aristotle's logic. Its shape is: all A are C, all B are C, so all A are B. Knights ride horses and bandits ride horses, but that does not make knights bandits. The shared category, the middle term, touches both sides without ever linking them.

A neurologist described a brain-injured patient who reasoned that because money is green and so are trees, cash must sprout from branches. Both premises are true, but the colour is merely something money and leaves have in common, and having a feature in common connects nothing; a green bill is no leaf.

Or take this: every student owns a backpack, and so does Grandfather, therefore Grandfather must be a student. The first premise puts students inside the group of backpack owners, but it never says that everyone in that group is a student. Grandfather and the students could sit in separate corners of the backpack crowd. Now change which fact does the bridging. Use the fact that Grandfather is a student as a starting premise instead of the conclusion, and infer from it that he carries a backpack. The argument becomes airtight, the valid form medieval students called Barbara.

The same slip powers guilt by association. In the 1960s some opponents of civil rights argued that the Communist Party supported civil rights, so supporting them made you a communist. But holding one opinion in common with a group does not enrol you in it, since many unrelated people can support one cause for reasons of their own. Edgar Allan Poe made a joke of it in The Purloined Letter, where the detective Dupin mocks a police chief who moves from all fools are poets to all poets are fools. The chief let an overlap that runs one way quietly run backwards.

Recast this kind of argument in if-then form and you get the error called affirming the consequent. Rain soaks the ground, and the ground is soaked, therefore it rained. That leaps from the result back to a single cause, as though rain were the only thing that could wet the ground, when a sprinkler or a hose could do it too.

the-masked-man-fallacy.context_blurb:
The masked man fallacy is a subtle swap: treating what someone believes or knows about a thing as if it were a fact about the thing itself. Two true descriptions can pick out one person without your knowing it, and your ignorance does not change who that person is. Philosophers of language from Frege to Quine have studied the puzzle closely.

A knight reasons that he knows his own brother, that he does not know the masked rider before him, and therefore that the rider cannot be his brother. But the masked rider is in fact that very brother. Both starting claims are true, yet the conclusion is false, because failing to recognize the man is a fact about what is going on in the knight's head, not about who is really standing there.

Lois Lane is sure that Superman can fly and sure that Clark Kent, at the next desk, cannot. In fact they are one man. It does not follow that Superman and Clark are two people. All that follows is a fact about Lois: she believes that Superman and Clark are not the same man. Critics find the same slip in Rene Descartes, who argued that he could doubt his body exists but not his mind, so his mind is not his body. Whether Descartes can doubt something is a fact about Descartes, not a real property of the body, so it cannot pry the two apart.

the-conjunction-fallacy-linda-the-activi.context_blurb:
The conjunction fallacy is judging that two things together are more likely than one of them alone. That is impossible, because every case of "A and B" is already a case of A. The psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman made it famous with their Linda problem in the early 1980s, and it shows how far our feeling of likelihood can drift from the arithmetic.

The simplest versions use plain cases. Mia forecasts rain; Sam forecasts rain, thunder, and clearing by lunch. Sam's forecast sounds sharper, but every day that fits all three of his demands is already a rainy day, so Mia's call can come true on more days. Kahneman summed up the lesson as less is more. The same goes for Bill, who is sharp at maths but dull and unimaginative. "Accountant who plays jazz" fits him so well that it feels likelier than "plays jazz," yet every jazz-playing accountant is already a jazz player, so the bare claim covers at least as many cases. In a dice game, a die with four green faces and two red is rolled for a prize. Most players bet on the sequence GRGRRR because it looks more like the green-heavy die, but RGRRR sits inside every roll that contains GRGRRR, and turns up in other rolls besides, so the shorter sequence can only win more often.

Then came Linda: 31, outspoken and bright, a philosophy student who cared about social justice and marched against nuclear weapons. Asked whether she was more likely a bank teller or a bank teller who is also a feminist activist, 85 percent of students chose the second. But a feminist bank teller is still a bank teller, so adding "feminist" can only shrink the group. Defenders suggested that people heard plain "bank teller" as meaning a non-feminist teller. So Tversky and Kahneman had people rate each claim on its own instead of ranking the pair. With no rival in view, "bank teller" can only mean every bank teller, yet 82 percent still gave that bigger group the lower score.

What drives the error? When the researchers stripped out Linda's personality and called her just a 31-year-old woman, nearly every subject put plain "bank teller" on top, as logic demands. The trap needs the tempting profile: the vivid detail is what makes a richer description feel likelier. Experts fall too. Practising internists judged a patient more likely to have a rare one-sided weakness plus common shortness of breath than the rare weakness alone, in 73 to 100 percent of cases. That is impossible, because every patient with both symptoms already has the rare one.

Ralph Hertwig and Gerd Gigerenzer later argued that the slippery word "probable" does some of the damage. Asked instead to count, out of a hundred women matching Linda's sketch, the tellers and then the feminist tellers, people stumbled far less: the error rate dropped from 50-90 percent to 0-25 percent. Once you are counting heads, no one claims a smaller group has more members than the larger group it sits inside. The fallacy has a darker courtroom form. People judged that a smuggler, Mr. P., was more likely to have killed an employee to keep the man from going to the police than simply to have killed an employee. But naming that one motive can only lower the odds, since a killing for that reason is just a slice of all the killings he might have done for any reason.

necessary-vs-sufficient-conditions.context_blurb:
Two small ideas sit under every if-then puzzle. A sufficient condition is enough: its presence guarantees the result. A necessary condition is required: without it the result cannot happen. Oxygen is necessary for fire but not sufficient, since a room can be full of oxygen with nothing burning. Telling "needed for" from "enough for" is one of logic's great clarifiers, studied from Aristotle to modern logic.

Striking a match in open air almost always yields a flame, so it comes close to being enough. But it is not required, since sparks, lighters and lightning make flames with no match at all. Being odd works the other way round for whole numbers above two. Every prime above two is odd, so oddness is required for such a number to be prime, yet 9 is odd and not prime, so oddness is not enough. A student who decides from 9 that oddness has nothing to do with primes has over-corrected. Now and then one condition does both jobs. If daylight comes exactly when the sun has risen over the horizon, and at no other time, then the sun's rising is at once enough for daylight and indispensable to it.

One if-then sentence names one condition of each kind. In "if it rained, the pavement is soaked," the rain is enough to guarantee wet pavement, while wet pavement is merely required by the rain. Forgetting that the arrow runs one way breeds a famous error. A detective reasons that a broken lamp would darken the room, finds the room dark, and declares the lamp broken. But many things can darken a room, a broken lamp being just one and a flicked switch another, so darkness alone cannot point to the lamp. Medicine offers a clean real case. Robert Koch identified the tuberculosis bacterium in 1882, and no one ever develops TB without it. Yet many people who carry it never fall ill, because their immune systems wall it off, so finding the bacterium does not prove active disease: it is required for TB but not enough on its own.

J. L. Mackie asked why we blame a short circuit for a house fire rather than the surrounding air's oxygen, when the blaze needed both and neither could start it alone. His answer was that without the short circuit this particular fire would never have started, while oxygen is around every house all the time, so it never marks out one fire from another. He called such a cause an INUS condition: one indispensable piece of a set of conditions that together are enough, though other sets could do the job too. The same confusion powers a classic blunder. Grant that a ringing alarm always means smoke is present. A student who notices smoke and concludes that the alarm must have sounded has treated smoke, which merely has to be present when the alarm rings, as though only the alarm could have produced it, when a stove or a candle makes smoke too. That move is affirming the consequent.

false-equivalence.context_blurb:
False equivalence treats two cases as comparable because they share a label, when they differ enormously in size or substance. A king who taxed one coin and a king who burned a province both abused power, but hardly to the same degree. Its cousin, the middle-ground fallacy, assumes that the truth must sit halfway between any two claims. Both slips are hard to spot because the shared feature is often real; the error is the leap from a shared label to a shared weight.

A tanker that pours 210 million gallons of crude into the sea and a neighbor who drips half a liter on his driveway have both spilled oil, but one spill is hundreds of millions of times larger, and lumping them together hides the actual damage. A housecat and a jaguar really do belong to the same cat family, yet the family tie is tiny next to the differences that make one a lap animal and the other able to kill you. Staying inside one category is not what makes a comparison fair, since apples and oranges can be fairly compared on sweetness or price. What makes a comparison fair is that the two things match in the respect that matters to the point being made, while an unfair comparison seizes on some likeness that is beside the point. So when a news anchor calls both a peaceful, lawful rally and an arson mob crowds in the street, the honest report spells out how the two groups behaved and what damage each did, without crowning either cause.

The middle-ground fallacy is easiest to see in color. When one witness calls the midday sky blue and another calls it yellow, a bystander who settles on green has not been fair, because averaging a truth with a falsehood simply manufactures a fresh falsehood. Hagglers exploit the same reflex. If your car is honestly worth $20,000 and a buyer offers $1, then proposes to split the difference at $10,000, his absurd opening bid has pulled the so-called middle toward him, so the fair-sounding offer is really a lowball in disguise. As the logician Bo Bennett put it, there is no compromise when it comes to truth.

False equivalence is a fallacy of degree. A debater who claims the right to bear arms covers a private nuclear submarine, since rifles and submarines are both arms, has the label right, yet the gulf in destructive power is so vast that the common word decides nothing; spotting that settles no question of gun policy. Journalism has its own version. In the late 1940s the Texas newspaperman Hubert Mewhinney mocked reporters who simply print both quotes when two politicians disagree about whether it is raining, instead of doing the one useful thing: a real reporter, he said, should glance outside to see which of them is lying. A magazine that sets a geologist who dates the Earth at billions of years beside James Ussher, the seventeenth-century scholar whose biblical arithmetic put creation at 4004 BC, commits the same fault. The lie is in what goes unsaid: the experts who study the question agree, and one weak source has been dressed up as an equal side.

Flattening can bury moral distinctions too. An orator lumps a president who orders a wartime strike that kills civilians together with an ordinary mass murderer, since both caused deaths. But the bare word deaths hides real differences in the circumstances, in who bears how much responsibility, and in what each man intended; naming those differences does not decide which case is worse. Broadcasters call the media form of the fallacy false balance. For years the BBC set leading climate researchers against a handful of deniers to sound even-handed, until staff guidance around 2018 admitted that its climate coverage had too often gone wrong. The network concluded that a climate denier is not required to make the coverage balanced, because equal airtime is not equal evidence.

the-motte-and-bailey.context_blurb:
The motte-and-bailey is a trick of argument named after a kind of medieval castle. The philosopher Nicholas Shackel gave it that name in a 2005 paper, and the writer Scott Alexander made it famous in 2014. Once you can see it, you will spot it everywhere: in sermons, in politics, in newspaper columns and in arguments at the lunch table.

A castle of this kind has two parts. The bailey is a wide, sunny yard where life is pleasant, but its low wall falls easily to raiders. The motte is a cold stone tower on a steep mound of earth, miserable to live in but almost impossible to take. When raiders come, everyone runs to the tower; when they leave, everyone goes back to the yard. The arguer does the same. He makes the bold, exciting claim, and the moment someone challenges it, he slips back to a safe, dull claim nobody could deny, insisting that was all he ever meant. The real tell comes after the challenger has walked away, when he moves straight back into the bold claim he never truly gave up.

Take the sentence morality is socially constructed. Pressed, the speaker shelters in a harmless point: what people believe about good and evil is learned from the society that raised them. But the bold claim the sentence keeps carrying is that right and wrong do not exist at all. Scott Alexander gave a religious case. A preacher proclaims a God who makes universes, forms the first woman out of a rib, splits the sea and cures the sick. When a skeptic says none of that can be shown, the preacher answers that by God he only means the beauty and order of nature, and digs in there. The fault is not believing in miracles. He never really traded the miracle-worker away; he defends only the gentle claim while still holding the one he never argued for.

The same shelter works in politics. A speaker pressing a bundle of specific, arguable positions under the name of feminism can fall back on the writer Marie Shear's 1986 quip defining feminism as the radical idea that women are people. The quip makes a perfect tower because it commits to so little that a critic finds nothing to push against. The positions themselves stay open to argument; the point is to spot the slogan used as a shield. Shackel also calls the trick Humpty Dumptying, after Lewis Carroll's egg, who boasts that his words mean whatever he chooses. A single word hides a mild meaning and a daring one. The arguer proves the easy meaning, then acts as though he has proven the hard one.

Shackel coined the name in a paper attacking postmodern philosophers, and his chief target was the French thinker Michel Foucault. Foucault starts from something modest: those in power influence which ideas a society treats as true. On Shackel's reading he then leans on that to carry a far larger thesis, that truth is nothing but power. Shackel found the same pattern in the sociologist David Bloor's strong programme for studying science. Bloor begins from the bland remark that a community counts as knowledge whatever its members accept, then reaches for a startling claim: that scientific knowledge is just another accepted belief, and that whether it is true plays no role in why people hold it.

A defender might plead that the arguer was merely redefining his terms. Shackel replied that this excuse never touches the cheat. The redefinition may be real enough, but the dishonesty lives elsewhere: in offering the arguments for the modest claim as though they were arguments for the bold one. The trick is a kind of equivocation, trading one idea for another halfway through. Ordinary equivocation works because two meanings sit close together; here they are plainly different, so the switch should be easy to catch. The arguer gets away with it by first dressing up the double-meaning phrase as something deep, so that the switch feels like insight.

the-isolated-demand-for-rigor.context_blurb:
The isolated demand for rigor is the move of holding a claim you dislike to sky-high standards of proof while waving your own side's claims through. The writer Scott Alexander made the name popular for one-way skepticism dressed up as care. Each demand sounds reasonable on its own; the cheat lies in aiming it only one way, and catching it means watching how someone argues across many cases.

A man sure that a mineral supplement cures cancer has one study on his side and twenty against. He dismisses the twenty as tiny, slanted and hunting for a result. Those flaws are real and can wreck a study, but he aims his doubt only at the studies he dislikes and never at the one he loves, so his doubt filters out unwelcome evidence instead of testing the truth. The move belongs to the family of special pleading. A diner's no-animals rule fairly lets in a blind woman's guide dog, because the dog meets a need the rule was never meant to block. A regular who wants his pet admitted because he is a regular offers no relevant difference at all; the rule is simply inconvenient for him.

Alexander's examples run across politics in both directions. A commentator who opposes a military strike demands it pass a strict dollars-per-life test against the cost of malaria nets, a bar no real government program could clear, while sparing programs he favours, public broadcasting among them. Pointing an impossible standard only at the option you already oppose is a rigged contest, whatever the strike's real merits. In another scene a Science Czar keeps raising the bar for a study showing a minimum-wage benefit, until the researchers run a full random-assignment experiment that still shows the benefit. Then a faint, statistically meaningless hint of harm from six restaurants in one town makes him declare the matter closed. A man who demanded a randomized trial before believing one result now believes the opposite on the strength of six restaurants. So the test is direction, not height: a high bar is honest if a person also turns it on his own favourite plans, and a cheat if it only ever points at everyone else's.

The essay's seed image is Heraclitus, who taught that everything is in constant flux. When a rustler takes an ox Heraclitus has bought, arguing that the beast has changed and is no longer the same ox, Heraclitus suddenly insists on the plain, everyday sense of the same ox. He wants flux when it undercuts other people's claims and stable identity the moment his own property is at stake. In Alexander's joking Wild West ending, the relativist Protagoras boasts that he never felt tempted to abandon his position, since his self-interest decided what was true. Socrates answers him with a grim jest: the only truly consistent people are dead men. And whenever Alexander catches someone pointing a standard one way only, his verdict is the same: whoever applies it unevenly is just stealing cows again.

relative-privation.context_blurb:
Relative privation, also called the appeal to worse problems, dismisses a real complaint by pointing to a bigger problem somewhere else. It sounds morally serious, but it never argues that the complaint is false, only that something else is worse. Spotting it means separating two questions: is this complaint true, and is it the biggest problem in the world?

A squire warns his knight that his blade must be honed before he rides out again, and the knight snaps that soldiers are dying while the boy frets about a sword. Yet both troubles can exist together, and the graver one does not cancel the lesser; a dull sword stays dull. Tell a host that his roast chicken came out tough, and he may retort that starving people would gladly eat a burnt one. His point may be true, but the existence of hungry people elsewhere says nothing about whether this particular chicken was overcooked.

The move often swaps one question for another. An employee complains that the firm's aging software drags everyone down and loses sales, and the boss replies that at least the company has software, unlike rivals who still work by hand. He has swapped the real issue, speed, for a question nobody raised, whether the firm has software at all. A legend tells of a girl who, ordered to eat her peas for the sake of starving children, scraped them into an envelope and mailed them. Her stunt exposes the gap, because eating her dinner would not put a single bite in a hungry child's mouth. The move runs upward too. A son announces an A on his physics exam, and his father asks why it was not an A-plus. The father compares a real achievement with an imagined flawless one, so the win looks like a loss.

Sometimes treating the worse problem first is sound. On a battlefield a medic who treats the worst wound first is reasoning well, because there are too few hands to save everyone at once. The cheat begins where no such shortage exists, as when someone disfigured by acid is made to wait for repair surgery until every deadly illness in the world is conquered; nothing actually forces that wait. The everyday version is "First World problem." Said about yourself, it is a harmless joke. Flung at a girl who grumbles about slow café wifi, it brushes her complaint aside as trivial because bigger miseries exist elsewhere.

the-gish-gallop.context_blurb:
The Gish gallop is a debate tactic named after the American creationist Duane Gish, who was known for firing off claim after claim faster than any opponent could answer. Each unanswered claim is then treated as if it stood, and the sheer pile passes for a strong case. It is not a formal fallacy but an abuse of debate itself, and it still thrives online and on television.

Imagine a debater spraying out twenty dubious claims in one timed turn. Most go unanswered, and the crowd decides the fast talker won. But a claim left unanswered only because the clock ran out has not thereby been shown to be true; quantity is being passed off as quality. Gish held a real doctorate in biochemistry from Berkeley and boasted of more than 300 debates against biologists, delivered quickly and with complete assurance. Even his critics granted the degree was real, but neither a genuine degree nor a confident manner can make a torrent of claims true.

Its ingredients are flimsy: vague talk, anecdotes dressed as data, facts bent out of context, outright lies, side issues and showy jargon. Every piece is a bluff that falls apart as soon as anyone pauses to check it, which is why slowing down and examining a single claim breaks the trick. The honest side still pays a price. A false claim takes three seconds to say and minutes to take apart, so while she patiently corrects one, he fires off five more; the clock punishes whoever cleans up the mess. In 1994 Eugenie Scott, head of America's National Center for Science Education, named the tactic. She blamed the format: one side got so much unchecked airtime that falsehood could outrun any reply.

The trick has relatives. The neuroscientist Steven Novella describes a reverse gallop, sometimes called weaponized pedantry: the opponent waits for one tiny slip, such as saying clip when you meant magazine, and declares your whole argument about gun safety dead. But a true conclusion can survive a small slip in a detail, so one stray error does not sink it. In a squid-ink dump, every single fact checks out, and still the opponent goes under, because not one of those facts bears on the question at issue. Truth is not the same as relevance.

confirmation-bias.context_blurb:
Confirmation bias is the mind's habit of noticing, seeking and remembering the evidence that fits what it already believes, while explaining away whatever does not. Psychologists named it in the twentieth century, but the English philosopher Francis Bacon described it in 1620, and the trap is far older than either. Much of science's machinery, its controls, blind tests and repeated experiments, exists to fight this one habit.

Start with an alchemist who swears by his luck potion. He drinks it every morning, his days go well, and he has never skipped it to see what happens. He counts each time it seemed to help and lets each failure slip away, so the potion can only ever look proven. Bacon mocked believers who notice the prophecies that come true and pass over the misses, though misses are far more common. He saw the deeper mechanism too. Once the mind settles on a first verdict, it bends every new fact to defend that verdict instead of testing it, so a man who decides his new neighbor is a liar files each kindness as an act and each slip as proof.

Memory plays the same trick. Many people with aching joints feel sure that rain makes them hurt, so in the 1990s the physician Donald Redelmeier and the psychologist Amos Tversky checked 18 arthritis patients' pain against the real weather for over a year and found no link. The patients stayed certain because they recalled the wet days their joints ached and forgot the wet days they felt fine. The ancient skeptic Diagoras saw through a grander version. A priest showed him a temple wall of painted tablets, each left by a seaman whose prayers in a storm had brought him home alive, as proof that the gods answer prayer. Diagoras asked where the paintings were of the sailors who had prayed just as hard and drowned. Dead men hang no tablets, so the wall showed only the hits.

In 1960 the psychologist Peter Wason turned the trap into a game. He showed people the numbers 2, 4 and 6, said they obeyed a secret rule, and let them try triples of their own. Most guessed something like rising by two and tried only triples that fit the guess, piling up agreement that proved nothing. The one useful move was to offer a triple they expected him to reject, such as 1-2-3, a deliberate attempt to break their own guess.

Bacon had already explained why that move matters. The mind is stirred more by agreeing cases than by contrary ones, yet for finding truth a single contradicting fact is the stronger clue, because one true exception can topple a rule that a hundred agreements never prove. A detective sure of his suspect should weigh the clue that denies his theory above the one that fits it. Experiments show the bias reshaping memory. In a study by Snyder and Swann, two groups read the same profile of a woman, partly shy and bookish, partly outgoing. Those judging her for a library job later remembered mostly her quiet moments, and those judging her for sales remembered mostly her talkative ones. In a 1979 Stanford study by Lord, Ross and Lepper, backers and critics of the death penalty read the same two invented studies, one for deterrence and one against. Each side praised the study it liked and tore apart the other, and both camps left more convinced of their first view than before.

During the 1930s the philosopher Karl Popper noticed that sweeping theories such as Marxism and Freud's psychology seemed confirmed by everything, and that was the problem. Confirmations are easy to find if you look for them, he argued, so one counts only when it comes from a risky prediction that the theory could easily have got wrong. When Popper showed the psychologist Adler a case that seemed not to fit, Adler explained it instantly, citing his thousandfold experience. Popper replied that with this case it was presumably thousand-and-one-fold, and the theory was still untested. The old witch-hunters' swimming test was rigged the same way: a bound woman who floated was a witch, and one who sank was innocent, so only drowning could clear her. Brains are no shield. Keith Stanovich and other researchers found that intelligence barely predicts who resists favoring his own side. What helps is a deliberate habit of searching hard for the case against your own first idea.

anchoring.context_blurb:
Anchoring is a bias in which the first number you meet drags every later judgment toward it, even when that number is arbitrary. Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman named it in the 1970s. The mind grabs any reference point when it has nothing better, and the first one sticks even after it has been exposed as meaningless, which is why stores and negotiators work so hard to plant it.

A tag that reads "was $200, now $90" makes the jacket feel like a steal, even if the store never once charged $200 and printed the higher figure only to strike it out. The struck-out price sets the bar, so shoppers judge $90 against an invented number rather than against what the jacket is really worth. In a 1998 study by Wansink, Kent and Hoch, soup at 79 cents sold about three cans per shopper with no sign. A sign reading "Limit 12 per person" pushed that to about seven. Shoppers began at twelve and adjusted down from it, ending far higher than if they had started counting up from zero.

The classic experiment used a rigged wheel of fortune that stopped only on 10 or 65. Tversky and Kahneman then asked what share of African countries belonged to the United Nations. Those shown 10 guessed around 25 percent, and those shown 65 around 45. A number they knew was meaningless had pulled an unrelated estimate toward itself. Their explanation was anchoring-and-adjustment: you start from the number in front of you, nudge toward your real guess, and stop too soon. In negotiation studies, a high opening bid tends to end in a high price and a low one in a low price, because the opening figure becomes the point from which both sides measure every counteroffer, so it fixes the range the final price falls in, unless it is so extreme that the other side walks away.

Expertise does not cure it. Seasoned judges were given one shoplifting file and a pair of dice, secretly loaded, whose roll counted as a sentencing demand. A high roll produced sentences of about 7.8 months, a low roll about 5.3. The roll fixed the scale each judge started from; he moved away from it only until the sentence felt fair, which left him near a figure he knew was meaningless, yet about four in five believed the roll had played no part. Real estate agents toured the same house carrying different listing prices, and their appraisals followed the listing, yet only about 19 percent mentioned it as an influence. Most were moved without feeling it and gave the credit to their own judgment. Warnings and willpower barely help. What works is a move called consider-the-opposite: before you commit, make yourself write down specific ways the number could be far off, and arguing against it frees your estimate from its pull. Simply knowing an anchor is arbitrary does not switch it off.

the-appeal-to-nature.context_blurb:
The appeal to nature is the leap from "this is natural" to "this is good or safe," or its mirror image, "this is man-made, so it is bad." The philosopher G. E. Moore named a close cousin of it the naturalistic fallacy. The leap survives because natural is a warm, friendly word that seems to carry moral weight the speaker has never earned.

A hedge-witch vouches for her root tea on the grounds that it sprang wild from the earth instead of coming from a workshop. Yet the deadly poison hemlock thrives in those very ditches, often mistaken for wild carrot, and every bit of the plant is poisonous. Where a plant grows tells you nothing about whether it will harm you. The mirror argument fails too. Eyeglasses, aspirin, antibiotics and the pacemakers that keep failing hearts going are all man-made, so being man-made cannot by itself make a thing bad; you still need evidence about what it actually does. A label that brags of being all natural therefore tells you almost nothing about safety. Cyanide hides in apple seeds and cherry pits, and arsenic and mercury are natural poisons. The opposite overreaction, that natural means harmful, is just as wrong.

What really decides is often the dose. Foxglove is a deadly poison and also the source of digoxin, a real heart medicine. The toxic amount is only about 1.6 times the helpful one, so whether it heals a failing heart or stops it depends on a carefully measured dose, not on whether it was picked wild. Folk healers long used willow bark against pain, but the bark gave uneven, often weak amounts of its helpful ingredient. The chemist Felix Hoffmann changed the molecule in his lab, making it gentler on the stomach and steady in strength, and that lab-made version, aspirin, is safer than the natural bark. Still, the pull of the word is strong. In one study people were told plainly that a natural and a synthetic drug were equally safe and effective, and about 70 percent still chose the natural one; even when told it was less safe, one in five picked it. People also rated cigarettes labelled natural as safer, though they were no different. The word creates a feeling of safety that the facts do not back up.

The deepest version of the mistake was flagged by the Scottish philosopher David Hume in 1739. He noticed writers piling up facts about what is and then sliding, all at once, into claims about what ought to be. No heap of facts about how animals or anything else naturally behave can, by itself, prove how we ought to live. Hemlock gives the fallacy a grim last word. In 399 BC Athens executed Socrates with a cup of it. Its poison, coniine, paralyses the nerves, so his breathing slowly failed while his thoughts stayed sharp to the end.

appeal-to-tradition-vs-appeal-to-novelty.context_blurb:
The appeal to tradition and the appeal to novelty are a matched pair of fallacies about time. One says a practice must be right because we have always followed it; the other says a scheme must be better because it is new. Real arguments sit close by, since an old practice may hold hard-won wisdom and a new discovery may truly improve on the old. The fallacies are the lazy versions that skip explaining why.

In 1985 Coca-Cola replaced its old recipe with a sweeter New Coke. The new flavor had even won blind taste tests, picked by 61 percent of some 200,000 people. Yet customers flooded the company with angry calls, and after 77 days the original came back as Coca-Cola Classic. Being new had never made the drink better; what customers valued was the taste they knew. The mirror mistake brought down Blockbuster and Tower Records, which kept insisting that the old ways still made money. Past earnings prove only that a strategy once fit its market, not that it still fits a changed one. In 1977 Bert Lance, who ran the federal budget for Jimmy Carter, coined the slogan that you shouldn't fix what isn't broken. As a caution it can be sound, but as a flat rule it assumes the one thing it never checks: that the thing is not already broken.

Put the two errors side by side and they turn out to be one. "It's how we've always done it" and "it is the way of the future" both let the date on a thing, ancient or brand-new, stand in for proof that it is true or good. Tradition can kill. In 1847 Ignaz Semmelweis made the doctors on his Vienna ward clean their hands with chlorinated lime, and deaths from childbed fever plunged from 18.3 percent to 2.2. The other doctors turned the practice down all the same, because scrubbing up was not how medicine had ever been practised, and they refused to depart from custom. A simple test exposes the lazy version: strike out the words old or new and see whether any reason survives. A custom called right because it is traditional collapses. A practice that has lasted because generation after generation tested it against hard cases still stands, because its reason was the testing, never the date.

Change can be justified too, when it names its reason. Two reformers back new methods. One shows exactly how the old method broke down and how his repairs that flaw without new dangers. The other says only that his is the modern solution, so buy it. It is the second who commits the fallacy, selling the newness without naming any real improvement. In 1929 G.K. Chesterton gave the classic rule for the other direction. A reformer finds a fence across a road and wants it cleared away because he sees no use for it. Chesterton's wiser reformer refuses until he has first found out why the fence was built; only then may he take it down. Not knowing a thing's purpose is a fact about your ignorance, not about the fence.

In 1790, attacking the French Revolution, Edmund Burke gave custom its best defense. Each person's private stock of reason is small, he argued, so people do better to draw on a shared bank of wisdom, the capital that whole nations build up over the ages and test across the generations. That is an argument, not the fallacy. Burke's claim was never that old means right, but that inherited practice may hold tested wisdom no single mind could rebuild alone, and the Burkean still has to show that the wisdom is really there.

the-fallacy-fallacy.context_blurb:
The fallacy fallacy is the mistake of saying, "Your argument is flawed, so your conclusion is false." A bad reason for a claim is not a disproof of the claim. Students who have just learned the names of the fallacies are tempted to use them as weapons, so this last lesson is one of humility: the tools of logic judge arguments, and they do not by themselves settle what is true.

Alex argues that since every fox has a tail and this creature has one, it must be a fox. The argument fails, because plenty of other animals have tails. But when Bob declares that the animal is therefore not a fox, he makes the opposite mistake. All Alex did was fail to show it is a fox; it may be one all the same. In the same way, a knight who defends a court's verdict with a flimsy reason has not shown the verdict wrong when his reason collapses. Only that one argument has failed, and the verdict may still be right on other grounds. The error runs the other way too. A stopped clock shows the right time twice a day, yet no one would call it a good clock. A true result never proves the method behind it was sound, because a broken process can still land on the truth by accident.

Keep two kinds of failure apart. A fallacy is a defect in the reasoning that links premises to a claim, while truth and falsity belong to the claim itself. So catching a real flaw earns you the right to throw out that argument and ask for a better one, but it does not show the claim to be false; for that you need separate evidence. One bad defense is weak evidence against a position anyway, because it is easy to cook up a fallacious argument for almost any claim, true or false. Finding one tells you only that this defender argued poorly.

History offers a grand example. Fermat's Last Theorem defeated every attempt at proof for more than three and a half centuries. Gabriel Lame announced a proof, and Joseph Liouville showed that it assumed a property numbers do not always have. Anyone who decided from the pile of wrecked proofs that the theorem was false would have been wrong: every collapse showed only that one particular proof did not work, and in 1994 Andrew Wiles proved the theorem true. The lesson also guards against a debating trick, shouting the names of fallacies, such as straw man or ad hominem, as if a label won the argument. Naming a fallacy without showing the actual error in the reasoning proves nothing, and a heap of labels can derail thinking rather than do it.

the-backfire-effect-and-motivated-reason.context_blurb:
Motivated reasoning starts from the conclusion you want, then gathers arguments like a lawyer for a client: the verdict comes first, and the reasons are hired later. Its darker cousin, the backfire effect, makes a believer cling harder when the evidence turns against him. The humbling lesson of the experiments: the easiest person to fool is yourself.

In a 1992 experiment by Ditto and Lopez, people tested a strip said to reveal a dangerous enzyme problem, and bad news made them doubt the test and check it again far longer, while good news was accepted at once, because news we do not want to hear must clear a much higher bar. Jonathan Haidt calls it two different questions: for a claim we like we ask, "Can I believe it?" and one scrap of evidence lets us stop, but for a claim we dislike we ask, "Must I believe it?" and one doubt lets us dismiss it, so where each of us sets the bar depends on the verdict we secretly hope for.

In 1979 Lord, Ross and Lepper gave people on both sides of the capital-punishment debate one packet with a study for deterrence and one against. Each camp praised the study it liked, picked apart the other, and left more certain than before, so the identical mixed evidence drove the sides further apart.

Ziva Kunda pinned down the difference in 1990: honest inquiry asks what is true, while motivated reasoning picks its conclusion first and only then recruits reasons to defend it. Being clever is no cure. In Dan Kahan's 2017 experiment, strong math students on every side solved a numbers puzzle about a skin cream, but when the same numbers described gun control, they solved it mainly when the truth suited their politics. So the more skilled at math people were, the further apart the two camps ended up, because their skill went into defending the answer they wanted.

Dorothy Martin's group expected a catastrophic flood on the morning of December 21, 1954, and three psychologists had secretly joined it to watch. When nothing happened, Martin announced a new message, that the believers had spread so much light that God had saved the world, and the most committed began preaching harder than ever, turning the failure into proof. Against the soldier, who defends a fortress of beliefs, Julia Galef sets the scout. The scout goes beyond the walls wanting an accurate picture of the land, welcome or not: in Galef's words, to see things as they are, not as you wish they were.

occams-razor-used-rightly.context_blurb:
Occam's razor is a rule of thumb named for William of Ockham, a 14th-century English Franciscan friar: when two explanations fit the same evidence equally well, prefer the one that makes fewer assumptions. It is a tie-breaker and a first bet, not a bludgeon, and it never promises that the simplest story is true. Its everyday use is as a guard against piling up mysteries the evidence never asked for.

A guard at a castle keep hears hoofbeats on the road at night before he can see the animal. His best first bet is a stray farm horse, the guess that asks him to believe the least that is new; if a horn appears, he can change his mind. In the 1940s Dr. Theodore Woodward warned his medical students at the University of Maryland not to hunt zebras on Greene Street, and his advice spread through medicine as a rule of thumb: hearing hoofbeats, think of horses before zebras. Doctors still call a rare, exotic diagnosis a zebra. But the razor is no license to ignore clues. If the cookie jar is empty, its lid screwed back on, a chair pulled up to the counter and crumbs on a boy's chin, the cat is not the simple answer. The rule chooses among stories that account for all the clues, and here only one does: the boy.

Aristotle and Ptolemy praised the same idea centuries earlier, and Thomas Aquinas wrote that it is superfluous to suppose many causes where a few will do. The friar's name stuck because he used it more relentlessly and to sharper effect than anyone before him, until it was known as his. Used rightly, the razor can even tell you to add something new. In 1846 Uranus kept wandering off the path Newton's laws laid out for it, and the astronomer Urbain Le Verrier, after a mountain of calculation, proposed a single cause that left the law of gravity alone: an unknown eighth planet. Johann Galle aimed where Le Verrier told him and found Neptune within a degree of the spot. The simplest model is still only the leading guess. When a new measurement refuses to fit, a careful thinker keeps the simple model as the favorite while staying willing to abandon it if the data force him.

Ockham never wrote the famous line about not multiplying entities beyond necessity; the Irish Franciscan John Punch coined it in 1639. What Ockham actually warned against piling up was assumptions, unneeded suppositions, rather than things themselves, which is why the razor can welcome a new planet. In 1930 energy seemed to vanish in beta decay, and Wolfgang Pauli wrote to a physics meeting, addressing his "Dear Radioactive Ladies and Gentlemen," with a fix he himself called desperate: an unseen, nearly weightless particle slipping off with the lost energy. One ghostly particle was a smaller leap than abandoning the law that energy is never lost, and the neutrino was confirmed in 1956. A story told by W. W. Rouse Ball, in an 1888 history, says Napoleon teased Pierre-Simon Laplace that his vast work on the heavens left out God, and Laplace answered that he had had no need of that hypothesis. His point was parsimony: his equations already fit the orbits, so a divine-intervention term would have done no work.

The razor has limits its careless users forget. Preferring the simpler of two theories is rational only when, all else equal, no test can yet tell them apart, so a debater whose simple theory quietly skips awkward results has misused it. Galileo mocked anyone who treated fewness alone as the test of a theory, since by that standard the alphabet's two dozen letters could explain the whole universe. A theory must still fit the evidence, and letters predict no orbit. Francis Crick, co-discoverer of DNA's structure, called the razor a dangerous implement in biology, because living things really are messy, full of evolution's patches and exceptions, so the tidiest hypothesis frequently turns out false. Finally, simplicity has two measures that can pull apart: the number of things a theory populates the world with, and the number and neatness of its laws. Adding one planet kept gravity's laws clean, so used rightly, the razor weighs everything a theory costs, its laws as well as its list of things.

steelmanning-and-the-principle-of-charit.context_blurb:
Steelmanning means rebuilding the other side's argument in its strongest form before you answer it, the opposite of attacking a straw man. Its older cousin, the principle of charity, tells you to read an unclear claim in the way that makes the best sense of it. Thinkers from John Stuart Mill to Donald Davidson have argued that both are far more than politeness: they are the backbone of good reasoning.

Picture a girl whose brother makes a clumsy case for a later curfew. She could pounce on his awkward wording, but that would settle nothing, because he could simply say he meant something better. So she builds the strongest version of his case she can and answers that. A boy in a debate club who mocks the silliest form of a classmate's view has won nothing for the same reason: he defeated a position she never held, and she can shrug that it is not what she meant. Straw is easy to knock down; steel stands up. A test for a fair restatement comes from the game theorist Anatol Rapoport, whose rules the philosopher Daniel Dennett made famous. Put the other person's view so clearly and fairly that he thanks you and wishes he had phrased it that way himself. His thanks is not flattery or surrender; it proves you captured his position in words he would gladly adopt. And someone who always dodges the strongest form of the other side gives himself away. As the writer Chana Messinger put it, facing the strong version shows real confidence, while avoiding it shows a secret fear that it might be right.

Rapoport's recipe has four steps, and criticism comes last. First restate the view so well that its owner thanks you; then list every point where you agree; then say what you have learned from him. Only then may you rebut. Dennett was blunt that this is a winning tactic, not mere manners: by the time you criticize, the first three steps have turned your opponent into a receptive audience. The idea is old. In On Liberty (1859) John Stuart Mill insisted on hearing opposing views from people who truly believe them, warning that a man who knows only his own side of a case knows little even of that. Long before, by tradition, the Jewish sage Rabbi Meir taught that no one speaks without a reason, so treat another person's words as carrying a sensible intent worth taking seriously, not as nonsense to brush aside. The word itself began as a joke. In an online discussion in August 2003, Paul C. Anagnostopoulos mocked an opponent's overblown straw man as so big and strong it was turning into steel. Thinkers picked up the jab and flipped it, so an insult became the name of a virtue: building your opponent's case at its strongest.

Mill pressed harder. Suppose your opinion is true and no one has refuted it, yet you cannot answer the best objections to it. Then, he said, you are right by luck rather than by knowledge, because you cannot show why you are right. The rule of charity got its name from Neil L. Wilson in 1959. If a new student says nobody passed the test when three classmates plainly did, read her as meaning her own study group, since that reading keeps the most of her words true. W. V. O. Quine, working out in 1960 how anyone could translate a wholly foreign language, made the same move: when your translation makes people sound absurd, the likelier explanation is that you have translated them badly, because deep silliness is rarer than a bad translation.

Donald Davidson went furthest. Charity, he argued, is not a favour you may grant or withhold; it is a precondition of understanding anyone at all. Unless you assume that other people mostly believe truly and reason soundly, their words collapse into noise. So a man who tried to abandon charity entirely would not understand others more strictly; he would lose the power to treat them as speakers at all.
